Framework → estimation → fundamentals → caching → databases → consensus → messaging → event-driven → APIs → reliability → classic designs.

Core must know Important asked often Tough where senior interviews are decided ★★★★★ interview frequency

1️⃣ The Interview Framework & Estimation

A system design interview is not a test of whether you know the "right" architecture — it is a test of whether you can turn a vague prompt into requirements, numbers, a design, and defensible trade-offs in 45 minutes. This section gives you the operating system for every other section: what interviewers actually score, the 4-step framework with a time budget, back-of-envelope math you can do at the whiteboard, and the vocabulary of trade-offs that makes you sound senior. Master this first; every design question in later sections assumes it.

What interviewers actually evaluate

Why interviewers ask: there is no answer key. The interviewer writes feedback against a rubric of signals — structure, trade-off reasoning, depth, communication — and a candidate who names a perfect architecture without showing those signals still fails.

Four signals dominate every rubric. Structure: do you drive the conversation through requirements → design → deep dive, or do you free-associate boxes? Trade-off reasoning: for every choice, do you name the alternative and why you rejected it ("Postgres over Cassandra because we need transactions and the write volume is only 60 QPS")? Depth: when the interviewer probes ("what breaks first at 10× load?", "what if this node dies mid-write?"), can you go two levels down into one component? Communication: do you narrate while drawing, check in ("want me to go deeper on the cache or move on?"), and adapt when they redirect you?

Analogy: it is a driving test, not a race — the examiner cares whether you check mirrors and signal, not whether you arrive somewhere impressive. The depth probes are deliberate: interviewers keep pushing on one component until you run out of depth, precisely to find where your knowledge ends. Saying "I don't know the exact internals, but I'd reason about it like this…" scores better than bluffing, which is usually detected in one follow-up.

Expectations scale with level. A junior/mid candidate passes with a coherent single-region design and correct component roles. A senior candidate must drive the process unprompted, bring numbers, and defend trade-offs. A staff candidate is additionally judged on requirement push-back ("do we really need strong consistency here?"), cost awareness, evolution over time, and cross-team concerns (migrations, on-call, org boundaries).

LevelWhat passesTypical failure mode
Junior / midCoherent design with correct component roles when guided; knows what a load balancer, cache, queue doCannot explain why a component is there; freezes on "what if it fails?"
SeniorDrives the whole session: clarifies requirements, estimates load, proposes design, picks 2–3 deep dives, names trade-offs with numbersWaits to be led; decisions without alternatives ("we'll use Kafka") or without numbers
Staff / principalEverything senior, plus challenges the problem statement, discusses cost, migration path, failure domains, team/ownership boundariesOver-engineering a simple problem; depth in one pet area but no breadth
Interview angle: at Walmart-scale companies the written feedback is literally organized as "problem exploration / design / deep dive / communication". A useful meta-move: at minute 1, say "Let me spend a few minutes on requirements and rough numbers, then draw the high-level design, then we can pick a couple of areas to go deep — sound good?" You have just scored the structure signal before drawing a single box.

Pitfalls

  • Optimizing for the "impressive" answer instead of the scored behaviors — a well-reasoned monolith beats an unjustified microservice mesh.
  • Treating interviewer interruptions as attacks. They are usually steering you toward the area they need signal on; follow them immediately.
  • Silent drawing. Two minutes of quiet whiteboarding reads as "cannot communicate"; narrate every box as you draw it.
  • Answering depth probes with breadth ("we could also add a CDN…") — a probe on the cache wants more about the cache.
Interview questions
  • How do you decide what to spend time on in a 45-minute design interview? — Time-box: ~10 min requirements + estimation, ~10 min high-level design, ~20 min on the 2–3 hardest bottlenecks the numbers revealed, ~5 min failure modes and wrap-up. Say the plan out loud and re-check it at the 20-minute mark.
  • The interviewer says "assume infinite scale, skip requirements" — what do you do? — Comply, but state the assumptions you are baking in ("then I'll assume read-heavy, eventual consistency acceptable, ~1M QPS") so your later choices still have a basis.
  • You realize mid-interview an earlier decision was wrong. Do you hide it? — No: flag it, fix it, explain the trigger ("the estimate says 2 TB/day, so the single Postgres I drew won't hold 2 years of data — let me partition it"). Self-correction is a positive senior signal.
  • What separates a senior from a staff answer on the same question? — Staff answers question the requirements, quantify cost, plan evolution (v1 → v2 migration without downtime), and name operational load (on-call, capacity reviews); senior answers execute a sound design well.
  • What is the interviewer doing when they keep asking "and what if that fails?" — Depth-probing to find where your understanding ends; go down the stack (process → node → AZ → region) and stop honestly when you reach your limit.

The 4-step framework & the 45-minute time budget

Why interviewers ask: candidates fail more often on process than knowledge — 25 minutes on requirements, or a deep dive that never happens. A rehearsed framework with a clock is the single highest-ROI interview preparation.

Step 1 — Requirements (≈5 min). Split into functional (what it does: "post a photo, follow users, see a feed"), non-functional (how well: availability target, latency budget, consistency needs, durability, compliance) and explicitly out-of-scope ("I'll skip auth and abuse detection unless you want them"). Then ask the sizing questions: how many users? DAU? actions per user? read:write ratio? data size per item? latency target? is stale data acceptable, and for how long? Writing "500M DAU, feed p99 < 200 ms, eventual consistency OK for feeds, never lose a posted photo" in the corner of the board anchors every later decision.

Step 2 — High-level design (≈10 min). Three artifacts, in order: the API (a handful of endpoints with request/response shapes), the data model (core entities and who owns them), and the diagram (client → edge → services → storage, left to right). Keep it boring and correct; resist detail. Step 3 — Deep dives (≈20 min). Pick the 2–3 components your estimation says will hurt — the fan-out path, the hot partition, the cache invalidation — and go deep: data structures, failure handling, exact consistency behavior. Let the interviewer's interest steer the pick. Step 4 — Wrap-up (≈5 min). Failure modes ("what breaks if the cache cluster dies?"), monitoring (the 3 metrics you would page on), and evolution ("at 10× we shard the follow graph; v1 ships without the ranking service").

Analogy: it is a surgical checklist — the steps are trivial to read and the point is that under pressure you do them in order anyway.

Phase45-min budgetOutput on the boardSignal it scores
1. Requirements + estimation~10 minFunctional / non-functional / out-of-scope list; QPS, storage, bandwidth numbersStructure, business sense
2. High-level design~10 minAPI sketch, entities, one left-to-right diagramBreadth, correctness
3. Deep dives (2–3)~20 minZoomed diagrams, data structures, consistency and failure behaviorDepth — the hire signal
4. Wrap-up~5 minFailure modes, top metrics, evolution planOperational maturity

Pitfalls

  • Spending 20 minutes on requirements. Ten questions maximum; if the interviewer says "assume whatever is reasonable", state assumptions and move.
  • Perfecting the high-level diagram. It is scaffolding for deep dives, not the deliverable.
  • Choosing deep dives by comfort ("let me talk about caching, I know caching") instead of by where the numbers say the pain is.
  • Skipping wrap-up entirely — the 2-minute "here's what breaks and what I'd monitor" close is cheap and scores operational maturity.
Interview questions
  • Walk me through how you'd start "Design WhatsApp". — "First functional scope: 1:1 chat, group chat, delivery/read receipts, media? Then non-functional: message latency < 500 ms, no message loss, ~2B users. Out of scope: calls, stories. Then numbers: say 1B DAU × 40 messages/day ≈ 460k messages/s average, ~1M/s peak…" — i.e., demonstrate step 1 concretely, not abstractly.
  • What are non-functional requirements? Name the ones that change designs most. — Qualities, not features: availability, latency percentile targets, consistency, durability, scale ceiling, cost, compliance. Consistency and latency change architectures the most: strong consistency forbids many caching/replication tricks; a p99 < 100 ms budget forbids cross-region synchronous hops.
  • How do you pick which deep dives to do? — From the estimation: whatever number is scariest (write QPS on one row range, fan-out multiplier, storage growth) plus whatever the interviewer leans toward. Name 4 candidate areas and let them pick 2.
  • The interview is 60 minutes, not 45 — what changes? — Scale the budget, spend nearly all extra time on deep dives (roughly 10/15/30/5), and add a third deep dive rather than more breadth.
  • What belongs in a wrap-up? — Single points of failure and their blast radius, the 3 metrics you would page on (e.g. p99 latency, error rate, queue lag), and one sentence on 10× evolution. Ends the interview on an operational-maturity note.

Back-of-envelope estimation: latency numbers, QPS, storage, bandwidth

Why interviewers ask: numbers are what separate engineering from vibes. "We'll shard the database" is empty until you show the database actually needs sharding; five lines of arithmetic tell you — and the interviewer — where the real problem is.

Memorize three conversion tools. Powers of 2 ↔ 10: 210 ≈ 103 (KB), 220 ≈ 106 (MB), 230 ≈ 109 (GB), 240 ≈ 1012 (TB); in interviews always round to powers of 10 and say you are rounding. Time: a day is 86,400 s — call it ~100,000 s, so X per day ÷ 100k = X QPS: 1M/day ≈ 10–12 QPS, 100M/day ≈ 1,150 QPS, 1B/day ≈ 11,500 QPS. Peak factor: traffic is not uniform — peak ≈ 2–5× average for consumer apps (higher for spiky events: on-sales, flash sales can be 10–100×). Size everything for peak.

The four standard calculations: QPS = DAU × actions/user/day ÷ 86,400, then × peak factor, split into read QPS and write QPS (the ratio drives the whole design). Storage = items/day × bytes/item × retention days × replication factor (usually 3); do metadata and blobs separately — they differ by orders of magnitude and live in different systems. Bandwidth = QPS × average payload size (remember 1 Gbps = 125 MB/s). Server count = peak QPS ÷ per-server capacity, then add headroom (target ~50–60% utilization) and at least N+1 for failure.

Per-server ballparks worth stating (then say "order of magnitude, we'd load-test"): a stateless app server handles ~1k–10k RPS of real business logic (simple proxying: 10k–100k); a tuned Postgres/MySQL node does ~5k–20k simple transactions/s and is comfortable up to a few TB; Redis does ~100k+ ops/s on one core; a Kafka partition sustains ~1–10 MB/s (plan ~10k msg/s each); one machine holds ~10k–100k concurrent WebSocket/TCP connections per process with tuning (up to ~1M with dedicated engineering). Analogy: estimation is Fermi math — you are not pricing the groceries, you are checking whether the bill is $30 or $3,000.

photo = 2 MB original + 200 KB display copy → 2.2 MB stored

# Writes
uploads/day = 10M / 10 = 1M
write QPS   = 1M / 86,400 ≈ 12 avg  → ×5 peak ≈ 60 QPS

# Reads

read QPS  = 200M / 86,400 ≈ 2,300 avg → peak ≈ 7–12k QPS

# Storage

  1. State assumptions and get agreement before computing anything.
  2. Writes: 1M/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 12 QPS avg, ~60 peak. Writes are a non-problem.
  3. Reads: 200M/day ≈ 2,300 QPS avg, ~7–12k peak. Read:write ≈ 200:1.
  4. Storage: 2.2 TB/day of blobs → ~2.4 PB/yr replicated; metadata ~180 GB/yr.
  5. Bandwidth: ~460 MB/s ≈ 3.7 Gbps sustained egress; peaks beyond one NIC.
  6. Conclusion: read-heavy → CDN + object store; the numbers picked the deep dives for you.
Interview angle: precision is a smell. "12.3472 QPS" costs you credibility; "call it 12 QPS, so ~60 at peak — a rounding error for any database" earns it. Interviewers also love the sanity-check move: "460 MB/s egress… that's ~4 Gbps, so a single 10 Gbps NIC could technically carry the average but not the peak — CDN it is."

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting the peak factor and sizing for the average — the design then dies every evening at 8 pm.
  • Mixing bits and bytes: bandwidth is quoted in bits (1 Gbps = 125 MB/s). Off by 8× is a very visible interview mistake.
  • Estimating storage without replication (×3) and retention (×days) — both multiply, and "×3 ×365" turns GB into PB.
  • Computing one blended QPS. Reads and writes go to different systems; blend them and you cannot justify any storage choice.
  • Doing arithmetic silently and announcing a result. Show the two-line derivation; a wrong number with visible reasoning is recoverable, a bare wrong number is not.
Interview questions
  • Your service gets 100M requests/day. What's the QPS? — ~1,150 average (100M ÷ 86,400), plan 3–5k at peak. Answering instantly and adding the peak unprompted is the point of the question.
  • Why do I care that a same-DC round trip is 0.5 ms if RAM is 100 ns? — Every network hop costs ~5,000× a memory access, so chatty designs (N+1 calls, per-item cache gets) blow latency budgets; batch, pipeline, or co-locate instead.
  • How many servers for 50k RPS of a simple API? — At ~5k RPS/server of real work: 10 at full load; run at ~50% utilization plus failover → 20–25. State the per-server assumption first, since it dominates the answer.
  • Estimate storage for 500M tweets/day. — ~1 KB metadata each → 500 GB/day → ~180 TB/yr → ~550 TB replicated, before media. Media (say 10% × 200 KB) adds ~10 TB/day — media dominates, store it separately.
  • What can a single Postgres box actually take? — Order of 5k–20k simple transactions/s and a few TB comfortably; beyond that read replicas, then partitioning/sharding. Saying "it depends, we'd load-test, but the order of magnitude is…" is the expected form.
  • When is peak 100× average rather than 3×? — Scheduled events: ticket on-sales, flash sales, lottery results, midnight game launches. Those designs need queues/waiting rooms and load shedding, not just more servers.
  • Cross-region sync replication — what does physics cost you? — 50–150 ms RTT per round trip; a commit that waits for a cross-continent ack cannot beat ~100 ms, so strong cross-region consistency and sub-100 ms writes are mutually exclusive.

Requirements → architecture: the mapping table

Why interviewers ask: the fastest tell of a senior candidate is that their components follow from the requirements ("read-heavy, staleness OK → cache-aside + replicas") instead of arriving as fashion ("we'll use Kafka and DynamoDB").

Every workload sits on three axes, and each axis has standard levers. Read-heavy vs write-heavy: read-heavy (feeds, catalogs, search — often 100:1) is solved with caching layers, CDNs, read replicas, denormalization/precomputation; write-heavy (metrics, chat, IoT, orders at spike) is solved with partitioning/sharding, append-only log-structured stores (LSM: Cassandra, RocksDB-based), queues to absorb bursts, and batching. Latency-sensitive vs throughput-oriented: latency-sensitive paths (checkout, chat send, search-as-you-type) want in-memory data, few network hops, co-location, and precomputed answers; throughput-oriented paths (analytics, ETL, ML pipelines) want batching, sequential I/O, columnar formats, and can queue freely. Consistency needs: strong consistency (money, inventory, seat booking) points to single-leader SQL, transactions, per-key linearizability, synchronous replication; eventual consistency (likes, view counts, feeds, profiles) unlocks async replication, caches, multi-region active-active.

Analogy: it is a decision table, not inspiration — like choosing a vehicle: heavy cargo → truck, one passenger fast → motorbike. Nobody "prefers" trucks. The interview move: after estimation, say the classification out loud — "this is read-heavy, latency-sensitive on reads, eventual consistency is fine for the feed but the payment ledger needs strong consistency" — and then let each component cite one of those clauses as its justification.

Requirement signalReach forConcrete examples
Read-heavy (≥10:1), staleness OKCache-aside + TTL, CDN for static/media, read replicas, materialized viewsProduct catalog, news feed, profile pages
Write-heavy / bursty ingestPartitioned queue/log in front, LSM stores, sharding by key, batch + async processingClickstream, telemetry, chat history (Kafka → Cassandra/ClickHouse)
Low read latency (p99 < 50–100 ms)In-memory store or cache as primary read path, denormalized precomputed data, same-region servingRedis-backed session/feed, search suggestions
High throughput, latency-tolerantBatching, sequential/columnar storage, workers pulling from queuesNightly reports, ML feature pipelines, warehouse loads
Strong consistency / transactionsSingle-leader RDBMS, serializable or RC transactions, sync replication, idempotent writes; or per-key conditional writesPayments ledger, inventory decrement, seat holds
Eventual consistency acceptableAsync replication, multi-region active-active, caches everywhere, CRDT-ish countersLike counts, follower counts, presence
Large blobs (MB+)Object store + CDN; only metadata in the databasePhotos/video (S3/GCS-like), backups
Fan-out / decoupled consumersPub-sub log with consumer groups, outbox pattern from the DBOrder events → email, analytics, inventory services
Interview angle: a favorite probe is to flip one requirement and watch the design change: "same product catalog, but prices must update globally within 1 second — what changes?" Good answer: the cache TTL story dies; move to event-driven invalidation (pub-sub broadcast of price changes to edge caches) or accept serving prices from a replicated store with bounded lag, and re-validate price at checkout either way.

Pitfalls

  • Classifying the whole system once. Systems have paths: the feed read path and the payment write path in the same app get opposite treatments.
  • Claiming strong consistency "to be safe" everywhere — it silently forbids the caches and async replication your read QPS needs.
  • Reaching for sharding before caching on a read-heavy workload; a 95% hit-rate cache removes 20× load with a tenth of the complexity.
  • Putting blobs in the database because "it's transactional" — store a URL/key, keep the bytes in an object store.
Interview questions
  • Your API is 99% reads with 5-minute staleness tolerance. Architecture? — CDN/edge cache for anonymous responses, cache-aside Redis with a 1–5 min TTL for per-user data, read replicas behind that; writes go to the primary and either invalidate or just age out. Cache hit rate becomes the KPI.
  • Write-heavy telemetry at 1M events/s — what's the shape? — Load balancer → stateless collectors → partitioned Kafka (absorbs bursts, decouples) → batch consumers into an LSM/columnar store (Cassandra/ClickHouse). Never synchronous writes into a B-tree RDBMS at that rate.
  • Where do you need strong consistency in an e-commerce checkout? — Payment capture, order creation, inventory decrement — ideally in one transactional boundary or a saga with idempotency. Product pages, reviews, recommendations are all eventual.
  • Latency-sensitive AND write-heavy — like a multiplayer game position feed? — Keep state in memory (sharded by session/region), replicate async for durability, accept loss of last few updates; sometimes UDP-style fire-and-forget beats durable queues. Durability is the axis you trade away.
  • Why does "consistency needs" change the caching story? — A cache is a replica you refresh lazily; strong consistency requires read-your-write, which plain TTL caches violate. You then need write-through + invalidation, or you bypass the cache on that path.

API design in interviews: REST, pagination, idempotency, versioning

Why interviewers ask: the API is the first concrete artifact of step 2, and it quietly exposes whether you have run a public API in production — cursor pagination, idempotency keys, and error contracts are the three tells.

Default to REST over HTTPS with JSON: nouns as resources (POST /v1/orders, GET /v1/orders/{id}, GET /v1/users/{id}/orders?status=OPEN), plural nouns, no verbs in paths, standard status codes (200/201/204, 400 validation, 401/403, 404, 409 conflict, 429 rate-limited, 5xx). Pagination: offset (?page=3&size=20 → SQL OFFSET 40) is simple but degrades linearly (the DB scans and discards 40 rows — page 10,000 scans 200k) and skips/duplicates items when rows are inserted between pages; cursor (?limit=20&cursor=eyJpZCI6O…, an opaque token encoding the last-seen sort key, becoming WHERE (created_at,id) < (?,?) ORDER BY … LIMIT 20) is O(1) per page and stable under writes — the default for feeds and infinite scroll. Offset survives only where users jump to arbitrary page numbers (admin tables).

Idempotency: GET/PUT/DELETE are naturally idempotent; POST /payments is not, and clients retry on timeout — the classic double-charge. Fix: client sends an Idempotency-Key header (UUID); the server stores key → response (unique constraint, with TTL) and replays the stored response on retry. This is how Stripe works and it is the expected answer verbatim. Versioning: additive changes (new optional fields) need no version; breaking changes get /v2/… (visible, cacheable, the pragmatic default) or a header/content-type version. Error contract: a consistent envelope — {"error":{"code":"ORDER_NOT_FOUND","message":"…","traceId":"…"}} — machine-readable code, human message, correlation id; never leak stack traces.

When not REST: gRPC for internal service-to-service calls (binary protobuf, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming, generated clients, ~2–10× cheaper serialization) — poor fit for browsers; GraphQL when many client shapes aggregate many backends (mobile wants 5 fields, web wants 50) — costs server complexity, caching pain, and N+1 risk; WebSocket (or SSE for one-way) when the server must push: chat, live scores, collaborative editing. Analogy: REST is certified mail, gRPC is the internal phone system, WebSocket is an open phone line, GraphQL is a personal shopper.

POST /v1/orders                     Idempotency-Key: 7f3a…-uuid
  { "items":[{"sku":"A1","qty":2}], "addressId":"addr_9" }
  → 201 { "orderId":"ord_123", "status":"PLACED" }
  (same key retried → 201, same body, no second order)

GET /v1/users/42/orders?status=OPEN&limit=20&cursor=eyJjcmVhdGVkIjoi…
  → 200 { "items":[…20…], "nextCursor":"eyJjcmVhdGVkIjoi…" }

Error envelope (every endpoint, same shape):
  → 409 { "error": { "code":"DUPLICATE_ORDER",
                     "message":"Order already placed",
                     "traceId":"a1b2c3" } }
StyleUse whenCost you must mention
REST/JSONPublic APIs, browser clients, CRUD — the defaultOver/under-fetching; verbose payloads
gRPCInternal microservice calls, streaming, tight latencyBrowser-hostile (needs proxy), binary debugging, schema tooling
GraphQLMany client shapes over many sources (BFF role)Server complexity, HTTP-cache loss, N+1 and query-cost control
WebSocket / SSEServer push: chat, presence, live updatesStateful connections → sticky routing, harder LB and failover

Pitfalls

  • Designing endpoints as verbs (/createOrder, /getUserOrders) — instant junior tell; model resources.
  • Offering offset pagination for a feed, then being unable to explain what happens when a new post arrives between page 1 and page 2 (items shift → duplicates).
  • Forgetting idempotency on any money- or order-creating POST; interviewers ask "the client timed out and retried — how many orders exist?"
  • Returning different error shapes per endpoint, or 200 with {"success":false}.
  • Skipping rate limiting: mention 429 + Retry-After and a token-bucket per API key at the gateway.
Interview questions
  • Cursor vs offset pagination — when and why? — Cursor for feeds/infinite scroll: O(1) page fetch via indexed seek, stable under concurrent inserts, hides internal ids; offset only when arbitrary page jumps are a real requirement, accepting O(n) scans and drift.
  • How do you make POST /payments safe to retry? — Client-generated Idempotency-Key; server inserts it with a unique constraint before processing and stores the final response against it; a retry hits the constraint and replays the stored response. Key TTL ~24 h.
  • How would you version this API? — Never break: additive fields are unversioned; breaking changes go to /v2 run side by side, with deprecation headers, metrics on v1 traffic, and a sunset date. Header-based versioning is cleaner in theory but hides versions from logs, caches, and curl.
  • When would you pick gRPC over REST here? — For the internal hop (e.g. api-gateway → inventory service): typed contracts, HTTP/2 multiplexing, deadline propagation, streaming; keep REST at the public edge.
  • Client needs live order status — polling or push? — Poll with ETag/backoff if updates are rare and latency tolerance is ~seconds (cheapest, stateless); SSE for one-way sub-second push; WebSocket only if the client also sends frequent messages. Say the fallback: push systems still need a reconcile-on-reconnect poll.
  • What belongs in your error response? — Stable machine code, human message, correlation/trace id, optionally a field-errors array for 400s; consistent envelope across all endpoints so clients can write one handler.

Data model first-pass: access patterns before schema, SQL vs NoSQL

Why interviewers ask: "SQL or NoSQL?" is a trap when answered as a preference. The senior answer derives the store from the access patterns and the numbers — and most interview problems turn out to need both, for different data.

First-pass method: name the entities (User, Photo, Follow, Comment) and their rough cardinalities, then — before any schema — list the access patterns as queries with frequencies: "get feed for user (7k QPS)", "get photo metadata by id (2k QPS)", "list a user's photos (500 QPS)", "record a like (300 QPS)". Relational modeling starts from the data's shape; NoSQL modeling starts from the queries — in an interview, do the query list first regardless, because it also picks your indexes, caches, and partitions.

The decision tree (animated below) in words: need multi-row ACID transactions or flexible ad-hoc queries/joins → relational (Postgres/MySQL). Otherwise, is access by a single key at a scale one node cannot hold (millions of writes/s, hundreds of TB) → key-value/wide-column (DynamoDB, Cassandra) with the partition key chosen from the dominant query. Otherwise a specialized shape: full-text search → Elasticsearch/OpenSearch; deep relationship traversals → graph DB; time-ordered append + range scans → time-series/columnar (ClickHouse, Timescale); big blobs → object store + CDN, never the database. Analogy: it is a flowchart at the hardware store — you do not "prefer" screws over nails, you look at what you are joining.

Two honesty clauses that score points: modern Postgres stretches far (JSONB for flexible fields, read replicas, partitioning, ~few-TB comfort), so the default is relational until a number forbids it; and NoSQL's price must be named — no joins (you denormalize and maintain copies), limited transactions, query patterns frozen at design time (a new access pattern can mean a new table/GSI or a backfill).

Question the interviewer asksWhat your query list must already contain
"What's your partition key?"The highest-QPS access pattern — its lookup field is the partition key
"How do you list X by Y?"Either an index that serves it, or the denormalized copy you maintain
"What happens when you need a new query?"SQL: add an index. KV: new GSI/table + backfill — say this cost aloud

Pitfalls

  • Designing tables before queries — in NoSQL this produces a model that cannot answer the second question the interviewer asks.
  • "NoSQL because scale" with 60 writes/s on the board. Your own estimate contradicts you; interviewers check for that.
  • Forgetting that denormalized copies must be maintained: every write now fans out, and you own the consistency between copies.
  • One store for everything — blobs in Postgres or transactions in Cassandra both invite the follow-up that sinks you.
Interview questions
  • SQL or NoSQL for this design? — Reframe: "per data set". Then run the tree out loud with your numbers. The reframing itself is the senior signal.
  • Why not DynamoDB/Cassandra for the orders table? — Orders need multi-row transactions (order + items + payment + inventory) and back-office ad-hoc queries; write volume (from your estimate) is well within one SQL cluster. KV would force sagas and denormalization with no scale need.
  • You chose Cassandra for messages — what did you give up? — Joins, multi-partition transactions, ad-hoc queries; you commit to a partition key (conversation id) and time-ordered clustering, and any new access pattern (search messages by text) means a separate index/system.
  • How would you model "list a user's orders, newest first" in a KV store? — Partition key userId, sort key createdAt (descending scan with limit) — i.e., show that the query became the schema.
  • When does Postgres stop being enough? — When a number says so: sustained write QPS beyond a beefy primary (~tens of k/s), working set far beyond RAM with hot random reads, table sizes making index maintenance/vacuum painful (multi-TB), or cross-region write latency needs. Then: replicas → partitioning → sharding/managed NewSQL, in that order.

The vocabulary of trade-offs

Why interviewers ask: "there's no right answer, only trade-offs" is the genre convention of the interview. Being able to name the axis you are trading on — in one sentence, with an example — is how every decision should be delivered.

The form of a senior answer is always: "I chose A over B; that buys us X at the cost of Y, which is acceptable here because Z." The table below is the standard set of axes. Two get name-dropped by interviewers directly: CAP — during a network partition a distributed system must choose to keep serving (availability, risking stale/conflicting data) or refuse/wait (consistency); and its practical extension PACELC — even with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency (waiting for replica acks vs answering from the nearest, possibly stale, copy).

Analogy: trade-off vocabulary is chess notation — the moves existed anyway, but naming them lets you discuss three ahead.

AxisThe trade in one lineOne-line example
Availability vs consistencyUnder partition/failure: serve possibly-stale data, or refuse until certainShopping cart stays writable in both halves (merge later); bank transfer blocks instead of double-spending
Latency vs consistency (PACELC)Answer from the nearest replica now, or the leader after a round tripRead follower for a profile page (ms, maybe stale); read leader after your own write ("read-your-writes")
Latency vs durabilityAck when buffered, or ack when fsynced/replicatedRedis default acks before disk (fast, can lose ~1 s); Kafka acks=all waits for replicas (slower, survives a broker loss)
Cost vs redundancyEvery extra copy/region/standby is paid-for insurance3-replica multi-AZ Postgres vs single node: ~3× cost for surviving an AZ loss
Throughput vs latencyBatching amortizes overhead but delays each itemKafka linger.ms=20: fewer, fuller batches — every message waits up to 20 ms
Space vs freshness (precompute)Materialize answers ahead of time, then keep them freshPrecomputed feed per user: O(1) reads, but a fan-out job and staleness to manage
Push vs pullProducer delivers to consumers, or consumers fetch on demandPush feeds (fast reads, celebrity fan-out explodes) vs pull feeds (cheap writes, slow reads) — hybrids win
Build vs buyControl and cost-at-scale vs time-to-market and ops burdenManaged Kafka/SQS first; build your own only when volume, features, or unit cost force it
Simplicity vs optimalityThe boring design ships and is debuggable at 3 amMonolith + Postgres for v1; split services when team/scale pain is measured, not predicted
Interview angle: when stuck, the phrase "the trade-off here is…" followed by any correct axis buys you ten seconds and scores communication. When the interviewer proposes an alternative ("why not push the feed?"), the answer is never yes/no — it is the axis: "push trades write amplification for read latency; with a 5M-follower account that is 5M writes per post, so I'd push for normal users and pull for celebrities."

Pitfalls

  • Presenting choices with only upsides. If you cannot name what your choice costs, the interviewer will, and now they are driving.
  • Misquoting CAP as "pick 2 of 3 at all times" — the choice only exists during a partition, and PACELC covers the rest of the time.
  • Calling something "more scalable" without the axis — scalable in reads? writes? storage? cost?
  • Choosing consistency by default for data that is obviously tolerant (like counts), spending your latency budget on nothing.
Interview questions
  • Explain CAP with a real system. — During a partition: Cassandra (tunable, typically AP) keeps accepting writes on both sides and reconciles; an RDBMS with synchronous replication or a quorum system (e.g. etcd/ZooKeeper, CP) refuses writes on the minority side. No partition → CAP says nothing; PACELC takes over.
  • Give one place you'd trade durability for latency. — A metrics/clickstream buffer: losing one second of samples on a crash is fine, so buffer in memory and flush in batches; never do this for orders or payments.
  • Push or pull for a notification system? — Push (WebSocket/mobile push) for online users needing sub-second delivery; pull (badge count on app open) as the always-correct fallback; the reconcile-on-reconnect pull is what makes push safe to lose.
  • Build vs buy for rate limiting at the gateway? — Buy/adopt (envoy/NGINX/cloud gateway features or Redis + a library) — it is undifferentiated; build only if you need exotic semantics (global limits across regions with strict fairness), and say the ops cost of building.
  • Your interviewer says "just make it strongly consistent everywhere". — Quantify the price: every write waits on quorum/cross-AZ round trips, caches on that path die, multi-region active-active becomes leader-per-key or gets ~100 ms writes; then propose strong consistency only on the money path.

Common interview anti-patterns (and their fixes)

Why interviewers ask: they don't ask — they watch. Interviewers see the same five failure modes weekly and often steer you into terrain where they show; knowing them by name is the cheapest way to not be that candidate.

1. Buzzword-first design — opening with microservices, Kafka, and Kubernetes before any requirement exists. The fix is sequencing: requirements → numbers → then components, each justified by a number ("60 write QPS — a single Postgres primary is bored"). 2. Ignoring the question asked — answering the "design a URL shortener" you rehearsed instead of the "design bulk link analytics for marketers" that was asked; repeat the problem back in your own words in the first minute and re-check when the interviewer redirects. 3. No numbers — every sizing claim ("we'll need to shard") floating free; the fix is the 5-line estimate before the diagram. 4. A single point of failure left standing — one load balancer, one cache node, one DB primary, never mentioned; do an explicit SPOF sweep in wrap-up: point at each box and say what happens when it dies. 5. "Just use DynamoDB / Kafka / the cloud" — outsourcing the question to a product name; the interviewer will happily ask "and how does DynamoDB do that?" — you must know the mechanism (partitioning, quorums, LSM) one level below the brand.

Analogy: these are the "checkmate in one" blunders of the format — avoiding them doesn't win the game, but committing them loses it regardless of everything else.

Anti-patternWhat the interviewer writes downThe 10-second fix
Microservices/Kafka on line one"Complexity without justification""Given ~X QPS, I'll start with a modular monolith and split where the numbers demand"
Answering a different question"Didn't listen / rehearsed"Restate the problem + scope in minute 1; confirm
No estimation"Cannot size systems"5 lines: DAU → r/w QPS → storage → bandwidth
SPOF left standing"Not production-minded"Wrap-up sweep: "LB is paired, cache has replicas, DB fails over in ~30 s"
"Just use <product>""Brand-deep knowledge"Name the mechanism: "a partitioned, quorum-replicated KV store — e.g. DynamoDB"
Silent whiteboarding"Communication concerns"Narrate every box as it is drawn

Pitfalls

  • Over-correcting into minimalism theatre — refusing a queue the requirements clearly need is the same error mirrored.
  • Treating the SPOF sweep as optional polish; at senior level an unexamined single DB primary is often an automatic down-level.
  • Defending a rejected idea for minutes. Concede fast ("you're right, at this scale that's overkill"), adapt, move — stubbornness is a recorded signal.
  • Vendor lock-in of the mouth: if every sentence contains an AWS product, interviewers at non-AWS shops (or vendor-neutral ones like Walmart) will probe the mechanism underneath.
Interview questions
  • "Why did you pick Kafka here?" — The pass: "we need a replayable, partitioned log to decouple N consumers from bursty writes at ~X MB/s; Kafka/Pulsar/Kinesis all fit — I'll say Kafka." The fail: "it's the standard."
  • "Where does your design lose data or go down?" — Expected answer walks the SPOF sweep unprompted: LB (paired, anycast/DNS), app (stateless, N+1), cache (replicated, and losing it means a thundering herd — mention warming), DB (replica + failover, RPO/RTO stated).
  • "Your design is very complex for 100 QPS, defend it." — Don't. Concede and simplify; the question is a planted test of ego vs judgment.
  • "You said DynamoDB — what's happening inside when you write?" — Hash of the partition key routes to a partition's replica group, write is quorum-acknowledged across AZs, LSM-style storage; if you can't say roughly this, don't lead with the brand.
  • "We only have 15 minutes — what do you cut?" — Cut breadth, not requirements: 2 minutes of scope + numbers, one thin vertical slice of design, one deep dive. Never cut the numbers.

Whiteboard conventions & how to narrate

Why interviewers ask: the diagram is your shared memory with the interviewer. A clean, conventional layout lets them ask better questions; a tangle of arrows makes them spend the deep-dive time deciphering instead of probing.

Conventions that read instantly: left → right = request flow (client at far left, storage at far right); boxes are components, cylinders are databases, stacked boxes mean "N replicas"; label every arrow with the protocol or verb ("HTTPS", "gRPC GetUser", "publish order-events") and put numbers on hot arrows ("7k QPS", "2 TB/day"); dashed arrows for async, solid for sync. Draw the boring skeleton first — client → DNS/CDN → LB → API → service(s) → cache + DB — then modify it as the design evolves rather than redrawing. Keep one diagram; deep dives get a fresh zoomed-in drawing of a single box rather than more clutter on the main one.

Narration protocol: announce, draw, justify — "requests hit a load balancer (drawing) so app servers stay stateless and horizontally scalable". After each phase, summarize in one sentence and offer a fork: "that's the write path; want me to do the read path or dig into the fan-out?" — this hands the interviewer the steering wheel at the moments you want feedback, and turns the session into the collaborative design discussion it is scored as. In virtual interviews (Excalidraw/Miro is the norm), pre-agree the tool, use text labels liberally since drawing is slower, and never let the tool cause silence — keep talking while dragging boxes.

Analogy: narrate like a surgeon in a teaching hospital — every action is announced before, during, and after, so the room is never guessing what the hands are doing.

Interview angle: the single highest-leverage habit is writing the requirements and the estimate in a corner of the board and pointing back at them when justifying choices ("we said p99 < 200 ms, so this extra hop needs to go"). It visually demonstrates requirement-driven design for the whole session.

Pitfalls

  • Unlabeled arrows. "What's this arrow?" is a question you made the interviewer waste time on.
  • Drawing every replica, AZ, and sidecar on the main diagram — say "each of these is replicated ×3" and keep the picture readable.
  • Erasing and redrawing from scratch mid-interview; it burns 5 minutes and loses the shared context.
  • Asking "does this look right?" (invites a grade) instead of "want me to deep-dive A or B?" (invites collaboration).
Interview questions
  • The interviewer points at an arrow: "what exactly goes over this?" — Be ready with verb + payload + rate for every arrow you drew: "gRPC GetFeed(userId, cursor), ~7k QPS peak, returns 20 post ids the client hydrates from the CDN."
  • "Can you zoom into the cache box?" — Start a fresh small diagram: client keys, node topology (replicas/shards), eviction, invalidation path — never scribble internals onto the system diagram.
  • "Summarize your design in 30 seconds" (often at the end) — Practice the closing summary: flow left to right, the two key trade-offs, the one thing you'd build first. It is frequently what the interviewer writes down verbatim.

1. The interviewer says "Design Instagram." What is the strongest first move?

c. Requirements and numbers anchor every later decision and score the structure signal. (a) draws before knowing what for — the skeleton may be right but you can't justify it; (b) is the buzzword-first anti-pattern; (d) delegates your job to the interviewer.

2. A service gets 100M requests/day. Roughly what average QPS is that, and what should you size for?

b. 100M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,150 QPS (the "divide by ~100k" rule), and consumer traffic peaks at 2–5× average, so plan ~3–5k. (c) is the answer for 1B/day — off by 10×; (a)/(d) misplace the decimal, and sizing for average guarantees a nightly outage at peak.

3. Users post 500M tweets/day at ~1 KB of metadata each. Ignoring media, roughly how much metadata storage per year before replication?

c. 500M × 1 KB = 500 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 182 TB/yr. With ×3 replication it becomes ~550 TB — which is why you compute replication as a separate, stated multiplier. (b) forgets ~10× of days, (d) adds a stray ×10; both are classic slipped-zero errors — write the two-line derivation.

4. Which ordering of latencies is correct, smallest to largest?

b. RAM ~100 ns < NVMe SSD ~100 µs < same-DC RTT ~500 µs < cross-region ~50–150 ms. The tempting (a) swaps SSD and the DC round trip — they are the closest pair (local SSD is usually a few times faster than a network hop), which is exactly why "cache on local SSD vs remote Redis" is a real trade-off.

5. Your feed API uses ?page=51&size=20 (offset pagination). Users report seeing the same post twice while scrolling. Why, and what's the fix?

c. Offset counts rows from the top; a new post pushes yesterday's row 40 into position 41, so page 3 re-serves it. A cursor ("everything older than the last item I saw") is stable under inserts and O(1) via an index seek. (a) and (d) can cause staleness, not systematic duplicates at page boundaries.

6. A client calls POST /payments, times out, and retries. What prevents a double charge?

b. The Stripe pattern: the key, not the payload, defines "the same operation"; the unique constraint makes the race safe and the stored response makes retries observationally identical. (a) renames the problem — two PUTs to a "create" endpoint still need a stable identity; (c) is unreliable (legitimate identical payments exist) and no LB does this statefully.

7. Estimation shows 100:1 read:write, staleness of minutes is acceptable, and the primary DB is at 80% CPU from reads. Best first lever?

a. Read-heavy + staleness-tolerant is the textbook cache case: a 95%-hit cache removes ~20× read load with modest complexity. (b) sharding is the most invasive lever and solves write/storage scaling you don't have; (c) is buzzword-first; (d) buys time but was offered as the tempting "safe" option — it fails the trade-off-reasoning signal.

8. A candidate opens with: "I'd split this into 12 microservices communicating over Kafka, deployed on Kubernetes with DynamoDB." What's the core problem?

d. The failure is sequencing, not tool choice: with no functional scope, QPS, or consistency needs on the board, neither 12 services nor 4 (c) can be justified — swapping brands (a, b) repeats the same anti-pattern with different logos. The fix is requirements → estimate → then let components cite the numbers.

Practice

Estimation drill: storage & QPS for a Twitter-like feed

You are designing a Twitter-like service. Assume: 200M DAU; 100M new posts/day; each post is ~1 KB of text + metadata; 10% of posts carry media averaging 500 KB; each user loads their feed 5×/day, 20 posts per load. Estimate: (1) write QPS, (2) feed-read QPS, (3) storage per day and per year with 3× replication, (4) which number should drive the design.

Show every line of arithmetic; round aggressively and say so.

Hint 1Divide per-day counts by ~100,000 seconds to get average QPS, then apply a peak factor. Keep metadata and media storage separate.
Hint 2Feed reads multiply twice: loads/day → QPS, then ×20 posts per load if you need "posts served per second" for the cache sizing.
Solution 
Writes
  100M posts/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160 QPS avg  → peak ×3–5 ≈ 3.5–6k QPS

Feed reads
  loads/day  = 200M × 5 = 1B  → 1B ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,600 QPS avg
  peak ≈ ×3 ≈ 35k feed loads/s
  posts served ≈ 35k × 20 = 700k posts/s at peak  ← cache territory

Storage — metadata
  100M × 1 KB = 100 GB/day
  × 365 ≈ 36.5 TB/yr  → ×3 replication ≈ 110 TB/yr

Storage — media
  10M posts × 500 KB = 5 TB/day
  × 365 ≈ 1.8 PB/yr → ×3 ≈ 5.5 PB/yr   (≈ 50× the metadata)

What drives the design: reads outnumber writes ~10:1 on loads but ~700k posts-served/s at peak means the feed cannot be assembled by querying the posts table — it must be served from a precomputed/cached feed (the fan-out deep dive). Media dominates storage by ~50× → object store + CDN; the 110 TB/yr of metadata is modest and shardable later. Saying "media and metadata are different problems" is the main scoring moment.

Estimation drill: ticket-booking QPS at an on-sale spike

Concert tickets for a 50,000-seat stadium go on sale at 10:00. 10M fans are expected, half arriving within the first 5 minutes. While waiting, a naive client polls seat availability every 2 seconds. Estimate: (1) arrival rate, (2) steady-state polling QPS if 5M users are on the seat map at once, (3) the actual purchase-write rate, (4) what the numbers say the architecture must be.

This is a peak-factor problem: the interesting result is the ratio between the numbers.

Hint 1Polling QPS = concurrent users × polls per second per user. Compare that with what any database can do.
Hint 2Only 50k purchases can ever succeed. How many writes/second is that spread over even 10 minutes?
Solution 
Arrivals
  5M fans ÷ 300 s ≈ 17k new sessions/s  (plus asset load → CDN)

Polling storm (the killer number)
  5M concurrent × 1 poll / 2 s = 2.5M QPS on seat availability
  → no OLTP database survives this; even a Redis cluster is stressed

Purchases (the tiny number)
  50k seats over ~10 min = 50,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 83 writes/s
  with holds/failures ×5 attempts ≈ 400–500 writes/s — one SQL node

Ratio: reads outnumber meaningful writes by ~5,000:1

Architecture the numbers force: (1) a virtual waiting room / queue admitting users at a controlled rate (turn 2.5M pollers into a token stream); (2) seat map served as a CDN-cached snapshot updated every 1–2 s or pushed via SSE — per-user polling of the origin must die; (3) purchases through a small, strongly consistent path: seat hold with TTL (e.g. row lock or Redis SET NX PX) then payment then confirm; (4) load shedding + rate limits so the 83 writes/s that matter are never queued behind junk traffic. The interview point: the transactional core is tiny — the entire problem is shaping the read storm.

Estimation drill: daily log volume for a 10k-server fleet

Your platform runs 10,000 servers. Each emits on average 200 log lines/s at ~250 bytes/line. Estimate: (1) fleet ingest in MB/s and events/s, (2) raw volume per day, (3) stored volume with 10:1 compression and 30-day retention ×2 replication, (4) how many Kafka partitions the ingest pipe needs at ~10 MB/s per partition.

Watch the bits-vs-bytes trap when you quote the network number.

Hint 1Per-server bytes/s first, then multiply by fleet size; convert to per-day with ×86,400.
Solution 
Per server: 200 lines/s × 250 B = 50 KB/s
Fleet ingest: 10,000 × 50 KB/s = 500 MB/s  (= 4 Gbps on the wire)
Events/s:    10,000 × 200 = 2M events/s

Per day (raw): 500 MB/s × 86,400 ≈ 43 TB/day

Stored: 43 TB ÷ 10 (compression) ≈ 4.3 TB/day
  30-day retention: 4.3 × 30 ≈ 130 TB
  × 2 replication  ≈ 260 TB kept online

Kafka partitions: 500 MB/s ÷ 10 MB/s ≈ 50 minimum
  → provision ~100–150 for headroom, hot-spot skew and failure

Takeaways to say: 2M events/s rules out anything but a partitioned log + batch consumers into a columnar/LSM store (ClickHouse, Loki-style); compression is a 10× lever so it appears in the estimate, not after it; and retention is a product decision worth challenging — "do we need 30 days hot, or 7 days hot + 90 in object storage?" turns 260 TB of expensive storage into ~60 TB.

Requirements gathering: from vague prompt to interview-ready scope

The interviewer says only: "Design a system that lets store associates check the price and stock of any item from a handheld device." Produce what a strong candidate would write on the board in the first 8 minutes: functional requirements, non-functional requirements (with numbers you propose), explicit out-of-scope items, and the 5 sizing questions you would ask.

There is no single right list — the scoring is on coverage, numbers, and explicitly proposing assumptions for the interviewer to veto.

Hint 1Non-functional requirements need numbers even if invented: propose them ("I'll assume p99 < 500 ms — reasonable?") rather than leaving qualities vague.
Hint 2Think about the two data freshness questions separately: how fresh must price be vs how fresh must stock be? They likely differ.
Solution (model answer)

Functional: (1) scan barcode / search by name or SKU; (2) show current price incl. active promotions for this store; (3) show on-hand stock for this store, and nearby-store stock as fallback; (4) show aisle/bin location; (5) works on managed handheld devices over store Wi-Fi.

Non-functional (proposed numbers, to be vetoed): ~10,000 stores × ~100 associates ≈ 1M potential users, maybe 200k concurrent at peak; ~5 lookups/associate/hour → 200k × 5 / 3,600 ≈ ~300 QPS steady, plan 1–2k peak (holiday season) — small! Latency p99 < 500 ms on store Wi-Fi; price must be exact (legal/trust: read from an authoritative, transactionally updated source or short-TTL cache with event invalidation), stock may be ~1–2 min stale (it is an estimate anyway — theft, misplaced items); availability 99.9% with a degraded offline mode: last-synced local catalog on the device or an in-store edge cache, because store connectivity fails and associates still face customers.

Out of scope (say it): purchasing/checkout, inventory adjustment writes, customer-facing app, auth/device management details.

Five sizing questions: (1) how many stores/associates and what peak concurrency? (2) catalog size — how many SKUs (~hundreds of millions across stores, or per-store subset)? (3) how fresh must stock be, and where does inventory truth live today (per-store system vs central)? (4) is cross-store lookup day-1? (5) any offline requirement when the store WAN is down?

Why this scores: the QPS estimate reveals the surprise — the load is tiny, so the interesting problems are data freshness, per-store correctness of price, and offline resilience, not scale. Discovering "this is not a scaling problem" via your own numbers is exactly the signal the exercise exists to test.

⚡ Rapid-fire: numbers, conversions & capacities

  • Seconds in a day? — 86,400; use ~100k, so per-day ÷ 100k ≈ QPS.
  • 1M requests/day in QPS? — ~12 average.
  • 1B requests/day in QPS? — ~11,500 average.
  • Typical peak-to-average factor? — 2–5× for consumer traffic; 10–100× for scheduled events (on-sales, flash sales).
  • 210, 220, 230, 240? — ~103 (KB), 106 (MB), 109 (GB), 1012 (TB).
  • L1 cache vs RAM reference? — ~1 ns vs ~100 ns.
  • SSD random read? — ~100 µs (NVMe); ~1,000× RAM.
  • HDD seek? — ~10 ms; why random disk I/O is designed away.
  • Round trip within a datacenter? — ~0.5 ms.
  • Cross-region round trip? — ~50–80 ms same continent, ~100–150 ms cross-continent.
  • Read 1 MB from RAM vs SSD? — ~10 µs vs ~1 ms.
  • 1 Gbps in MB/s? — 125 MB/s (divide bits by 8).
  • Requests/s for one stateless app server? — ~1k–10k of real work; say "load-test to confirm".
  • Single Postgres/MySQL node ballpark? — ~5k–20k simple transactions/s, comfortable to a few TB.
  • Redis single node? — ~100k+ ops/s, sub-ms; memory-bound, not CPU-bound.
  • One Kafka partition? — ~1–10 MB/s, ~10k msgs/s; parallelism = partition count.
  • Concurrent WebSockets per server? — ~10k–100k with tuning; ~1M is a dedicated engineering effort.
  • Daily storage: 1M items × 1 KB? — 1 GB/day → ~365 GB/yr → ~1 TB/yr with 3× replication.
  • Standard replication factor to assume? — 3 copies (often across 3 AZs).
  • 99.9% availability in downtime? — ~8.8 h/yr (~43 min/month).
  • 99.99% availability? — ~52 min/yr; each extra nine is ~10× harder.
  • Object-store durability marketing number? — "11 nines" (99.999999999%) durability — a different axis from availability.
  • Bytes for an int64 / UUID string / timestamp? — 8 B / 36 B as text (16 B binary) / 8 B.
  • QPS formula? — DAU × actions per user per day ÷ 86,400, then × peak factor.
  • Storage formula? — items/day × bytes/item × retention days × replication factor.
  • Servers-needed formula? — peak QPS ÷ per-server QPS, at ~50–60% target utilization, +1 for failure (N+1).
  • Cache hit rate worth claiming? — 90–99% for skewed read-heavy workloads; each hit avoids a ~ms DB read.
  • A "good" p99 for a user-facing API? — ~100–300 ms end-to-end; each synchronous internal hop spends ~0.5–5 ms plus service time.

2️⃣ Networking & the Edge

Every design you draw starts with a request crossing the network, and interviewers love this layer because it is where hand-waving dies: how does the client find your server, what do those three-way handshakes cost, and what exactly does that "LB" box do when a node dies? This section walks the request path end-to-end — DNS, TCP/TLS, HTTP versions — then the machinery at the edge: load balancers, gateways, CDNs, real-time protocols, and the latency and failure numbers that let you defend every hop.

Anatomy of a request: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP, and where the milliseconds go

Why interviewers ask: "walk me through what happens when I type a URL" is the classic warm-up, but the senior version is quantitative: how many round trips before the first byte, which ones can you eliminate, and why does connection reuse matter more than most micro-optimizations.

A cold request pays for four phases in series. DNS resolution: the OS asks a recursive resolver, which walks root → TLD → authoritative servers if nothing is cached (~20–120 ms cold, ~0 when cached). TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, exactly 1 RTT before any data. TLS 1.3 handshake: ClientHello/ServerHello with key share, 1 RTT (TLS 1.2 needed 2; TLS 1.3 resumption can even send data in the first flight — 0-RTT, safe only for idempotent requests because it is replayable). HTTP exchange: 1 RTT plus server processing. Cold total ≈ DNS + 3 RTTs; at a 100 ms cross-region RTT that is ~300–400 ms before your code runs at all.

Analogy: calling a company — directory assistance for the number (DNS), the phone ringing and being picked up (TCP), agreeing to speak privately (TLS), and only then the actual conversation (HTTP).

The escape hatch is keep-alive and connection reuse: HTTP/1.1 keeps the TCP+TLS connection open by default, so request #2 pays only 1 RTT + server time. This is why clients and services maintain connection pools, why serverless cold paths that re-handshake per call hurt, and why "add an extra synchronous hop" costs more than its service time — each new hop may pay its own handshake tax unless pooled. Interview move: whenever you draw an arrow crossing a region, say the RTT out loud and multiply by the handshakes it needs.

Interview angle: when asked "why is our API slow only for the first request?", the expected answer chain is cold connection: DNS miss + TCP + TLS handshakes, fixed by connection pooling/pre-warming, TLS session resumption, and moving TLS termination close to the user (edge/CDN) so handshake RTTs are ~10 ms instead of ~100 ms.

Pitfalls

  • Counting only the HTTP RTT in a latency budget and "discovering" 300 ms of handshakes in production.
  • Enabling TLS 1.3 0-RTT for non-idempotent requests — 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker; keep it for GETs.
  • Creating a new HTTP client (and thus a new pool) per request in code — every call pays the full handshake tax.
  • Forgetting that DNS TTL caching happens at many layers (OS, JVM, resolver) — the JVM historically cached forever with a security manager; check networkaddress.cache.ttl.
Interview questions
  • How many round trips before the first byte of a cold HTTPS request, and how do you cut them? — ~3 (TCP 1, TLS 1.3 1, HTTP 1) plus DNS. Cut with keep-alive/pools, TLS resumption (0/1-RTT), HTTP/3 (combines transport+TLS in 1 RTT), and edge termination so RTTs are short.
  • Why does moving TLS termination to the edge help if the origin is still far away? — Handshakes are RTT-bound, not bandwidth-bound: 2–3 handshake RTTs happen over a ~10 ms user↔edge path, and the edge reuses long-lived, already-warm connections to the origin.
  • What's the danger of TLS 1.3 0-RTT? — Early data is replayable (no server-side freshness proof yet), so an attacker can resend the flight; restrict 0-RTT to idempotent requests or disable it.
  • Your service calls 5 downstream services in series, same region. Handshake cost? — Zero if pools are warm — that is the point of pooling; if each call opened a fresh TLS connection you would add ~5 × 2 RTT ≈ 5 ms in-region, and far worse cross-region.
  • Client latency histogram is bimodal: 20 ms and 320 ms. First hypothesis? — Two populations: warm connections vs cold (DNS + TCP + TLS). Check connection reuse rates before touching application code.

DNS as a system-design tool: TTLs, GeoDNS, and failover limits

Why interviewers ask: DNS is the first router of every design — it decides which region a user lands in — and its caching behavior is the reason "just flip DNS" is not an instant failover plan. Knowing its limits separates people who have run a failover from people who have read about one.

Two roles matter: recursive resolvers (your ISP's or 8.8.8.8 — they do the walking and the caching) and authoritative servers (the ones your DNS provider runs that hold the truth for your zone). Records carry a TTL; every resolver between the user and you may cache for that long. Providers layer routing policies on top: GeoDNS (answer differs by resolver location), latency-based routing (answer the region with lowest measured RTT), weighted (canary 5% of traffic to a new stack), and health-checked failover (stop returning an IP whose health check fails).

As a load-balancing/failover tool DNS is powerful but blunt. Strengths: it is the only global routing layer you get before any of your infrastructure is reached, so it is how multi-region actually works. Limits: TTL is a suggestion — some resolvers and OSes cache longer, browsers pin, JVMs cache; even with TTL 60 s expect a long tail of minutes to hours where old clients still hit the dead region. It balances per resolver, not per user (one ISP resolver may front millions of users), gives no feedback loop on server load, and cannot see connections. Analogy: DNS failover is changing the address on the company website — new visitors go to the new office, but everyone with the old address written down keeps showing up there for a while.

Design consequences: keep TTLs low (30–60 s) on records you may need to move, but not so low that resolver traffic and lookup latency spike; put a stable anycast IP (one IP announced from many locations, routed by BGP to the nearest) in front when you need instant rerouting — this is how large CDNs and Google's 8.8.8.8 avoid the TTL problem entirely.

MechanismGranularityReaction timeUse for
DNS weighted / GeoDNS / latencyPer resolverTTL + straggler tail (minutes+)Region steering, canary, coarse balancing
DNS health-checked failoverPer recordCheck interval + TTL tailRegion-level disaster failover
Anycast IP (BGP)Per network pathSeconds (route withdrawal)Edge/CDN/DNS itself; instant rerouting
Load balancerPer connection/requestSub-second health checksReal balancing inside a region
Interview angle: in a multi-region design say: "Route users by latency-based DNS with health checks and 60 s TTL; accept a tail of stale clients for a few minutes during regional failover, and make the surviving region able to serve them." Mentioning the straggler tail unprompted is a strong operational-experience signal.

Pitfalls

  • Claiming "DNS failover gives us instant multi-region HA" — the cached-resolver tail means minutes of partial outage; pair with anycast or client-side retry to the other region.
  • Setting TTL to 5 s "for agility" on a high-QPS domain — you just multiplied resolver load and added lookup latency to the long tail.
  • Forgetting GeoDNS sees the resolver's location, not the user's — a user on a VPN or a centralized corporate resolver lands in the wrong region (EDNS Client Subnet mitigates, partially).
  • Round-robin DNS as "load balancing" — no health awareness, no even spread (resolver caching skews it badly).
Interview questions
  • You flip DNS to the standby region. When does traffic actually move? — New lookups move within TTL (~60 s); a straggler tail (resolvers ignoring TTL, OS/JVM caches, keep-alive connections already established) persists for minutes to hours. Plan for the old region to keep answering or redirect.
  • DNS round-robin vs a real load balancer? — DNS RR has no health checks, no per-request granularity, and resolver caching skews distribution; use it only to spread across LB IPs, and let the LB do the real balancing.
  • How does GeoDNS decide where a user is? — By the recursive resolver's IP (optionally refined by EDNS Client Subnet). Wrong for VPNs and centralized resolvers — one reason latency-based beats geo-based routing.
  • What is anycast and why do CDNs prefer it over DNS steering? — The same IP is announced via BGP from many PoPs; the network routes each user to the nearest one, and a failed PoP just withdraws the route — rerouting in seconds with no TTL tail.
  • How would you canary a new stack with DNS? — Weighted records: 95/5 between old and new, watch error rates, ramp weights. Caveat: per-resolver granularity makes the split approximate, and rollback still pays the TTL tail.
  • Where can a single DNS misconfiguration take down everything? — Expired domain, bad zone push, or the authoritative provider going down (the 2016 Dyn DDoS): mitigate with long-ish TTLs on stable records, secondary DNS providers, and infrastructure-as-code review on zone changes.

HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: multiplexing and the two head-of-line blockings

Why interviewers ask: "why did HTTP/2 exist, and why wasn't it enough?" tests whether you understand layering: HTTP/2 fixed HTTP's head-of-line blocking but exposed TCP's, and HTTP/3 had to replace the transport to fix that. It also explains real decisions: gRPC needs H2, mobile apps love H3.

HTTP/1.1: one request at a time per TCP connection (pipelining existed but was unusable), so browsers open ~6 parallel connections per host and engineers invented spriting and domain sharding. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams as binary frames over one TCP connection, adds header compression (HPACK) and stream priorities: request #2 no longer waits for response #1 — HTTP-level head-of-line blocking is gone.

But TCP guarantees a single ordered byte stream. Lose one packet and TCP holds back all later bytes until retransmission — even bytes belonging to unrelated H2 streams. That is TCP head-of-line blocking, and on lossy links (mobile!) H2 can degrade below H1's six independent connections. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP: QUIC implements reliability per stream in user space, integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake (1 RTT to an encrypted connection, 0-RTT resumption), and identifies connections by ID rather than the IP/port 4-tuple — so a phone hopping from Wi-Fi to LTE keeps its connection alive (connection migration).

Analogy: H1 is one checkout lane per customer; H2 is one lane where everyone's items are interleaved on a single belt — if the belt jams, everyone waits; H3 gives every customer their own belt through the same door.

HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3
TransportTCPTCP (TLS in practice)QUIC over UDP (TLS 1.3 built in)
Concurrency1 req/connection → ~6 connectionsMany streams, 1 connectionMany streams, 1 connection
HOL blockingAt HTTP level (per connection)Fixed at HTTP, remains at TCPFixed at both (per-stream loss recovery)
Handshake to encryptedTCP + TLS: 2 RTTTCP + TLS 1.3: 2 RTT1 RTT (0-RTT resumption)
ExtrasSimple, debuggable, universalHPACK header compression, priorities; required by gRPCConnection migration across networks (mobile)
Interview angle: practical stance to state: "browser ↔ edge on HTTP/3 where supported (lossy last mile is where it pays), edge ↔ services on HTTP/2 (gRPC), and I don't chase H3 inside a datacenter — in-DC loss is rare so TCP HOL barely bites." Shows you optimize where the problem lives.

Pitfalls

  • Saying "HTTP/2 removes head-of-line blocking" without the TCP caveat — that caveat is usually the whole point of the question.
  • Domain sharding and asset spriting carried over to H2 — they now hurt (more connections, worse compression and prioritization).
  • Assuming H3 works everywhere — some corporate networks and middleboxes throttle or block UDP/443; clients must fall back to H2.
  • Believing gRPC runs over H3 in browsers — browser gRPC needs gRPC-Web + a proxy; native gRPC is H2.
Interview questions
  • Why can HTTP/2 be slower than HTTP/1.1 on a lossy mobile link? — All streams share one TCP connection; any loss stalls every stream (TCP HOL), while H1's ~6 independent connections let 5 keep flowing. H3 solves this properly.
  • Why does QUIC use UDP instead of a new IP protocol? — Middleboxes and NATs drop unknown protocols; UDP passes everywhere, and QUIC builds reliability, congestion control, and TLS on top in user space, which also makes it evolvable without OS kernel upgrades.
  • What is QUIC connection migration and who cares? — Connections are identified by a connection ID, not the 4-tuple, so a phone switching Wi-Fi→LTE keeps its connection (no re-handshake, no dropped download). Mobile-heavy products care a lot.
  • Server push in HTTP/2 — would you use it? — No; it was hard to cache-coordinate and browsers removed it. Use 103 Early Hints / preload instead. Knowing it is effectively dead is the senior answer.
  • Does HTTP/2 help service-to-service calls? — Yes: one pooled connection carries many concurrent RPCs (gRPC's model), fewer sockets and handshakes; but watch max concurrent streams limits and per-connection flow control on very hot links.

Load balancing: L4 vs L7, algorithms, health checks, and who balances the balancer

Why interviewers ask: every diagram has an LB box; the probes are "what layer is it, what algorithm, how does it know a node is dead, and what happens to in-flight requests during a deploy?" — and the staff-level twist: "your LB is a single point of failure; now what?"

L4 (transport) balancers see IPs and ports only: they forward TCP/UDP flows without touching bytes above the transport — millions of connections, microsecond latency, but no routing by URL and one connection maps to one backend for its lifetime (example: AWS NLB, IPVS, HAProxy in TCP mode). L7 (application) balancers terminate the connection, parse HTTP, and can route by path/host/header, retry, rewrite, compress, and handle TLS (AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy in HTTP mode). L7 costs more CPU per request but is where the useful features live. A common stack is L4 in front of a fleet of L7 proxies. Hardware appliances (F5) still exist in enterprises; software (NGINX/Envoy/HAProxy) and cloud-managed LBs are the default answer now.

Algorithms: round-robin (fine when requests are uniform), weighted (heterogeneous instances, canaries), least-connections (better when request durations vary wildly), power-of-two-choices (pick 2 random backends, send to the less loaded — nearly as good as global least-loaded but needs no global state; the right answer for distributed LB fleets), and consistent hashing on a key (client IP, user id, session cookie) when the same client should land on the same backend — for cache locality or session affinity. Affinity is a smell for state that belongs in Redis/DB, but it is legitimate for per-user in-memory caches and WebSocket termination.

Health checks: active (LB probes /healthz every few seconds; N failures → out, M successes → back in) and passive (watch real traffic: consecutive 5xx/timeouts eject the node — Envoy's outlier detection). Use both: active catches dead nodes, passive catches "healthy-but-failing" ones. Connection draining (deregistration delay): on deploy/scale-in, stop sending new requests but let in-flight ones finish within a grace period — the difference between zero-downtime deploys and a spray of 502s. Analogy: a restaurant host who stops seating new tables in a closing section but lets diners finish.

The LB's own HA: a managed cloud LB is already a distributed fleet behind DNS/anycast. Self-hosted pairs use VRRP/keepalived — two boxes share a floating virtual IP; the standby claims it on failure in ~1–3 s. At global scale, anycast announces the same VIP from many sites. There is no single magic box — it is layers: DNS → anycast VIP → L4 fleet → L7 fleet → services.

AlgorithmBest whenWatch out
Round-robin / weightedUniform, short requests; canary weightsLong-tail requests pile up on unlucky nodes
Least-connectionsHighly variable request durationsNeeds shared state; a fast-failing node looks "least loaded" (the black-hole effect)
Power-of-two-choicesDistributed LB fleet, no shared stateNear-optimal in theory and practice; know the name
Consistent hash / affinityPer-key cache locality, WebSocketsHot keys skew load; node changes remap ~1/N of keys
Interview angle: the "black-hole" trap is a favorite: a node that fails instantly (connection refused, fast 500) has the fewest active connections, so least-connections sends it more traffic. The fix is passive outlier ejection — success rate, not connection count, decides membership. Naming this unprompted lands very well.

Pitfalls

  • Health endpoint that checks dependencies (DB, downstream) — one DB blip makes every node "unhealthy" and the LB ejects the whole fleet. Liveness = process health; keep deep checks for readiness/alerting.
  • No connection draining on deploys — every rollout emits a burst of 502/reset errors that gets misdiagnosed as app bugs.
  • Sticky sessions as the availability story — node death still loses the session; externalize session state and keep affinity only as an optimization.
  • Forgetting the LB's own limits: L7 proxies are CPU-bound on TLS and parsing; an L4 tier or bigger fleet fronts them when connections/s spike.
Interview questions
  • NLB vs ALB — when do you pick which? — ALB (L7) for HTTP routing, TLS, WAF, path-based fan-out; NLB (L4) for extreme connection counts, non-HTTP protocols, static IPs/zonal IPs, or when you must preserve source IP and add microsecond-level latency only.
  • How does the client's IP survive an L7 hop? — It doesn't natively; the proxy adds X-Forwarded-For (or PROXY protocol at L4). Trust it only from your own edge, or attackers spoof it and break rate limiting.
  • Your LB is a single point of failure — how is it made HA? — Managed LBs are fleets across AZs behind DNS; self-hosted: VRRP/keepalived floating IP pair in a DC, anycast across sites, DNS with health checks above that. Layers, not one box.
  • What happens to WebSockets behind an LB during a deploy? — Draining only helps requests that end; long-lived connections must be closed (send GOAWAY/close frame), clients reconnect with jittered backoff, and the connection registry rebalances — design the reconnect storm, not just the happy path.
  • Why power-of-two-choices instead of global least-connections? — Global least-conn needs every LB instance to share load state (stale by the time it's used, and herds onto the "least loaded" node); two random probes get within a constant factor of optimal with zero coordination.
  • Health checks pass but users get errors — how? — Shallow check (200 on /healthz while the app's DB pool is exhausted), port checked ≠ port served, security-group/route asymmetry, or draining misconfigured to 0 s. Passive checks on real traffic close the gap.

Reverse proxies, API gateways, BFFs and the service mesh

Why interviewers ask: candidates draw "API Gateway" reflexively; the probe is what it actually does, what belongs at the edge vs in services, and whether you know a gateway, a reverse proxy, a BFF, and a mesh sidecar are the same machinery playing four different roles.

A reverse proxy (NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy) sits in front of servers and handles cross-cutting plumbing: TLS termination (decrypt once at the edge; internal traffic re-encrypted via mTLS or trusted network), compression (gzip/brotli responses), request routing (host/path → service), buffering slow clients, caching, and rewriting. An API gateway is a reverse proxy plus API-management policy: authn at the edge (validate JWT/OAuth once, forward identity in a trusted header so every service doesn't re-implement it), rate limiting (best at the edge — reject junk before it consumes backend capacity; often a second, per-service limiter deeper in for defense in depth), API keys, request/response transformation, and per-route quotas (Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Zuul/Spring Cloud Gateway).

The BFF pattern (backend-for-frontend): instead of one generic API contorting itself for web, iOS, and partner integrations, each client type gets its own thin gateway that aggregates and shapes responses for that UI (mobile wants one round trip and small payloads; web can chattier). It kills the "one API, N unhappy clients" problem at the cost of some duplicated aggregation logic owned by each frontend team.

A service mesh (Istio/Linkerd, dataplane = Envoy sidecars) takes the same proxy and puts one next to every service instance, so service-to-service traffic gets mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and telemetry uniformly, configured centrally instead of in every codebase. Analogy: the gateway is the building's front desk; the mesh gives every office its own assistant who screens calls the same way. Cost: an extra hop (~0.5–2 ms per side), fleet-wide proxy upgrades, and real operational complexity — say "I'd adopt a mesh when the polyglot service count makes library-based resilience unmaintainable, not by default."

RoleSitsOwnsExamples
Reverse proxyIn front of serversTLS, compression, routing, buffering, cachingNGINX, HAProxy, Envoy
API gatewayPublic edge of your APIsAuthn, rate limits, quotas, API versioning/shapingKong, AWS API GW, Spring Cloud Gateway
BFFOne per client typeAggregation + response shaping for that UICustom Node/Spring service per app
Mesh sidecarNext to every instancemTLS, retries, timeouts, telemetry for east-west trafficEnvoy via Istio/Linkerd
Interview angle: a clean edge story to narrate: "TLS terminates at the CDN/edge proxy; the gateway validates the JWT once and injects X-User-Id over an internal-only trusted channel; coarse rate limits at the gateway (per API key/IP), business-aware limits in the service (per tenant); mobile goes through its BFF to make the feed one round trip." Every clause answers a probe before it's asked.

Pitfalls

  • Business logic creeping into the gateway — it becomes a shared, contended deploy bottleneck (the ESB anti-pattern reborn).
  • Trusting X-User-Id/X-Forwarded-For headers that can arrive from the internet — strip and re-set them at the trust boundary.
  • Terminating TLS at the edge and forgetting the internal leg entirely — state plaintext-vs-mTLS as an explicit decision, or the security interviewer will.
  • Rate limiting only deep in the stack — by then the junk request already consumed a connection, a thread, and a downstream call.
Interview questions
  • Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer — same box? — Overlapping machinery, different roles: LB = distribute across replicas; reverse proxy = protocol plumbing in front of servers; gateway = API policy (auth, limits, quotas). One Envoy/NGINX can play all three; name the role, not the binary.
  • Where do you put rate limiting and why? — Cheap, coarse limits at the edge (per IP/key — protect capacity), precise business limits near the service (per tenant/operation — protect fairness), backed by a shared store (Redis token bucket) when limits must be global across gateway instances.
  • Why authenticate at the edge instead of in each service? — One hardened implementation, one token-validation cache, uniform logging; services then do authorization (what this user may do) which is domain logic. Zero-trust variants still verify a signed identity token per service — via the mesh.
  • When is a BFF worth it? — When client needs diverge (mobile latency budgets vs web richness vs partner stability) and the generic API is accumulating ?include= flags; not worth it for one web client — that's just your API.
  • What does a service mesh buy that libraries (Resilience4j) don't? — Language-agnostic, centrally configured retries/mTLS/telemetry with no code changes — pays off with many polyglot services; the cost is 2 proxy hops and a control plane to run. With five Java services, a shared library is the honest answer.

CDN: edge PoPs, cache keys, TTL vs purge, and what belongs on it

Why interviewers ask: a CDN is the single biggest latency and offload lever in most consumer designs — often 90%+ of requests never reach you — and the follow-ups (cache key design, invalidation on breaking news, private content) test whether you have operated one rather than just drawn the box.

A CDN is thousands of edge PoPs (points of presence) that terminate user connections ~5–30 ms away and serve cached responses.
