Two fill models: origin pull (default — a miss at the edge fetches from your origin, caches per response headers, serves; first user per PoP pays the miss) and push (you pre-upload, e.g. a product launch's assets or video). Large CDNs add a mid-tier / origin shield so 200 PoPs missing simultaneously produce one origin fetch, not 200.

The cache key decides correctness: by default URL + host; you extend it deliberately (device class, Accept-Encoding, country, API version header) and normalize aggressively — every needless query-param permutation fragments the cache and tanks the hit ratio. Freshness is TTL (Cache-Control: s-maxage) plus purge/invalidation for "it must change now" (breaking-news headline, pulled product). Purge is seconds-to-a-minute across PoPs and per-URL or by surrogate key/tag ("purge everything tagged product-123"). The robust pattern avoids purging on the hot path entirely: versioned/fingerprinted URLs (app.3f9c2.js) with year-long TTLs — deploy new HTML referencing new URLs, never invalidate. Private content uses signed URLs/cookies (time-limited signature checked at the edge) so the CDN can serve videos or downloads without your auth service in the path.

What to put on it: all static assets and media, video segments (HLS/DASH — this is how streaming scales at all), and — with care — anonymous API GETs (search suggestions, product listings) with short TTLs (1–30 s): at 50k RPS even a 5 s TTL collapses load to ~0.2 QPS per PoP per key. Never cache per-user or authenticated responses unless the user is in the cache key (and usually not then). Dynamic acceleration helps even uncacheable calls: users terminate TLS at the nearby edge, then ride the CDN's warm, pooled, optimized-route connections to origin — typically tens of ms saved plus handshake elimination. Expect hit ratios of 90–99% for static and media; each hit is ~10–30 ms vs ~100–300 ms from a far origin. Analogy: neighborhood warehouses for a mail-order company — most orders ship from up the street, and only unusual items come from the national depot.

Interview angle: the numbers to volunteer: "static hit ratio 95–99%, so origin egress and load drop ~20–100×; user TTFB goes from ~200–400 ms to ~20–50 ms; even for uncacheable APIs, edge termination saves the 2–3 handshake RTTs." For video: "no one serves video from origin — segments on the CDN are the design."

Pitfalls

  • Caching a response that varies by user without the varying dimension in the cache key — the classic "user A saw user B's cart" incident. Authenticated responses default to no-store.
  • Unnormalized query strings (?utm_source=…, param order) fragmenting the cache — hit ratio quietly halves.
  • Relying on purge for deploys instead of fingerprinted asset URLs — purge is an emergency lever, not a release mechanism.
  • Ignoring the thundering herd on expiry of a hot key — use origin shield plus stale-while-revalidate so one fetch refreshes while stale is served.
Interview questions
  • What exactly is a cache key and how would you design it for a product API? — The tuple identifying a cached variant: normalized path + whitelisted query params + selected headers (country, device class, API version). Whitelist, sort, and drop everything else (tracking params) to protect hit ratio.
  • TTL vs purge — how do you choose? — TTL for tolerable staleness (30 s on listings), purge/surrogate-tag for correctness events (price fix, pulled article, DMCA), fingerprinted URLs + long TTL for assets so neither is needed. Real systems use all three.
  • Can you CDN-cache API responses? — Anonymous GETs, yes: short TTL (1–30 s) + stale-while-revalidate turns 50k RPS into a trickle. Personalized responses: no — or split the payload so the shared part is cached and the personal part is a small separate call.
  • How do signed URLs work for private video? — Origin/app issues a URL with an expiry and HMAC/RSA signature; every edge validates the signature locally — no auth-service call per segment. Rotate keys, keep expiries short, sign the cookie instead when there are hundreds of segment URLs.
  • The CDN is down — what's your story? — Rare but real (June 2021 Fastly). Options: multi-CDN with DNS/anycast steering and health checks, origin sized to survive a "raw" hit ratio for core paths, feature-flag degraded mode (no images, cached HTML). Saying "multi-CDN costs cache-warmth" shows depth.
  • What is origin shield / request coalescing and why does it matter? — A designated mid-tier PoP that all edges miss through, coalescing concurrent misses for one key into a single origin fetch — it turns "every PoP misses at once after a purge" from 200 origin hits into 1.

Real-time delivery: short polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket (and scaling the fan-out)

Why interviewers ask: chat, notifications, live scores, and driver tracking all hinge on "how does the server tell the client something happened?" — and the deep probe is never the protocol choice, it is "you have 5M open connections; how does a message find its socket?"

Short polling: client asks every N seconds. Trivial, cache-friendly, proxy-proof — and either laggy (big N) or wasteful (small N: 1M clients polling every 2 s = 500k QPS of mostly-empty 200s). Long polling: server holds the request open until data arrives or ~30 s elapses, then the client immediately re-asks. Near-real-time on plain HTTP, but each waiting client parks a request; herds of simultaneous reconnects need jitter. SSE (Server-Sent Events): one long-lived HTTP response streaming text/event-stream — server→client only, auto-reconnect with Last-Event-ID built into the browser, rides HTTP/2 cleanly. Ideal for feeds, tickers, notifications. WebSocket: an HTTP request Upgrades into a full-duplex TCP-framed channel — the only choice when the client also streams (chat typing, games, collaborative editing). Cost: every proxy/LB/gateway in the path must support upgrades and long-lived idle connections (timeouts, heartbeats), and connections are state.

Scaling pushes everything to the same architecture: a tier of WS/SSE gateway nodes holding connections (~50k–200k each with tuning), with business services publishing events into a pub/sub backbone (Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, NATS) that gateways subscribe to. The routing question has two answers: sticky/affinity (hash user→gateway so publishers know where to send — simple, but hot users and node death hurt) or a connection registry (on connect, gateway writes user → gateway-id into Redis; publishers look up and target, or every gateway subscribes to a topic partition and filters). For group fan-out (a 100k-member channel), publish once per channel topic and let each gateway deliver to its local members — never once per member. Analogy: polling is calling the post office every hour; long polling is a clerk who stays silent on the line until a letter arrives; SSE is a radio broadcast to you; WebSocket is a phone call.

WebRTC, in one paragraph: peer-to-peer UDP media/data channels between browsers, set up via your signaling server (often over WebSocket), with STUN for NAT discovery and TURN relays when direct connection fails (~10–20% of pairs). It is the answer for sub-second voice/video/screen-share; for server-sourced data it is overkill — say so and move on.

Short pollLong pollSSEWebSocket
LatencyUp to interval~Instant~Instant~Instant
DirectionClient pullsClient pulls (held)Server → clientBoth
Server costQPS burnHeld request each1 connection each1 connection each (state!)
Proxy/LB frictionNoneLow (timeout tuning)Low (disable buffering)High (upgrade + idle timeouts + affinity/registry)
Reconnect storyN/ABuilt into the loopAuto + Last-Event-IDYou build it (backoff + jitter + resume)
Interview angle: for "design chat", the winning shape is: WS gateways (stateless business-wise, stateful connection-wise) → Kafka/Redis pub/sub → delivery service; user→gateway registry in Redis with TTL heartbeats; messages persisted first, then fanned out, so offline users sync on reconnect via the same cursor API. Mention the reconnect storm after a gateway dies — that is the differentiator.

Pitfalls

  • Choosing WebSocket for server→client-only feeds — you inherit upgrade-hostile proxies and a custom reconnect protocol for nothing; SSE was enough.
  • No heartbeats/ping-pong — NATs and LBs silently drop idle connections (~60 s is common) and both sides keep believing the socket is alive.
  • Fan-out by publishing one message per recipient into pub/sub — a 100k-member channel becomes 100k messages; publish per-channel, deliver locally per gateway.
  • Sticky sessions as the routing story with no registry — a gateway crash orphans its users until DNS/affinity heals; registry + reconnect with jitter is the resilient version.
Interview questions
  • 5M concurrent users need notifications. WebSocket or SSE, and how many nodes? — SSE (one-way). At ~100k connections/node ≈ 50 nodes + headroom (say 70 across 3 AZs). Gateways subscribe to a partitioned topic; a registry maps user→node. WS only if clients also send.
  • How does a message find the right socket among 50 gateways? — On connect the gateway registers user → gateway (Redis, TTL-refreshed); publishers route to that gateway's topic/queue. Alternative: broadcast to all gateways and filter — simpler, fine until fleet × message volume makes it quadratic-ish.
  • A gateway with 100k connections dies. What happens next? — 100k clients reconnect at once: exponential backoff with jitter, LB spreads them, registry entries expire via TTL, clients resume with a cursor (last-seen message id) so nothing is lost. Without jitter you DDoS yourself.
  • Why do proxies break long-lived connections and what do you configure? — Idle/read timeouts (NGINX proxy_read_timeout default 60 s), response buffering (must be off for SSE), upgrade header handling for WS, and LB idle timeouts (ALB default 60 s) — plus app-level heartbeats under the smallest timeout in the path.
  • When is short polling the right answer? — Low-frequency updates (order status every 30 s), tiny scale, hostile networks, or when responses are CDN-cacheable — 1M clients polling a 5 s-TTL edge-cached endpoint may cost origin almost nothing. "Boring and cacheable" beats "real-time" when the product doesn't need sub-second.
  • Where does WebRTC fit? — Peer-to-peer UDP for voice/video/screen-share with STUN/TURN for NAT traversal, signaling over your WS server; not for server-pushed data. One sentence, then return to the actual problem.

gRPC vs REST vs GraphQL: contracts, streaming, and when each wins

Why interviewers ask: "why gRPC between services but REST at the edge?" is a near-universal probe, and GraphQL's N+1 problem is the standard test of whether you have actually run it rather than admired it.

REST: resources + HTTP verbs + JSON. Universal clients, human-debuggable, and it inherits the entire HTTP ecosystem — caching (ETags, CDN), status codes, proxies. Contract is by convention (OpenAPI helps but is optional), payloads are text-heavy, and clients over- or under-fetch what the resource shape dictates.

gRPC: RPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf contracts — the .proto file is a compiler-enforced, versioned schema generating typed client/server stubs in every language. Binary encoding is ~3–10× smaller and much cheaper to parse than JSON; HTTP/2 gives multiplexed calls on pooled connections; and it has first-class streaming (server-, client-, and bidirectional) plus built-in deadlines that propagate down the call chain. Weaknesses: browsers cannot speak native gRPC (no control over HTTP/2 frames) — you front it with gRPC-Web + a proxy or a REST/JSON transcoding gateway; binary payloads need tooling (grpcurl) to debug; and plain HTTP caching does not apply.

GraphQL: one endpoint, client-specified queries against a typed schema. Kills mobile over-fetching (one round trip returns exactly the fields needed across entities) and lets frontend teams evolve without backend deploys. Costs: the flexible query is the attack/perf surface — an innocent query resolving posts { author { name } } executes 1 query for posts + N for authors (N+1) unless every resolver batches via DataLoader-style batching+caching; you need query-depth/complexity limits and per-field cost analysis; and HTTP caching is largely lost (POSTs to one URL) so you rebuild caching at the persisted-query or field level. Analogy: REST is a fixed menu, GraphQL is à la carte (the kitchen must survive any order), gRPC is the kitchens' internal ticket system.

RESTgRPCGraphQL
ContractConvention / OpenAPIProtobuf IDL, codegen, enforcedTyped schema, introspectable
EncodingJSON (text)Protobuf (binary, 3–10× smaller)JSON
Transport fitAny HTTP; CDN/proxy caching worksHTTP/2 required; pooled + multiplexed; streaming built inHTTP POST to one endpoint; caching DIY
Browser supportNativeVia gRPC-Web/gateway onlyNative (it's just POST)
Classic failure modeOver/under-fetching; contract driftDebugging opacity; edge frictionN+1 resolvers; unbounded query cost
Sweet spotPublic APIs, CRUD, cacheable readsInternal service-to-service, low latency, streamingBFF layer for diverse UI clients
Interview angle: the defensible default: "REST (or GraphQL if clients are diverse) at the public edge, gRPC inside — protobuf contracts and deadline propagation are worth more between 40 internal services than JSON's debuggability; at the boundary a gateway transcodes." Then volunteer the N+1 story: "every GraphQL resolver goes through DataLoader batching, and queries carry a complexity budget."

Pitfalls

  • Renaming or renumbering protobuf fields — wire compatibility lives in field numbers; never reuse a number, reserve deleted ones.
  • GraphQL without depth/complexity limits — one crafted (or naive) nested query can fan out to millions of resolver calls.
  • Choosing gRPC for a public third-party API — partners want curl-able JSON and stable REST semantics; keep gRPC where you control both ends.
  • Comparing "gRPC is faster" without saying why — the wins are binary encoding, HTTP/2 connection reuse, and no JSON parse; on tiny QPS the difference is irrelevant and tooling should decide.
Interview questions
  • Why is gRPC faster than REST+JSON, concretely? — Smaller binary payloads (no field names on the wire), cheap serialization vs JSON parse, multiplexed pooled HTTP/2 connections (no per-call handshakes), and codegen'd stubs skipping reflection. Typically single-digit ms and big CPU savings at high QPS.
  • How do you version a protobuf API safely? — Add fields with new numbers (unknown fields are ignored by old readers), never change a field's number/type, reserved removed numbers, additive evolution within v1; breaking changes get a new service version run side by side.
  • What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and the fix? — Nested resolvers issue one query per parent item (1 posts query + N author queries). Fix: batch and cache per-request with DataLoader (collect ids in one tick → single WHERE id IN (…)), or push the join into the data layer.
  • How does a browser call your gRPC services? — It doesn't directly: gRPC-Web through an Envoy proxy, a REST-transcoding gateway (annotations map RPCs to routes), or a BFF that speaks JSON out and gRPC in. Connect-RPC exists to blur this; know the pattern, not just a brand.
  • When does GraphQL clearly beat REST? — Many client types with divergent data needs iterating fast against many backend entities (mobile home screens aggregating 6 services in one round trip). Single client, stable shapes, heavy caching → REST stays simpler and CDN-friendly.
  • What are gRPC deadlines and why do they matter in a call chain? — The caller sets a deadline that propagates in metadata; every downstream hop sees remaining time and aborts work that can no longer be used — the built-in version of the timeout-budget pattern, and a big reason gRPC suits deep service graphs.

Timeouts, retries and hedging: surviving a flaky network without amplifying it

Why interviewers ask: the network will partition, and naive retry logic converts a 1-minute blip into a self-inflicted outage. "Your downstream got slow — what do your clients do?" is where resilience knowledge becomes visible.

Split the timeout: connect timeout (establish TCP/TLS — should be short, ~1 s: if the SYN isn't answered fast, the host is likely down and you want to fail over to another instance) vs read/request timeout (waiting for the response — sized from the callee's p99 plus margin, e.g. p99 = 200 ms → 500 ms). One number for both is a classic bug: a 30 s "timeout" means 30 s hanging on a dead host. In deep call chains, use a propagated deadline/timeout budget: the edge grants 2 s total and each hop passes the remaining time down, so nobody computes an answer the user already abandoned.

Retries are load multipliers. Rules that keep them safe: retry only idempotent or idempotency-keyed operations; retry on connect errors and 5xx/timeouts, never on 4xx; use exponential backoff with full jitter (sleep = rand(0, base×2^attempt)) so failures don't synchronize clients; and cap the damage with a retry budget (e.g. retries may add ≤10% extra load, tracked per client — Envoy/Finagle style) instead of a per-call "3 retries", because 3 retries at every one of 5 layers compounds to 35 ≈ 243 attempts at the bottom of the stack during an outage — the retry storm. Analogy: everyone redialing a congested phone line the instant it drops is why it stays congested.

Hedged requests attack tail latency instead of failure: send the request, and if no reply within ~the p95, fire a duplicate to another replica and take the first answer (cancel the loser). Google's classic result cuts p99 dramatically for a few percent extra load — but only for idempotent reads. The thundering herd on reconnect is the same synchronization disease at the connection level: after a restart or network blip, thousands of clients reconnect and re-warm caches simultaneously; the cures are jittered reconnects, connection-rate limiting at the LB, and request coalescing (one flight refills a hot cache key, the rest wait).

During a true partition, remember what the client can know: a timeout does not mean the operation failed — it may have succeeded and the ACK died. Every "retry a write" story must therefore pass through idempotency (keys, dedup tables) — this is the network-layer root of the exactly-once discussion in the messaging section.

Client → A → B → C, each layer: timeout 1 s, 3 retries, no jitter, no budget
C has a 90-second brownout…
  attempts hitting C  = 3 (A's) × 3 (B's) × 3 (C's callers) = 27×
  every attempt also holds a thread/connection in A and B while waiting
fix: deadline budget from the edge + retry budget ≤10% + full jitter + circuit breaker
Interview angle: the crisp numbers to state: "connect timeout 1 s; read timeout = downstream p99 × 2–3; retries: 1–2 max, full jitter, budget-capped at 10%; hedge reads at p95 for tail-sensitive paths; writes retry only with an idempotency key." Five clauses, and you have pre-answered the entire resilience probe.

Pitfalls

  • Retrying non-idempotent writes on timeout — the double-charge generator; the timeout may hide a success.
  • Backoff without jitter — all clients sleep the same schedule and re-arrive as a synchronized wave, re-killing the recovering service.
  • Timeouts that grow up the stack (edge 2 s but a deep dependency at 10 s) — the deep layer keeps computing for callers that already gave up; deadlines must shrink downward.
  • Hedging writes or hedging without cancellation — you double write traffic exactly when the system is struggling.
Interview questions
  • Connect vs read timeout — why separate values? — Connect failure means "host unreachable" and should fail fast (~1 s) so you try another replica; read time reflects real work and is sized from the callee's latency distribution. One merged 30 s value gives you 30 s black holes.
  • What is a retry budget and why is it better than "3 retries"? — A cap on retry volume (e.g. retries ≤10% of requests). Per-call counts compound multiplicatively across layers during outages (3×3×3…); a budget makes the amplification bounded and self-limiting exactly when the system is sick.
  • Explain hedged requests and their preconditions. — Duplicate a slow request to a second replica after ~p95 latency, take the first response, cancel the other. Needs idempotent reads, per-request cancellation, and headroom for ~5% extra load; wrong tool for writes or overloaded fleets.
  • Your service recovered from a 2-minute outage and immediately fell over again. Why? — Thundering herd: synchronized retries/reconnects plus cold caches produce a load spike far above steady state. Fixes: jitter everywhere, connection-rate limits, cache warm-up or coalescing, circuit breakers half-opening gradually, load shedding by priority.
  • A timeout fired on a payment call. What may be true, and what must the client do? — Three possibilities: never arrived, failed mid-flight, or succeeded and the response was lost. The client must not blind-retry: reuse the idempotency key so the server dedupes, or query operation status first.
  • Where do circuit breakers fit relative to retries? — Retries handle transient single-request failures; the breaker watches the error rate and stops calling a sick dependency entirely (fail fast, serve fallback), then probes with limited traffic (half-open). Retry inside the breaker, never around it.

Regions, AZs and where the milliseconds (and dollars) go

Why interviewers ask: "should this be multi-AZ or multi-region?" has a cost/latency/complexity answer, not a fashion answer, and the numbers — 0.5 ms vs 2 ms vs 70 ms, and per-GB egress pricing — are what make it defensible.

A region is a geographic cluster of datacenters; an availability zone is an isolated datacenter (power, cooling, network) within it. AZs are close enough for synchronous replication (~1–2 ms RTT) but fail independently — so multi-AZ is the default availability story: three replicas across three AZs, synchronous or near-synchronous, and an AZ loss is a non-event. Cross-region RTTs (~50–150 ms) make synchronous replication user-visible, so multi-region designs are either active-passive (async replica, RPO > 0), active-active with conflict handling, or geo-partitioned (EU users' data lives in EU) — that is a later section's deep dive; here, know the physics that forces the choice.

The egress cost dimension surprises people: cloud ingress is free, but data leaving costs real money — internet egress ~$0.05–0.09/GB, cross-region ~$0.02/GB, and even cross-AZ transfer is billed (~$0.01–0.02/GB total). A chatty microservice mesh shipping 1 PB/month across AZs is ~$10–20k/month of pure network bill; CDNs exist partly because their egress is cheaper than serving from origin. Edge computing (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) runs small logic in the PoPs themselves — auth token checks, A/B routing, personalization stitching — buying ~10–30 ms responses for logic that doesn't need your database, at the price of a constrained runtime and distributed-state headaches.

PathTypical RTTSync replication?Cost note
Same host / loopback~0.05 ms—Free
Same AZ~0.2–0.5 msYesFree (usually)
Cross-AZ, same region~1–2 msYes — the HA sweet spot~$0.01–0.02/GB — chatty meshes add up
Cross-region, same continent~30–80 msPainful — async is the norm~$0.02/GB
Cross-continent~100–150 msNo (physics: ~5 ms per 1000 km one-way in fiber)~$0.02–0.08/GB
User → nearest edge PoP~5–30 ms—CDN egress cheaper than origin egress
Interview angle: the default posture to state early: "single region, three AZs, synchronous replication — that survives any single DC failure with zero data loss. I go multi-region only for a named reason: latency to far users (then CDN/edge first, it's 10× cheaper), regulatory data residency, or region-level DR with an explicit RPO/RTO." Naming the trigger conditions is the senior move.

Pitfalls

  • "Multi-region for availability" as a reflex — a region-wide outage is rare; you accept replication lag, conflict resolution, and 2× cost to insure against it. Say the trade explicitly.
  • Synchronous cross-region writes on the user path — every write eats 100+ ms of physics; no tuning fixes the speed of light.
  • Ignoring cross-AZ transfer costs in a chatty design — AZ-aware routing (prefer same-AZ replicas, e.g. Kafka follower fetch) is a real line item.
  • Confusing durability with availability: 3 AZ replicas protect data; a bad deploy replicates a bug to all three instantly. Backups and staged rollouts still matter.
Interview questions
  • Multi-AZ vs multi-region — what does each protect against? — Multi-AZ: host/rack/DC failure, with sync replication and no user-visible latency cost. Multi-region: regional disaster, and latency for far users — paid for with async replication (RPO > 0) or conflict resolution, plus double infrastructure.
  • Why can't you synchronously replicate NY ↔ Frankfurt? — ~80–90 ms RTT of physics per acknowledged write; a checkout doing 3 sequential writes gains ~270 ms. Light in fiber is ~200,000 km/s — no vendor changes that.
  • Your AWS bill shows $30k/month of "data transfer". Where do you look? — Cross-AZ chatter between services and DB replicas, cross-region replication volume, and internet egress bypassing the CDN. Fixes: AZ-aware routing, compression, batching, put cacheable egress behind the CDN.
  • When does edge computing beat adding a region? — When the logic needs no strongly consistent central data: auth verification, redirects, personalization assembly, geo-blocking. It's ~10–30 ms everywhere with no new database to operate — a region is a last resort, an edge function is a config push.
  • What RTO/RPO does an async standby region give? — RPO = replication lag (seconds typically — data written in that window is lost on failover); RTO = detection + DNS/traffic shift + promotion (minutes unless heavily automated and rehearsed). If they answer "zero and zero", it wasn't async.

IP, ports, NAT — and the resource limits that bite: ephemeral ports, FDs, SYN floods

Why interviewers ask: "how many connections can one box hold?" and "why did your proxy die at 28k outbound connections?" test whether the fundamentals — the 4-tuple, ephemeral ports, file descriptors — are actually load-bearing in your head.

A TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port). A server listening on one port can hold millions of inbound connections — each remote (IP, port) pair makes a distinct tuple; the practical ceilings are memory (~tens of KB per connection) and file descriptors (every socket is an FD; default ulimit -n is often 1024 — raise it to 100k+ or the C10k problem greets you as Too many open files). The famous 65,535 limit applies to outbound connections: a client reaching one (dst IP, dst port) can only vary its source port, and the OS hands out ~28k ephemeral ports by default (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range). A proxy hammering one upstream exhausts them — worsened by TIME_WAIT, which parks a closed connection's tuple for ~60 s. Fixes: connection pooling/keep-alive (the real fix), more upstream IPs/ports, wider port range, SO_REUSEADDR-family tuning.

NAT maps many private IPs through one public IP by rewriting ports and keeping a translation table — why your laptop is unreachable from the internet, why data-center servers get (expensive) public IPs or sit behind NAT gateways, and why long-idle connections die: the NAT entry expires (~minutes) unless keep-alives refresh it. A SYN flood abuses the handshake: attackers send SYNs (often from spoofed sources) and never ACK, filling the half-open connection backlog so real users can't connect. Mitigations: SYN cookies (encode the connection state in the SYN-ACK sequence number — no memory held until the ACK proves liveness), bigger backlogs, and upstream filtering. Broader DDoS basics: volumetric floods (100s of Gbps of UDP junk) are absorbed by anycast CDN/scrubbing capacity — never by your origin; protocol attacks (SYN floods) by cookies and stateless edges; application-layer floods (expensive-looking HTTP requests) by rate limits, caching, and challenges. Your origin's best defense is being unreachable except via the edge. Analogy: a SYN flood is prank-calling every table's reservation line and never showing up — the restaurant "fills" while standing empty; SYN cookies are the host who writes nothing down until the party physically arrives.

outbound to ONE upstream (ip:port fixed) → only src port varies
  ephemeral range default ≈ 32768–60999  → ~28k concurrent
  + TIME_WAIT holds tuples ~60 s after close
  churn limit ≈ 28,000 / 60 s ≈ ~470 new conns/s to one upstream
fix: keep-alive pool (100 conns reused) instead of connect-per-request
inbound on ONE listening port → limited by FDs + RAM, not ports
  ulimit -n 1024 (default!) → raise to 1M for a WS gateway
Interview angle: this card is the substrate for two favorite debugging questions: "proxy suddenly can't reach its upstream under load" (ephemeral port/TIME_WAIT exhaustion from connect-per-request — check ss -s, fix with pooling) and "gateway crashes at 1024 users" (FD limit). Volunteering ulimit -n and TIME_WAIT by name is instant credibility.

Pitfalls

  • Believing "65k max connections per server" — that is the outbound-to-one-destination limit; inbound scales to millions with RAM and FDs.
  • Disabling TIME_WAIT recycling blindly (tcp_tw_recycle — removed from Linux for breaking NAT'd clients); pool connections instead.
  • Load-testing from a single client machine and hitting your own ephemeral-port limit, then blaming the server.
  • Leaving health-check or metrics endpoints reachable from the internet — free ammunition for application-layer floods.
Interview questions
  • How many WebSocket connections can one gateway hold? — Port-wise unlimited inbound (one listen port, distinct 4-tuples); really bounded by FDs (raise ulimit), memory (~20–100 KB/conn with buffers → 1M conns ≈ tens of GB), and CPU for heartbeats/broadcast. 100k–1M with tuning.
  • Your sidecar proxy fails connecting to one upstream at high QPS with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Diagnose. — Ephemeral port exhaustion: connect-per-request to a single (ip,port) caps at ~28k live + TIME_WAIT churn. Fix with keep-alive pools; secondarily widen ip_local_port_range or add upstream addresses.
  • What is a SYN cookie? — A stateless SYN-ACK whose sequence number cryptographically encodes the connection parameters; the server allocates nothing until the client's ACK echoes it back, so spoofed SYNs cost the server ~zero memory.
  • Why do idle connections through NATs/firewalls die, and whose job is it to fix? — Translation-table entries expire after idle minutes; the endpoints must send keep-alives (TCP keep-alive or app-level pings) under that interval — a core reason WebSocket protocols mandate ping/pong.
  • Sketch the DDoS defense stack for a public API. — Anycast CDN/scrubbing absorbs volumetric; SYN cookies + stateless edge for protocol attacks; per-key/IP rate limits, caching, and challenges for L7 floods; origin firewalled to accept only edge IPs; and load shedding so overload degrades by priority instead of collapsing.

1. A cold HTTPS request (TLS 1.3, no resumption) to a server 100 ms away, DNS uncached (~50 ms). Roughly how long before the first response byte can arrive?

c. The phases run in series: ~50 ms DNS, 100 ms TCP handshake, 100 ms TLS 1.3 handshake, 100 ms request/response ≈ 350 ms. (d) describes TLS 1.2's two-RTT handshake; (a) is the reused-connection cost — which is exactly why keep-alive and pooling are worth 3.5× here.

2. Your team enables TLS 1.3 0-RTT everywhere to shave latency. What is the actual risk?

b. Early data is sent before the server proves freshness, so a captured flight can be resent; servers can't distinguish the replay. Encryption strength is unchanged (a). The standard policy: allow 0-RTT for idempotent GETs, reject or force-retry it for everything else.

3. On a lossy mobile link, a page over HTTP/2 loads slower than it did over HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections. Why?

c. TCP delivers one ordered byte stream: a hole blocks all later bytes, including frames of unrelated streams — TCP head-of-line blocking. H1's six connections are six independent orderings, so loss on one leaves five flowing. This is precisely the problem QUIC/H3 solves with per-stream reliability; (a) and (b) are real but negligible effects.

4. Which benefit is unique to HTTP/3/QUIC rather than HTTP/2?

b. QUIC identifies connections by connection ID instead of the (IP, port) 4-tuple, so a network switch — which changes the client's IP — migrates the connection instead of killing it. Multiplexing (a) and header compression (c) arrived with H2; TLS (d) is standard on both.

5. Behind a least-connections LB, one node starts instantly returning "connection refused". Traffic to it increases. Why?

c. Least-connections reads "no open connections" as "least loaded" — a fast-failing node looks ideal and swallows ever more traffic. The fix is passive health/outlier ejection based on success rate, plus active probes. (b) describes a different algorithm; the question said least-connections.

6. Every deploy produces a ~20-second burst of 502s even though new pods pass health checks before old ones stop. Most likely cause?

b. The signature of missing draining/deregistration delay: old instances receive SIGTERM and drop live connections, or the LB briefly routes to instances that already stopped listening → 502 from the proxy. Fix: deregister first, drain in-flight with a grace period, then terminate. (c) would show as elevated latency/504s, not an exact deploy-window 502 burst.

7. You need to push live order-status updates to browsers (server → client only, ~1 update/min per user, millions of users). Best-fit transport?

b. The traffic is strictly server→client: SSE gives instant push, rides HTTP/2, survives proxies more easily, and auto-reconnects with Last-Event-ID. WebSocket (a) adds upgrade friction and a hand-rolled reconnect protocol for a direction you don't use; (c) at 1 poll/s × millions of users is a huge QPS bill for minute-granularity data; (d) is for peer-to-peer media.

8. A WS gateway holding 100k connections crashes. Which design detail matters MOST for what happens next?

c. The failure itself is cheap; the danger is 100k clients reconnecting in the same second (thundering herd) and stale user→gateway routing entries black-holing messages. Jitter spreads the storm, cursors make the reconnect lossless, TTLs self-heal the registry. (a), (b), (d) change constants, not the failure mode.

9. Primary region fails; you update the DNS record (TTL 60 s) to point at the standby. Two hours later some users still hit the dead region. Why?

c. TTL is advisory: misbehaving resolvers, OS caches, JVM address caching, and long-lived pooled connections all outlive it. This tail is why DNS failover is a coarse tool — pair it with anycast, client retry-to-alternate-endpoint logic, or keep the old IPs answering with redirects. (b) confuses record changes with delegation propagation.

Practice

Design the edge for a global news site (CDN, cache keys, breaking-news purge)

A news site serves 50M readers/day worldwide from a single US-East origin. Pages: article HTML, images, a personalized "for you" strip, and a live homepage that must update within 5 seconds when news breaks. Design the edge: what is cached where, the cache keys and TTLs, and exactly what happens when a breaking story lands.

Cover: hit-ratio expectations, the personalization problem, and the purge-vs-TTL decision per asset class.

Hint 1Separate asset classes: immutable assets, article bodies, the homepage, the personalized strip. Each gets its own key/TTL/invalidations story.
Hint 2Personalized content and cached content can share a page if the page is assembled client-side (or edge-side) from a cached shell + a small uncached API call.
Solution

Asset classes:

static assets (js/css/img)  key: fingerprinted URL        TTL: 1 year, immutable — never purged
article images              key: URL (+device-class)       TTL: days; purge only on legal takedown
article HTML/JSON           key: normalized URL            TTL: 5 min + stale-while-revalidate
                            surrogate tag: article-{id}, section-{politics}
homepage / breaking module  key: URL + country             TTL: 30 s + SWR  ← purged on breaking news
personalized "for you"      NOT edge-cached: small API call (Cache-Control: private)
                            page ships as cached shell + client/edge include

Breaking-news flow (must beat 5 s): editor publishes → CMS emits event → purge-by-surrogate-tag (homepage, section-*) issued to the CDN API → PoPs invalidate in ~1–2 s → next request per PoP triggers one origin pull via origin shield (request coalescing turns 200 PoPs' misses into ~1 origin fetch) → globally fresh within ~3 s. TTL alone (30 s) misses the deadline; purge alone without shield invites a herd.

Numbers to state: 50M readers × ~10 requests ≈ 500M req/day ≈ ~6k RPS average, 20–30k peak — but with 97–99% hit ratio the origin sees only ~100–500 RPS plus purges; TTFB for far readers drops from ~300 ms (cross-ocean to US-East) to ~30 ms. On a giant story, traffic may spike 10× yet the origin load barely moves — the edge absorbs it, which is the whole point. Mention signed URLs only if there's a paywall: cached paywalled articles served via signed cookie checks at the edge.

WebSocket chat at 5M concurrent: gateway count and message routing

Design the connection tier for a chat app with 5M concurrent users, each sending on average 1 message/min, messages averaging 300 bytes, mostly 1:1 chats plus some 10k-member group channels. How many gateway nodes? How does a message from user A reach user B's socket on another node? What happens when a gateway dies?

An estimation-plus-mechanism problem: sizes first, then the routing design, then the failure story.

Hint 1Pick a defensible connections-per-node number (memory and FD math), then add headroom for AZ failure and reconnect storms.
Hint 2Two routing options: user→gateway registry with targeted delivery, or topic broadcast with local filtering. Compare their costs at this fleet size.
Solution 
Connections/node: budget ~50 KB/conn (buffers, TLS, heartbeat state)
  100k conns/node ≈ 5 GB conn memory → comfortable on a 16–32 GB box
  ulimit -n → 1M; heartbeat every 30 s → 100k/30 ≈ 3.3k pings/s/node — fine

Fleet: 5M ÷ 100k = 50 nodes minimum
  ×1.5 headroom (AZ loss + reconnect storm + deploys) ≈ 75 nodes / 3 AZs

Message volume: 5M × 1 msg/min ÷ 60 ≈ ~83k msgs/s ingress
  ~2× egress (1:1 delivery) + group amplification
  83k × 300 B ≈ 25 MB/s — trivial bandwidth; the cost is fan-out, not bytes

Routing: gateways are dumb pipes: on connect, write userId → gatewayId to a Redis registry (TTL 60 s, heartbeat-refreshed). A sends "to B" → gateway publishes to a chat service → service persists the message (source of truth first!), looks up B's gateway, and pushes via that gateway's queue/topic (e.g. one pub/sub channel per gateway). B offline → skip push; B syncs by cursor on reconnect. Group channels: never 10k targeted sends — publish once to channel-{id}; each gateway holding members of that channel subscribes and delivers locally (subscription map maintained on join/leave). Broadcast-to-all-gateways-and-filter is acceptable at 75 nodes for simplicity, but per-gateway targeting scales better as fleet × volume grows.

Gateway death: 100k clients reconnect with full-jitter backoff over ~30–60 s (LB spreads them across surviving 74 nodes — each takes ~1.4k extra, fine with headroom); registry entries expire by TTL so no black-holed pushes; messages were persisted before push, so reconnect + cursor sync loses nothing. State the sticky-session alternative and reject it: affinity without a registry means node death orphans users and uneven rebalancing; the registry is the design.

Estimation drill: handshake tax on a cross-region API, and the fix

A mobile app in Sydney calls your API in US-East (Virginia), RTT ≈ 200 ms. The app's HTTP client opens a fresh HTTPS connection per request (TLS 1.3), DNS cached. The API itself computes in 30 ms. Estimate (1) end-to-end latency per request today, (2) with connection reuse, (3) with an edge PoP 10 ms from the user terminating TLS and holding warm origin connections, (4) which fix you ship first.

Count round trips explicitly — the arithmetic is the answer.

Hint 1Fresh HTTPS connection = TCP (1 RTT) + TLS 1.3 (1 RTT) + request/response (1 RTT), all at 200 ms each.
Hint 2With edge termination, which legs run at 10 ms RTT and which at ~190 ms — and how many round trips remain on the long leg?
Solution 
(1) Today, cold connection every request:
    TCP 200 + TLS 200 + HTTP 200 + server 30  ≈ 630 ms per request

(2) Keep-alive / pooled connection (handshakes amortized):
    HTTP 200 + server 30                      ≈ 230 ms   (−63%)

(3) Edge termination (user↔edge 10 ms, edge↔origin warm H2 pool):
    TCP 10 + TLS 10 + HTTP 10 (to edge)
    + edge→origin on warm conn ≈ 1 × 190
    + server 30                               ≈ 250 ms cold,
    and ≈ 230 ms warm — but EVERY request now costs ~230–250 ms,
    including each user's first (no more 630 ms cold starts)

(4) Ship order: fix the client's connection reuse first — it is a
    config/code change, no infrastructure — then add edge termination
    to kill cold-start tax for all users and enable 0-RTT resumption.

Extra credit to mention: HTTP/3 to the edge merges transport+TLS into ~1 RTT of setup (10 ms here); the remaining 190 ms is physics — the only way below it is moving compute or data closer (regional replica, edge cache for reads), which is a different (and much bigger) design conversation than shaving handshakes.

Debug: LB health checks pass, users see 502s

Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway from your ALB. Target-group health checks (HTTP 200 on /healthz, every 10 s) are all green and stay green. List the hypotheses you would check, in order, with the signal that confirms each.

A 502 means the proxy could not get a valid response from the backend for that request — while the probe requests succeed. Enumerate the gaps between those two facts.

Hint 1What is different between a health-check request and a real request? Path, duration, payload size, connection lifecycle, timing relative to deploys.
Hint 2Compare idle-timeout settings on both sides of the LB, and correlate the 502 timestamps with deploy/scale events.
Solution

Ordered hypotheses:

1. Idle-timeout mismatch (top cause): backend keep-alive timeout
   (e.g. app server 30 s) < ALB idle timeout (60 s). Backend closes
   a pooled connection exactly as the ALB reuses it → race → 502.
   Signal: 502s uncorrelated with load/deploys; backend keepAliveTimeout
   < LB idle timeout in config. Fix: backend timeout > LB timeout.

2. Deploy/scale-in without draining: instance terminates with requests
   in flight, or LB routes briefly to a stopped process.
   Signal: 502 bursts align with deploy/autoscaling timestamps.

3. Shallow health check: /healthz returns 200 from a trivial handler
   while real requests crash (OOM kills of workers, exhausted DB pool,
   panic on a specific route). Signal: app error logs / worker restarts
   at 502 times; /healthz shares nothing with the failing path.

4. Request-shape limits: large uploads or long streams exceeding
   backend header/body limits or worker timeout → connection reset.
   Signal: 502s cluster on specific routes/payload sizes.

5. Conn/FD exhaustion under peak: backend accepts probes (tiny, rare)
   but resets under real concurrency. Signal: 502 rate tracks traffic;
   `ss -s`, ulimit, listen backlog overflows (`netstat -s`).

Method to narrate: pull the LB access logs (they record which target and an error reason per 502), correlate timestamps with deploys and load, then reproduce with a long-duration request during a rolling restart. The interview-winning sentence: "green health checks only prove the probe path works between probes — 502s live in the gaps: connection lifecycle races, draining, and paths the probe never exercises."

⚡ Rapid-fire: networking & edge one-liners

  • RTTs before first byte on a cold HTTPS (TLS 1.3) connection? — 3: TCP, TLS, HTTP (+ DNS if uncached).
  • TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 handshake? — 2 RTT vs 1 RTT; 1.3 adds 0-RTT resumption (replay-risky).
  • What does keep-alive save? — TCP+TLS handshakes per request: 2 RTTs and the CPU of key exchange.
  • DNS recursive vs authoritative? — Recursive resolves and caches for clients; authoritative holds the zone's truth.
  • Why is DNS failover slow? — TTL caching plus resolvers that ignore TTLs: a straggler tail of minutes+.
  • Anycast in one line? — Same IP announced from many sites; BGP routes each user to the nearest; failover = route withdrawal in seconds.
  • L4 vs L7 LB? — L4 forwards TCP/UDP flows (fast, blind); L7 parses HTTP (route by path, retry, terminate TLS).
  • Power-of-two-choices? — Probe 2 random backends, pick the less loaded — near-optimal, no shared state.
  • Least-connections black hole? — A fast-failing node looks idle and attracts traffic; fix with outlier ejection.
  • Active vs passive health checks? — Probe endpoint on a timer vs watch real traffic for 5xx/timeouts; use both.
  • Connection draining? — Stop new requests to a terminating node, let in-flight finish — zero-downtime deploys.
  • HTTP/2's unfixed problem? — TCP head-of-line blocking: one lost packet stalls all streams.
  • HTTP/3's three headline wins? — Per-stream loss recovery, 1-RTT setup, connection migration across networks.
  • Why H1 browsers opened ~6 connections/host? — One request at a time per connection; parallelism needed more sockets.
  • Reverse proxy vs API gateway? — Plumbing (TLS, routing, compression) vs API policy (authn, rate limits, quotas).
  • BFF pattern? — One aggregation gateway per client type, shaping responses for that UI.
  • Where does rate limiting go? — Coarse at the edge (protect capacity), precise per-tenant near the service (protect fairness).
  • CDN origin pull vs push? — Miss-triggered fetch-and-cache vs pre-uploading content to the edge.
  • Cache key? — Normalized URL + whitelisted params/headers; every stray param fragments the cache.
  • TTL vs purge? — TTL for tolerable staleness; purge/surrogate tags for "must change now"; fingerprinted URLs to avoid both.
  • Typical CDN hit ratio and win? — 90–99% on static; ~20–50 ms edge vs ~200–400 ms far origin, and 10–100× origin offload.
  • Signed URL? — Time-limited signature the edge verifies locally — private content without an auth call per request.
  • Short poll vs long poll? — Ask on a timer (laggy, wasteful) vs server holds the request until data (near-instant).
  • SSE vs WebSocket in one line? — One-way HTTP stream with auto-reconnect vs full-duplex socket you manage yourself.
  • Routing a message to 1 of 5M sockets? — Registry: user → gateway in Redis (TTL heartbeats); publish to that gateway.
  • Why heartbeats on WS/SSE? — NATs, LBs and firewalls kill idle connections silently (~60 s defaults).
  • gRPC's edge over REST? — Protobuf contracts + binary encoding + multiplexed H2 + streaming + propagated deadlines.
  • GraphQL's N+1? — Nested resolvers fire a query per parent row; fix with DataLoader batching.
  • Connect vs read timeout? — ~1 s to reach the host (fail over fast) vs p99-based wait for the response.
  • Retry budget? — Cap retries at ~10% of traffic so layered retries can't multiply into a storm.
  • Full jitter backoff formula? — sleep = rand(0, base × 2^attempt); randomness prevents synchronized waves.
  • Hedged request? — Duplicate a slow read at ~p95 to another replica, take the first answer — tail-latency killer.
  • Same-AZ / cross-AZ / cross-region RTT? — ~0.3 ms / ~1–2 ms / ~50–150 ms.
  • Cross-AZ traffic price trap? — ~$0.01–0.02/GB — chatty meshes and replicas turn it into a real bill.
  • Outbound connections to one upstream ip:port? — ~28k by default (ephemeral port range), worsened by TIME_WAIT; pool connections.
  • First two knobs for a million-connection gateway? — ulimit -n (FDs) and per-connection buffer memory.
  • SYN cookie? — State encoded in the SYN-ACK sequence number; no server memory until the client proves liveness.
  • DDoS defense in one line? — Absorb volumetric at anycast edge, SYN cookies for protocol floods, rate-limit/cache/challenge L7, hide the origin.

3️⃣ Databases & Storage at Scale

Almost every system design interview is won or lost at the data layer: the store you pick fixes your consistency, your failure modes, and the questions you can answer cheaply forever after. This section goes bottom-up — how a single node stores bytes (B-tree vs LSM), then how data survives node death (replication), outgrows one node (sharding), and what you give up along the way (CAP, consistency models, distributed transactions) — ending with the NoSQL family map and a worked "which store for which system" decision.

How databases store data: B-tree vs LSM-tree, WAL, and the three amplifications

Why interviewers ask: "why is Cassandra fast for writes?" and "why did your Postgres p99 spike?" are both storage-engine questions. Knowing which engine sits under each database lets you predict its behavior instead of memorizing vendor claims.

Both engine families start every write the same way: append the change to a write-ahead log (WAL) — a sequential file that is fsynced before the write is acknowledged, so a crash can be replayed. WAL is why "durable" and "fast" can coexist: sequential appends run at disk streaming speed (~500 MB/s on SSD) while the fancy data structures are updated lazily.

A B-tree (Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB, Oracle, SQL Server, MongoDB's WiredTiger) keeps rows in fixed-size pages (8 KB Postgres, 16 KB InnoDB) organized as a wide, shallow tree — 3–4 levels reach billions of rows, so a point read is 3–4 page fetches, mostly cached. Writes update pages in place; a full leaf triggers a page split that ripples upward. Analogy: a filing cabinet with labeled folders — finding anything is fast, but inserting into a full folder means splitting it and relabeling the drawer.

An LSM-tree (Cassandra, HBase, RocksDB, LevelDB, ScyllaDB — and RocksDB powers MyRocks and many NewSQL engines) never updates in place. Writes go to an in-RAM sorted memtable; when full (~64 MB) it is flushed as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Reads must check memtable + several SSTables (newest wins), helped by bloom filters that skip files guaranteed not to hold the key. Background compaction merges SSTables, dropping overwritten values and tombstones (delete markers). Analogy: an inbox — you always drop new mail on top (fast), and a janitor periodically merges the piles into sorted archives.

The trade is captured by three amplifications: write amp (bytes written to disk per byte of data — LSM compaction rewrites each row ~10–30× over its life; B-trees rewrite whole pages for one row), read amp (structures consulted per read — LSM checks many SSTables; B-tree is a bounded 3–4 pages), and space amp (dead versions awaiting compaction/vacuum). You optimize two at the expense of the third.

B-treeLSM-tree
Write pathIn-place page update (random I/O)Memtable append → sequential flush
Read path3–4 page fetches, boundedMemtable + N SSTables (bloom filters help)
Write ampPage splits, full-page writesCompaction rewrites, 10–30×
Range scansExcellent (leaf pages linked)Good but merges across SSTables
DeletesImmediate (space reclaimed by vacuum)Tombstones until compaction — reads slow down
Used byPostgres, MySQL/InnoDB, SQL Server, WiredTigerCassandra, HBase, RocksDB/LevelDB, ScyllaDB
Best forRead-heavy, transactional, range queriesWrite-heavy, append-mostly, time-series

Pitfalls

  • "LSM is always faster" — only for writes. A read-heavy workload on an LSM store pays compaction CPU + multi-file reads for nothing.
  • Compaction storms: under sustained write load, compaction falls behind, SSTables pile up, and read latency degrades — then compaction catches up and steals all the I/O. This is the classic Cassandra p99 sawtooth.
  • Mass deletes in Cassandra create tombstone walls: a query scanning 100k tombstones to return 10 rows will time out (tombstone_failure_threshold).
  • Turning off fsync (synchronous_commit=off) buys latency but a crash loses the last few hundred ms of "acknowledged" writes — say the trade out loud, don't do it silently.
Interview questions
  • Why can Cassandra absorb 1M writes/s per cluster but Postgres struggles past tens of thousands per node? — Cassandra's write is a WAL append + memtable insert (no read, no in-place page update) and scales linearly across nodes; Postgres pays index updates, page writes, and MVCC bookkeeping per row on one primary.
  • What is write amplification and why does it matter on SSDs? — Bytes physically written per logical byte; LSM compaction can be 10–30×. It burns SSD endurance and steals I/O bandwidth from foreground reads.
  • How does an LSM store make "key not found" fast? — Bloom filters per SSTable: a negative answer is definitive, so absent keys skip all file reads.
  • Why do databases need a WAL if the data files are updated anyway? — Crash consistency: the sequential log is fsynced first so a torn page or crash mid-update can be replayed/undone; it also feeds replication.
  • Your LSM store's disk usage is 3× the data size — is that a bug? — Likely space amplification: obsolete versions and tombstones awaiting compaction (size-tiered compaction is worst). Check compaction backlog before adding disks.
  • When would you pick a B-tree engine for a write-heavy system? — When those writes need transactional reads-after-write, secondary-index consistency, or range scans dominate; or when write volume fits one node and operational simplicity wins.

Indexes: secondary, composite, covering — and what each one costs your writes

Why interviewers ask: "just add an index" is the junior reflex; the senior answer knows an index is a second data structure you now maintain on every write, and that index design (column order, covering) decides whether a query is 1 I/O or a million.

A secondary index is another sorted structure (usually a B-tree) mapping indexed value → primary key / row pointer. A query on the indexed column walks the index, then fetches each matching row from the table — that second hop is the hidden cost: 1,000 matches can mean 1,000 random page reads.

A composite index on (a, b, c) is sorted by a, then b, then c — so it serves predicates on a, (a,b), (a,b,c), but not b alone (the leftmost-prefix rule). Order columns: equality filters first, then the range/sort column. A covering index includes every column the query needs (Postgres INCLUDE, or just listing them), enabling an index-only scan that never touches the table. Analogy: a book's index normally gives page numbers (you still flip to the page); a covering index prints the quote right in the index.

The bill: every index is an extra write per row change. A table with 5 secondary indexes turns one INSERT into 6 structure updates plus their WAL — and an UPDATE of an indexed column deletes+inserts in that index. This is why write-heavy tables carry few indexes, and why LSM stores handle secondary indexes awkwardly (Cassandra's built-in secondary indexes are node-local and mostly an anti-pattern — you denormalize into a second table keyed by the query instead).

-- Access pattern: recent orders for a user, showing status + total
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (status, total_cents);   -- covering: index-only scan, no heap hit
-- Serves: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
-- Does NOT serve: WHERE created_at > ?   (leftmost prefix violated)
Index choiceRead winWrite cost
Single-column secondaryPoint/range on that column, then row fetches+1 index update per write
Composite (equality→range order)Filter + sort in one scan+1 update; larger keys
Covering / INCLUDEIndex-only scan — no table I/OBigger index; more columns trigger index writes
Partial (WHERE status='active')Tiny index over hot subsetOnly matching rows pay

Pitfalls

  • Indexing low-selectivity columns (status with 3 values) — the planner ignores it, you pay writes for nothing; consider a partial index instead.
  • Redundant indexes: (a) alongside (a,b) — the first is nearly always subsumed and just taxes writes.
  • Functions in predicates (WHERE lower(email)=?) skip a plain index on email — you need an expression index.
  • On MySQL/InnoDB every secondary index stores the primary key — a fat 64-byte PK bloats every index.
Interview questions
  • Your write TPS dropped 40% after a release — what storage-level cause do you check? — New indexes: each one adds a structure update + WAL per write; also index bloat forcing page splits.
  • Index on (user_id, created_at) — will WHERE created_at > now() - '1 day' use it? — No: leftmost prefix. It needs an index leading with created_at.
  • What is an index-only scan and when does it fail to be "only"? — Serving the query entirely from the index; in Postgres it still visits the heap for pages not marked all-visible (vacuum matters).
  • Why are Cassandra's secondary indexes discouraged? — They are local to each node, so a lookup fans out to the whole cluster; the idiom is a second denormalized table keyed by the query.
  • How many indexes is too many? — When write amplification hurts: each write updates every index. OLTP tables commonly cap at ~5; append-heavy event tables often have 1–2.

Leader–follower replication: async vs sync, lag, and read-your-writes

Why interviewers ask: "add read replicas" is on every whiteboard, and the follow-up — "so what happens right after a user updates their profile?" — separates people who have operated replication from people who have drawn it.

One node, the leader, takes all writes and appends them to its replication log (the WAL again); followers replay that stream and serve reads. The single knob that matters is when the leader acknowledges: async — ack after local commit, followers catch up later (fast, but an unlucky crash loses acked writes); sync — wait for a follower's ack (no loss, but one slow follower stalls every write); semi-sync — wait for one of N followers (the common production compromise, e.g. Postgres synchronous_standby_names, MySQL semi-sync).

Replication lag — typically milliseconds, but seconds-to-minutes under load, long transactions, or a follower rebuild — makes replicas eventually consistent. The classic user-visible bug is a read-your-writes violation: save profile → hit "back" → the read goes to a lagging replica → your edit is "gone". Fixes: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after their write; sticky-route a session to one replica; or track the leader's log position (LSN/GTID) in the session and only read from replicas that have replayed past it. Analogy: a newsroom — one editor writes the master copy, printers around the country reprint it; a reader near a slow printer sees yesterday's edition.

Failover is where async replication draws blood: if the leader dies, you promote the most caught-up follower — any writes it hadn't received are simply lost (or worse, an old leader comes back and diverges — split brain, prevented by fencing and epoch numbers). Automated failover needs consensus (Patroni + etcd for Postgres, Raft-based election in modern systems) — a topic interviewers love to walk toward.

ModeWrite latencyData loss on leader crashUsed when
AsyncLocal commit only (fastest)Yes — unshipped tail lostDefault for read replicas, cross-region copies
Semi-sync (any 1 of N)+1 follower RTTNo (one synchronous copy)Production OLTP wanting durability
Fully sync+slowest followerNoRare; small clusters, strict RPO=0

Pitfalls

  • Sending reads "to the replicas" without naming which reads tolerate staleness — checkout and auth flows usually cannot.
  • Monitoring lag in bytes, not seconds — a small byte lag on a huge transaction can still be minutes of replay.
  • Automated failover on a flappy network without fencing: two leaders both accepting writes (split brain) is far worse than a minute of downtime.
  • Forgetting that replicas don't add write capacity — the leader still applies every write; replicas only scale reads.
Interview questions
  • You added 5 read replicas and write latency got worse — why might that be? — Semi-sync waiting on a slow follower, network saturation from 5 log streams, or the leader throttling to let replicas keep up (e.g. flow control in Galera-style setups).
  • How do you guarantee a user sees their own write? — Leader reads for that user for a short window, session stickiness to a caught-up replica, or LSN/GTID tokens compared against replica replay position.
  • What's your RPO with async replication? — The replication lag at crash time: typically < 1 s, but unbounded under load. If RPO must be 0, you need at least semi-sync.
  • Walk me through a safe failover. — Detect via quorum (not one ping), fence the old leader (kill/isolate, bump epoch), promote the most-advanced follower, repoint clients (DNS/proxy/VIP), then re-attach the old leader as a follower after rewinding divergent WAL (e.g. pg_rewind).
  • Can replicas serve strongly consistent reads? — Only with extra machinery: wait until the replica's applied position ≥ the leader's current commit (adds latency), or use a lease-holder/consensus read as NewSQL systems do.
  • Your service does 50k reads/s and 2k writes/s — how does replication help? — Perfectly: 1 leader takes 2k writes/s comfortably; 3–4 replicas share the 50k reads/s. State the staleness contract per endpoint.

Multi-leader replication: conflicts, why LWW loses data, CRDTs

Why interviewers ask: "make it active-active across regions" sounds like an availability upgrade; the probe is whether you know you just bought a distributed conflict-resolution problem.

Multi-leader (active-active) lets several nodes accept writes — one leader per region, replicating asynchronously to the others. Wins: local write latency in every region, and surviving a whole region's loss. The price: two users can concurrently update the same row in different regions, and both writes are already acknowledged — conflicts are now inevitable and must be resolved, not prevented.

The default resolver almost everywhere is last-write-wins (LWW): keep the write with the larger timestamp. It is simple and silently discards data — clock skew between servers (even with NTP, milliseconds; without, unbounded) means the "last" write may actually be the earlier one, and the losing write vanishes with no error. Cassandra's cell-level LWW is a famous source of "my update disappeared" tickets. Better options: keep siblings and let the application merge (Riak, early Dynamo carts — where merge-by-union famously resurrected deleted items), detect concurrency with version vectors, or design the data so conflicts cannot occur (partition writes by home region, or make operations commutative).

CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) are the principled version of "commutative by design": counters, sets, and registers whose merge function is mathematically guaranteed to converge regardless of delivery order — a G-counter merges by taking per-node maxima; an OR-set tags adds with unique ids so add/remove conflicts resolve deterministically. Redis Enterprise's active-active geo-replication and collaborative editors (Figma-style, Yjs/Automerge) run on them. The limit: only some data shapes fit, and "converged" is not the same as "what the user intended".

StrategyHowRisk
AvoidanceHome-region routing: each record has one writing regionRegion failover reintroduces conflicts
LWWLargest timestamp winsSilent data loss under clock skew
Siblings + app mergeStore both, merge on readComplex; merge bugs (deleted items return)
CRDTsCommutative merge functionsLimited data types; semantic surprises

Pitfalls

  • Proposing active-active "for availability" when the workload has natural single-region owners — you inherit conflicts for no benefit over leader-per-shard.
  • Trusting server timestamps for LWW ordering — clock skew makes causality lie; at minimum use hybrid logical clocks.
  • Auto-incrementing IDs in two leaders — instant collisions; use region-prefixed or random IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake).
Interview questions
  • When is multi-leader actually the right call? — Multi-region write latency requirements, offline-capable clients (each device is a "leader"), or collaborative editing — anywhere writes must be accepted without cross-region coordination.
  • Why is LWW dangerous, concretely? — Two concurrent updates: the one with the smaller timestamp is discarded with no error; clock skew can even discard the later real-world write. Fine for ephemeral data (presence), unacceptable for money.
  • How would you make a distributed like-counter correct? — CRDT G-counter: each node increments its own slot, merge = element-wise max, total = sum. No coordination, converges exactly.
  • How do you even detect that two writes conflict? — Version vectors: each replica tracks per-node counters; if neither vector dominates the other, the writes were concurrent → conflict.

Leaderless replication & quorums: N/R/W, sloppy quorums, repair

Why interviewers ask: Dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB's ancestry) power half the "design a scalable X" answers; interviewers check you can do the R+W>N arithmetic and know the repair machinery that makes "eventually consistent" actually converge.

No leader: a client (or coordinator node) sends each write to all N replicas of a key and considers it successful after W acknowledgments; reads query R replicas and take the newest version. If R + W > N, read and write sets must overlap in at least one node, so a read sees the latest successful write — quorum consistency. Typical: N=3, W=2, R=2. Dial W=1 for write speed (risking loss), R=1 for read speed (risking staleness); W=N gives read-anything at the cost of writes failing when any replica is down. Analogy: leaving a message with 2 of a person's 3 assistants and later asking 2 of the 3 — at least one you ask must have heard it.

Availability machinery when nodes fail: a sloppy quorum accepts the write on substitute nodes outside the home set so W can still be met; the substitute stores a hinted handoff — "this belongs to node C" — and forwards it when C recovers. Note: during sloppiness, R+W>N no longer guarantees overlap — you traded consistency for write availability. Convergence machinery: read repair (a read that sees a stale replica writes the newer version back to it) and anti-entropy (background process comparing replicas via Merkle trees so only differing ranges are transferred — Cassandra's nodetool repair).

Cassandra exposes all of this per query as consistency levels: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM (quorum within the local datacenter — the multi-region workhorse), ALL. A common production recipe: write LOCAL_QUORUM, read LOCAL_QUORUM for consistency-sensitive tables; ONE for high-volume telemetry.

Setting (N=3)BehaviorUse for
W=2, R=2Quorum consistency, tolerates 1 node down for both opsDefault for user-facing state
W=1, R=1Fastest, stale reads and lost-write windows possibleMetrics, logs, feeds
W=3 (ALL), R=1Reads cheap and fresh; writes fail if any replica downRarely-written config-style data
LOCAL_QUORUMQuorum within the region; async cross-regionMulti-DC Cassandra standard

Pitfalls

  • Claiming R+W>N gives linearizability — it does not: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, and partial write failures can still surface anomalies (a failed write with 1 ack is visible to some reads).
  • Never running anti-entropy repair — deleted data can resurrect after gc_grace_seconds when a node that missed the tombstone rejoins.
  • Reading at ONE and writing at ONE for "performance" on data users re-read immediately — you rebuilt the read-your-writes bug with extra steps.
Interview questions
  • N=3: pick W and R for a shopping cart vs a page-view counter. — Cart: W=2/R=2 (quorum, users notice loss). Counter: W=1/R=1 — staleness is invisible and volume is huge.
  • Does W=2,R=2,N=3 survive a datacenter losing one replica? — Yes for both reads and writes (2 of 3 remain). Two down: strict quorum fails; sloppy quorum keeps writes alive with hints.
  • How do replicas that missed writes catch up without a leader's log? — Three mechanisms: read repair (foreground, hot keys), hinted handoff (short outages), anti-entropy Merkle repair (everything else).
  • Why Merkle trees for anti-entropy? — Comparing hashes level by level localizes differences in O(log n) exchanges, so two 1 TB replicas sync by transferring only differing ranges, not the whole dataset.
  • What does a sloppy quorum sacrifice? — The overlap guarantee: reads may miss the hinted writes until handoff completes — it converts consistency into availability during failures.

Partitioning & sharding: key-range vs hash, consistent hashing, virtual nodes

Why interviewers ask: sharding is the canonical "scale beyond one node" move, and the probe order is predictable: why shard at all → what's the key → what happens when you add a node. Consistent hashing is the single most-requested whiteboard drawing in this space.

When do you actually need it? A well-tuned single Postgres primary comfortably handles roughly 10–50k write TPS, a few TB of hot data, and low-single-digit-TB tables before index maintenance, vacuum, and failover-rebuild times get painful (read load is solved by replicas first). Shard when a number — write TPS, data volume, working set vs RAM — exceeds one node with headroom, not before: sharding forfeits cross-shard joins, transactions, and unique constraints, and you own that complexity forever.

Two ways to split by key. Key-range partitioning (HBase, Bigtable, Vitess range shards, Postgres declarative partitions) keeps sort order — great for range scans — but sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment) hammer the last shard. Hash partitioning spreads uniformly but destroys range queries. Naive hash(key) mod N has a fatal flaw: changing N remaps almost every key — adding node 11 to 10 moves ~91% of data.

Consistent hashing fixes rebalancing: hash both nodes and keys onto a ring (0…2³²); each key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only the keys in one arc — about 1/N of the data, from/to its immediate neighbor. Analogy: mailboxes on a circular street — a new house takes over only the stretch of street just before it. One node = one point is lumpy (uneven arcs, and a leaving node dumps its whole load on one neighbor), so real systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak) give each physical node 100–256 virtual nodes: arcs even out statistically, and a departing node's load spreads across many machines. Alternative used by Dynamo/DynamoDB-style and Vitess/CockroachDB: fixed pre-split partitions (say 1024) mapped to nodes by a directory — rebalancing moves whole partitions, no hashing math at runtime.

SchemeRange queriesLoad spreadRebalance costExamples
Key-rangeYes (sorted)Skew-prone (hot ranges)Split/merge rangesHBase, Bigtable, Postgres partitions
Hash mod NNoEvenCatastrophic (~all keys)Naive app-level sharding
Consistent hash + vnodesNoEven~1/N per node changeCassandra, DynamoDB, Memcached clients
Fixed partitions + directoryPer-partitionEven; movableMove whole partitionsVitess, CockroachDB, Kafka

Pitfalls

  • Sharding at 60 writes/s "for scale" — your own estimate contradicts the design; replicas + partitioning inside Postgres come first.
  • Timestamp or auto-increment shard keys with range partitioning: all inserts land on the newest shard (the "hot tail").
  • Forgetting the router: someone must map key→shard (client library, proxy like Vitess/Envoy, or coordinator nodes) and hold the topology — that component needs HA too.
Interview questions
  • When do you shard vs add replicas? — Replicas scale reads; sharding scales writes and data volume. Shard only when write TPS or data size exceeds one primary with headroom (~tens of k TPS / low TB).
  • Draw consistent hashing and explain what virtual nodes buy you. — Ring + clockwise ownership; vnodes even the load, spread a dead node's keys across many survivors, and let heterogeneous hardware take proportional shares.
  • What's your shard key for a multi-tenant SaaS? — tenant_id: queries are tenant-scoped so they stay single-shard; but plan for whale tenants (dedicated shard or sub-sharding a tenant).
  • How does DynamoDB decide where your item lives? — Hash of the partition key onto partitions (consistent-hash lineage); each partition has throughput and ~10 GB size limits, splitting as it grows.
  • Why does Kafka's model look like "fixed partitions + directory"? — Partition count is chosen up front; rebalancing moves partition ownership between brokers rather than rehashing messages.

Life after sharding: hot keys, secondary indexes, cross-shard queries, resharding

Why interviewers ask: picking a shard key is the easy half. The follow-ups — "what about Justin Bieber's row?", "how do you find users by email now?", "how do you go from 4 shards to 16 live?" — test whether you have lived with a sharded system.

Hot keys (the celebrity problem). Hashing spreads keys evenly, not load: one celebrity's post receives millions of reads/writes on a single shard. Mitigations, in escalation order: cache the hot entity aggressively (a hot read key is a cache problem); for hot write keys, split the key by appending a random suffix (post123#0..15 spread over 16 shards, aggregated on read — "write sharding"); isolate whales on dedicated shards; or handle celebrity fan-out differently at the application layer (the hybrid push/pull feed pattern).

Secondary indexes across shards. A local index lives inside each shard, indexing only that shard's rows: writes stay single-shard (cheap), but a query by the indexed value must scatter-gather across all shards (read cost O(shards)). A global index is itself partitioned by the indexed value: queries hit one index shard (cheap reads), but every write may touch a second shard, asynchronously in practice — DynamoDB GSIs are exactly this, eventually consistent by design. Rule of thumb: local for write-heavy, global for read-heavy lookups like "user by email".

Cross-shard queries and transactions. Joins across shards happen in the application or a query layer (scatter-gather, then merge — Vitess and Citus do this for you), so co-locate data that must join (put a user's orders on the user's shard). Cross-shard transactions need 2PC (slow, blocking) or sagas; most sharded designs instead pick keys so that money-moving operations stay within one shard. Resharding live: pre-split into many logical shards mapped to few physical nodes (moving a logical shard is easy; changing the hash isn't), or migrate with the dual-write + backfill playbook — write both old and new layouts, backfill history, verify checksums, cut reads over, drop the old — the same choreography as any online migration.

ProblemCheap fixRobust fix
Hot read keyCache in front (Redis/CDN)Replicate the hot entity to all shards
Hot write keyRandom-suffix write sharding + read aggregationDedicated shard / app-level redesign (feed hybrid)
Lookup by non-shard-keyScatter-gather over local indexesGlobal secondary index (async-updated)
Cross-shard transactionChoose keys so it doesn't happenSaga / outbox (see section 6)
Adding capacityMove pre-split logical shardsDual-write + backfill migration

Pitfalls

  • Global unique constraints (email!) silently stop working when you shard by user_id — you need a global index or a claim-check table, stated explicitly.
  • Scatter-gather latency is the slowest shard's latency — p99 amplifies with shard count (one laggard drags every query).
  • Resharding by "just rehash everything over the weekend" — at 10 TB and 100 MB/s effective copy rate that's ~28 hours of moving data while writes keep arriving; you need dual-write, not downtime.
Interview questions
  • Your metrics show one shard at 90% CPU while others idle — walk me through it. — Identify the hot key (top-K by traffic), then: cache if read-hot; suffix-shard if write-hot; isolate the tenant if it's a whale; check for a bad shard key (low cardinality, skewed distribution) as the root cause.
  • Shard by user_id — now support login by email. — Global index mapping email → user_id (itself sharded by email), or a small lookup table/service; accept that it's a second write on signup and must be idempotent.
  • DynamoDB GSI vs LSI in one breath? — GSI: different partition key, eventually consistent, own capacity — a global index. LSI: same partition key, different sort key, strongly consistent — a local index within the partition.
  • How do you go from 4 to 16 shards with zero downtime? — If pre-split into e.g. 4096 logical shards: reassign logical→physical mapping and copy shard files. If not: dual-write to the new layout, backfill old data, verify, flip reads, retire — weeks, not a weekend.
  • Why co-locate orders with users on the same shard? — "User's order history" becomes single-shard, and order-placement transactions stay local — you designed the transaction boundary into the shard key.

CAP & PACELC properly: what partition tolerance really means

Why interviewers ask: everyone can recite "pick two of three"; almost everyone recites it wrong. Stating CAP precisely — and extending it with PACELC — is a cheap, reliable senior signal.

The precise statement: when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write — linearizability) and availability (every request to a live node gets a non-error answer). Partition tolerance is not optional — networks partition whether you like it or not (switch failures, GC pauses long enough to look like death, misconfigured firewalls) — so "CA distributed system" is marketing: it describes either a single node or a system that simply hasn't met its partition yet. The real choice is CP vs AP, and only during a partition.

CP examples: ZooKeeper/etcd (a minority partition refuses to serve — that's the point of quorum), Spanner, HBase, single-leader Postgres with sync replication where the minority side blocks. AP examples: Cassandra and Dynamo-style stores at low consistency levels, DNS, most caches — every side keeps answering, and divergence is reconciled later. Note it's per-operation, not per-database: Cassandra at QUORUM behaves CP-ish; at ONE it's AP.

PACELC completes the picture: if Partition, trade A vs C; Else (normal operation, which is 99.99% of life) trade Latency vs Consistency. Even with a healthy network, making a write consistent means waiting for replicas — cross-region, that's 50–150 ms per coordination round. Spanner is PC/EC (waits for quorum always); Dynamo/Cassandra are PA/EL (fast and loose both times); MySQL semi-sync is roughly PC/EC-lite. PACELC is why "we'll just use strong consistency" has a latency bill even on a good day.

SystemPACELCDuring partitionNormal operation
ZooKeeper / etcdPC/ECMinority stops servingQuorum on writes (latency)
Spanner / CockroachDBPC/ECConsistent, minority unavailableQuorum + commit-wait latency
Cassandra / Dynamo (ONE)PA/ELAll sides serve, divergeFast, eventual
MongoDB (majority)PC/EC-ishMinority can't elect, stallsMajority write concern latency

Pitfalls

  • "We'll pick CA" — instant credibility loss. The available choices are how you behave when (not if) the network splits.
  • Treating CAP as a database-wide constant: consistency level, write concern, and read preference make it per-operation.
