  • Ignoring PACELC's "else": teams pick strong consistency, then wonder why every cross-region write costs 100+ ms on a healthy network.
Interview questions
  • Is Cassandra AP or CP? — Per-query: QUORUM/QUORUM leans CP (minority side fails requests); ONE/ONE is AP. The tunable is the answer.
  • What does partition tolerance actually mean? — The system keeps operating (per its chosen guarantee) when messages between nodes are lost or delayed — including false partitions from GC pauses and packet loss.
  • Give a business case for AP and one for CP. — AP: shopping cart / likes — availability earns revenue and conflicts are mergeable. CP: inventory decrement, payments, leader election — a wrong answer is worse than an error.
  • Why does PACELC matter more than CAP day-to-day? — Partitions are rare; the latency-vs-consistency choice is paid on every request. Your p99 budget usually decides consistency, not partition philosophy.
  • Your PM asks for "always available AND always consistent" cross-region — what do you say? — Physics says pick per operation: reads can be consistent-with-latency or fast-and-stale; during partitions one property must yield. Then offer the split: strong for money paths, eventual elsewhere.

Consistency models: linearizability → causal → eventual, and session guarantees

Why interviewers ask: "eventual consistency" is the most-used, least-defined phrase in interviews. Naming the specific model — and the specific anomaly each one forbids — shows you can reason about what users will actually observe.

The spectrum, strongest first. Linearizability: the system behaves as if there were a single copy, and every operation takes effect atomically at some instant between its start and end — once any client reads the new value, no client may read the older one. This is what people mean by "strong consistency"; it's what CAP's C is, what a compare-and-swap needs, and what ZooKeeper/etcd give for writes (and Spanner for everything). Sequential consistency relaxes real-time: all clients see operations in the same order, but that order may lag reality. Causal consistency only orders operations that are causally related — a reply is never seen before its question — while concurrent writes may appear in different orders to different observers. Eventual consistency promises only convergence: stop writing, and replicas eventually agree; it forbids nothing along the way.

Between causal and eventual live the practical session guarantees: read-your-writes (you see your own updates), monotonic reads (time never goes backward across your successive reads — no seeing a comment, refreshing, and watching it vanish), monotonic writes (your writes apply in order), and writes-follow-reads. They're properties of one client's session, cheap to provide (sticky routing or version tokens) and usually exactly what the product actually needs — most "we need strong consistency" requirements are really "we need session guarantees". Analogy: linearizability is one shared whiteboard everyone reads; causal is gossip that never delivers an answer before its question; eventual is rumor — everyone hears everything, eventually, in some order.

Where each shows up: Postgres single-node — linearizable per row for committed reads (it's one copy). ZooKeeper/etcd — linearizable writes; ZK reads are stale-able unless you sync(), etcd offers serializable (fast) vs linearizable (quorum) reads. Dynamo-style — eventual by default, quorum tunable, no linearizability guarantee even at R+W>N. MongoDB — tunable via read/write concern up to linearizable single-document. Spanner/CockroachDB — external consistency (linearizability across the globe) via TrueTime/HLC.

ModelGuaranteeForbidden anomalyLives in
LinearizableSingle-copy, real-time orderAny stale read after a newer one seenetcd/ZK writes, Spanner, single Postgres
SequentialOne global order (may lag)Clients disagreeing on orderSome replicated state machines
CausalCause before effectReply visible before its postMongoDB causal sessions, COPS-style stores
Session guaranteesPer-client sanity (RYW, monotonic)Own write invisible; time reversal per clientSticky replicas, LSN tokens
EventualConvergence onlyNothing until quiescenceDynamo-style, DNS, caches

Pitfalls

  • Saying "strong consistency" when you mean "read-your-writes" — you'll be asked to pay linearizability's latency price for a session-guarantee problem.
  • Believing R+W>N ⇒ linearizable — partial writes and concurrent operations still produce non-linearizable histories (Kleppmann's classic counterexample).
  • Serving a linearizable system's reads from followers "for scale" — you just downgraded the guarantee without telling anyone.
Interview questions
  • Which operations in an e-commerce system need linearizability? — Inventory decrement at checkout, payment state transitions, coupon redemption (once-only), auth token revocation. Catalog, reviews, recommendations: eventual with session guarantees.
  • Linearizability vs serializability? — Linearizability: real-time ordering of single operations on one object. Serializability: transactions over many objects appear in some serial order (not necessarily real-time). Strictest is both: strict serializability (Spanner).
  • How does a lagging replica break monotonic reads, and the cheapest fix? — Successive reads load-balanced across replicas with different lag; fix with session stickiness or a last-seen-LSN token the replica must have passed.
  • Why are ZooKeeper reads not linearizable by default? — Reads are served locally by any member for throughput; they may lag the quorum. sync() before read buys linearizability when needed.
  • What model do you need for a chat app's message ordering? — Causal (replies after their parents, per-conversation order); global linearizability across all chats is unnecessary and unaffordable.

Distributed transactions: 2PC and why applications route around it

Why interviewers ask: the moment your design has two stores ("orders in Postgres, event to Kafka"), the interviewer asks how both happen atomically. Knowing why 2PC exists, why it blocks, and what teams use instead is a standard senior checkpoint.

Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks every participant to prepare (do the work, hold locks, write a durable "I can commit" record, vote yes/no); if all vote yes, the coordinator durably logs COMMIT and tells everyone to commit; any no → abort all. It gives atomicity across systems (XA in the Java world, still under the hood of Spanner-style databases per shard-group). The fatal flaw is blocking: a participant that voted yes is in-doubt — it may neither commit nor abort on its own, holding row locks, until the coordinator tells it the outcome. Coordinator crashes after prepare → participants hold locks indefinitely; throughput on those rows drops to zero. Plus: latency is two round trips to every participant, and availability is the product of all participants' availability.

3PC adds a pre-commit phase so participants can time out and decide, removing the block — but it assumes bounded network delay (no partitions), which real networks don't grant, so it's a textbook mention, not a production tool. The production-grade descendants change the model instead: Google Percolator (BigTable + MVCC, primary-lock trick) powers snapshot-isolated transactions at scale; Spanner runs 2PC across Paxos groups — the "coordinator" is itself replicated, so it can't die as a single process — and uses TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks exposing a bounded uncertainty interval; commit waits out the uncertainty, ~few ms) to hand out globally ordered timestamps, giving external consistency without a global lock. Calvin/deterministic databases pre-order transactions in a replicated log so every node executes the same schedule with no commit protocol at all.

Applications, though, mostly avoid the problem: make one store the system of record and drive the rest asynchronously — the outbox pattern (write business row + event in one local transaction, relay publishes it) and sagas (sequence of local transactions with compensations) trade atomicity for availability and loose coupling. Details and choreography live in section 6.

ApproachAtomicityBlocking?CostUse
2PC / XAYes, all-or-nothingYes (in-doubt holds locks)2 RTT × participants, coupled availabilityInside DBs; rare between services
Spanner-style (2PC over Paxos + TrueTime)Yes + external consistencyNo single-process coordinatorCommit-wait ms; infra heftNewSQL internals
Saga + outboxEventual, via compensationNoDesign work: compensations, idempotencyMicroservices default (§6)

Pitfalls

  • Proposing XA between your service, Kafka, and a REST API — heterogeneous 2PC across services is an availability trap and often not even supported.
  • "We'll write the DB, then publish the event" without outbox — the crash between the two steps is exactly the dual-write bug 2PC was solving.
  • Citing 3PC as the fix — it's non-blocking only without partitions, i.e., in a network you don't have.
Interview questions
  • Why is 2PC called blocking, precisely? — A yes-voting participant cannot unilaterally decide after prepare; if the coordinator vanishes it holds locks until the outcome arrives — safety is preserved, liveness is not.
  • How does Spanner make cross-shard transactions practical? — Each shard group is a Paxos-replicated state machine (coordinator can't die), and TrueTime's bounded clock uncertainty lets commits get globally ordered timestamps — a few-ms commit wait instead of global locks.
  • Order must be saved AND an event published — atomically. Options? — Outbox (one local txn, relay publishes; at-least-once + idempotent consumers), CDC from the WAL, or listen-to-yourself. Not XA to Kafka.
  • When is 2PC still the right answer? — Within one database system's shards (it controls recovery), or short-lived, few-participant, same-datacenter commits where the operational blast radius is understood.

The NoSQL family map: which store for which shape of problem

Why interviewers ask: after "SQL or NoSQL" (section 1's decision tree) comes "which NoSQL, and what will bite you". Each family has one defining strength and one classic operational scar — knowing both is the difference between name-dropping and choosing.

Key-value (Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB in its plainest use): opaque value by key, microsecond–millisecond lookups, the substrate of caches, sessions, counters, feature flags. Wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase): two-level keys — a partition key locating the node and a clustering key sorting rows within the partition — built for huge write volume and "give me a time-ordered slice of one partition" queries. Partition-key design is the data model: every query must name the partition key, partitions should stay under ~100 MB, and deletes write tombstones that haunt reads until compaction. Document (MongoDB, Couchbase): JSON-shaped aggregates, schema-flexible, secondary indexes and rich single-document queries — the pragmatic default when entities are self-contained and the team wants Mongo's ergonomics; joins and multi-document transactions exist but are not the strong suit.

Graph (Neo4j, Neptune): when the traversal is the query — fraud rings, social paths, dependency graphs; an n-hop walk that would be n self-joins in SQL is native here. Time-series (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, ClickHouse for analytics): append-heavy, time-bucketed compression, downsampling and retention policies as first-class features. Search (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch): an inverted index — term → list of documents — makes full-text and faceted queries cheap; it is near-real-time (documents become searchable on the next refresh, default every 1 s) and it is a secondary system fed from your source of truth, never the source of truth itself.

NewSQL / distributed SQL closes the loop: Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB give SQL + serializable transactions over Raft/Paxos-replicated, auto-sharded ranges — you pay coordination latency (quorum per write) and operational sophistication. Vitess is the other road: keep MySQL, add a sharding/routing layer on top (YouTube's path, now Slack's and GitHub's playbook via similar approaches).

FamilyExemplarsData model / superpowerClassic scarReach for it when
Key-valueRedis, Memcached, DynamoDBKey → value; µs–ms latency, trivial scalingNo queries beyond the key; Redis persistence ≠ durability by defaultCache, session, counter, rate limiter
Wide-columnCassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase(partition, clustering) keys; massive write throughput, linear scaleTombstones, hot partitions, query patterns frozen at designTime-ordered data at high write volume: messages, events, IoT
DocumentMongoDB, CouchbaseJSON aggregates, flexible schema, secondary indexesUnbounded document growth; cross-document consistencySelf-contained entities: catalogs, profiles, CMS
GraphNeo4j, NeptuneNodes/edges; n-hop traversals without joinsSharding a graph is genuinely hardFraud rings, recommendations, org/dependency graphs
Time-seriesTimescale, InfluxDB, ClickHouseTime-bucketed compression, retention, rollupsLate/out-of-order data; cardinality explosionsMetrics, telemetry, sensor data
SearchElasticsearch, OpenSearchInverted index; full-text, facets, relevanceNRT (~1 s refresh), rebuild-from-source disciplineSearch boxes, log analytics — beside a source of truth
NewSQLSpanner, CockroachDB, Yugabyte; Vitess (sharded MySQL)SQL + serializable txns, auto-sharded, replicatedQuorum latency per write; ops complexity/costRelational semantics beyond one node's limits
-- Cassandra: the query IS the schema
CREATE TABLE messages (
  chat_id   uuid,
  bucket    int,          -- e.g. month: caps partition size
  sent_at   timeuuid,
  author_id uuid,
  body      text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id, bucket), sent_at)   -- partition key, clustering key
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);
-- serves: last N messages of a chat = one partition, one sorted slice

Pitfalls

  • Elasticsearch as the system of record — a refresh-interval search index with looser durability guarantees holding your only copy is an outage story; keep truth in a database and reindex from it.
  • Cassandra partitions that grow forever (partition key = user_id for an events table) — add a time bucket to the key before the 100 MB+ partition melts reads.
  • Redis as a durable store with default persistence — RDB snapshots lose the tail; even AOF everysec loses ~1 s. Say the durability setting out loud.
  • Choosing by hype cycle: "graph database" for data with a couple of foreign keys, or NewSQL for a workload one Postgres could hold.
Interview questions
  • Chat app, 1M msgs/min: which store and why? — Wide-column (Cassandra/Scylla): partition (chat_id, bucket), clustering sent_at DESC — write-heavy, time-sliced reads, linear scale. Postgres for users/membership; ES for message search if required.
  • How does an inverted index make search fast? — Terms are pre-mapped to posting lists of doc IDs; a query intersects/unions small sorted lists instead of scanning documents — plus per-term stats power relevance scoring.
  • Why is a just-written Elasticsearch doc not searchable? — Docs sit in an in-memory buffer until refresh (default 1 s) creates a searchable segment; durability comes separately from the translog. Tuning refresh to 30 s is a standard bulk-index speedup.
  • DynamoDB vs Cassandra in one minute? — Same lineage (Dynamo paper). DynamoDB: fully managed, per-request pricing, GSIs, 400 KB item cap, capacity units to plan. Cassandra: self-run (or Astra), tunable consistency per query, no item-size cliff, you own repairs/compaction.
  • When NewSQL over sharded Postgres/Vitess? — When you need serializable cross-shard transactions and global distribution without building 2PC/routing yourself, and can pay quorum-write latency; if the workload shards cleanly by tenant, Vitess-style is cheaper and boring-in-a-good-way.
  • Where do graph databases actually win? — Variable-depth traversals (find fraud rings ≤ 4 hops): SQL needs recursive self-joins that explode; adjacency-native storage walks edges in ~constant time per hop.

Object storage & the analytics split: S3, lakes, warehouses, columnar files

Why interviewers ask: every design with photos, videos, exports, or ML data needs the "files don't go in the database" move — and the follow-up "where do analysts query this?" checks you know the OLTP/OLAP split.

S3 semantics (and GCS/Azure Blob equivalents): a flat key → blob store with 11 nines of durability (objects erasure-coded across devices and zones — losing data is designed to be a once-per-10,000-years-per-10M-objects event) and, since 2020, strong read-after-write consistency (the old "eventual for overwrites" caveat is gone — worth saying, it's a common stale fact). Objects are immutable — "update" is a full replace; there are no appends, no partial writes. Big files go up via multipart upload (parallel 5 MB–5 GB parts, resumable). Latency is tens-of-ms to first byte with effectively unlimited aggregate throughput — a blob store, not a database: no queries, list operations are slow, and per-request cost means "millions of tiny objects" is the anti-pattern (batch or pack them).

When files beat rows: anything over a few hundred KB that's read as a unit — images, video, PDFs, backups, model weights. The pattern is always the same: the database keeps a metadata row (owner, size, content-type, S3 key), the blob lives in object storage, and clients transfer directly using presigned URLs — time-limited signed links so uploads/downloads bypass your servers entirely (your API signs, the client talks to S3, your bandwidth bill and latency both drop).

The OLTP/OLAP split: your row-store (Postgres) is built for many small transactions; analytics scans millions of rows per query and would flatten it. So operational data is replicated (CDC, nightly exports) into an analytics side: a data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift — schema-on-write, SQL, fast columnar scans) or a data lake (raw files in S3, schema-on-read, queried by Spark/Athena/Trino; table formats like Iceberg/Delta add transactions — the "lakehouse"). Both rest on columnar formats (Parquet, ORC): storing each column contiguously means a query touching 3 of 100 columns reads ~3% of the bytes, and same-typed runs compress 5–10×. Analogy: row store = filing cabinet of complete dossiers; column store = one binder per field — computing "average age" means flipping one thin binder, not every dossier.

OLTP (Postgres)Warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery)Lake (S3 + Parquet + Trino)
Unit of workSmall transactions, point readsScans/aggregations over millions of rowsSame, plus raw/semi-structured data
SchemaOn write, strictOn write, modeledOn read, flexible (Iceberg/Delta add ACID)
LayoutRow (B-tree pages)ColumnarColumnar files
Latencymssecondsseconds–minutes
Feeds fromthe appCDC / ETL out of OLTP — never analysts querying prod

Pitfalls

  • BLOBs in Postgres "for transactional safety" — backups balloon, vacuum crawls, cache is wasted; store the pointer, not the pixels.
  • Proxying file bytes through your API servers instead of presigning — you pay double bandwidth and turn app servers into file pipes.
  • Letting the BI tool point at the production primary — one analyst's SELECT * over a year of orders is a self-inflicted outage.
  • Millions of 2 KB objects in S3 — request costs and list latency dominate; pack small records into larger files (or use a database).
Interview questions
  • Design photo upload for 10M users — where do bytes flow? — Client asks API for a presigned PUT, uploads straight to S3 (multipart if large), S3 event or client callback confirms, DB stores metadata + key, CDN serves reads via signed URLs.
  • What does 11 nines of durability actually mean, and what doesn't it cover? — Probability of the store losing the object is astronomically low (erasure coding across zones); it does not cover you deleting it — versioning, object lock, and cross-region replication handle human error and region loss.
  • Why is Parquet so much faster for analytics than CSV or row pages? — Column pruning (read only referenced columns), predicate pushdown via min/max stats per chunk, and 5–10× compression on homogeneous columns — often 10–100× less I/O per query.
  • Warehouse or lake? — Warehouse: curated, SQL-first, BI dashboards, predictable schemas. Lake: raw + diverse data (logs, events, ML features), cheaper at PB scale, schema evolves; lakehouse formats blur the line. Many shops run lake → warehouse as bronze→gold.

Schema design for scale: denormalization, fan-out, soft deletes, online migrations

Why interviewers ask: schema choices are where "it worked in the demo" meets "the feed takes 4 seconds at 100M users". Fan-out direction and zero-downtime migration are two of the most reused patterns across all design questions.

Normalize until reads hurt. Normalization (one fact, one place) keeps writes cheap and consistent; at scale, hot read paths buy speed by denormalizing — storing derived copies: a like_count on the post instead of COUNT(*), the author's name embedded in the feed item. The contract you sign: every copy must be maintained (trigger, event, or batch), will drift, and needs a reconciliation story. Denormalize named read paths backed by numbers, not "for performance".

Fan-out on write vs read is the same trade at feature scale — the Twitter-feed classic. Fan-out on write (push): when Alice posts, insert the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed list — reads are O(1), writes are O(followers), and a 50M-follower celebrity means 50M inserts for one tweet. Fan-out on read (pull): store the post once; building a feed reads all followees' recent posts and merges — writes O(1), reads O(followees). The production answer is hybrid: push for normal users, pull-and-merge for celebrities. Rule of thumb: push when read:write ratio is high and audience per write is bounded.

Soft deletes (deleted_at timestamp instead of DELETE) preserve audit trails, undo, and referential sanity — at the cost of every query filtering WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (partial indexes help), unique constraints needing care (unique on email where not deleted), and GDPR requiring true erasure eventually. Migrations at scale never lock: big tables change via expand → migrate → contract: (1) add the new nullable column/table (instant, no lock — but beware ALTERs that rewrite: adding a column with a volatile default, changing types); (2) dual-write old + new from the app; (3) backfill history in throttled batches; (4) verify with checksums; (5) switch reads; (6) drop the old shape releases later. Tools: gh-ost/pt-online-schema-change for MySQL, careful CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY + batched updates for Postgres. The same choreography reshards databases and swaps datastores entirely.

Expand → migrate → contract (rename users.name → full_name, zero downtime)
1. ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text;        -- expand (nullable, no rewrite)
2. deploy: app writes BOTH name and full_name          -- dual-write
3. backfill: UPDATE ... WHERE full_name IS NULL LIMIT 10k, sleep, repeat
4. verify: counts + checksums old vs new
5. deploy: app reads full_name                          -- reads switch
6. later release: stop writing name; ALTER ... DROP COLUMN name   -- contract

Pitfalls

  • Backfilling at full speed — the UPDATE storm saturates the WAL and replication lag knocks out your read replicas; throttle and batch.
  • Dual-write without idempotency/ordering — retries interleave old and new writes; guard with upserts keyed on immutable IDs.
  • Counters via COUNT(*) on hot paths at scale — precompute; but naive UPDATE post SET likes=likes+1 serializes on one row (hot-row contention) — batch or shard the counter.
  • Soft deletes leaking through forgotten query paths — deleted users appearing in exports; centralize the filter (view or default scope).
Interview questions
  • Design the Twitter home timeline — push or pull? — Hybrid: fan-out on write into follower feed caches (Redis lists) for normal accounts; celebrities excluded and merged at read time. State the celebrity threshold and the merge.
  • How do you change a column type on a 2 TB table with zero downtime? — Expand-contract: new column, dual-write, throttled backfill, checksum verify, switch reads, contract. Never in-place ALTER that rewrites under lock.
  • Your denormalized like_count drifts from reality — what's the plan? — Expected: increments are lossy under retries/races. Reconcile with a periodic batch recount (or event-sourced rebuild); design consumers to tolerate small drift.
  • Why not just always normalize — the textbook says so? — The textbook optimizes writes and integrity; at 10k feed-reads/s a 6-way join per read costs more than maintaining a derived copy. Numbers, not doctrine, pick the point on the spectrum.

Choosing storage in the interview: three worked decisions

Why interviewers ask: the storage choice is where all your section-3 knowledge gets cashed in. The winning form is always the same: access patterns + numbers → store per data set → trade-off named aloud.

The 60-second script: (1) restate the access patterns with QPS and sizes from your estimation; (2) run the decision per data set — most systems end polyglot: relational core + cache + blob store, plus one specialist if a number demands it; (3) for each pick, name what you gave up and the mitigation. Below, the script applied to three interview staples.

URL shortenerChat (WhatsApp-scale)E-commerce orders
NumbersReads ≫ writes (100:1), ~200 B/row, billions of rows, key lookup only~1M msg/min writes, reads = recent slice per chat, append-only~1k orders/s peak, multi-row invariants (order+items+payment+stock)
Dominant accessGET code → urllast N messages of chat_idtxn on order; "my orders"; back-office queries
PickKV (DynamoDB/Redis-fronted); even sharded Postgres works — say why either is fineCassandra/Scylla: partition (chat_id, bucket), clustering sent_at DESCPostgres (sharded by user/tenant when numbers demand) or NewSQL at global scale
Cache/CDNRedis + CDN on hot codes (Zipf: tiny hot set, huge hit ratio)Recent messages per chat in Redis for open conversationsRead replicas for browse; cart in Redis
What you gave upAd-hoc queries (analytics via CDC to warehouse)Joins, ad-hoc queries; search needs ES sidecarWrite scale headroom — mitigated by sharding plan on tenant/user
Interview angle: notice that all three answers cite a number before naming a product, split data sets rather than picking "one database", and volunteer the sacrifice before the interviewer asks. That sequence — number, split, sacrifice — is the rubric's "justifies trade-offs" box, and it is entirely rehearsable.
Interview questions
  • "Why not Cassandra for the URL shortener too?" — It would work; but the workload (read-heavy, tiny rows, cacheable) is dominated by the cache layer, so the source of truth can be boring. Choose the simplest store the numbers permit.
  • "Your orders DB hits write limits — first move?" — Verify it's writes not indexes/locks; then shard by user_id (orders co-located), sagas for anything crossing shards, and revisit which indexes each write pays for.
  • "Where does search live in all three?" — A separate Elasticsearch fed by CDC/outbox — search is a projection, never the source of truth.
  • "What's the one number that changes the chat answer?" — Write volume. At 1k msgs/min, Postgres with partitioning is fine; at 1M/min, LSM wide-column is the honest answer. Same design method, different number, different store.

1. Why can an LSM-tree store (Cassandra, RocksDB) sustain much higher write throughput per node than a B-tree store?

b. The LSM write path is sequential-only: WAL append + sorted in-memory insert; SSTables are flushed sequentially later. A B-tree must find and rewrite pages in place (random I/O, splits). (a) is wrong — LSM stores keep a WAL precisely so the memtable can be recovered; (d) describes an unsafe cache, not an LSM: durability comes from the WAL, not shutdown flushes.

2. A Cassandra table's read latency degrades week over week although data volume is flat. Deletes run nightly. Most likely storage-level cause?

c. LSM deletes write tombstone markers that must be read past on every query until compaction purges them (after gc_grace_seconds) — heavy delete workloads create tombstone walls and even scan-abort errors. (a) misunderstands bloom filters (probabilistic, don't "fill up"); (d) is the wrong engine — Cassandra has no B-tree pages.

3. A user saves their profile, the app confirms, they refresh, and the old profile appears. Reads go to replicas, writes to the leader (async replication). What guarantee is missing, and the cheapest fix?

b. The write succeeded and is durable; the user just read a lagging replica — a read-your-writes (session) violation, fixable per-user with leader-pinning or LSN tokens. (a) works but throws away read scaling for every request to fix a per-session problem — the classic over-correction.

4. Postgres primary with async replicas; the primary's disk dies and a replica is promoted. Some orders confirmed to customers in the last seconds are gone. What was the actual engineering decision that caused this?

c. Async replication means "ack = durable on one node"; whatever hadn't streamed out dies with the primary. If those orders mattered, the design needed semi-sync (synchronous_standby_names, ack after 1 standby) — RPO=0 at the price of a follower RTT per commit. (b) matters too but even the best replica lacks the unshipped tail; (a) snapshots are far behind any replica.

5. Dynamo-style store, N=3. Which setting guarantees a read overlaps the latest successful write (no sloppy quorum in play)?

b. Overlap needs R+W>N: 2+2>3 ✓. (c) 1+2=3: the write might be on the one replica you didn't read. (d) 2+1=3: your single read can hit the one replica that missed the write. Note even (b) is quorum consistency, not linearizability — concurrent and partially-failed writes can still produce anomalies.

6. During a node outage, a Cassandra-style cluster keeps accepting writes via sloppy quorum + hinted handoff. What did the system trade away while hints are outstanding?

c. Substitute nodes aren't in the key's home replica set, so a quorum read of home replicas can miss the hinted writes — consistency was spent to buy write availability, the AP move. (a) is wrong: hints are stored durably on the substitute; (b) describes a strict quorum's behavior.

7. A cache tier maps keys to 10 nodes with hash(key) mod 10. You add an 11th node. Roughly what fraction of keys change owner — and with consistent hashing instead?

b. Under mod-N, a key stays only if hash mod 10 = hash mod 11 — about 1/11 of keys — so ~10/11 ≈ 91% move (a cache stampede on the origin). Consistent hashing moves only the arc the new node claims: ~1/N ≈ 9%. That asymmetry is the entire reason consistent hashing exists.

8. Orders are sharded by hash(user_id). A flash sale makes one seller's inventory row the write hotspot — one shard pegged, others idle. Best immediate mitigation for the hot write key?

c. A single logical key lives on one shard no matter how many shards exist — (a) doesn't help — and (b) caches reads while the pain is writes. Write-sharding the counter (suffix 0..k-1, sum on read) or batching reservations spreads the write load; hot keys are a per-key problem, not a capacity problem.

9. A user sees a comment, refreshes, and the comment is gone; a minute later it's back. No deletes occurred. Which consistency guarantee, if provided per session, would have prevented exactly this?

b. The refresh hit a replica lagging behind the one that served the first read — time ran backwards for this client. Monotonic reads (sticky replica routing or a last-seen-version token) forbids precisely that, far cheaper than (a). (c) is a different anomaly — it's about the reader's own writes, and this comment was someone else's; (d) is already true and prevented nothing.

10. In a payment flow you must guarantee that once the client is told "balance reserved", no subsequent read anywhere sees the unreserved balance. Which is the weakest model that suffices, and a system that provides it?

c. "Once anyone saw the new state, no one may see the old one, across all clients" is the definition of linearizability — single-copy behavior in real time. (b) causal only orders related operations for observers of the cause; an unrelated client could still read stale state. Session guarantees (d) protect one client, not "any subsequent read anywhere".

Practice

Shard a users + orders schema for 500M users

Your Postgres monolith holds users (500M rows) and orders (10B rows, 3k writes/s peak, growing). Design the sharded layout: shard key, routing, how "user's order history" and "login by email" work, hot-key handling, and what happens to cross-user analytics.

Covers: shard key choice · co-location · global indexes · scatter-gather

Hint 1

List the access patterns first: login (by email), profile (by user_id), order history (by user_id), place order (touches one user's data), analytics (all users). Which key makes the most frequent ones single-shard?

Hint 2

Co-locate orders with their user. Then only two patterns are not single-shard: email login and analytics. Each has a standard dedicated fix.

Solution

Shard key: user_id, hash-based, pre-split. Hash (not range — sequential IDs would hot-tail); pre-split into e.g. 4096 logical shards mapped to ~16–32 physical nodes via a directory, so scaling out = remapping logical shards, never rehashing. Route in a proxy layer (Vitess-style) or client library holding the shard map.

Co-location: orders is sharded by its user_id too, so "order history for user X" and order placement are single-shard, and an order+items+payment write is a local ACID transaction. This is the key design sentence to say aloud.

Login by email: a global lookup index — a small email → user_id table itself sharded by email (or kept in a KV store). Written at signup in the same saga as user creation, idempotently; uniqueness of email is enforced here, since per-shard unique constraints can't span shards.

Hot keys: whale accounts (a marketplace megaseller with 1M orders) skew their shard. Monitor top-K per shard; mitigations: their reads are cached; if one account's write volume dominates, sub-shard that account's orders by (user_id, month) or move the tenant to a dedicated shard via the directory.

Cross-shard queries: analytics and back-office search do NOT scatter-gather production shards — CDC (Debezium) streams every shard into a warehouse/Elasticsearch; ad-hoc queries live there. In-request cross-shard needs (rare) go scatter-gather with per-shard limits and merged pagination, accepting p99 = slowest shard.

Migration path: dual-write old monolith + shards, backfill by user_id range with throttling, checksum-verify, flip reads per-tenant percentage-wise, retire the monolith. Storage math sanity: 10B orders × ~1 KB ≈ 10 TB data (+ indexes ≈ 15–20 TB) over 32 nodes ≈ ~600 GB/node — comfortable.

Cassandra partition key for chat messages — why (chat_id, bucket)?

You store chat messages in Cassandra. A teammate proposes PRIMARY KEY (chat_id, sent_at). Group chats live for years; some have 50k messages/day. Explain what goes wrong, and design the correct key for "load the latest 50 messages, scroll back in time".

Covers: partition sizing · clustering order · bucketing · tombstones

Hint 1

With partition key = chat_id alone, where do five years of one busy group's messages live? How big is that partition?

Solution

The failure: partition key chat_id puts a chat's entire history in ONE partition on one replica set forever. A 50k-msg/day group at ~300 B/msg grows ~15 MB/day → 5+ GB/year, sailing past the ~100 MB guidance: unbalanced nodes, slow compactions, repair pain, and eventually unreadable partitions. Unbounded partition growth is the #1 Cassandra modeling error.

The fix — add a time bucket to the partition key:

PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id, bucket), sent_at)
WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC)
-- bucket = month for busy chats, e.g. 202609

Why it works: the composite partition key (chat_id, bucket) caps each partition at one month (~450 MB/mo is still too big for the 50k/day whale → use day or week buckets for those, or size the bucket to the p99 chat: the interview point is bucket size is derived from message-rate × row-size ≤ ~100 MB). Clustering by sent_at DESC makes "latest 50" a single-partition, already-sorted LIMIT 50 read. Scrolling back pages within the bucket, then steps to the previous bucket — the client walks buckets newest→oldest, usually 1–2 partitions per screen.

Bonus points: use timeuuid for sent_at (uniqueness under same-ms sends); TTL-based retention deletes whole partitions as buckets age out — which conveniently sidesteps tombstone walls that row-level deletes would create.

Estimation drill: a year of orders, with replication and snapshots

An e-commerce platform does 2M orders/day, average order row + items ≈ 2 KB. Storage runs with replication factor 3, daily snapshots retained 30 days, and you plan 2 years ahead. (a) Raw new data per year? (b) Total footprint after year 1 including replication and snapshots? (c) Async replication lag is 200 ms at p50 / 5 s at p99 — during peak (100 orders/s), how many orders can a freshly-promoted replica be missing?

Covers: storage arithmetic · replication overhead · snapshot retention · lag → RPO

Hint 1

2M/day × 2 KB — round to powers of ten and keep units visible: KB → GB → TB. Snapshots: what fraction of each daily snapshot is new bytes matters only if incremental; assume full snapshots first, then refine.

Solution

(a) Raw: 2M × 2 KB = 4 GB/day. × 365 ≈ 1.5 TB/year of primary data (add ~50% for indexes → ~2.2 TB logical).

(b) Footprint at end of year 1: live data ≈ 2.2 TB × RF 3 = ~6.6 TB on cluster disks. Snapshots: a full daily snapshot of ~2.2 TB × 30 retained = 66 TB if naive fulls — which is why nobody does fulls: with incremental snapshots you store one full (~2.2 TB) + 30 days of deltas (~4 GB/day × 1.5 ≈ 6 GB/day ≈ 0.2 TB) ≈ ~2.4 TB in object storage. Total ≈ 9 TB — and the interview point is showing the full-vs-incremental fork out loud. (2-year plan: ~13 TB cluster + snapshots; still one modest cluster — numbers argue against premature sharding.)

(c) Lag → potential loss (RPO): at 100 orders/s, p50 lag 200 ms ≈ 100 × 0.2 = ~20 orders in flight; p99 lag 5 s ≈ ~500 orders unshipped at the worst moment. If losing 500 confirmed orders in a failover is unacceptable, async is the wrong setting for this table: semi-sync (ack after 1 standby) makes RPO 0 for ~+1 RTT (<1–2 ms same-DC) per commit — cheap insurance, and exactly the trade to narrate.

Post-incident: reads are stale after last night's failover — what happened?

Overnight, the primary database was auto-failed-over. This morning: (1) some customers' recent orders are missing entirely; (2) a few customers see orders they had cancelled yesterday as active again; (3) for an hour after the failover, some app servers kept erroring on writes while others were fine. Reconstruct the mechanics behind each symptom.

Covers: async replication loss · divergence/rewind · stale topology & split brain risk

Hint 1

Symptom 1 is about what the promoted replica never received. Symptom 2 is subtler: the cancellation was received by whom, and who got promoted?

Hint 2

Symptom 3: after promotion, how do 40 app servers learn who the new primary is — and what happens to connection pools full of sockets to the old one?

Solution

(1) Missing orders — async replication tail loss. The primary acked writes after local commit only; the replica promoted at failover was seconds behind, and the unshipped WAL died with the primary (RPO > 0, realized). Fix: semi-sync for order-writing transactions, or accept and document the RPO with reconciliation from the payment provider's records.

(2) Cancelled orders back — divergence between replicas. The cancellations reached the OLD primary (and maybe one replica), but the PROMOTED replica was a different, more-lagged node — or the old primary briefly served after the new one took over. Promotion should pick the most-advanced replica (compare LSN/GTID); anything the old primary had beyond the promoted node's position must be rewound (pg_rewind) before it rejoins — replaying it would fork history. If both accepted writes simultaneously, that's split brain: fencing (STONITH, epoch/generation numbers checked per write) is the missing control.

(3) An hour of partial write errors — stale topology. App servers cached the old primary's address (DNS TTL, stale VIP, or long-lived pooled connections that never re-resolved). Servers that restarted or re-resolved found the new primary; the rest kept hitting a fenced/dead node. Fix: failover via a proxy layer (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy/Envoy) or service discovery with connection-pool invalidation on topology change — and health checks that verify writability, not just TCP.

Interview framing: one incident, three separate mechanisms — durability (RPO), consistency (divergence/fencing), and discovery (topology propagation). Naming all three layers is what "walk me through a failover" is really asking for.

⚡ Rapid-fire: storage one-liners

  • B-tree vs LSM in one line? — Update-in-place pages (read-optimized) vs append-and-compact (write-optimized).
  • What's a WAL for? — Sequential durable log fsynced before ack: crash recovery + feeds replication.
  • The three amplifications? — Write (bytes written per byte changed), read (structures checked per read), space (dead versions on disk).
  • Bloom filter's job in LSM? — Skip SSTables that definitely lack the key; false positives possible, false negatives never.
  • Tombstone? — LSM delete marker that persists (and slows reads) until compaction purges it.
  • Composite index (a,b): serves b alone? — No — leftmost-prefix rule.
  • Covering index? — Index containing all queried columns → index-only scan, no table hit.
  • Cost of each extra index? — One more structure updated (+ WAL) on every write.
  • Async vs semi-sync replication? — Ack locally (fast, can lose tail) vs ack after ≥1 follower (RPO 0, +1 RTT).
  • Read-your-writes fix in 5 words? — Pin reads to leader briefly (or LSN tokens).
  • Replication lag hides where? — Any replica read: profile "vanishing" edits, stale carts, monotonic-read violations.
  • Split brain prevention? — Fencing + epochs: old leader must be provably unable to accept writes.
  • Do replicas scale writes? — No — every replica applies every write; only reads scale.
  • Why is LWW dangerous? — Clock skew silently discards concurrent (even later) writes.
  • CRDT in one line? — Data type whose merge is commutative/associative/idempotent, so replicas converge without coordination.
  • Quorum rule? — R + W > N ⇒ read set intersects write set (strict quorums only).
  • Hinted handoff? — Substitute node stores a write "for" a down node and delivers it on recovery.
  • Read repair vs anti-entropy? — Fix stale replicas during reads (hot keys) vs background Merkle-tree sync (everything).
  • Why consistent hashing? — Node add/remove moves ~1/N of keys, vs ~all under mod-N.
  • Virtual nodes buy…? — Even load and rebalances spread across many nodes, plus weighting for big machines.
  • Celebrity/hot-key fixes? — Cache hot reads; suffix-shard hot writes; isolate whales; redesign fan-out.
  • Local vs global secondary index? — Per-shard (cheap writes, scatter reads) vs indexed-value-sharded (cheap reads, extra write hop).
  • When to shard, in numbers? — When write TPS or data outgrows one primary (~tens of k TPS / low TB) after replicas + partitioning.
  • CAP, correctly stated? — During a partition choose consistency or availability; P is not optional.
  • PACELC's addition? — Even without partitions, consistency costs latency on every operation.
  • Linearizability in one line? — The system behaves as one copy; reads respect real-time order.
  • 2PC's weakness? — Blocking: in-doubt participants hold locks if the coordinator dies.
  • Spanner's trick? — Paxos-replicated participants + TrueTime bounded clocks → external consistency (short commit-wait).
  • App-level alternative to 2PC? — Outbox + sagas: local transactions, async events, compensations.
  • Cassandra partition key rule? — Every query names it; bucket it so partitions stay ≤ ~100 MB.
  • Elasticsearch freshness? — Near-real-time: searchable after refresh (~1 s default); never the source of truth.
  • S3 consistency today? — Strong read-after-write (since 2020); durability 11 nines; objects immutable, multipart for big files.
  • Presigned URL? — Time-limited signed link letting clients hit object storage directly, bypassing your servers.
  • Why columnar for analytics? — Read only needed columns + 5–10× compression → 10–100× less I/O per scan.
  • Zero-downtime migration recipe? — Expand → dual-write → backfill (throttled) → verify → switch reads → contract.

4️⃣ Caching

Caching is the highest-leverage tool in system design — a 99% hit ratio turns a 100k-RPS problem into a 1k-RPS problem — and also the source of the hardest bugs you will be asked about: stale reads, stampedes, and flip-flopping data. This section walks the cache hierarchy top to bottom, then the patterns (cache-aside, write-through…), then the two classic failure modes (staleness races and thundering herds), then eviction, then Redis deep enough for a dedicated grilling. CDN internals live in section 2; the DB's own caching (buffer pool, memtables) in section 3 — here we own everything in between.

Why cache & where: the cache hierarchy and hit-ratio math

Why interviewers ask: "add a cache" is the reflex answer to every scaling question; the senior signal is knowing which layer to add it at, what each layer buys, and being able to do the hit-ratio arithmetic that says whether it actually saved you.

A request can be answered at six places before it touches disk, each roughly 10–100× slower than the last: browser cache (Cache-Control headers; 0 network, saves everything), CDN edge (~10–50 ms from the user, absorbs global read traffic — details in §2), gateway/reverse-proxy cache (nginx/Varnish in your DC, ~1 ms, shields all app instances for shared responses), app-local in-process cache (Caffeine/Guava HashMap-with-eviction, ~100 ns, no network hop, but per-instance and incoherent), distributed cache (Redis/Memcached, ~0.3–1 ms same-DC, shared by all instances, the workhorse layer), and finally the DB buffer pool (InnoDB/Postgres shared_buffers — the database caching its own pages in RAM, ~1–5 ms including query work; see §3). Only after all six misses do you pay a disk read.

Analogy: answering a question from memory, then your desk notes, then the office library, then ordering the book — each step is an order of magnitude slower, so you want the answer as close as possible. The design skill is matching data to layer: immutable static assets → browser+CDN with year-long TTLs; shared hot API responses → gateway or Redis; tiny ultra-hot config/feature flags → in-process; everything relational → at least the buffer pool, sized so the working set fits in RAM.

The arithmetic that justifies a cache: effective latency = hit_ratio × hit_latency + (1 − hit_ratio) × miss_latency, and origin load = total_RPS × (1 − hit_ratio). At 100k RPS with a 200 ms origin: 95% hits → 5,000 RPS to origin; 99% → 1,000 RPS. That last 4 points of hit ratio cuts origin load 5× — which is why hit ratio, not cache latency, is the metric you tune first. Note also what a cache does not fix: it helps p50 dramatically but your p99 is still the miss path (1% of requests at 200 ms), so you must size the origin for miss traffic, especially at cold start.

LayerTypical latencyScope / coherenceBest for
Browser0 (no network)Per user; only TTL expiry, no server-side purge of already-cached copiesStatic assets, immutable versioned URLs
CDN edge~10–50 msPer PoP; purge API, seconds to propagateImages, JS/CSS, cacheable API GETs
Gateway (nginx/Varnish)~1 msPer DC, shared across instancesHot shared responses, microcaching (1–5 s TTL)
In-process (Caffeine)~100 ns–1 µsPer instance — incoherent across fleetUltra-hot small data: config, flags, top-N
Distributed (Redis/Memcached)~0.3–1 msShared, single logical copySessions, computed views, DB offload — the default
DB buffer pool~1–5 ms (with query)Inside the DB, always onEverything — size it so the working set fits
Interview angle: when told "the product page is slow", walk the hierarchy out loud top-down and place the fix: "Is it cacheable per-user or shared? Shared and static → CDN. Shared and dynamic → Redis with a 60 s TTL takes the DB from 100k to 1k RPS…" Then quote the formula and compute origin load at the hit ratio you claim — interviewers upgrade you the moment arithmetic appears.

Pitfalls

  • Quoting cache latency as the win. The win is mostly origin load reduction; a 0.5 ms hit hardly matters if misses melt the DB.
  • Ignoring the cold-start problem: after a deploy or Redis flush, hit ratio is 0% and the origin sees full traffic — size origin for that, or warm the cache first.
  • Caching per-user data at a shared layer (CDN/gateway) — the classic "user A sees user B's cart" incident. Shared layers only for shared responses (or key by session explicitly).
  • Adding Redis while the DB buffer pool is thrashing. Sometimes the honest fix is more DB RAM, not another layer to keep consistent.
Interview questions
  • Your API does 50k RPS with a 100 ms DB query — walk me through adding caching. — Classify the response: shared or per-user, staleness tolerance. Shared + minutes of staleness OK → Redis cache-aside with TTL; compute the win: at 98% hits, DB sees 1k RPS and effective latency ≈ 0.98×1 ms + 0.02×100 ms ≈ 3 ms. Then name invalidation and stampede protection before the interviewer asks.
  • Hit ratio is 95%; is going to 99% worth engineering effort? — Yes when origin-bound: miss traffic drops 5× (5% → 1%), which may halve your DB fleet. The lever is usually TTL increase, better key design (fewer variants), or a larger cache — measure which misses dominate first (compulsory vs capacity vs invalidation misses).
  • What breaks first when the distributed cache dies? — The DB takes the full read load (20× normal at 95% hits) and usually collapses; then everything upstream times out. Mitigations: circuit breaker + degraded mode, request coalescing, cache replicas, and never sizing the DB assuming the cache exists ("cache as optimization, not load-bearing" — or accept it is load-bearing and make it HA).
  • Where would you cache personalized data? — Not at CDN/gateway (shared). Redis keyed by user (session, computed feed), or in a signed cookie/JWT if small and slow-changing. In-process only if you accept per-instance staleness.
  • Why is p99 barely improved after adding a cache with 99% hits? — p99 is dominated by the miss path: ~1% of requests miss and pay full origin latency, and p99 measures exactly the worst 1%. To fix p99 you must speed up misses (better DB) or hide them (refresh-ahead, serve-stale).
  • What's the DB buffer pool and why do you care? — The DB's own page cache in RAM (InnoDB buffer pool, Postgres shared_buffers + OS page cache). A "slow query" is often just a cold buffer pool; before adding external caches, check the working set fits — RAM at ~100 ns/page beats any network cache.

Caching patterns: cache-aside, read/write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead

Why interviewers ask: "how do you keep the cache and DB in sync?" has a different answer per pattern, and the follow-up "who owns consistency?" separates candidates who have run caches from those who have read about them.

Cache-aside (lazy loading) — the application owns everything: read → try cache → on miss, read DB, put into cache with TTL; write → write DB, then delete (not update) the cache key. It is the default in ~90% of systems: only requested data is cached, cache failure degrades to a slow system rather than a broken one, and the cache can be any dumb key-value store. Cost: every miss pays two trips (DB + cache put), first reads are cold, and the app carries the invalidation logic — with the races covered in the next card.

Read-through moves the miss logic into the cache layer: the app always asks the cache; the cache itself loads from the DB on miss (Caffeine's LoadingCache, DynamoDB DAX, a cache service with loaders). Same data flow as cache-aside, but the loader lives in one place — which enables per-key locking so concurrent misses trigger one DB load, your built-in stampede guard. Write-through is its write twin: writes go to the cache, which synchronously writes the DB before acking. Cache and DB never diverge and reads-after-writes hit warm data, but every write pays both latencies and you cache data that may never be read.

Write-behind (write-back) acks after writing the cache only, flushing to the DB asynchronously in batches. Massive write throughput (this is literally how CPU caches and the InnoDB buffer pool work) — but now the cache is the system of record for unflushed data: lose the cache node, lose committed-looking writes. Only acceptable with a replicated cache and for data that tolerates loss (metrics, view counters, like counts). Refresh-ahead is an optimization on any read pattern: for hot keys, asynchronously re-load shortly before TTL expiry, so hot readers never see a miss — p99 flattens at the price of some wasted refreshes. Analogy: cache-aside is fetching a book yourself when the shelf is empty; read-through is a librarian who fetches it for you; write-through is the librarian filing every new book immediately; write-behind is a pile on the desk filed "later" — fine until the desk catches fire.

PatternRead pathWrite pathConsistency ownerRisk / costUse when
Cache-asideapp: cache → miss → DB → putDB write, then cache deleteApplicationstale-window races, cold missesDefault; general read-mostly data
Read-throughcache loads from DB itself(pair with a write pattern)Cache layer/loaderneeds a smart cache; same staleness as asideLoader reuse + built-in single-flight (Caffeine, DAX)
Write-throughusually read-throughcache → sync DB write → ackCache layerwrite latency ×2; caches never-read dataRead-after-write correctness matters, moderate writes
Write-behindcachecache ack, async batched DB flushCache layer (buffered)data loss if cache dies before flush; reorderingCounters, metrics, absorbing write bursts
Refresh-aheadhit; async reload near expiry—Cache layerwasted refreshes on cold keysHot keys where p99 (miss spikes) matters
Interview angle: in a design, say the pattern and the owner in one breath: "Cache-aside on Redis, TTL 5 min, delete-on-write — the service owns invalidation; I'll protect the hot keys with single-flight." For a like-counter: "write-behind: INCR in Redis, flush aggregates to the DB every 10 s; losing 10 s of likes on a crash is acceptable, and I'd note that explicitly." Naming the acceptable loss is the senior move.

Pitfalls

  • Updating (SET) the cache on write instead of deleting: two concurrent writers can interleave DB-write and cache-SET in opposite orders, pinning a stale value until TTL — delete is race-tolerant, set is not.
  • Write-behind on data you cannot lose (orders, payments). If the interviewer hears "async flush" for money, the follow-up is always "and when Redis restarts?"
  • Choosing write-through "for consistency" but reading via a different path that bypasses the cache layer — you only get its guarantee if all reads and writes go through it.
  • Forgetting the TTL on cache-aside puts: a delete-based scheme with a missed delete (bug, crash between DB write and delete) then serves stale data forever. TTL is your backstop, always set one.
Interview questions
  • Why delete rather than update the cache on write? — Update races: writer A (v1) and B (v2) can hit the DB as v1→v2 but the cache as SET v2 → SET v1, pinning stale v1. Delete converges: worst case an extra miss. Also the new value may need data you don't have at the write site (rendered/joined view).
  • Cache-aside vs read-through — is there a real difference? — Data flow is identical; the difference is where the loader lives. Read-through centralizes it, enabling per-key locking (one DB load per concurrent miss) and consistent serialization. Cache-aside spreads loaders across call sites — flexible, but every site re-implements stampede control.
  • When is write-behind the right call? — High write rate + tolerance for bounded loss + values that aggregate (counters, telemetry, last-seen timestamps). Quantify the exposure: "flush every 5 s, replicated Redis → we lose ≤5 s of increments on simultaneous replica loss." Never for records of truth.
  • How does refresh-ahead differ from a longer TTL? — A longer TTL increases staleness; refresh-ahead keeps the TTL (staleness bound) but hides the miss by reloading early — freshness of a short TTL, p99 of a long one, at the cost of extra reads for keys that stay hot.
  • Your write-through cache acked but the DB write failed — what now? — The cache must roll back (delete the key) or the pair is inconsistent; strictly you need the cache write and DB write to be atomic, which they aren't across systems — so real write-through implementations write DB first or hold the entry invisible until DB acks. This is why cache-aside's "DB is always the source of truth" is easier to reason about.
  • Which pattern does DynamoDB DAX / Caffeine LoadingCache implement? — Read-through (+ write-through for DAX writes); Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite is refresh-ahead, and its loader gives per-key single-flight for free.

Invalidation & consistency: TTLs, races, and the delete-after-commit rules

Why interviewers ask: "there are only two hard things in computer science…" — this is the first one. Any candidate can add Redis; the deep-dive is "walk me through how a stale value gets into your cache and how long it stays there."

Cache and DB are two systems with no shared transaction — a mini two-generals problem: no ordering of {DB write, cache op} is atomic, and a crash or a concurrent reader between the two steps leaves them disagreeing. So you never aim for "always consistent"; you aim for a bounded, known staleness window and pick the tools that shrink it: TTL as the universal backstop (staleness ≤ TTL even when every other mechanism fails — tune per key class: seconds for prices, hours for profiles), explicit invalidation (delete the key when you write the DB) to shrink typical staleness to near zero, and event-driven invalidation — a consumer tails the DB's change stream (MySQL binlog / Postgres logical decoding via Debezium-style CDC) and deletes affected keys, which catches every writer including out-of-band updates, batch jobs, and other services, and cannot be skipped by an app crash after commit.

Explicit invalidation has a famous race, the read-repopulates-stale window: reader R misses the cache and reads v1 from the DB; writer W updates the DB to v2 and deletes the key; R (slow, GC pause, retried) then SETs v1 back into the cache — a value older than a completed delete now lives there until TTL. Orderings matter too: delete-then-write (delete cache, then write DB) is worse — any reader in between reloads the old DB value; hence the rule write DB first, commit, then delete. The residual race above is narrowed by delayed double delete: delete after commit, then delete the same key again ~500 ms later, killing whatever a straggling reader re-inserted. Alternatives that sidestep deletion entirely: versioned keys — write new data under product:42:v7 and flip the pointer/version the readers use, so stale entries are never served, just orphaned until TTL/eviction (this is also how CDN cache-busting via hashed asset URLs works).

Stale-while-revalidate reframes the problem: serve the expired value immediately and refresh it asynchronously in the background (HTTP's stale-while-revalidate directive; same idea in-process). Readers never block on a miss, staleness is bounded by expiry + refresh time, and it doubles as stampede protection. Analogy: a newspaper stand that hands you yesterday's paper the second you ask, while sending a runner for today's — nobody queues, and the paper is at most one edition old.

MechanismStaleness windowCatches out-of-band writes?Cost / complexity
TTL only≤ TTL (choose per key class)Yes (eventually)Trivial; stale up to full TTL
Delete-on-write (+TTL backstop)~0 normally; race window until TTLNo — only writers that remember to deleteLow; racy as shown above
Delayed double delete~0; race shrunk to ~delayNoLow; needs an async second delete
Versioned keys / cache busting~0 for readers of the new versionN/A (nothing overwritten)Medium; version pointer to manage, orphans until eviction
CDC / binlog-driven deletereplication+pipeline lag (~ms–s)Yes — every committed writeHigh; Debezium-style infra, but decouples all writers from cache logic
Stale-while-revalidateexpiry + refresh time, non-blockingVia whatever triggers revalidateLow–medium; readers may see one stale response
Interview angle: the phrase to say unprompted: "cache and DB have no shared transaction, so I bound staleness instead of eliminating it: delete after commit, delayed double delete for the read-repopulate race, TTL of 5 minutes as the backstop, and if other services also write this table, CDC-driven invalidation so the cache doesn't depend on every writer behaving." That sentence covers four follow-ups before they're asked.

Pitfalls

  • Delete-then-write ordering: deleting the cache before the DB commit invites any concurrent reader to reload and cache the old value — strictly worse than delete-after-commit.
  • Deleting inside the DB transaction: if the transaction rolls back you evicted for nothing (harmless) — but if you delete after the write yet before commit, a reader can cache the uncommitted value's predecessor… and if you delete after commit but the app crashes in between, the delete never happens. TTL backstop is non-negotiable.
  • No TTL because "we invalidate explicitly" — one missed code path (new batch job, manual SQL fix) and the cache is wrong forever.
  • Invalidating by SET-with-new-value from the writer: reintroduces the write-write race that delete avoids (see patterns card).
Interview questions
  • Why can't the cache update be in the DB transaction? — Redis isn't a participant in the DB's transaction; 2PC across DB+cache would serialize every write on the slowest party and still leaves in-doubt states. Standard answer: commit DB, then best-effort delete, TTL backstop; or a transactional outbox/CDC feed doing the delete reliably after commit.
  • Walk me through how a stale value survives a correct delete. — The read-repopulate race: reader loads v1 pre-write, writer commits v2 + deletes, reader then SETs v1. Fixes: delayed double delete, SETNX-style guards with version checks, versioned keys, or short TTL. (This is the animation above — be able to draw it.)
  • TTL: how do you pick it? — Business staleness tolerance first ("price wrong for how long is acceptable?"), then load: origin misses/s ≈ keys × (1/TTL) worst-case; longer TTL raises hit ratio and staleness together. Different TTL per key class, jittered (see stampede card), never one global constant.
  • What does CDC-based invalidation buy over app-side deletes? — Completeness (every committed write, from any service, batch job, or DBA) and crash-safety (the log survives an app dying post-commit). Costs: infra (Debezium/Kafka), ms-to-s lag, and ordering care when one key maps to many cache entries.
  • What is stale-while-revalidate and where is it native? — Serve expired content immediately, refresh async; native in HTTP caching (Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate=30, honored by CDNs) and in Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite. It converts miss latency spikes into bounded staleness — usually the right trade for read-heavy pages.
  • Two services cache the same entity differently — who is right? — Trick question: neither, both are caches; the DB is the source of truth. Real answer is to converge invalidation: shared CDC stream or a shared cache tier, and an explicit staleness SLO per consumer.

Cache stampede, penetration & avalanche — and the fixes

Why interviewers ask: "your hot key's TTL just expired at 100k RPS — what happens?" is a favorite because the naive cache design fails at exactly the moment it matters most, and the fixes (single-flight, jitter, negative caching) are cheap once you can name them.

Stampede / thundering herd / dogpile: a hot key expires; until someone repopulates it, every concurrent request misses and goes to the DB. At 10k RPS on that key with a 100 ms DB query, ~1,000 identical queries pile onto the DB in the first 100 ms — the DB slows, the recompute takes longer, more requests pile up: a self-amplifying spike from a single expiry. Fixes, cheapest first: per-key mutex / single-flight — the first misser takes a lock (in-process, or SET lock:key NX PX 3000 in Redis) and recomputes; everyone else either waits briefly or serves the just-expired stale value (Go's singleflight, Caffeine's per-key loading does this natively). Request coalescing is the same idea applied at proxies (nginx proxy_cache_lock, CDN origin shield collapses concurrent origin fetches). Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): each hit refreshes early with a probability that rises as expiry approaches (refresh when now − Δ·β·ln(rand()) ≥ expiry), so one lucky request renews the key before it ever expires — no lock, no herd.

Avalanche is the fleet-wide cousin: many keys expire at once (deploy warmed them together, or a Redis node restarts empty) and the aggregate miss rate crushes the DB. Fix: jittered TTLs (TTL = base ± random 10–20% so expiries spread), staged warm-up after restarts, and a circuit breaker so the DB degrades gracefully instead of dying. Penetration is different again: requests for keys that don't exist (bad IDs, or an attacker iterating them) always miss and always hit the DB — the cache can't help because there's nothing to cache. Fixes: negative caching (cache "not found" with a short TTL, e.g. 30–60 s) and a Bloom filter of all valid IDs in front of the cache — "definitely absent" answers skip the DB entirely, false positives (~1% at 10 bits/key) just fall through harmlessly. Analogy: stampede is everyone running to the kitchen the second the buffet tray empties — single-flight sends one waiter while everyone else keeps eating what's on their plate.

ProblemTriggerPrimary fixBackstops
Stampede (dogpile)Hot key expires under concurrent loadPer-key mutex / single-flight; serve stale meanwhileProbabilistic early refresh (XFetch), refresh-ahead, request coalescing at proxy/CDN
AvalancheMass simultaneous expiry or cold cache restartJittered TTLs (±10–20%)Staged warm-up, circuit breaker to DB, cache replicas/persistence
PenetrationQueries for nonexistent keys (bugs or attack)Negative caching (short-TTL "not found")Bloom filter of valid IDs, input validation, rate limiting
Interview angle: when you add a cache to any design, immediately volunteer: "hot keys get single-flight so an expiry sends one query, TTLs are jittered ±15% so a deploy doesn't synchronize expiries, and missing IDs are negative-cached for 30 s so a scanner can't turn my cache into a DB DDoS tool." Three sentences, three classic incidents pre-empted.

Pitfalls

  • A distributed lock with no expiry: the lock holder crashes mid-recompute and the key can never be refreshed. Always NX PX, and treat lock timeout as "someone else may also be computing" (idempotent SET, or check-and-set).
  • Waiting (blocking) behind the lock instead of serving stale: under load you've replaced a DB pile-up with a thread-pool pile-up. Serve-stale is almost always the right waiter behavior.
  • Negative caching with a long TTL: a newly created ID stays "not found" for the whole TTL — keep it to seconds, and delete the negative entry on create.
  • A Bloom filter you never rebuild: deletes aren't supported, so after churn its effective false-positive rate drifts — rebuild periodically or use a counting variant.
Interview questions
  • Hot key at 50k RPS expires; DB query takes 200 ms — quantify the damage. — 50k × 0.2 s = up to ~10,000 concurrent identical queries before the first completes; the DB's connection pool (say 100 conns) saturates, latency balloons, and unrelated queries starve. With single-flight: exactly 1 query, others serve stale for ≤200 ms.
  • Single-flight across many app instances — how? — In-process single-flight still lets N instances send N queries (often fine: 30 vs 10,000). For true global single-flight, a Redis lock (SET lock:key NX PX) or coalescing at a shared layer (gateway cache lock, origin shield). Name the trade-off: global lock = extra hop + lock liveness concerns.
  • How does probabilistic early refresh avoid both herd and lock? — Each request may refresh early with probability growing near expiry (XFetch: refresh if now − Δ·β·ln(rand()) ≥ expiry, Δ = recompute cost); statistically one request refreshes just-in-time, the key never actually expires, and there is no lock to manage — but it only protects keys that are being read; a key hot only in bursts can still expire cold.
  • Cache penetration vs stampede — difference in one line? — Stampede: real key, temporarily absent (expiry) → herd until repopulated. Penetration: key never exists → every request is a permanent miss; only negative caching or an existence filter helps.
  • Where does a Bloom filter sit and what are its numbers? — In front of cache/DB, holding all valid IDs: ~10 bits per key ≈ 1% false positives (120 MB for 100M IDs). "Absent" is definitive → reject without DB; "present" may be wrong 1% of the time → fall through normally. No deletes; rebuild on schedule.
  • Redis restarted empty during peak — what happens and what do you wish you'd built? — Avalanche: 100% miss rate, DB takes full load and likely tips over; cascading timeouts upstream. Wish list: Redis persistence/replica promotion (so it doesn't restart empty), warm-up from a snapshot before taking traffic, DB circuit breaker + load shedding, and per-endpoint serve-stale.

Eviction policies: LRU, LFU, TinyLFU — and sizing the cache

Why interviewers ask: "the cache is full — what gets thrown out?" tests whether you know caches are a bet on the future reference pattern, and the LRU-fails-on-scan story is a reliable depth probe.

Eviction is a prediction: which resident entry is least likely to be needed again? LRU (least recently used) bets on temporal locality — recently touched things get touched again. It's the default (a doubly-linked list + hashmap, O(1)) and usually right, but it has a famous failure: a one-off scan (batch export, crawler, full-table report) touches millions of keys once, and pure LRU dutifully evicts your entire hot working set to hold garbage that will never be read twice. LFU (least frequently used) bets on frequency instead — scan-resistant, but it hoards: a key hot last week keeps a high count and squats in the cache after going cold ("cache pollution"), and it needs aging to fix that. FIFO and random sound dumb but are cheap and nearly LRU-quality at large sizes — Redis actually implements approximated LRU/LFU by sampling (default 5) random keys and evicting the best candidate, because true LRU bookkeeping across millions of keys isn't worth the memory.

The modern answer is W-TinyLFU (Caffeine's policy): keep a tiny admission window (~1% of capacity, plain LRU) for new keys, and guard the main region with a frequency sketch — a count-min sketch that remembers approximate access counts in a few bits per entry, periodically halved so history ages out. A key evicted from the window is admitted to the main region only if its sketch frequency beats the frequency of the main region's eviction victim. Result: one-hit-wonders (scans!) die in the tiny window and never displace proven-hot entries — near-optimal hit ratios with ~zero per-entry overhead. Analogy: a nightclub with a small entry lounge and a doorman who only lets you into the main room if you've shown up more often than the person he'd have to kick out.

Sizing and measuring: size for the working set — the set of keys that gets, say, 95%+ of accesses (usually Zipf-distributed: a small fraction of keys takes most traffic) — not for the whole corpus. Then measure honestly: hit ratio = hits / (hits + misses) per key class and per time window, not one global lifetime number that hides a broken class behind a healthy one. Watch the eviction rate too: high evictions + high miss rate = capacity misses → grow the cache or fix admission; low evictions + high miss rate = compulsory or invalidation misses → a bigger cache won't help, fix TTLs/keys instead. That distinction — which kind of miss dominates — is the whole diagnosis skill.

PolicyBets onStrengthWeaknessSeen in
LRURecencySimple, O(1), right for most workloadsOne-off scans flush the hot setDefault everywhere; Redis approximates by sampling
LFUFrequencyScan-resistant, protects proven-hot keysStale hot keys squat without aging; heavier bookkeepingRedis allkeys-lfu (Morris counters + decay)
FIFO / RandomNothingTrivial, cheap, no metadata~5–15% worse hit ratio at small sizesMemcached slab reuse; Redis fallback
W-TinyLFURecency + frequency sketchScan-resistant AND recency-aware; near-optimalComplexity (sketch, window tuning)Caffeine (JVM), Ristretto (Go)
Interview angle: the story to tell: "we ran a nightly product export; every morning the first hour of traffic was slow. Pure LRU had evicted the hot set for scan garbage. Fixes: W-TinyLFU (admission control), or exclude the batch path from the cache entirely." Then the sizing math: Zipf traffic → caching 20% of the catalog often captures 90%+ of reads — never say "cache everything".

Pitfalls

  • Reporting one global lifetime hit ratio. A 92% overall can hide a 40% ratio on the endpoint that matters; slice by key class and time window.
  • Growing the cache to fix a miss rate caused by invalidation or short TTLs — capacity was never the problem; check eviction rate first.
  • Letting batch/analytics traffic share the online cache — either bypass the cache for scans or use an admission policy that filters them.
  • Assuming Redis LRU is exact: it samples maxmemory-samples (5) random keys per eviction — good enough, but "true LRU" answers lose points with a Redis-savvy interviewer.
Interview questions
  • Why does LRU fail on a table scan, and what fixes it? — A scan touches each key exactly once; LRU ranks "just touched" highest, so scan garbage evicts the hot set. Fixes: admission control (TinyLFU sketch — one-timers never enter the main region), a scan-bypass flag, or segmented LRU (probation vs protected segments, e.g. SLRU / Postgres's buffer-ring trick for seqscans).
  • How does W-TinyLFU decide admission? — New keys live in a ~1% LRU window; on window eviction, compare the candidate's approximate frequency (count-min sketch, periodically halved) with the main region's victim; higher frequency wins. The sketch costs a few bits/entry and ages, so old fame expires.
  • How big should the cache be? — Working set, not corpus: with Zipf-like access, find the fraction of keys covering your target hit ratio (often 10–20% of keys → 90–95% of reads). Compute bytes = keys × (value + key + ~50–100 B overhead), add 20–30% headroom, verify by plotting hit ratio vs size in a shadow test — it flattens where the working set ends.
  • Hit ratio is 85% and you want 95 — walk your diagnosis. — Classify the misses: compulsory (first access — warmup/refresh-ahead), capacity (evictions high — grow or better policy), invalidation/TTL (short TTL churn — retune), fragmentation of keys (per-user keys for shared data — normalize the key). Each has a different fix; growing RAM only fixes one of the four.
  • Which Redis eviction policy for a pure cache vs a cache with must-keep keys? — Pure cache: allkeys-lfu (or allkeys-lru). Mixed: volatile-lru/lfu evicts only keys with TTLs, so no-TTL keys are protected — but if everything has a TTL volatile-* can find nothing to evict and writes fail with OOM. Details in the Redis card.

Redis in depth: data structures, persistence, Cluster, and the sharp edges

Why interviewers ask: Redis shows up in nearly every design, so interviewers use it as a depth ladder: data-structure choice → persistence semantics → single-threaded implications → Cluster mechanics → hot/big key war stories. Each rung filters candidates.

Data structures are the point — Redis is not a string cache, it's a server of in-memory data structures with atomic operations. Sorted sets (skiplist + hashmap): ZADD leaderboard 9214 user:7, ZREVRANGE 0 9 for top-10, ZREVRANK for "your rank" — all O(log N), the canonical leaderboard/priority-queue answer. Hashes for objects (field-level updates without rewriting the value, memory-efficient via listpack for small sizes). Lists for simple queues (BRPOPLPUSH), Streams for real queues (consumer groups, acks, replay — a mini-Kafka). Sets for membership/intersection (mutual friends), HyperLogLog for unique counts in 12 KB with ~0.81% error (daily uniques over 100M users), Geo (sorted-set-encoded geohashes) for "drivers near me", bitmaps for per-user daily-active flags. Choosing the structure IS the design answer.

Persistence & what "cache vs store" really means: RDB forks and snapshots the dataset every N minutes — compact, fast restarts, but loses everything since the last snapshot. AOF appends every write command, fsync policy everysec by default → ≤1 s loss; always is durable-ish but slow. Common production setup: both, AOF for recovery, RDB for backups. But even AOF+replication is not a database-grade guarantee: replication is async, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes. Rule: Redis as a cache → persistence optional (warm restarts are the only benefit); Redis as a store (sessions, counters, queues) → AOF everysec + replicas, and accept the documented small-loss window — say this trade-off out loud.

Single-threaded model: one thread executes all commands (I/O threads since 6.0 only parse/write sockets) — that's why every command is atomic with zero locks, and why Redis still does ~100k+ ops/s/node: it's RAM-bound, not CPU-bound. Two consequences: a slow command (KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a 10M set, O(N) LRANGE) blocks everything — the classic self-inflicted outage; and network round-trips dominate latency, so pipelining (send N commands without waiting) turns 10k sequential ops at 0.5 ms RTT = 5 s into ~a few ms. Lua scripts / functions run atomically server-side (check-and-set logic, rate limiters); MULTI/EXEC queues commands and runs them atomically (no rollback — a failed command doesn't undo the others), with WATCH for optimistic CAS. Distributed locks (SET NX PX and the Redlock debate) are covered in section 5 with the other coordination primitives.

Scaling out: Replication + Sentinel = one primary (all writes), async replicas, Sentinels doing failure detection and automated promotion — HA for a dataset that fits one node. Redis Cluster = actual sharding: the keyspace is divided into 16,384 hash slots; a key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384; each primary owns a slot range. Smart clients cache the slot→node map and go straight to the right node; hit the wrong one and you get MOVED 12539 10.0.0.2:6379 — a redirect that also tells the client to refresh its map. Resharding moves slots live (keys migrate; mid-migration you may see ASK redirects for individual keys). Multi-key ops must stay in one slot — hash tags ({user:7}:cart, {user:7}:profile — only the braces part is hashed) co-locate related keys deliberately.
