Analogy: 16,384 numbered PO boxes distributed among post offices; your key's number is fixed by hashing, and a wrong office hands you a MOVED slip with the right address instead of forwarding the mail.

Sharp edges interviewers love: a hot key (one celebrity's counter) concentrates on one shard no matter how many nodes you add — fix by client-side caching of that key, read replicas, or key splitting (counter:{1..10}, sum on read). A big key (a 5M-member set) makes every operation on it slow and blocks the single thread, and deleting it synchronously can stall the node for seconds — use UNLINK (async free), SCAN-based incremental deletes, and design keys small. Memory eviction: maxmemory + policy — noeviction (default! writes fail at the limit), allkeys-lru/lfu for pure caches, volatile-* to evict only TTL'd keys — a "cache" left on noeviction becomes an outage at the limit.

# Leaderboard in four commands (sorted set, all O(log N))
ZADD lb:2026-09 9214 user:7042          # set/update score
ZINCRBY lb:2026-09 50 user:7042         # atomic increment
ZREVRANGE lb:2026-09 0 9 WITHSCORES     # top-10
ZREVRANK lb:2026-09 user:7042           # this user's rank (0-based)
# Cluster co-location: hash tags — only "{u:7042}" is hashed
GET {u:7042}:cart   GET {u:7042}:profile   # same slot → MGET/Lua allowed
DeploymentGives youDoesn't give youChoose when
Single nodeSimplicity, full command setHA, capacity beyond one boxDev, small non-critical caches
Replication + SentinelHA (auto-failover), read replicasSharding; sync durability (async repl can lose acked writes on failover)Data fits one node, you need failover
Redis ClusterSharding (16,384 slots) + per-shard replicas + failoverMulti-key ops across slots (need hash tags), some client simplicity, SELECT/db numbersDataset or throughput exceeds one node
Interview angle: upgrade every Redis mention with one internal detail: "sorted set — skiplist, so rank queries are O(log N) even at 50M members"; "I'll pipeline the 200 lookups: one RTT instead of 200"; "cluster mode, so the rate-limiter's Lua script needs hash-tagged keys to stay in one slot". And volunteer the failure story: "hot key goes to one shard — I'd split the counter into 10 subkeys and sum on read."

Pitfalls

  • KEYS * / SMEMBERS / DEL on big keys in production: O(N) on the single thread stalls every client. Use SCAN, SSCAN, UNLINK.
  • Treating Redis as durable because AOF is on: async replication means a failover can drop acked writes; everysec can drop ~1 s. Fine for sessions, not for money.
  • Default maxmemory-policy noeviction on a "cache": at the memory limit writes start failing instead of evicting — set allkeys-lfu explicitly.
  • MULTI/EXEC as a transaction with rollback: there is no rollback — runtime errors in one command leave the others applied. Use Lua for all-or-nothing logic.
  • Cross-slot multi-key commands in Cluster (MGET a b) fail with CROSSSLOT — design hash tags up front, not after the migration.
Interview questions
  • Design a leaderboard for 50M users — why Redis sorted sets? — Skiplist gives O(log N) insert/rank/range: top-K is ZREVRANGE 0 K-1, a user's rank is ZREVRANK — milliseconds at 50M, no SQL ORDER BY over 50M rows per request. Memory ~50M × ~100 B ≈ 5–6 GB: one node holds it; shard by season/region if not.
  • Why is single-threaded Redis so fast, and when does it stop being fast? — All data in RAM, no locks, event-loop I/O; the bottleneck is the network, not CPU. It stops being fast when a single O(N) command runs (blocks everyone), or when you need >1 node of CPU for small ops — then pipeline, split big keys, or go Cluster.
  • RDB vs AOF — and what do you run for a session store? — RDB: periodic fork+snapshot, loses minutes, fast restore. AOF: per-command log, everysec loses ≤1 s, bigger files, slower restore (AOF rewrite compacts). Session store: AOF everysec + a replica + Sentinel; state the residual loss window and that re-login is the fallback.
  • MOVED vs ASK? — MOVED: slot permanently reassigned — go there and update your slot map. ASK: slot mid-migration, this one key already moved — ask the target once (with ASKING), don't update the map. Confusing them breaks clients during resharding.
  • How do you find and fix a hot key? — Find: redis-cli --hotkeys (LFU mode), per-node QPS skew, MONITOR sampling. Fix: client-side/in-process cache of that key (ms TTL), read replicas for reads, or split writes across N subkeys and aggregate on read. Adding shards does nothing — one key lives on one shard.
  • Can you do multi-key atomic ops in Cluster? — Only same-slot: hash tags ({order:9}:items) force co-location, then MULTI/Lua work. Cross-slot atomicity doesn't exist — restructure keys or accept two-step with idempotency.
  • Sentinel vs Cluster in one line? — Sentinel: HA for an unsharded primary (monitor + failover vote). Cluster: sharding with built-in per-shard failover. Data > one node or throughput > one primary → Cluster; otherwise Sentinel is simpler.
  • Distributed lock in Redis? — SET lock val NX PX 30000, delete-if-owner via Lua. Single-instance is fine for efficiency locks (stampede control); for correctness locks Redlock is debated (Kleppmann's clock/GC objections) — prefer fencing tokens from a consensus store. Full treatment in section 5.

Memcached vs Redis vs in-process (Caffeine)

Why interviewers ask: "why Redis and not Memcached?" is a two-line answer most candidates fumble into "Redis is newer". The honest answer is that each wins a different column.

Memcached is a deliberately dumb, multithreaded byte cache: get/set/delete on strings, slab allocation, scales vertically across cores on one box (a big Memcached node can push millions of ops/s), client-side consistent hashing for distribution, nothing persisted, no replication. Redis trades some raw simplicity for data structures, atomic server-side operations, optional persistence, replication/failover, and Cluster. Caffeine (in-process) removes the network entirely — ~100 ns hits and zero serialization — at the price of per-instance capacity (it shares your JVM heap and GC) and no coherence across the fleet (see next card).

The honest decision rule: pure look-aside byte cache at extreme throughput on fat boxes → Memcached; anything needing structures, atomicity, persistence, or HA → Redis; ultra-hot small read-mostly data where nanoseconds or per-call cost matter → Caffeine in front of either. In practice most shops standardize on Redis for operational uniformity and add Caffeine as an L1.

MemcachedRedisCaffeine (in-process)
Data modelOpaque bytes, get/set/delete/incrStrings, hashes, lists, sets, zsets, streams, HLL, geo, bitmapsJava objects (no serialization)
ThreadingMultithreaded — one node uses all coresSingle command thread (+I/O threads ≥6.0)Caller's threads, lock-free reads
Latency (hit)~0.3–1 ms (network)~0.3–1 ms (network)~100 ns — 1000× less
Persistence / HANone — restart = empty; client rehash on node lossRDB/AOF; replicas, Sentinel, ClusterDies with the process
Scale-outClient-side consistent hashingRedis Cluster (16,384 slots), server-coordinatedOne per instance; no sharing
EvictionLRU per slab classConfigurable: LRU/LFU approx, volatile-*W-TinyLFU (near-optimal)
Memory efficiencySlab allocator — very low overhead, but slab-size wasteHigher per-key overhead (~50–90 B), rich encodings for small valuesHeap objects + GC pressure
Best atMassive flat KV throughput per nodeGeneral default: structures + atomicity + HAL1 for ultra-hot data; per-call nanoseconds
Interview angle: the crisp answer: "Memcached when I want a dumb, multithreaded look-aside cache and nothing else — it uses all cores of a big box, which single-threaded Redis won't. Redis when I want any structure, atomic ops, or survival across restarts. Caffeine as L1 in the service for the top-1000 keys. Default to Redis for ops uniformity." Facebook's Memcache paper (billions of gets/s look-aside tier) is the classic Memcached-at-scale citation.

Pitfalls

  • "Redis is always better" — a Memcached node saturates all cores; a Redis node saturates one command thread. For flat KV at extreme QPS per box, Memcached still wins.
  • Forgetting serialization cost in the Redis column: a 100 KB JSON blob costs (de)serialization + network per hit; Caffeine hands you the live object.
  • Using Caffeine for data that must be consistent across instances — that's the flip-flopping-reads bug in the next card.
Interview questions
  • When would you actually pick Memcached today? — A pure look-aside byte cache where per-node throughput and memory efficiency dominate and loss-on-restart is fine — e.g. an HTML-fragment cache in front of rendering, on fat multi-core boxes. No structures, no persistence needed.
  • Why is Caffeine "free" performance and what's the catch? — No network, no serialization, W-TinyLFU hit ratios: ~ns hits. Catch: N instances = N incoherent copies + N× memory + GC pressure, so it's for small hot read-mostly sets with tolerable staleness.
  • Two-level cache (Caffeine L1 + Redis L2) — how do reads/writes flow? — Read: L1 → L2 → DB, populating backwards. Write: DB → invalidate L2 → broadcast invalidation to all L1s (pub/sub). Short L1 TTL (seconds) bounds staleness even if the broadcast is missed.

Local caches behind a load balancer: coherence and the flip-flop bug

Why interviewers ask: "a user updates their profile and sees the old name on refresh, the new one on the next refresh, then the old one again — what's happening?" is a real-incident question with exactly one right diagnosis: incoherent per-instance caches behind a round-robin LB.

Put a Caffeine cache in each of 30 instances and every instance has its own copy with its own load time. A write updates the DB (and even Redis) but each instance's local copy expires on its own clock. A user whose requests round-robin across instances sees flip-flopping data: instance 7 has the new value, instance 12 still holds the old one, and consecutive refreshes disagree — worse than uniformly stale, because it looks broken rather than merely behind. Analogy: thirty receptionists each keeping their own sticky note of your address; you told one of them you moved, and which address the company uses depends on who picks up the phone.

Fixes in increasing strength: (1) short TTLs (1–10 s) — bound the disagreement window, often enough for config/flags; (2) pub/sub invalidation broadcast — writers publish the changed key on a Redis channel (PUBLISH cache-inv product:42); every instance subscribes and evicts locally, shrinking incoherence to milliseconds. Pub/sub is fire-and-forget (a disconnected subscriber misses messages), so keep the TTL as backstop — this is exactly the near-cache pattern that Hazelcast/Ignite/Redis client-side caching (RESP3 CLIENT TRACKING, server pushes invalidations for keys a client has read) productize; (3) version check — store a version/etag per key in Redis; instances serve the local copy only after a cheap version compare, trading a fast Redis GET per read for near-coherence; (4) don't cache locally — for anything where flip-flops are user-visible and harmful, Redis-only is the honest choice.

Also decide what is allowed in L1: shared, read-mostly, small, staleness-tolerant (catalog metadata, feature flags, top-N lists — yes); per-user or write-after-read data (cart, profile being edited — no, or session-affinity so the same user lands on the same instance's copy).

Coherence approachStaleness boundCostFailure mode
TTL onlyTTL (per instance, unsynchronized)ZeroFlip-flops for the whole TTL
Pub/sub invalidation + TTL backstop~ms after write (TTL if a message is missed)Channel + subscriber per instanceMissed messages during disconnects → rely on TTL
Version check per read~one Redis RTTRedis GET per read (loses most of L1's latency win, keeps deserialization win)Redis down → choose serve-local or fail
No local cache (Redis only)Single shared copy~0.5 ms per readNone of the above — the default for correctness-sensitive data
Interview angle: diagnose the flip-flop story in one sentence ("per-instance caches with independent expiry behind round-robin"), then fix it in one more: "pub/sub eviction broadcast with a 30 s TTL backstop — and the cart never goes in the local cache at all." Mentioning RESP3 client-side caching (the server tracks what each client read and pushes invalidations) marks you as current.

Pitfalls

  • Relying on pub/sub alone: Redis pub/sub has no delivery guarantee — an instance that was reconnecting missed the eviction and serves stale until… the TTL you hopefully kept.
  • Broadcasting the new value instead of an eviction: now every instance applies updates in possibly different orders — broadcast "evict key", let each instance reload.
  • Letting L1 hold per-user data "because it's hot": correct only with sticky sessions, and then you've coupled cache correctness to LB affinity.
  • Unbounded L1s: 30 instances × 2 GB of duplicated cache is 60 GB of heap that Redis would hold once — size L1 for the top keys only.
Interview questions
  • User sees old/new/old data on refreshes — walk the diagnosis. — Round-robin LB + per-instance caches with independent load times. Confirm by pinning to one instance (cookie) — flip-flop disappears. Fix: eviction broadcast + TTL backstop, or drop L1 for that data class.
  • Why broadcast evictions rather than updated values? — Value broadcasts race: two writes can arrive in different orders at different instances, permanently diverging copies. Evictions are idempotent and order-insensitive; each instance reloads the authoritative value on next use.
  • What is a near cache? — A small per-client L1 kept coherent by the L2/server pushing invalidations for exactly the entries that client holds (Hazelcast near cache, Redis RESP3 CLIENT TRACKING). Formalized version of the pub/sub pattern with per-client precision.
  • Is sticky-session routing a fix for cache coherence? — Partially: one user consistently sees one instance's copy, hiding flip-flops. But data is still stale cross-users, and stickiness costs LB flexibility and blast-radius (instance death = those users' state gone). Better as UX mitigation than as the coherence strategy.

What NOT to cache — and cache poisoning

Why interviewers ask: a candidate who caches everything is as junior as one who caches nothing. Knowing the categories that must not be cached — and that a shared cache is an attack surface — is cheap senior signal.

Don't cache: writes of record — the order, the payment, the inventory decrement are DB transactions, not cache entries; "cache the order and flush later" is write-behind on money (see patterns) and loses orders on a node death. Personalized-and-cheap — a per-user query that already runs in 2 ms from a warm buffer pool gains almost nothing (hit ratio per user is low, memory cost per user is high) and adds an invalidation problem; cache shared expensive things first. Auth decisions — caching "user X may access Y" turns every permission revocation into a security incident window; if you must (auth service at 100k RPS), keep TTLs of seconds, cache token validation (signature check results) rather than authorization grants, and provide a kill-switch purge. Also on the list: fast-moving counters used in decisions (available stock at checkout — reserve transactionally instead), and anything where the staleness conversation with product ends in "never".

Cache poisoning is the security flip-side of shared caches: if any unkeyed input (a header like X-Forwarded-Host, a query param the cache key ignores) can change the response, an attacker crafts one poisoned request and the cache serves the result to everyone until TTL — one request, thousands of victims. Related: web cache deception — tricking a CDN into caching a personalized page under a static-looking URL (/account/settings/style.css), exposing user A's data to whoever requests that URL. Defenses: cache key must include every input that affects the response (correct Vary), never cache responses with Set-Cookie/Authorization unless explicitly keyed per user, strict cacheable-content-type/path allowlists at the CDN, and short TTLs + fast purge as blast-radius control. Analogy: a shared cache is a communal whiteboard — anything anyone manages to write on it becomes everyone's truth until it's wiped.

Interview angle: after presenting a cache design, spend one sentence on the negative space: "orders and stock decrements never touch the cache path; permission checks are cached at most 30 s with purge-on-revoke; and the CDN key includes every header that can vary the response, so a poisoned variant can't fan out." That last clause answers the security follow-up before it's asked.

Pitfalls

  • Caching an authorization result for the session lifetime: revoked users keep access until logout — bound it in seconds and purge on revoke events.
  • CDN-caching any response that carries Set-Cookie — you may hand one user's session to many.
  • "We cache it because it's slow" applied to a query that's slow because it's wrong (missing index) — caching a bad query hides the bug and adds staleness.
  • Cache key narrower than the response's real inputs (locale, currency, device, A/B bucket) — users see each other's variants; the same bug class as poisoning, self-inflicted.
Interview questions
  • Would you cache inventory counts on a product page? — For display, yes (short TTL, "low stock" is approximate anyway). For the checkout decision, no — reserve stock in a transaction; the display cache must never be the thing that authorizes a sale.
  • How does a cache poisoning attack work end to end? — Find an unkeyed input that alters the response (e.g. a reflected header), send one request timed to land on a cache miss so the poisoned response is stored, and every user of that cache key gets it until TTL/purge. Defense: key on all varying inputs, validate/strip suspicious headers at the edge, short TTLs, fast purge.
  • Caching auth tokens vs auth decisions — difference? — Token validation (is this JWT signature valid, not expired) is deterministic on the token → safe to cache/memoize briefly. Authorization (may X do Y now) depends on mutable state (roles, revocations) → cache only seconds, with event-driven purge on revoke.
  • What's web cache deception? — Luring a victim to /account/style.css-style URLs so the CDN, keying on the static-looking path, caches the personalized account page publicly. Fix: only cache allowlisted static paths/types, and have the origin mark private pages Cache-Control: private, no-store.

Session storage: sticky vs external store vs stateless JWT

Why interviewers ask: "where do sessions live when you scale to 30 instances?" is the classic bridge from single-server to distributed thinking, and the JWT-revocation follow-up catches everyone who answered "stateless!" too fast.

Sticky sessions: session state stays in instance memory; the LB pins each user to one instance (cookie-based affinity). Zero extra infrastructure and the fastest reads — but an instance death logs out its users, deploys/scale-in shed state, autoscaling skews (old instances hoard sessions), and the LB must do L7 cookie inspection. Acceptable for small systems and as a latency optimization on top of an external store; as the only mechanism it's the thing you're expected to grow out of.

External session store (Redis via Spring Session, Memcached): instances are stateless; every request loads the session by cookie ID (~0.5 ms). Any instance serves any user, deploys and crashes are invisible, sessions get TTL-based expiry for free, and logout/revocation is a DEL. Costs: a Redis dependency on the hot path (make it HA — Sentinel/Cluster, see Redis card), and a serialization discipline (keep sessions small — a session that grows to 100 KB of cart+preferences is a big key and a bandwidth tax per request).

Stateless JWT: the session is the cookie — claims signed by the server, verified by signature on each request, no store lookup at all. Perfect horizontal scaling and cross-service auth (any service with the public key can verify). The catches: revocation — a stolen or logged-out token stays valid until exp, so you either keep tokens short-lived (5–15 min) with refresh tokens (whose store is… stateful again), or maintain a denylist checked per request (stateful again); size — claims ride on every request (keep < ~1 KB); secrets — key rotation needs kid headers and overlap windows; and claims are readable (base64, not encrypted) — never put PII/secrets in them. Analogy: sticky = your regular barber who remembers you (and retires with your history); Redis = a shared client file any barber can pull; JWT = you carry a signed card listing your haircut — nobody keeps a file, but a stolen card works until it expires.

Sticky sessionsExternal store (Redis)Stateless JWT
Instance dies / deployThose users logged outInvisibleInvisible
Per-request cost0 (local RAM)~0.5 ms Redis GETSignature verify (~µs) + payload bytes
Logout / revoke nowLocal deleteDEL — immediateNot until exp, unless denylist (re-stateful)
LB requirementL7 cookie affinityAnyAny
Cross-service authNoShared store accessYes — verify with public key
Scaling storyPoor (state gravity)Good; Redis is the scaling unitPerfect (no server state)
Interview angle: the balanced production answer: "short-lived JWT access token (10 min) for stateless verification everywhere + refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie backed by Redis — so routine requests hit no store, but logout/compromise revokes the refresh token and the exposure window is minutes. Pure sticky sessions only if we're two instances and shipping this week." Naming the exposure window is what makes it senior.

Pitfalls

  • "JWT = logout is impossible" and "JWT = fully solved" are both wrong: short expiry + revocable refresh tokens is the standard middle; a per-request denylist re-creates the session store you were avoiding.
  • Sticky sessions + autoscaling: scale-in kills sessions, and new instances get no traffic from pinned users — affinity fights elasticity.
  • Sessions ballooning in Redis (cart, view history, personalization stuffed in): per-request bandwidth tax and big-key trouble — store IDs in the session, data elsewhere.
  • JWTs in localStorage (XSS-readable) — HttpOnly cookies for browsers; and never skip signature verification "internally".
Interview questions
  • You move from 1 to 30 instances — what happens to login? — In-memory sessions break (each instance has its own). Options in order of preference: external Redis store (Spring Session is a drop-in), JWT if cross-service and scale demand it, sticky sessions only as a stopgap — then walk the revocation trade-off unprompted.
  • How do you revoke a JWT? — You can't revoke the signature; you bound it: short exp (minutes) + refresh-token rotation with server-side revocation, or a denylist of jti/session-version checked per request (cheap Redis SISMEMBER), or bump a per-user token-version claim and compare. State which you'd pick and why (usually short-exp + refresh).
  • Session store goes down — what do users experience and how do you soften it? — Every request 401s or errors: effectively a full outage. Soften: Redis HA with replica failover, client-side retry, degraded read-only mode for anonymous traffic, and (if acceptable) short-TTL local caching of recently seen sessions as an emergency shim.
  • Why are sticky sessions still used at all? — Zero infra, zero per-request latency, and they also help non-auth locality (warm local caches, WebSocket termination). Common hybrid: external store for correctness + affinity as a performance hint, so failover merely costs latency, not logouts.

1. Your service does 100k RPS through a cache with a 95% hit ratio; the origin query takes 200 ms. You improve the hit ratio to 99%. What happens to origin load?

c. Origin load = total × (1 − h): 100k × 5% = 5,000 RPS vs 100k × 1% = 1,000 RPS. The "4 percentage points" framing (a) hides the real lever — miss rate went from 5% to 1%, a 5× cut in the only traffic the origin sees. (d) inverts it: hit ratio is primarily an origin load story; latency p99 stays ≈ the miss path either way.

2. In cache-aside, why is the standard advice to delete the cache key on write rather than SET the new value?

b. With SET, writers A (v1) and B (v2) can commit to the DB as v1→v2 but reach the cache as SET v2 → SET v1: the cache now holds v1 until TTL with no further trigger to fix it. DEL is order-insensitive — worst case is an extra miss that reloads the committed value. (a), (d) are trivia-level non-reasons; (c) is backwards — you'd set a TTL anyway.

3. Which pattern is this: writes are acked after updating the cache only, and flushed to the database asynchronously in batches — and what is its defining risk?

c. Write-behind (write-back) makes the cache temporarily the only holder of committed-looking data — crash before flush = silent loss, which is why it's reserved for tolerant data (counters, metrics). (a) describes the synchronous twin, whose cost is latency, not loss. (b) and (d) are read-path patterns.

4. Reader R misses the cache and reads v1 from the DB, then pauses. Writer W updates the DB to v2 and deletes the cache key. R wakes and SETs v1. What state are you in, and which mitigation targets exactly this?

b. R's late SET lands after W's delete, so the cache holds v1 while the DB says v2 — and nothing else will fix it before TTL, because reads now hit the (stale) cache. The delayed second delete outlives any straggling reader and forces a fresh reload. (c): a SET on a deleted key just recreates it. (d): hits don't "repair" — that's the trap.

5. A hot key serving 20k RPS expires; the recompute takes 100 ms. With plain cache-aside, roughly how many identical origin queries launch, and what is the standard fix?

c. Every request during the 100 ms recompute window misses: 20,000/s × 0.1 s ≈ 2,000 concurrent identical queries — a stampede. Single-flight (per-key mutex, SET lock NX PX) sends exactly one; the rest serve the just-expired value. (a) is the naive assumption the race disproves; (b) replicas don't help — they all miss too; (d) trades a stampede for permanent staleness with no invalidation backstop.

6. Attackers hammer your API with random nonexistent product IDs and every request reaches the DB despite your cache. What is this called, and what fixes it?

a. Keys that don't exist can never hit — the cache is bypassed by construction. Caching the miss ("not found", TTL 30–60 s) stops repeats, and a Bloom filter answers "definitely absent" without touching the DB (~10 bits/key for 1% false positives). (b) is mass simultaneous expiry, (c) is one hot existing key, (d) is an attacker storing a bad response — different mechanism entirely.

7. A nightly batch export scans the full catalog through the service and every morning the cache hit ratio craters. Which eviction-policy reasoning is correct?

d. A scan touches millions of keys exactly once; pure LRU treats "just touched" as precious and flushes the real working set. W-TinyLFU admits a new key only if its sketch frequency beats the would-be victim's, so one-timers die in the small window. (a) is backwards — scan keys have frequency 1; (b) helps only until the scan exceeds the new size too; (c) random still evicts hot keys proportionally.

8. A Redis Cluster client sends GET user:7042 to a node that doesn't own the key's slot. What happens?

b. Cluster nodes never proxy (a) — the client is expected to be smart: MOVED = permanent reassignment, refresh your CRC16→slot→node map. (d) inverts the two redirects: ASK is the temporary, one-request redirect used mid-slot-migration and must NOT update the map. (c) CROSSSLOT is for multi-key commands spanning slots, not a single GET.

9. For a session store on Redis you enable AOF with appendfsync everysec and one async replica with Sentinel. Which durability statement is honest?

c. everysec fsyncs once per second (≤1 s loss window), and replication is async, so a failover can promote a replica missing acked writes. Users re-login: fine. Orders: not fine. (a) overstates — the ack does not wait for fsync at everysec; (b) understates — persistence exists, with documented windows; (d) reverses the two mechanisms' roles.

Practice

Design drill: product page at 100k RPS with a 200 ms origin

A retail product page serves 100k RPS globally. Rendering from origin takes 200 ms (DB + pricing service). Page = shared catalog data (title, images, description) + semi-dynamic data (price, updated up to every few minutes) + personalized data (cart badge, recommendations). Design the cache layers, state TTLs and invalidation per data class, and compute origin load and effective latency at 95% and 99% combined hit ratio. What protects you when a flash-sale price change lands on the hottest SKU?

Split the page by data class first; one cache policy per class, not per page.

Hint 1Immutable/shared → push to browser+CDN with long TTLs. Semi-dynamic shared → short-TTL Redis (or CDN with purge). Personalized → per-user fetch or Redis keyed by user; never a shared cache.
Hint 2Origin RPS = 100k × (1 − h). Effective latency ≈ h × t_hit + (1 − h) × 200 ms. The flash-sale question is a hot-key expiry — name the stampede control.
Solution 
Split the page (never cache "the page" as one unit):
  images/JS/CSS   → hashed URLs, CDN + browser, TTL 1 year, invalidate by new URL
  title/desc      → CDN + gateway, TTL 10 min, CDN purge on catalog edit
  price           → Redis cache-aside, TTL 60 s, delete-on-write + CDC backstop
  cart/recs       → per-user API, Redis keyed user:{id}, or client-side fetch; NOT CDN

Origin math (misses that reach render path):
  h = 95%: 100k × 0.05 = 5,000 RPS  → at 200 ms each ≈ 1,000 concurrent renders
  h = 99%: 100k × 0.01 = 1,000 RPS  → ≈ 200 concurrent renders (5× less fleet)
Effective latency (cache hit ~5 ms at edge/Redis):
  h = 95%: 0.95×5 + 0.05×200 ≈ 14.75 ms
  h = 99%: 0.99×5 + 0.01×200 ≈  6.95 ms   (p99 still ≈ 200 ms — the miss path)

Flash sale on the hottest SKU: price write → DB commit → delete price:sku (+ delayed double delete). The next instant, thousands of readers miss simultaneously → single-flight per key (SET lock:price:sku NX PX 2000), waiters serve the just-expired price for ≤ recompute time (~ms), one query recomputes. Jittered TTLs stop all SKUs of the sale expiring together (avalanche), and the pricing service sits behind a circuit breaker so a cache-layer failure degrades to slower pages, not a dead site. Bonus senior point: cold-start plan — after a deploy that flushes Redis, origin must survive ~100k RPS briefly, so warm the top-N SKUs from the previous cache snapshot before shifting traffic.

Leaderboard with Redis sorted sets: top-K and "your rank" at 50M users

Design a game leaderboard: 50M users, score updates at 20k writes/s at peak, queries are "global top-10", "my rank", and "10 players around me". Pick the data structure, write the exact commands, size the memory, and handle: monthly reset, ties, and what changes if one celebrity player's rank page is viewed 100k times/s.

Name complexity per operation; the follow-ups are resets, ties, and hot keys.

Hint 1One sorted set per period: lb:2026-09. ZADD/ZINCRBY for writes; ZREVRANGE / ZREVRANK / ZREVRANGE around rank for the three queries.
Hint 2Memory ≈ members × (id + score + skiplist/hash overhead ~100 B). Ties: encode a tiebreaker into the score's decimal part. Celebrity: the *read* is hot, not the write.
Solution 
Structure: one ZSET per season → monthly "reset" = new key lb:2026-10
  ZINCRBY lb:2026-09 120 user:7042        # score update, O(log N)
  ZREVRANGE lb:2026-09 0 9 WITHSCORES     # top-10, O(log N + 10)
  r = ZREVRANK lb:2026-09 user:7042       # my rank, O(log N)
  ZREVRANGE lb:2026-09 r-5 r+5            # 10 around me

Memory: 50M × ~100 B (8B score + member string + skiplist+dict overhead)
        ≈ 5 GB → one node OK; else shard by region/league, merge top-K
        (top-10 across S shards = ZREVRANGE 0 9 per shard, merge 10·S items)

Ties: score = points + (1 - ts/1e13) fraction → earlier scorer ranks first
      (or composite integer score: points * 2^20 + inverted-timestamp bits)

Writes: 20k/s of O(log 50M ≈ 26) ops — well within one Redis node (~100k op/s);
        pipeline batched updates from game servers.

Celebrity rank page at 100k reads/s: a hot key — one shard answers all of it regardless of cluster size. Cache the rendered rank snippet in-process (Caffeine, 1–2 s TTL) and/or serve rank from a periodically refreshed snapshot ("rank refreshes every 5 s" is a product decision that removes the problem). Old seasons: persist final standings to the DB, drop the ZSET. Mention that exact live rank for everyone at huge scale is usually relaxed to bucketed/approximate ranks — knowing when to degrade the requirement is the senior answer.

Debug: cache and DB disagree after a deploy

After a Friday deploy, support tickets say some product prices are wrong. The DB has the correct new prices (a bulk repricing job ran during the deploy window). Redis holds old prices for a subset of SKUs, TTL is 24 h, and the app does cache-aside with delete-on-write. Walk the mechanism that produced this, explain why it self-heals so slowly, and give the immediate fix plus three design changes that prevent recurrence.

Two plausible mechanisms exist — name both. "Restart Redis" is not an acceptable immediate fix.

Hint 1Mechanism 1: the repricing job wrote the DB directly — did it delete cache keys? Mechanism 2: deletes did happen, but in-flight readers repopulated old values (the read-repopulate race) at deploy scale.
Hint 2Why slow to heal: reads now HIT the stale cache, so nothing ever consults the DB again until the 24 h TTL. The fix must force misses for affected keys only.
Solution

Mechanism (either or both): (1) The bulk repricing job wrote the DB out-of-band — it never ran the app's delete-on-write path, so cached SKUs kept their old values. (2) Where deletes did fire, the deploy created a perfect storm for the read-repopulate race: instances draining during rollout held reads that loaded old prices pre-commit, then SET them after the job's deletes — stale values written after a correct invalidation. Both leave DB=new, cache=old.

Why it self-heals slowly: cache-aside reads stop at a hit. A stale hit generates no DB read and no correction — the stale entry is load-bearing until its 24 h TTL. High TTL = high hit ratio and long wrongness.

Immediate fix: targeted invalidation — replay the repricing job's SKU list and UNLINK price:{sku} for each (SCAN-based, rate-limited; never FLUSHALL — a full flush at peak = self-inflicted avalanche, 0% hit ratio into the DB).

Prevent recurrence: (1) CDC-driven invalidation — a Debezium-style consumer on the prices table deletes keys for every committed write, app-path or batch; no writer can forget. (2) Sane TTLs — prices at 24 h were indefensible; 1–5 min TTL bounds any future incident, jittered. (3) Delayed double delete around bulk jobs (second delete pass minutes after completion) to sweep race-reinserted values; and versioned keys (price:v{n}:{sku} with the version flipped after the job) if repricing is routine. Monitoring: an alert on cache-vs-DB sampled divergence would have caught this Friday, not Monday.

Estimation drill: memory to cache 20% of a 2 TB catalog

Your product catalog is 2 TB in the DB: 500M items averaging 4 KB each (per-item document after joins). Access is Zipf-like: analysis shows 20% of items get ~95% of reads. Size a Redis cache tier for that hot set (include overheads and headroom), decide node count with 64 GB usable per node, choose the eviction policy, and state what hit ratio you'd expect and how you'd verify the sizing.

Show the arithmetic line by line; round aggressively and say so.

Hint 1Hot set bytes = 500M × 20% × 4 KB, then add ~15–25% for key names + Redis per-key overhead, then 20–30% operating headroom.
Hint 2The right policy must resist scans and evict the coldest of the hot set as the working set drifts. What does Redis actually offer, and is its LRU exact?
Solution 
Hot set:        500M × 0.20 = 100M items
Payload:        100M × 4 KB = 400 GB
Overhead:       key (~30 B) + Redis entry overhead (~60–90 B) ≈ +100 B/item
                → ~10 GB — noise next to 4 KB values (≈ +2.5%)  → ~410 GB
Headroom:       ×1.25 (fragmentation, growth, replication buffers) ≈ 512 GB

Nodes:          512 GB ÷ 64 GB usable ≈ 8 primaries (Redis Cluster)
                + 8 replicas for HA → 16 nodes total
Expected hits:  ~95% by construction (the measured hot-set share) —
                minus invalidation/TTL churn; expect ~90–93% in practice.

Eviction policy: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu — a pure cache (evict anything), and LFU keeps the frequently-read core resident as the working set drifts, resisting scan-ish batch reads better than LRU. Note Redis LRU/LFU are approximate (samples maxmemory-samples keys). Never leave the default noeviction — at 512 GB the tier would stop accepting writes.

Verification: shadow-load production key traffic against a scaled-down node and plot hit ratio vs memory — the curve flattens where the true working set ends; if it flattens at 300 GB you've saved 4 nodes, if it's still climbing at 512 GB the 20%/95% analysis was optimistic. In steady state watch per-class hit ratio + eviction rate: rising evictions with falling hits = working set outgrew the tier (capacity misses) → add a shard; stable evictions with falling hits = invalidation churn → fix TTLs, not RAM.

⚡ Rapid-fire: caching

  • Effective latency formula? — h × t_hit + (1 − h) × t_miss.
  • Origin load at hit ratio h? — total RPS × (1 − h); 95%→99% cuts it 5×.
  • Cache hierarchy, fast to slow? — Browser → CDN → gateway → in-process → Redis → DB buffer pool → disk.
  • Typical latencies: in-process / Redis / same-DC RTT? — ~100 ns / ~0.5 ms / ~0.5 ms (Redis ≈ one RTT + µs of work).
  • Default caching pattern and its consistency owner? — Cache-aside; the application owns invalidation.
  • Why delete, not update, the cache on write? — Concurrent SETs can land out of order and pin stale data; deletes converge.
  • Write order for cache-aside writes? — DB write, commit, then cache delete (delete-first invites re-caching the old value).
  • Write-behind's defining risk? — Acked writes lost if the cache dies before the async flush.
  • Refresh-ahead in one line? — Reload hot keys just before expiry so readers never see the miss.
  • The read-repopulate race? — Reader loads old value, writer commits+deletes, reader SETs the old value back — stale until TTL.
  • Its cheap mitigation? — Delayed double delete (~500 ms after commit), plus a TTL backstop always.
  • What does CDC-driven invalidation uniquely catch? — Every committed write: batch jobs, other services, manual SQL — not just well-behaved app code.
  • Stale-while-revalidate? — Serve the expired value now, refresh async; native in HTTP Cache-Control and Caffeine refreshAfterWrite.
  • Stampede vs penetration vs avalanche? — Hot key expires (herd) / key never exists (cache useless) / many keys expire at once (mass miss).
  • Single-flight in Redis? — SET lock:key token NX PX ttl; one recomputes, others serve stale.
  • Bloom filter numbers? — ~10 bits/key ≈ 1% false positives; "absent" is definitive, no deletes.
  • Why does LRU fail on scans? — One-touch keys rank "most recent" and evict the hot working set.
  • W-TinyLFU's trick? — Small LRU admission window + frequency sketch: newcomers must out-score the eviction victim to enter.
  • Redis leaderboard commands? — ZADD/ZINCRBY to score, ZREVRANGE 0 9 for top-10, ZREVRANK for rank — O(log N).
  • Unique visitor count for 100M users in 12 KB? — HyperLogLog, ~0.81% error.
  • RDB vs AOF? — Periodic snapshot (loses minutes, fast restore) vs command log (everysec loses ≤1 s, bigger, slower restore).
  • Why is single-threaded Redis fast? — RAM-bound event loop, zero locking; commands are atomic by construction.
  • What blocks all of Redis? — Any O(N) command on a big structure: KEYS, SMEMBERS, sync DEL — use SCAN/UNLINK.
  • Pipelining buys what? — N commands in one round-trip: 10k ops at 0.5 ms RTT go from 5 s to ~ms.
  • Redis Cluster slot math? — CRC16(key) mod 16384; hash tags {…} hash only the braced part to co-locate keys.
  • MOVED vs ASK? — Permanent "update your slot map" vs one-request mid-migration redirect.
  • Sentinel vs Cluster? — Failover for one unsharded primary vs sharding with per-shard failover.
  • Hot key fix? — Client/local cache, read replicas, or split into N subkeys and aggregate — more shards won't help.
  • Big key fix? — Design them small; delete with UNLINK/SCAN, never sync DEL.
  • Dangerous default at maxmemory? — noeviction: writes fail; set allkeys-lfu/lru for caches.
  • MULTI/EXEC gotcha? — No rollback; failed commands don't undo the rest — use Lua for atomic logic.
  • Memcached beats Redis when? — Flat byte-cache at extreme per-node throughput: multithreaded, all cores, minimal overhead.
  • Flip-flopping reads behind an LB? — Incoherent per-instance caches; fix with pub/sub eviction broadcast + TTL backstop.
  • Why broadcast evictions, not values? — Value order can differ per instance and diverge forever; evictions are idempotent.
  • Never cache? — Writes of record, authorization grants (beyond seconds), cheap personalized data, checkout-deciding counters.
  • Cache poisoning defense in one line? — Key on every input that varies the response; never cache Set-Cookie responses unkeyed.
  • JWT revocation? — You can't unsign it: short exp + revocable refresh tokens (or a denylist — which is state again).
  • Sticky sessions' failure mode? — Instance death logs users out; affinity fights autoscaling.

5️⃣ Distributed Systems Core

Sections 3–4 gave you the building blocks — replication, quorums, consistency models. This section is about why those blocks are hard to compose: networks lie, clocks lie, and any node can pause or die halfway through anything. The path: first internalize why distributed systems are hard (fallacies, partial failure, impossibility results), then the machinery that tames them — logical time, consensus, coordination services, locks and fencing, idempotency, failure detection — and finally how real teams keep such systems honest in production. This is the section where interviewers separate "has drawn boxes" from "has been paged at 3am".

Why distributed systems are hard: fallacies, partial failure & impossibility

Why interviewers ask: every follow-up in a design interview — "what if this node dies mid-write?", "what if the ack is lost?" — is really testing whether you assume the network works. Candidates who design as if RPC were a local call fail those probes instantly.

The 8 fallacies of distributed computing (Deutsch/Gosling, Sun, 1990s) are the assumptions every distributed design silently makes until production breaks them: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous. The first three cause most outages: packets are dropped, reordered and duplicated; same-DC RTT is ~0.5ms but tail latency spikes 100×; a "quick" N+1 chatter pattern that is invisible in-process becomes seconds over the wire.

The deeper problem is partial failure. A single machine fails atomically — it is up or it is down. In a distributed system, node A can be alive while B is dead, or the link between them is dead, or B is alive-but-slow. Crucially, a timeout is ambiguous: when your call to the payment service times out, you cannot know whether the request was never received, received-and-crashed, or received-and-succeeded with the reply lost. Analogy: you text a friend "book the restaurant?" and get no reply — did the text fail, did they not see it, or did they book it and their reply got lost? Any action you take now risks either no booking or two bookings. That ambiguity is why retries need idempotency (below).

Gray failures are worse than crashes: a node that answers health checks but serves at 100× latency, drops 1% of packets, or has a dying disk. Detectors say "healthy", users say "down". Mature systems measure health from the client's perspective (success rate, latency percentiles) rather than only asking the server "are you alive?".

Two classic results bound what is possible. The Two Generals problem: two armies must attack together, coordinating only by messengers who may be captured — no finite number of acks-of-acks ever yields certainty that both sides agree, so perfect agreement over a lossy channel is impossible; real systems settle for high probability plus reconciliation. FLP impossibility (Fischer–Lynch–Paterson, 1985): in an asynchronous system (no bound on message delay) where even one node may crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee it always terminates — you cannot distinguish "crashed" from "slow". Practical consensus (Raft, Paxos) does not violate FLP; it sidesteps it with randomized timeouts and partial-synchrony assumptions, guaranteeing safety always and liveness whenever the network behaves for long enough.

FallacyWhat actually happensDesign consequence
Network is reliableDrops, duplicates, reordering, partitionsRetries + idempotency + timeouts everywhere
Latency is zero~0.5ms same-DC, 50–150ms cross-region, fat tailsBatch calls, cache, avoid chatty designs; budget the tail
Bandwidth is infiniteNICs and cross-AZ links saturate; egress costs moneyCompress, paginate, don't ship full objects on every hop
Topology doesn't changeAutoscaling, deploys, failovers reshuffle addresses constantlyService discovery + client re-resolution, not hardcoded hosts
Interview angle: when asked "what breaks first?", the senior move is to attack the timeout ambiguity: "The client times out but the write may have landed — so every mutating endpoint needs an idempotency story before we talk about scaling it." That single sentence shows you understand partial failure better than ten boxes on a whiteboard.

Pitfalls

  • Treating a timeout as "it failed". It means "I don't know" — the most dangerous three words in distributed systems.
  • Health checks that only test "process is up" miss gray failures; check real dependencies and measure from the caller's side.
  • Quoting FLP as "consensus is impossible". It is impossible to guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous model — real systems assume partial synchrony and work fine in practice.
  • Designing retry storms: naive retries on a slow dependency multiply its load exactly when it can least afford it — always pair retries with exponential backoff + jitter and a budget.
Interview questions
  • Your RPC to the order service timed out. What are the three possibilities? — Never arrived; arrived and failed; arrived and succeeded with the reply lost. Only idempotent retries are safe against the third.
  • Why can't two services ever agree "definitely committed" over a lossy network? — Two Generals: the last message might always be lost, so someone always acts without confirmation. You get probabilistic agreement plus reconciliation (e.g. settlement jobs), not certainty.
  • What is a gray failure and why do load balancers miss it? — Degraded-but-alive (slow disk, partial packet loss). LB health checks are binary and cheap; they pass while p99 explodes. Fix: outlier ejection based on observed error rate/latency.
  • If FLP says consensus can't always terminate, how does Raft work? — Raft is always safe; it only needs a period where timeouts hold (partial synchrony) to elect a leader and make progress. Randomized timeouts make livelock vanishingly unlikely.
  • How would you make a health check catch a node with a dying disk? — Deep health check that touches the disk/dependency path with a latency budget, plus client-side metrics (per-instance error rate) feeding outlier ejection.
  • Why are distributed bugs so hard to reproduce? — They depend on message ordering, timing and partial failures — a combinatorial space a unit test never explores. Hence property-based testing, fault injection and Jepsen-style checkers (testing card).

Time & ordering: physical clocks, Lamport, vector clocks, HLC

Why interviewers ask: "just use timestamps" is the most common wrong answer in distributed design — for conflict resolution, event ordering, and TTLs. Knowing why wall clocks can't order events, and what replaces them, is a hallmark senior signal.

Physical clocks drift. Commodity quartz drifts ~10–200 ppm — up to several seconds per day uncorrected. NTP disciplines clocks toward a reference but over the public internet typical error is 10–100ms, sync can step clocks backwards, and a misconfigured node can be off by minutes. So two nodes stamping events with System.currentTimeMillis() can easily disagree by more than the interval between two related events — meaning timestamp order ≠ real order. With last-write-wins (LWW) conflict resolution (see multi-leader replication), a genuinely newer write can carry an older timestamp and be silently discarded: data loss with no error anywhere.

Lamport's fix: stop asking "what time is it" and ask "what happened before what". Event A happened-before B if they're on the same node in that order, or A is the send and B the receive of a message, or transitively. A Lamport clock is one counter per node: increment on every local event; attach the counter to every message; on receive, set counter = max(local, received) + 1. Guarantee: if A → B (happened-before), then L(A) < L(B). The converse does not hold — two concurrent events also get ordered numbers, you just can't tell they were concurrent.

Vector clocks fix that: each node keeps a vector of counters, one slot per node, merged element-wise on receive. Now you can detect concurrency: if neither vector dominates the other, the writes conflicted and need resolution (Dynamo-style siblings). The cost: O(N) space per stamp, growing with the number of writers — which is why Dynamo/Riak prune them and Cassandra gave up and uses LWW timestamps (accepting the anomaly above). Analogy: Lamport is a single ticket-counter number — you know who was served first, not who queued independently. A vector clock is everyone's full stamp card — bulky, but you can see exactly who has seen whose work.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine both: a timestamp that tracks physical time when clocks agree, but carries a logical component that preserves happened-before when they don't — close to wall time, causally consistent, constant size. Used by CockroachDB and MongoDB. Spanner TrueTime is the hardware route: GPS + atomic clocks in every datacenter expose time as an interval [earliest, latest] with ε typically < 7ms; Spanner waits out the uncertainty ("commit wait") before making a transaction visible, buying external consistency (linearizable commit order) at the price of a few ms of latency and Google's infrastructure.

MechanismSizeGives youCannot doUsed by
Wall clock + NTP8 bytesHuman-readable time, TTLs, rough orderingOrder events across nodes (10–100ms error)Cassandra LWW (with known anomalies)
Lamport clock1 counterTotal order consistent with causalityDetect concurrency; relate to real timeTotal-order pieces of many protocols
Vector clockO(N) countersDetect concurrent (conflicting) writesStay small with many writersDynamo, Riak siblings
HLC~12 bytesCausality + close to wall time, constant sizeBound uncertainty without special hardwareCockroachDB, MongoDB
TrueTimeinterval [e,l]Bounded uncertainty (ε<7ms) → external consistencyExist without GPS/atomic clocks per DCGoogle Spanner (commit-wait)
Interview angle: in any multi-writer design, the moment you say "resolve conflicts by timestamp" expect: "whose timestamp?". The strong answer: "LWW with wall clocks can drop a causally newer write under skew; I'd use it only where losing an occasional concurrent update is acceptable (e.g. presence status), and use versioned writes (vector clocks/HLC) or single-writer-per-key partitioning where it isn't (e.g. cart, inventory)."

Pitfalls

  • Using timestamps as unique IDs or for cross-node ordering. Clocks step backwards on NTP correction; two nodes collide freely.
  • Believing Lamport L(A) < L(B) implies A caused B — it doesn't; the implication only runs the other way.
  • Vector clocks per key with client IDs in the vector grow unboundedly; prune or you'll store more clock than data.
  • Leap seconds and VM pauses: a "monotonic" duration measured with wall clock can be negative. Use System.nanoTime()-style monotonic clocks for durations, wall clocks only for points in time.
Interview questions
  • Why can't NTP-synced timestamps order events between two services? — NTP error (10–100ms WAN) exceeds typical event gaps; a later event can get an earlier stamp, and clocks can step backwards mid-run.
  • Lamport vs vector clocks in one line each? — Lamport: one counter, orders causally-related events, can't spot concurrency. Vector: N counters, additionally detects concurrent writes so you can surface conflicts.
  • How does Spanner get linearizable transactions across continents? — TrueTime exposes bounded clock uncertainty; commit waits out ε (<~7ms) before making a write visible, so timestamp order = real order.
  • Your dedupe logic keeps "the latest" record by timestamp and users report lost updates. Diagnosis? — Clock skew between writers: newer writes stamped older and discarded. Fix: HLC/sequence numbers, or route each key to a single writer.
  • What is happened-before, precisely? — The smallest partial order where same-node program order and message send→receive are ordered, closed under transitivity; events unordered by it are concurrent.
  • When is wall-clock LWW actually fine? — Low write concurrency per key, tolerance for losing one of two near-simultaneous updates, and a need for tiny metadata — e.g. last-seen presence, metrics gauges.

Leader election & consensus: Raft in plain English

Why interviewers ask: "who decides who the leader is?" sits underneath every HA design — failover, distributed locks, exactly-once Kafka, Kubernetes itself. You are rarely asked to implement Raft, but you must explain what it guarantees and where it hides in the systems you name.

Why consensus at all: replication (§3) needs one agreed leader per moment, and failover needs everyone to agree on the same new leader — otherwise two nodes both accept writes (split brain) and diverge. Consensus is the primitive that lets N nodes agree on a value (or a whole ordered log of values) despite crashes, as long as a majority is alive and talking: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Note the difference from Dynamo-style R/W quorums: those overlap reads with writes but do not by themselves give a single agreed order — consensus does.

Raft (2014, designed to be teachable) decomposes the problem. Time is divided into numbered terms; each term has at most one leader. Every node is follower, candidate, or leader. Followers expect heartbeats; if none arrives within a randomized election timeout (e.g. 150–300ms), the follower increments the term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and asks the rest for votes. A node grants one vote per term, first-come, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date as its own — this single rule is the heart of safety, guaranteeing an elected leader already holds every committed entry. If two candidates split the vote, nobody gets a majority; both time out with fresh random timeouts and one almost always wins the rerun — that randomness is Raft's practical answer to FLP.

Log replication: clients write to the leader; the leader appends the command to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers. Once a majority has persisted the entry, the leader advances its commit index, applies the entry to its state machine, and answers the client; followers learn the commit index on the next heartbeat and apply too. An entry acknowledged by a majority can never be lost: any future leader must win a majority, and majorities overlap, so at least one voter has the entry and the up-to-date rule forces the winner to have it. Analogy: a committee where any decision signed by a majority of members is binding — whoever chairs next must first collect a majority of signatures, and some signer will always be carrying the minute-book with that decision in it.

Relatives: Paxos (1989) is the original single-value consensus, famously hard to extend to a practical replicated log (Multi-Paxos ≈ what Raft specifies precisely); ZAB is Zookeeper's Raft-like atomic broadcast, predating Raft. Where consensus actually lives: etcd (Raft) under Kubernetes, Zookeeper (ZAB) under classic Kafka/HBase, Kafka KRaft mode replacing Zookeeper with its own Raft quorum, plus the control planes of Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, DynamoDB's metadata, Consul. You almost never build it: getting the edge cases (log truncation, membership change, snapshotting) right takes years — you rent consensus from etcd/Zookeeper via small leases and locks, and keep bulk data on cheaper replication.

ProtocolOne-linerWhere you meet it
PaxosThe original single-decision consensus; Multi-Paxos extends it to a log, famously under-specifiedChubby (Google), Spanner internals, academic questions
RaftMulti-Paxos re-designed for understandability: explicit leader, terms, log rulesetcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, Kafka KRaft, RabbitMQ quorum queues
ZABZookeeper's leader-based atomic broadcast; same guarantees family as RaftZookeeper (under classic Kafka, HBase, Solr)
Interview angle: the trap question is "why not run consensus across all 50 data nodes?". Answer: consensus costs a round-trip to a majority per write and degrades with cluster size and WAN latency; so real systems keep a tiny consensus group (3–5 voters) for metadata/leases/leadership, and use plain replication for bulk data. Kubernetes: 3-node etcd rules thousands of kubelets. Kafka: a small KRaft quorum rules hundreds of brokers.

Pitfalls

  • Even numbers of voters don't help: 4 nodes still tolerate only 1 failure (majority = 3) — run 3 or 5.
  • Reads from the leader are only linearizable if the leader confirms it is still leader (lease or read-index) — a deposed leader can serve stale reads.
  • Deploying a consensus trio across 2 datacenters: whichever DC has 1 node goes read-only when the link cuts; you need 3 failure domains.
  • Confusing Dynamo R/W quorums with consensus — overlapping quorums don't elect leaders or agree on an order (see §3 quorums).
Interview questions
  • Why randomized election timeouts? — To break symmetry: simultaneous candidates split the vote; random restart timers make one node retry first and win. This is Raft's practical dodge of FLP.
  • When is an entry "committed" in Raft, and why can't it be lost? — When the leader of its term has it on a majority. Any future leader needs a majority of votes; majorities intersect, and voters refuse candidates with less up-to-date logs.
  • A 5-node etcd cluster loses 3 nodes. What happens? — No majority: elections fail, writes (and linearizable reads) are refused. Data is safe; the cluster chooses consistency over availability (CP).
  • Why did Kafka move from Zookeeper to KRaft? — One system instead of two to operate; metadata as a Raft-replicated log scales to more partitions and makes controller failover much faster.
  • Can a client read stale data from a Raft system? — Yes, from followers (or an unconfirmed leader). Linearizable reads need leader read-index/lease; etcd offers serializable (possibly stale) reads as a cheaper option.
  • Would you ever implement Raft yourself? — Almost never: membership changes, snapshots and truncation edge cases take years to harden. Use etcd/Zookeeper for coordination, or a library (e.g. embedded raft in TiKV/Consul lineage) if it must be in-process.
  • Where is the consensus in a typical Kubernetes + Kafka + Postgres stack? — etcd (K8s control plane), KRaft or Zookeeper (Kafka metadata), and Patroni-style setups rent etcd/ZK consensus to elect the Postgres primary.

Coordination services: Zookeeper & etcd recipes

Why interviewers ask: "how do your 20 schedulers agree which one runs the nightly job?" The expected answer is not "implement Raft" but "use a coordination service correctly" — and knowing the recipes (and the blast radius) is the senior part.

A coordination service is a small, strongly consistent (consensus-replicated, CP) key-value store with two magic ingredients: sessions/leases and watches. Zookeeper models data as a tree of znodes; a client holds a heartbeat-maintained session, and ephemeral znodes vanish automatically when the session dies — presence with built-in cleanup. etcd (v3) is a flat keyspace with leases (TTL objects you attach keys to and keep alive) playing the same role. Watches push change notifications so clients don't poll.

The classic recipes: Leader election — everyone tries to create the same ephemeral node (or acquire the same lease-guarded key); the one that succeeds is leader; when its session dies the node vanishes and watchers race again (Zookeeper's sequential-node variant avoids the thundering herd by having each node watch only its predecessor). Service registry — each instance registers an ephemeral node under /services/payments/; consumers watch the directory and always see the live set. Distributed config / feature flags — write once, watchers everywhere converge in milliseconds. Distributed locks and fencing tokens — next card.

Analogy: a hotel front desk with a strict single ledger — you don't ask every guest who has room 5's key; the desk knows, and if a guest stops paying (session lapses), the key returns to the board automatically.

Why they must stay small: every write is a consensus round (majority ack, fsync) — think low thousands of writes/sec, values capped (etcd default request limit ~1.5MB, DB quota defaults ~2–8GB; Zookeeper znodes default max 1MB). They hold coordination state — leadership, membership, small config — never business data, queues, or metrics. And they are a blast-radius risk: everything depends on them, so an overloaded or misused coordination cluster takes the whole platform down (the classic outage: someone stores fat payloads or creates watch storms, etcd slows, Kubernetes controllers seize up). Mitigations: dedicated cluster per platform domain, quotas, client-side rate limits, and designing consumers to fail static — keep using the last-known config/membership when the coordinator is unreachable, rather than crashing.

Zookeeperetcd
ConsensusZABRaft
Data modelTree of znodes; ephemeral + sequential flavorsFlat KV + leases; MVCC revisions
Liveness primitiveSession (heartbeat) → ephemeral znodes vanishLease TTL, client keep-alive → attached keys vanish
Change notificationsOne-shot watches (must re-arm; can miss between)Streaming watches from a revision (no gaps)
Famous tenantsKafka (classic), HBase, SolrKubernetes, Rook; Consul is the Raft cousin with DNS/service-mesh features
Interview angle: for "design a cron/scheduler service", the crisp answer: "N schedulers, each campaigns for an etcd lease-guarded leader key; only the leader enqueues jobs; if it dies the lease lapses in ~10s and another wins. I'd also make job execution idempotent because leadership can briefly overlap with a paused old leader" — which tees up fencing tokens (next card).

Pitfalls

  • Storing business data (sessions, carts, queues) in Zookeeper/etcd — write throughput and size limits will end you; it's for coordination metadata only.
  • Herd effect: 500 clients watching one lock node all wake on release; use sequential nodes / watch-predecessor.
  • Session timeout tuning: too short → GC pause = false leader death and flapping; too long → slow failover. Typical 5–15s.
  • Treating "I hold an ephemeral node" as absolute truth — between your last heartbeat and now, the session may have expired. Act on leadership only with fencing.
Interview questions
  • How does ephemeral-node leader election work and what's the thundering-herd fix? — All create the same ephemeral znode; creator = leader; on session death it vanishes and watchers retry. Fix: ephemeral sequential nodes, each watching only its predecessor.
  • Why can't I use Redis as my service registry the same way? — Default Redis is a single AP-ish cache without consensus-backed sessions; entries don't reliably vanish when a holder dies, and failover can lose registrations. (Managed alternatives: Consul, Eureka, cloud-native discovery.)
  • What actually limits etcd/Zookeeper throughput? — Every write = consensus round: majority network RTT + fsync of the log. Order-of-thousands writes/sec, regardless of how big the machines are.
  • Kubernetes is "just" etcd plus controllers — what breaks if etcd is slow? — API server writes stall, controllers can't reconcile, leader leases lapse and flap. Running pods keep running (fail static) — the data plane outlives the control plane.
  • Zookeeper watch fired, then what? — It was one-shot: re-read the data AND re-arm the watch; design for missed intermediate states. etcd streaming watches from a revision avoid the gap.
  • How would you reduce the blast radius of a shared Zookeeper? — Separate ensembles per domain, quotas/ACLs, client rate limits, fail-static consumers, and observability on session churn + request latency.

Distributed locks: SETNX, Redlock & fencing tokens

Why interviewers ask: "only one worker may process this refund at a time" sounds like a mutex, and the naive Redis answer has a famous failure mode. Whether you know why TTL-based locks can't be trusted alone — and what a fencing token is — is a classic depth probe.

The standard recipe: SET lock:refund:42 <random-token> NX PX 10000 — set if not exists, with a TTL so a crashed holder can't lock the world forever. Release must be compare-and-delete (Lua: delete only if the value equals your token), otherwise you can delete a lock someone else now holds. This is fine as an efficiency lock (avoid duplicate work most of the time).

It is not a correctness lock, because of the TTL paradox: the TTL exists so the lock frees itself when a holder dies — but the lock service cannot tell "died" from "paused". A stop-the-world GC, a VM migration, a swapping host or a network stall can freeze the holder past the TTL; the lock expires, another client acquires it, and then the first client wakes up and keeps going, fully convinced it still holds the lock. Two writers, one resource. Raising the TTL just trades that risk for slower crash recovery.

Redlock (Redis's multi-node algorithm: acquire the lock on 3/5 independent Redis nodes within a drift budget) hardens against losing a single Redis, but Kleppmann's critique stands in one honest paragraph: Redlock still depends on bounded clock drift and bounded pauses — the exact assumptions the GC-pause scenario violates — so it cannot make a TTL lock safe against a paused-then-resumed holder either. Use Redlock if you want a sturdier efficiency lock; don't present it as a correctness guarantee.

The real fix is a fencing token: the lock service hands out a strictly monotonically increasing number with each grant (Zookeeper's zxid/czxid, etcd's revision, or a DB sequence), and the protected resource checks it — rejecting any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen. Now the stale holder's write bounces no matter how confused it is. Analogy: numbered deli tickets where the counter also refuses to serve ticket 33 after it has served 34 — a customer back from the bathroom can wave their old ticket all they like. Notice the requirement: the storage/downstream must be able to enforce the check (compare in a WHERE clause, conditional put, version column). If it can't, no lock protocol can save you. Alternatives: DB advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) — great when all workers already share one Postgres, since the lock dies with the session and the DB is the resource anyway; or best of all, redesign for idempotency — if processing the refund twice is harmless (upsert by refund id, conditional state transition WHERE status='PENDING'), you don't need the lock at all, and that is usually the strongest interview answer.

# efficiency lock (Redis)
SET lock:refund:42 8f3a-token NX PX 10000        # acquire, 10s TTL
# release: compare-and-delete via Lua (never plain DEL)
if GET lock:refund:42 == 8f3a-token then DEL lock:refund:42

# correctness: the RESOURCE enforces the fencing token
UPDATE refunds SET status='DONE', fence=34
 WHERE id=42 AND status='PENDING' AND fence < 34;   -- 0 rows → stale holder
OptionSafety under pausesWhen to use
Redis SETNX + TTLEfficiency only — stale holder can write after expiryDedup of cheap duplicate work; best-effort "one at a time"
Redlock (5 Redis nodes)Survives Redis node loss; still unsafe vs long pauses/clock jumpsSturdier efficiency lock; not a correctness proof
Zookeeper/etcd lock + fencing tokenSafe if the resource checks the tokenCorrectness-critical mutual exclusion
DB advisory / row lockSafe — lock and data share one transactional systemAll workers already share the DB; simplest correct option
Redesign: idempotent operationsNo lock to get wrongWhenever "do it twice safely" is achievable — prefer this

Pitfalls

  • Releasing with plain DEL: after your TTL expired, you delete the next holder's lock. Compare-and-delete with your random token.
  • Doing non-idempotent side effects (send email, call payment API) "under" a TTL lock — the external system can't check fencing tokens; you need idempotency keys there instead.
  • Extending TTLs with a watchdog thread — the watchdog freezes in the same GC pause as the work; it narrows but does not close the window.
  • Using a lock to serialize a hot path — you've built a 1-node bottleneck; partition the work by key instead so each key has one natural owner.
Interview questions
  • Why does a TTL make a distributed lock unsafe, when it's there for safety? — TTL frees locks of dead holders, but "dead" and "paused" are indistinguishable; a paused holder outliving its TTL resumes believing it holds the lock → two writers.
  • What is a fencing token, exactly? — A monotonically increasing number issued with each lock grant; the protected resource rejects writes with a token lower than the highest seen, neutralizing stale holders.
  • Give the one-paragraph honest take on Redlock. — It protects against Redis node failure by requiring a majority of independent Redises, but its safety still assumes bounded pauses and clock drift — Kleppmann's point — so it upgrades an efficiency lock, not to a correctness lock.
  • All my workers share one Postgres. Simplest correct mutual exclusion? — pg_advisory_lock (or SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the row): the lock lives and dies with the session in the same system that holds the data — no fencing needed.
  • When would you argue against any lock? — When the operation can be made idempotent or conditional (upsert, state-machine transition with WHERE guard, unique constraint): correctness moves into the data, and concurrency stops being scary.
  • Leader election is "just" a long-lived lock — same risks? — Yes: a deposed leader can act briefly after losing its lease. Same fix: epoch/fencing numbers on every action a leader takes (Raft terms are exactly this).

Idempotency & "exactly-once": keys, dedupe windows, upserts

Why interviewers ask: "the user clicked Pay once and was charged twice" is the single most common production war story, and "how do you prevent it?" appears in payment, ordering and messaging designs alike. The idempotency-key flow end-to-end is a must-know.

Because timeouts are ambiguous (fallacies card), every reliable client must retry — which means every mutating endpoint will receive duplicates. An operation is idempotent if doing it N times equals doing it once. Some operations are naturally idempotent: setting a value (status = 'PAID'), deleting by id, PUT-with-full-body. Others are not: incrementing, appending, "charge $50". The design move is either to reshape the operation into the natural kind (set an absolute value, upsert keyed by a deterministic id, guard with WHERE status='PENDING') or to bolt on an idempotency key.

The idempotency-key flow end-to-end: (1) the client generates a unique key per logical action — at button-click time, not per HTTP attempt — and sends it as a header (Idempotency-Key: 7f2c…, Stripe-style) on the first attempt and every retry. (2) The server, before executing, atomically claims the key (unique-constraint INSERT or Redis SET NX) storing status IN_PROGRESS. (3) It executes the operation and stores the response under the key. (4) A retry with the same key finds it: if DONE, replay the stored response; if IN_PROGRESS, return 409/wait — never execute twice. The claim and the business write should commit in one transaction where possible, so a crash between them can't strand a claimed-but-unexecuted key.

Dedupe windows: keys can't live forever, so they're kept with a TTL that must exceed the longest possible retry horizon (client retries + queue redelivery + human "click again tomorrow"? — pick consciously; 24–72h is common for payments). After the window, a duplicate becomes a new operation — which is why the key should also be derivable from business identity (order id + attempt) when true long-term dedupe matters, backed by a unique constraint on the business table itself.

"Exactly-once" honestly: exactly-once delivery is impossible over a lossy network — an ack can always be lost, forcing redelivery (Two Generals again). What is achievable is exactly-once processing (better: effectively-once): at-least-once delivery + deduplication/idempotency at the consumer, or atomically committing "the effect + the fact I processed offset N" in one transaction (Kafka read-process-write transactions, outbox pattern, or the consumer storing processed offsets in the same DB as the results). Analogy: the postal service may deliver the same letter twice, but you only act once because you check the reference number against your file before acting.

POST /v1/charges
Idempotency-Key: 7f2c9b1e-order-9182-attempt        # same on every retry

-- server side, atomically:
INSERT INTO idem_keys(key, status) VALUES ($1,'IN_PROGRESS');  -- unique → claim
-- duplicate key error → SELECT stored response (or 409 if IN_PROGRESS)
-- belt and braces: business-level uniqueness too
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT uq_payment UNIQUE(order_id, attempt_no);
LayerDedupe mechanismCatches
ClientOne key per action; disable button optimisticallyDouble-click, JS retry
Gateway / edgeShort-window key cache (e.g. Redis SETNX, minutes)Network-level retries, duplicate submits
HandlerIdempotency-key table, response replay, dedupe window 24h+All duplicate API attempts
DatabaseUnique constraints, conditional UPDATE (state machine)Everything above failing; race conditions
Consumer (async)Processed-ids table committed with the effect; or Kafka transactionsQueue redelivery (at-least-once)

Pitfalls

  • Generating the key per HTTP attempt (or server-side) — then retries carry different keys and dedupe nothing. It must identify the user action.
  • Checking "does key exist?" then inserting — TOCTOU race; two concurrent retries both pass the check. Claim must be one atomic write (unique constraint / SETNX).
  • Storing the key but not the response — the retry then returns 200 with an empty/different body, breaking clients that needed the original result.
  • Calling a non-idempotent third party (bank API) without passing their idempotency mechanism through — your dedupe protects your DB, not their ledger.
Interview questions
  • Why is exactly-once delivery impossible but exactly-once processing achievable? — Acks can be lost, so senders must redeliver (Two Generals). But the receiver can make duplicates harmless: dedupe by key, or commit effect + progress marker atomically. Duplicates arrive; effects apply once.
  • Where does the idempotency key come from and what makes a good one? — Client-generated at action time (UUID) or derived from business identity (order-id + attempt). Bad: timestamps, per-attempt UUIDs, anything the retry regenerates.
  • Setting vs incrementing — why does it matter? — SET balance=70 replayed is harmless; INCR balance BY 20 replayed corrupts. Prefer absolute writes, upserts and guarded state transitions; keep counters in append-only events dedup-able by id.
  • How long should the dedupe window be? — Longer than the maximum retry horizon across every layer (client backoff + gateway + queue redelivery + DLQ replay). Payments commonly 24–72h, plus a permanent unique constraint on business identity as the backstop.
  • Two concurrent requests arrive with the same key. What must happen? — Exactly one wins the atomic claim; the other sees IN_PROGRESS and waits or gets 409 Retry-After — it must NOT execute or immediately replay a half-baked response.
  • How does this interact with the outbox pattern? — Outbox gives at-least-once publishing (message written transactionally with the data, relayed later, maybe twice); consumers still need key-based dedupe — the two patterns are the producer and consumer halves of effectively-once.

Failure detection: heartbeats, phi accrual, gossip/SWIM & split brain

Why interviewers ask: "how does the cluster know a node is dead?" is the follow-up to every failover story — and the honest answer ("it can't know, it can only suspect") leads straight to quorums, fencing and the design of Cassandra/Consul-style membership.

The primitive is the heartbeat: "I'm alive" every T (or ping/ack on demand). The hard part is interpretation: a missed heartbeat means crashed, slow, or unreachable — you cannot tell which (FLP's shadow again). A fixed timeout is a blunt instrument: too short → false positives during GC pauses and load spikes (flapping, needless failovers); too long → minutes of downtime before anyone reacts. The phi accrual failure detector (Cassandra, Akka) replaces the binary verdict with suspicion: it models the historical distribution of heartbeat inter-arrival times and outputs φ, a continuously rising "how surprised am I" score; different subsystems act at different thresholds (stop routing reads at φ=5, evict at φ=10). Adaptive by construction — a normally-jittery network raises the bar.

Who watches whom? Central monitors don't scale and become SPOFs. Gossip protocols have each node exchange membership info with a few random peers per round; information spreads epidemically, reaching all N nodes in O(log N) rounds with constant per-node load. SWIM refines it: each round, ping one random member; on timeout, ask k other members to ping-req the target indirectly (distinguishing "node down" from "my link to it is bad"); still nothing → mark suspected and gossip that, giving the target time to refute with a higher incarnation number before it is declared dead. This is Serf/Consul's membership, memberlist, Cassandra's gossip cousin.

Split brain: a partition makes each side believe the other is dead; if both act (both elect a primary, both accept writes) you get divergence — the worst failure mode in stateful systems. The cure is never "better detection" (impossible) but quorum-based fencing: only the side holding a majority may act; the minority demotes itself to read-only or stops. Belt-and-braces in metal-era HA: STONITH ("shoot the other node in the head") — before promoting, power-fence the old primary via its management interface so it provably cannot write. Cloud equivalents: revoke the old leader's lease/credentials, detach its disk, or rely on fencing tokens (locks card).
