Interview angle: the trap is "we detect the primary is down and promote a replica". Probe: "detected by whom? What if it was a partition and the old primary still serves writers on its side?" The senior answer names the pieces: suspicion not certainty (phi accrual), a quorum decides (consensus service holds the leader lease), and the old primary is fenced — lease expiry stops it accepting writes, fencing tokens bounce anything in flight, STONITH if you're on metal.

Pitfalls

  • Aggressive timeouts "for fast failover" → flapping and failover storms under load spikes, which cause more downtime than they save.
  • Detection without fencing: promoting a new primary while the old one can still write is how you get two divergent databases.
  • Full-mesh heartbeating (everyone pings everyone) is O(N²) traffic — gossip/SWIM exists precisely to avoid it.
  • Forgetting the refutation path: without incarnation numbers, one slow node gets permanently evicted by a transient rumor.
Interview questions
  • Why can no failure detector be perfect? — Asynchronous networks make "crashed" and "slow" indistinguishable in finite time; any detector is either sometimes wrong (false positive) or sometimes late. You tune which error you prefer.
  • Phi accrual vs fixed timeout? — Fixed: binary verdict at an arbitrary threshold. Phi: continuous suspicion score from the observed heartbeat distribution — adaptive to network conditions, and different actions can trigger at different φ.
  • Why does SWIM probe indirectly before suspecting? — To rule out the prober's own link being the problem: k peers probe via independent paths, slashing false positives without longer timeouts.
  • How does gossip scale, concretely? — Constant fan-out per node per round; rumors reach N nodes in ~log₂(N) rounds. 1000 nodes ≈ 10 rounds ≈ a few seconds at 1 round/sec — with no coordinator to fail.
  • What prevents split brain in a 2-node primary/standby pair? — Nothing, inherently — 2 nodes have no majority. Add a third element: a quorum witness/tiebreaker, a consensus-held lease, or STONITH hardware fencing.
  • What is an incarnation number for? — A node's self-owned version counter: only the node itself can refute suspicion about itself, by gossiping a higher incarnation — preventing stale rumors from killing a live node.

HA topologies: active-passive vs active-active, RPO & RTO

Why interviewers ask: "what's your availability story?" must be answered with a topology, a failover mechanism, and two numbers — RPO (how much data you may lose) and RTO (how long you may be down). Vague "we have replicas" doesn't survive the follow-up.

Active-passive: one node/region serves writes; a standby replicates (see §3 leader–follower) and takes over on failure. Variants by warmth: cold (restore from backup — hours), warm (replica running, needs promotion — seconds-minutes), hot (synchronous replica, near-instant). Simple to reason about — one writer means no write conflicts — but the standby is paid-for idle capacity, and failover is a rare, scary, often-untested code path. Active-active: all nodes/regions serve traffic; capacity is fully used and "failover" is just weight-shifting — but if both sides accept writes to the same data you've bought multi-leader conflict resolution (§3). A very common middle path: active-active for stateless tiers + reads, single-writer (active-passive) per partition for the data tier.

Who decides to fail over? This is the consensus problem wearing an ops costume. Automatic promotion decided by one monitor = split-brain factory; the standard design (e.g. Patroni for Postgres) has candidates take a lease in etcd/ZK/Consul: the DB leader is whoever holds the consensus-backed lease, and losing it demotes you. Orchestrators (Redis Sentinel with its own quorum, MHA/Orchestrator for MySQL) follow the same shape: a majority of observers agrees before anyone promotes, and the old primary is fenced.

How traffic moves: within a subnet, a VIP (virtual IP / keepalived) or the load balancer's health checks flip in seconds. Across regions, DNS failover — but DNS TTLs are honored loosely (resolvers and apps cache; Java's default caching historically forever without networkaddress.cache.ttl), so budget minutes, not seconds; anycast/global load balancers (Route 53 health checks, GSLB, Cloudflare) narrow it. The two numbers: RPO (recovery point objective) = the data-loss window — with async replication it equals replication lag at crash time (could be seconds of committed-but-unshipped writes); sync replication buys RPO=0 for +1 RTT per commit. RTO (recovery time objective) = detection + decision + promotion + traffic switch + cache warm-up. Analogy: RPO is how much of your document you lose when the laptop dies (time since last autosave); RTO is how long until you're typing again on the spare.

TopologyRPORTOCost / complexityUse when
Backup + restore (cold)Hours (last backup)HoursCheapestDev, tolerable-loss internal tools
Active-passive, async replica (warm)Seconds (lag)30s–5min2× storage, idle standbyDefault for OLTP databases
Active-passive, sync replica (hot)0Seconds+1 RTT per commit; standby idleMoney paths where losing a committed write is unacceptable
Active-active, single-writer per partition0–seconds per partitionSeconds (shift weights)Routing complexityMulti-region serving with partitionable data (user-home-region)
Active-active multi-writer~0~0Conflict resolution foreverOnly when both regions must write the same data (rare; carts/CRDT-friendly data)
Interview angle: give numbers unprompted: "Async standby in a second AZ: RPO ≈ replication lag, call it <1s p99; RTO ≈ 30–60s — 10s detection (3 missed 3s health checks), lease-based promotion via etcd ~5s, VIP flip ~2s, plus connection re-establishment and cold caches. For checkout we'd pay the extra RTT for semi-sync so RPO=0." Then note the failover path must be exercised regularly (game days, testing card) — an untested failover is a second outage waiting.

Pitfalls

  • Advertising RPO=0 while running async replication — the lag at crash time IS lost data; only sync/semi-sync acks give zero.
  • DNS-based failover with optimistic TTL math: clients, JVMs and corporate resolvers cache past TTL; measure real convergence, assume minutes.
  • Failing over the database but not the things pointing at it: connection pools pinned to the old primary, hardcoded IPs, replicas replicating from a dead node.
  • Auto-failover with no fencing and no flap damping — a network blip triggers promotion, the old primary returns, and you have two primaries (see split brain).
Interview questions
  • Active-passive vs active-active — the one-line trade? — AP: simple single-writer semantics, idle capacity, real failover event. AA: full capacity use and near-zero RTO, but multi-writer data needs conflict resolution — so most AA designs keep a single writer per data partition.
  • Who should decide a failover and why not a monitoring box? — A quorum. One monitor partitioned from the primary would promote while the primary still serves — split brain. Lease in etcd/ZK (Patroni-style) or a sentinel quorum, plus fencing of the loser.
  • Walk me through the RTO budget of a Postgres failover. — Detect (health-check misses, ~10s) → quorum decision/lease expiry (~5–10s) → promote replica (replay remaining WAL, seconds) → repoint traffic (VIP seconds / DNS minutes) → warm caches (p99 elevated for minutes). Honest total: sub-minute switch, minutes to full performance.
  • When is RPO > 0 acceptable? — When the data is re-derivable or low-stakes (sessions, analytics events, caches) or the cost of sync replication (latency, availability coupling) exceeds the value of the tail writes. Never silently for financial ledgers.
  • How do you fail over across regions with stateful data? — Per-partition single writer with async cross-region replication; on region loss, promote partitions in the survivor (accepting RPO=lag), flip global LB/DNS, and reconcile when the region returns. Advertise degraded-writes honestly during the gap.
  • Why is the standby often broken exactly when needed? — It's an untested code path: config drift, expired credentials, undersized instance, stale replica. Cure: routine controlled failovers (game days) so failover is boring.

Delivery semantics between services: at-most / at-least / effectively-once

Why interviewers ask: every arrow between two boxes on your whiteboard has a delivery semantic, chosen by two knobs — when the sender stops retrying and when the receiver acks. Interviewers check you can name the semantic of each arrow you draw.

The semantics fall out mechanically. At-most-once: fire and forget — send, don't wait, never retry. Duplicates impossible, loss guaranteed eventually. At-least-once: retry until acked, and ack only after processing/persisting. Loss (practically) eliminated, duplicates guaranteed eventually — the ack that gets lost after successful processing forces a redelivery. "Exactly-once delivery" is impossible (Two Generals, fallacies card); what systems actually ship is effectively-once processing = at-least-once + dedupe/idempotency at the consumer (idempotency card) or transactional read-process-write (Kafka transactions, outbox + dedupe). The receiving side's ack timing matters just as much: ack-before-processing turns at-least-once transport into at-most-once processing (crash after ack = message gone).

SemanticSender behaviorReceiver ackCan loseCan duplicateUse for
At-most-onceSend once, no retryNone / immediateYesNoMetrics, logs, presence pings — where stale > retried
At-least-onceRetry with backoff until ackedAfter durable processingNo*YesDefault for anything that matters; pair with idempotent consumers
Effectively-onceRetry until ackedAfter processing, with dedupe/txnNo*Delivered yes, applied noPayments, orders, inventory — the real "exactly-once"

*within the broker's durability guarantees (e.g. Kafka acks=all + min.insync.replicas; SQS redrive to DLQ after max receives).

Interview angle: tie knobs to products: Kafka producer acks=0 ≈ at-most-once; acks=all + retries + enable.idempotence=true removes broker-side duplicates from producer retries; consumer semantics depend on when offsets are committed (commit-after-process = at-least-once; commit-before = at-most-once); end-to-end effectively-once = idempotent consumer or Kafka transactions. SQS standard = at-least-once; SQS FIFO adds 5-minute content/id dedupe — note that window, then your own key store takes over.

Pitfalls

  • Saying "we use Kafka so we get exactly-once" — Kafka transactions cover Kafka-in/Kafka-out topologies; the moment you write to an external DB or call an API, dedupe is on you.
  • Ack placement bugs: auto-ack/commit on receive silently converts your "reliable" pipeline to at-most-once processing.
  • Retrying without backoff/jitter into a struggling consumer — the retry storm outlasts the original incident.
Interview questions
  • Which two knobs define delivery semantics? — Sender retry policy and receiver ack timing. All three semantics are just settings of those two.
  • Why does at-least-once imply duplicates? — A lost ack after successful processing is indistinguishable from a lost message; the sender must resend, so the receiver sees it twice.
  • Your notification service may send the same push twice or drop one — which do you pick? — At-most-once (or short retry) — a duplicate "your order shipped" annoys less than a system built to dedupe pushes; for the order event itself, at-least-once + dedupe.
  • What does Kafka's idempotent producer actually dedupe? — Broker-side duplicates from producer retries (sequence numbers per partition). It does nothing about consumer-side reprocessing after a rebalance.
  • Where does the dedupe state live for effectively-once? — With the effect: processed-ids/offsets committed in the same transaction as the result, or an idempotency-key table in the target DB. State separate from the effect can desync.

Testing & operating distributed systems: chaos, Jepsen, game days

Why interviewers ask: a wrap-up favorite — "how do you know your failover/dedupe/replication actually works?" The senior answer is that you don't, until you test it in anger, on purpose, regularly.

Chaos engineering (Netflix's Chaos Monkey lineage): inject real faults into (eventually) production and verify the system holds a steady-state hypothesis — "kill 1 of 6 payment pods; p99 stays <300ms and error rate <0.1%". The discipline is scientific, not destructive: define steady state → hypothesize it survives fault X → inject with a minimal blast radius (one instance, one AZ, 1% of traffic) and an abort switch → widen only as confidence grows. Faults worth injecting, in rough order of yield: instance kill, dependency latency (+500ms on the DB), network partition, packet loss, disk full, clock skew, AZ evacuation. Tools: Chaos Monkey/ChaosKube (kill), Toxiproxy (latency/partition at the TCP proxy layer), AWS FIS, Gremlin, Litmus.

Jepsen in one paragraph: Kyle Kingsbury's framework (and blog series) that hammers a real database cluster with concurrent operations while injecting partitions, pauses and clock skew, records the full operation history, and checks it against the claimed consistency model (linearizability etc.) with the Knossos/Elle checkers. Its track record — finding lost writes, dirty reads and split-brain in etcd (early versions), MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Kafka, Redis-Redlock and dozens more — is why "has it been Jepsen-tested, and what did the report say?" is a legitimate database-selection question, and why you read a vendor's consistency claims with the report open.

Game days: scheduled fire drills for humans + systems — fail over the primary DB, evacuate an AZ, expire the TLS certs in staging, restore from backup with a stopwatch. They test what chaos tools can't: runbooks that have rotted, dashboards nobody can find, permissions the on-call doesn't have, and the RTO you claimed in the design review. Analogy: fire drills — the alarm hardware matters less than whether people know the exits. The operational trio to mention alongside: good observability (RED/USE metrics, tracing) so you can see the chaos land, runbooks updated by every drill, and blameless postmortems feeding fixes back.

Interview angle: close a design with one line: "I'd validate the failover path with quarterly game days and continuous small-blast chaos — kill one instance per service per day in staging, weekly dependency-latency injection — because the failover code path is the least-executed, highest-stakes code we own." That sentence lands harder than another cache tier.

Pitfalls

  • Chaos without observability or an abort switch — you learn nothing and might cause the outage you feared.
  • Only ever testing crash faults: gray failures (latency, partial packet loss) break more assumptions than clean kills.
  • Treating a Jepsen pass as permanent — results are per-version and per-configuration; defaults (e.g. write concerns) often differ from the tested setup.
Interview questions
  • What makes chaos engineering different from breaking things? — A steady-state hypothesis, minimal blast radius, an abort condition, and widening only with evidence — it's a controlled experiment, not vandalism.
  • What did Jepsen typically find, and what does that teach designers? — Systems violating their own consistency claims under partitions and clock skew (lost writes, stale reads, split brain). Lesson: trust measured behavior and explicit configs over marketing adjectives.
  • What does a game day catch that automated chaos doesn't? — Human/system integration: stale runbooks, missing permissions, unclear ownership, real restore times — the RTO is mostly people.
  • First three faults you'd inject into a new microservice? — Kill an instance (does the LB/retry mask it?), +500ms on its primary dependency (timeouts/bulkheads sized right?), and a full queue/DB-connection-pool exhaustion (backpressure or collapse?).

Your call to another service times out. What do you actually know?

A timeout is ambiguous: never-arrived, arrived-and-failed, or succeeded-with-lost-reply are indistinguishable. That's why (a) is the dangerous trap — retrying is only safe if the operation is idempotent — and why one timeout (d) is suspicion, not proof of death.

Two replicas use last-write-wins by wall-clock timestamp. Node B's clock runs 140ms behind. A user updates their cart on A, then 100ms later updates it again via B. After LWW merge, what happens?

B stamps the later write ~40ms earlier than A's stamp (100ms gap − 140ms skew), so max-timestamp keeps the older cart. LWW never errors or keeps siblings — that's (c)/(d) confusing it with vector-clock systems like Riak. Silent loss is precisely why "resolve by timestamp" needs the follow-up "whose clock?".

Lamport clocks give you L(A) < L(B). What can you conclude?

The guarantee runs one way: happened-before ⇒ smaller L. The converse (a) fails because concurrent events also receive ordered numbers. Detecting concurrency needs vector clocks; relating to wall time (d) needs synchronized physical clocks, which is the thing Lamport clocks exist to avoid.

In a 3-node Raft cluster, the leader appends an entry and gets an ack from one follower, then replies "committed" to the client and immediately crashes. Is the entry safe?

Leader + one follower = majority (2/3), which is Raft's commit condition — not all nodes (d). Any new leader needs a majority of votes; majorities overlap, and voters reject candidates whose logs are less up-to-date, so the winner provably holds the entry — no dependence on the crashed node (c).

Why do Raft nodes use randomized election timeouts?

If all followers timed out together, they'd repeatedly split the vote. Random timeouts mean one node usually campaigns first and wins. (b) is subtly wrong — FLP can't be "beaten"; randomness makes non-termination improbable, not impossible. Raft's ordering comes from terms and log rules, not clocks (c).

A worker holds a Redis lock (SETNX, TTL 10s), suffers a 25s GC pause, wakes, and writes to the protected resource. Another worker acquired the lock meanwhile. What actually prevents corruption?

Only the resource can stop a client that believes it holds the lock: it rejects writes with a token lower than the highest seen. Longer TTLs (a) just slow crash recovery and can still be outlived; Redlock (b) hardens against Redis failures, not client pauses; the watchdog (d) freezes in the same GC pause as the work.

Which operation is naturally idempotent — safe to blindly retry?

Setting an absolute value converges no matter how often it runs. Decrementing (a) compounds per retry — the classic double-charge shape; the keyless INSERT (c) duplicates rows (a unique business key would fix it); the email (d) is an external side effect needing its own dedupe key.

Why is exactly-once delivery impossible between two services over a network, even though effectively-once processing is achievable?

Two Generals: a lost ack means the sender either gives up (risking loss) or resends (risking duplicates) — delivery-count can't be exactly one. Processing can still be exactly-once-in-effect via consumer dedupe or atomic effect+offset commits. (d) is the marketing trap: Kafka's EOS is transactional processing within Kafka pipelines, not magic delivery.

In SWIM-style membership, node N1's direct ping to N3 times out. What does N1 do next, and why?

Indirect probes rule out N1's own link being the problem; suspicion (not a death sentence) plus incarnation-number refutation protects paused-but-alive nodes. Broadcast (a) is O(N) spam and trigger-happy; (b) causes divergent membership views; (c) just converts false positives into slow detection.

A payments database runs async replication to a warm standby with p99 replication lag of 2s. Marketing claims "zero data loss failover". What's the accurate statement?

Async means the primary acks before the standby has the bytes; whatever was in flight at crash time is gone — that window is the RPO. DNS caching (c) affects RTO (downtime), not data loss. (d) is nonsense: you can't fail over "before" losing data that never left the primary.

Practice

Design leader election for a scheduler on 3 nodes: DB lease vs etcd

A cron-style scheduler runs as 3 identical instances for HA, but exactly one should enqueue jobs at a time. The team already operates Postgres; there is no etcd/Zookeeper yet. Design leader election two ways — (a) a lease table in Postgres, (b) an etcd lease — and recommend one. Cover: acquisition, renewal, failover time, what happens during a GC pause on the leader, and what still requires idempotency.

Focus: leases, fencing, build-vs-rent for consensus · ~15 min whiteboard

Hint 1A lease is a lock with an expiry that must be actively renewed. In SQL, think one row + UPDATE … WHERE lease_until < now() OR holder = me, renewed every few seconds. What column gives you a fencing token for free?
Hint 2Both designs have the same hole: a leader paused past its lease keeps acting on stale belief. The question is not "which avoids it" but "which makes fencing and operations cheaper".
Solution

(a) Postgres lease table. One row: (name='scheduler', holder, lease_until, epoch). Acquire/renew in a single atomic statement:

UPDATE leases
   SET holder=$me, lease_until=now()+interval '10 seconds',
       epoch = epoch + (CASE WHEN holder=$me THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
 WHERE name='scheduler' AND (holder=$me OR lease_until < now())
 RETURNING epoch;   -- got a row → I am leader; epoch = fencing token

Renew every 3s; treat two consecutive failed renewals as "not leader — stop enqueueing". Failover time ≈ lease TTL + retry jitter ≈ 10–15s. Clock caveat: now() is evaluated on the DB server — one clock, so node skew doesn't matter; don't compare against app-server time. The epoch column is a free fencing token: stamp every enqueued job with it, and make the job store reject epochs lower than the highest seen.

(b) etcd lease. Campaign via a key guarded by a 10s lease with client keep-alives (etcd's election API packages this). Failover on lease lapse ≈ TTL. etcd's revision/election term is the fencing token. Watch-based notification means standbys learn instantly rather than polling.

GC-pause row (identical for both): a leader paused 30s loses the lease; another node wins; the old one wakes and enqueues stale jobs until its next renewal fails. Fencing epoch on writes + idempotent job enqueue (unique (job_id, scheduled_slot)) makes the overlap harmless — this is required in both designs, so "etcd is safer" is not by itself true.

Recommendation: Postgres lease. The team already operates it (the hard part of etcd is operating it); scheduler election is one tiny row with trivial load; the epoch column provides fencing; and the DB is likely where jobs live anyway, so lease + enqueue can share transactions. Introduce etcd only when several services need coordination (registry, config, many elections) — then the operational cost amortizes. Interview kicker: either way, say "correctness comes from the fencing epoch and idempotent enqueue, not from the election being perfect".

Two payments went through for one click — trace every layer that should have deduped

Incident: a customer clicked "Pay" once and was charged twice, 30 seconds apart. Path: browser → API gateway → order service → payment service → card processor, with the order service also consuming a "payment-completed" queue. List every layer where the duplicate could have been introduced AND the dedupe that layer should have had. Then state the minimal set of fixes you'd actually ship first.

Focus: idempotency end-to-end, retries, at-least-once queues · incident-review style

Hint 1Work the path hop by hop and ask at each: "who retries here, and on what evidence?" The 30s gap smells like a client- or gateway-level timeout retry, not a double click.
Hint 2Don't stop at your own services — the card processor accepts an idempotency reference too. And the queue consumer is a second, independent duplication source.
Solution
LayerHow it duplicatesDedupe it should have
BrowserDouble click; JS retry on timeout; user refresh + resubmitDisable button on submit; generate ONE idempotency key per checkout attempt and reuse it on retries
API gateway / LBAutomatic retry of timed-out POSTs (a 30s gap matches a gateway timeout + retry)Retry only idempotent methods, or forward the Idempotency-Key and short-window dedupe (Redis SETNX, ~minutes)
Order serviceIts own retry/hedging toward payment service; crash-and-rerun of a saga stepClaim the key atomically (unique INSERT) before calling payment; persist call-state so a rerun resumes, not repeats
Payment serviceProcesses two requests as two independent chargesIdempotency-key table with stored response replay + unique constraint on (order_id, attempt); conditional state machine WHERE status='PENDING'
Card processor callOur retry after its ambiguous timeout re-chargesPass the processor's idempotency reference (all major processors support one) so THEIR ledger dedupes
Payment-completed queueAt-least-once redelivery → order marked paid twice → double fulfilment (or a compensating flow re-triggering payment)Consumer processed-ids table committed atomically with the state change

Likely culprit for a single click + 30s gap: gateway or order-service timeout retry without a propagated idempotency key, hitting a payment service with no key store.

Minimal fixes to ship first: (1) unique constraint on payments(order_id, attempt) — one migration, stops the bleeding at the last line of defense; (2) idempotency key minted in the browser, propagated on every hop, claimed atomically in the payment service with response replay; (3) pass the processor's idempotency reference. Everything else is hardening. Also: an async reconciliation job comparing processor settlements vs internal ledger — because per Two Generals, some ambiguity always survives, and reconciliation is the backstop.

Design a distributed rate-limited counter across 5 nodes

Enforce "10,000 requests/min per API key" across 5 stateless gateway nodes behind round-robin LB. A naive teammate proposes: every request does INCR on a strongly consistent replicated counter and rejects at 10,000. Explain why exact global counting is a trap at this scale, then design something better. State the accuracy you actually guarantee.

Focus: coordination avoidance, why "exact" costs consensus, bounded error · classic Walmart-style probe

Hint 1What does each INCR cost if the counter is consensus-replicated? Multiply by peak RPS of a hot key. Then ask: what's the business cost of letting through request #10,050?
Hint 2Two families: centralize cheaply (single Redis, atomic Lua, no consensus) or decentralize with local budgets that sync asynchronously. What's the worst-case overshoot of each?
Solution

Why exact is a trap. A linearizable counter means every request pays a consensus round: majority RTT + fsync, and one Raft group serializes all increments for that key — a hot key at 10k/min is fine, but the same design at 10k/sec saturates a single consensus group, adds ~1–5ms to every request, and makes the rate limiter itself the availability bottleneck (limiter down → API down, for a feature whose whole job is protecting availability). And "exact" is fake precision anyway: requests in flight during the decision mean the boundary is always fuzzy.

Design A — central Redis, no consensus (good default): one Redis (or clustered by key) holding a fixed/sliding window per key, updated with an atomic Lua script (INCR + EXPIRE + check in one step, no TOCTOU). Cost: one ~0.3ms round trip per request; a single Redis does 100k+ ops/s. Failure policy is a choice: fail-open (protect availability, lose limiting) or fail-closed (protect the backend) — say it out loud. Accuracy: near-exact per window, modulo async replication on Redis failover.

Design B — local budgets + async sync (for the hot path): each of the 5 nodes gets budget 2,000/min (10,000 ÷ 5), enforced in-memory (token bucket, nanoseconds, zero network). Every ~1s, nodes report usage to Redis/gossip and rebalance unused budget. Skewed LB traffic wastes budget on cold nodes → borrow protocol or weighted split fixes most of it. Worst-case overshoot: 5 nodes × 1s sync interval × per-node peak rate — e.g. if a key can burst 500 rps/node, overshoot ≤ ~2,500 over the minute (~25%), tunable via sync interval.

What to guarantee: "approximately 10,000/min, overshoot bounded by (nodes × sync-interval × per-node rate), never more than 2× under partition" — and defend that: rate limiting is congestion control, not billing. If the counter is billing (paid quota), meter asynchronously from an event log with idempotent aggregation, and reconcile — never in the request path. The interview point: recognizing which counters need to be exact (money) and which need to be cheap (protection), and refusing to pay consensus prices for the latter.

Estimation drill: how much data does LWW lose under clock skew?

A two-region active-active user-profile store resolves conflicts with wall-clock LWW. Facts: 200 profile writes/sec globally; NTP keeps inter-region clock offset within ±50ms (assume a steady 50ms skew for the worst case); 0.5% of writes are "rapid pairs" — the same user writing twice within 100ms, with the second write landing on the other region (mobile/web race). Estimate: (a) how many writes/day are at risk of wrong-winner LWW, (b) the data-loss rate as a fraction of all writes, and (c) what skew budget would make losses negligible. Show arithmetic.

Focus: clock-skew window arithmetic, quantifying an anomaly instead of hand-waving · ~10 min

Hint 1A rapid pair resolves wrongly when the true gap between the two writes is smaller than the clock skew (second write gets an older stamp). If pair gaps are uniform in 0–100ms and skew is 50ms, what fraction of pairs flips?
Solution

(a) Writes at risk. Total: 200 × 86,400 ≈ 17.3M writes/day. Rapid pairs: 0.5% ≈ 86,400 pairs/day (conveniently, one per second). A pair flips when gap < skew: with gaps uniform over 0–100ms and skew 50ms, half flip → ≈ 43,000 wrong-winner merges/day. Each wrong merge silently discards one causally-newer write.

(b) Loss rate. 43,200 / 17.3M ≈ 0.25% of all writes — i.e. 1 in 400. That sounds small until you name it: tens of thousands of users per day whose latest edit reverts with no error logged. Support tickets say "the app forgot my change"; nothing in dashboards moves. This is why LWW loss is insidious: it's invisible to error-rate monitoring.

(c) Skew budget. Losses shrink with skew: at 5ms skew only pairs with gap < 5ms flip → 5/100 of pairs → 4,320/day (0.025%); at 1ms → ~860/day. To make cross-region losses truly negligible you need skew ≪ the minimum plausible write gap (~1ms), which public NTP can't promise across regions — that's PTP/TrueTime territory. So the realistic fixes are structural, not chronometric: (1) route each user's writes to a home region (single writer per key → skew irrelevant), (2) HLC or per-user version counters so causality, not wall time, picks winners, or (3) accept and detect: version vectors to surface conflicts for merge. In an interview, doing this 4-line arithmetic before proposing the fix is exactly the "quantify, then design" behavior the rubric rewards.

⚡ Rapid-fire: distributed systems one-liners

  • A timeout means? — "I don't know": failed, never arrived, or succeeded with the reply lost.
  • Two Generals in one line? — No finite acks-of-acks give certainty of agreement over a lossy link; settle for probability + reconciliation.
  • FLP in one line? — Fully-async consensus can't guarantee termination with even one possible crash; real systems assume partial synchrony + randomness.
  • Gray failure? — Alive to health checks, broken to users (slow disk, 1% packet loss); detect from the client's side.
  • Why can't timestamps order cross-node events? — NTP error (10–100ms) exceeds event gaps, and clocks step backwards.
  • Lamport clock rule? — Increment locally; on receive, max(local, received)+1. Causality ⇒ smaller L, not the converse.
  • Vector clock's superpower and cost? — Detects concurrent writes; O(N) metadata per stamp.
  • HLC? — Hybrid logical clock: wall-clock-close, causality-safe, constant size (CockroachDB, MongoDB).
  • TrueTime? — Time as a bounded interval (GPS+atomic); Spanner waits out the uncertainty before commit is visible.
  • Raft term? — A logical epoch with at most one leader; higher term always wins an argument.
  • When is a Raft entry committed? — On a majority of nodes via the current term's leader — then it can never be lost.
  • Split vote fix? — Randomized election timeouts; someone times out first and wins the rerun.
  • Why 3 or 5 voters, never 4? — 4 nodes still tolerate only 1 failure (majority 3); even numbers add cost, not tolerance.
  • Quorum (Dynamo) vs consensus? — Overlapping R/W sets vs an agreed single order + leader; overlap alone doesn't serialize.
  • Where does consensus hide in your stack? — etcd under Kubernetes, ZK/KRaft under Kafka, Patroni's DB leader lease, Consul.
  • Ephemeral znode / etcd lease? — Key that vanishes when its owner's session/lease dies — presence with automatic cleanup.
  • Why keep coordination services tiny? — Every write is a consensus round; and they're the blast radius for everything above them.
  • Why is a TTL lock unsafe alone? — A paused holder can outlive the TTL and resume writing; "dead" and "paused" look identical.
  • Fencing token? — Monotonic number per lock grant; the resource rejects lower-than-seen tokens.
  • Redlock verdict? — Sturdier efficiency lock; still assumes bounded pauses/drift, so not a correctness proof (Kleppmann).
  • Best lock is? — No lock: idempotent/conditional writes, unique constraints, one owner per key.
  • Idempotency key rule? — Minted once per logical action (client-side), resent on every retry, claimed atomically, response stored and replayed.
  • Setting vs incrementing? — SET replays harmlessly; INCR compounds — reshape counters into dedupe-able events.
  • Exactly-once, honestly? — Delivery: impossible. Processing: at-least-once + dedupe, or effect+offset committed atomically.
  • Phi accrual detector? — Continuous suspicion score from heartbeat history instead of a binary timeout; act at thresholds.
  • SWIM's two tricks? — Indirect ping-req via k peers (kills false positives) and suspicion + incarnation refutation (protects the slow).
  • Gossip speed? — Epidemic: all N nodes in O(log N) rounds at constant per-node load.
  • Split brain cure? — Not better detection — majorities: only the quorum side acts; fence the rest (lease expiry, tokens, STONITH).
  • RPO vs RTO? — Data you lose (≈ replication lag if async) vs time you're down (detect + decide + promote + repoint + warm).
  • Who decides failover? — A quorum holding the leader lease (Patroni/etcd pattern), never a lone monitor.
  • Jepsen? — Framework that partitions/pauses real clusters and checks histories against claimed consistency models; read the report before trusting the adjective.
  • Chaos engineering in one line? — Controlled fault injection against a steady-state hypothesis with minimal blast radius and an abort switch.

6️⃣ Async & Event-Driven Architecture

Every large system eventually stops doing everything in the request path: spikes get buffered, slow work gets deferred, and services get decoupled through messages. This section builds the async toolkit in order — why and when to go async, queues vs streams, Kafka mechanics at interview depth, then the hard part: keeping data correct across async boundaries (guarantees, outbox/CDC, sagas, event sourcing), and finally the operational layer — backpressure, scheduling, event design, and async request-reply. Delivery semantics fundamentals live in §5; this section is about applying them in real pipelines.

Why async: decoupling, load leveling, and the trade you pay

Why interviewers ask: "just put a queue there" is the most cargo-culted move in design interviews. The signal is whether you can name what the queue buys (decoupling, buffering), what it costs (latency, eventual completeness, a new failure domain), and when the boring synchronous call is the right answer.

A synchronous call couples two services in three ways at once: temporal (both must be up at the same instant), throughput (the caller can only go as fast as the callee), and failure (the callee's outage becomes the caller's outage). Putting a durable queue between them breaks all three: the producer writes and moves on, the consumer drains at its own pace, and a consumer outage just grows the backlog instead of failing user requests.

The second superpower is load leveling. Traffic is spiky (flash sale: 10× for 5 minutes) but provisioning for peak is expensive. A queue absorbs the spike and lets consumers drain it at steady provisioned rate — you size consumers for the average, not the peak, and pay for the difference in delay, not errors. Analogy: a dam on a river — floods fill the reservoir instead of the village, and the turbines run at constant flow.

The price is the latency vs completeness trade: the producer's "success" now means "durably enqueued", not "done". The user gets a 202 and the real work finishes seconds (or hours, during an incident) later — every downstream screen must tolerate "processing…" states, and you need visibility (lag metrics, status endpoints) instead of a synchronous error. When sync is right: the caller needs the answer to proceed (auth check, price lookup, inventory reservation shown to the user), the operation is fast and the dependency is reliable, or strong read-your-write semantics are required. Rule of thumb: queries are sync; state-changing work whose result the user does not need immediately is async.

Interview angle: when you drop a queue into a design, immediately say the three sentences that prove you understand it: what it decouples ("checkout no longer depends on the email service being up"), what the user sees now ("order confirmed, email arrives eventually"), and what you monitor ("age of oldest message / consumer lag, alert at 5 minutes"). That converts a box on the whiteboard into a senior signal.

Pitfalls

  • Making a call async but leaving the user waiting for its result anyway (spinner polling for 30 s) — you kept the latency and added infrastructure.
  • Queueing work that must be atomic with the request (e.g. reserving inventory after confirming the order) — async means the check can fail after you said yes.
  • Forgetting the queue is a new stateful dependency: it needs durability settings, monitoring, and a capacity story of its own.
  • Unbounded backlog as "resilience" — a 6-hour-old backlog of price updates is often worse than dropping them; stale work can be harmful work.
Interview questions
  • When would you deliberately keep a call synchronous? — When the caller needs the result to proceed (authz, price, availability shown to the user), when read-your-write is required, or when the dependency is fast and reliable enough that a queue only adds moving parts. Sync is the simpler default; async must earn its place.
  • Your checkout calls 6 services synchronously — what do you change? — Keep the ones whose answer gates the order (payment auth, inventory); move the rest (email, loyalty points, analytics, warehouse notify) behind events. Availability becomes the product of only the essential calls.
  • How do you size consumers if you buffer spikes instead of scaling for peak? — Size for average rate plus a drain target: consumers must sustain avg + (peak−avg)×spike_duration/acceptable_delay. If a 5-min 4k/s excess must drain in 10 min, you need ~2k/s of spare consumer capacity.
  • What breaks first when you introduce a queue? — Correctness assumptions: duplicates appear (at-least-once), ordering changes, and "it succeeded" now means "it will happen". Consumers must be idempotent and the UX must show pending states.
  • The product team says the email must arrive "immediately" — still async? — Yes: async ≠ slow. A healthy pipeline delivers in tens of milliseconds; async changes the failure behavior (email service down ⇒ delayed emails, not failed checkouts), not the happy-path speed.

Queues vs streams: two different contracts

Why interviewers ask: "Kafka or SQS?" is a genuine architecture fork, and many candidates treat them as interchangeable "message things". The probe is whether you know the contracts differ: a queue is a disappearing to-do list, a stream is a durable shared log — and each makes some designs easy and others impossible.

Queue model (SQS, RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ): the broker owns delivery state per message. A consumer receives a message, it becomes invisible to others (visibility timeout / unacked), and on ack the message is deleted forever. Scaling is trivial — add competing consumers and the broker deals messages out; no partition math. Brokers like Rabbit add per-message routing (exchanges, routing keys, priorities, per-message TTL, delayed delivery). What you give up: history. Once acked, a message is gone — no replay, no second consumer seeing the same data (you need fan-out topology like SNS→multiple SQS queues, or Rabbit exchange→multiple queues, decided at publish time).

Stream/log model (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, Redpanda): the broker stores an append-only log per partition and never mutates it on consumption. Consumers just remember an offset — "I have read up to position 4,182". Reading is non-destructive, so any number of independent consumer groups read the same data at their own pace, and any group can replay by rewinding its offset (yesterday's bug ⇒ reset to yesterday, reprocess). Data expires by retention policy (time/size, e.g. 7 days), not by being consumed. The cost: consumers manage position, parallelism is bounded by partition count, and "delete this one message" basically doesn't exist.

Analogy: a queue is a ticket dispenser at the deli — each ticket is taken once and torn up. A stream is the security-camera tape — everyone can watch it, rewind it, and the tape overwrites itself after a week.

Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ)Stream / log (Kafka, Kinesis)
On consumeMessage locked, then deleted on ackNothing changes; consumer advances an offset
Multiple readers of same dataOnly via publish-time fan-out (SNS→queues, exchanges)Native: any number of consumer groups
Replay / reprocessNo (message is gone)Yes — rewind offset within retention
ParallelismAny number of competing consumers≤ partitions per group (per partition: 1 consumer)
OrderingBest-effort (FIFO variants: limited throughput, e.g. SQS FIFO ~300 msg/s per group, 3k batched)Guaranteed per partition (per key with keyed partitioning)
Routing / delay / priorityRich per-message (routing keys, TTL, delay queues, priorities)Minimal — topics/partitions only; delay and priority are DIY
RetentionUntil consumed (or max age, SQS 14 days)Policy-based (time/size/compaction) regardless of consumption
Sweet spotTask/job distribution, work queues, RPC-ish commandsEvent backbone, CDC, analytics feed, multiple subscribers, audit
Interview angle: pick by contract, not by fashion. "Resize these images" (each message is a job, done once, no one else cares) → queue. "Order events that fulfillment, fraud, analytics, and the data lake all need — and we may add a subscriber next quarter" → stream. A strong senior answer names both and says: commands down queues, facts down streams.

Pitfalls

  • Using Kafka as a job queue: slow jobs block the partition behind them (head-of-line), parallelism is capped by partitions, and per-message retry/delay must be hand-built.
  • Using a queue as an event bus: the second team that needs the data forces a publish-side topology change, and there is no replay when they need history.
  • Assuming SQS standard preserves order or exact-once — it is best-effort order, at-least-once, with occasional duplicates by design.
  • Treating Kafka retention as a backup: default 7 days means a consumer down for 8 loses data silently unless retention/alerting says otherwise.
Interview questions
  • New consumer needs last month's events — queue or stream, and why? — Stream: reads are non-destructive and a new consumer group can start from any retained offset. In the queue model the data was deleted on ack; you'd have to rebuild it from a database.
  • How do competing consumers work in each model? — Queue: broker deals messages to any free consumer; add consumers freely. Stream: partitions are assigned exclusively within a group, so max useful consumers = partition count; beyond that they idle.
  • You need per-message delays (retry in 5 min) — which fits? — Queue-side features fit naturally (SQS delay/visibility timeout, Rabbit delayed exchange). On Kafka you build it: retry topics with delay consumers or a scheduler — a known Kafka weak spot.
  • Why does SQS FIFO cap throughput while Kafka scales ordered throughput? — SQS FIFO serializes per message group through the broker's delivery state machine (~300 msg/s/group, 3k batched, higher in high-throughput mode); Kafka only guarantees order within a partition and scales by adding partitions — order is scoped, so throughput is horizontal.
  • Could you build a work queue on Kafka anyway? — Yes, and big shops do, but you accept partition-grained parallelism, DIY per-message retries/DLQ, and head-of-line blocking; if you don't already run Kafka, a queue service is operationally cheaper.
  • What happens to unread Kafka data after retention expires? — Deleted (or compacted to latest-per-key on compacted topics) regardless of whether anyone read it — monitor consumer lag against retention as a data-loss guard.

Kafka at scale: partitions, groups, acks, and the levers that matter

Why interviewers ask: Kafka is the default event backbone, so "walk me through how Kafka scales" is a standard deep dive. The probe goes: partitions → ordering → consumer groups → what happens on rebalance → what acks=all actually waits for. Each level filters out candidates who have only used the client library.

Partitions are the unit of everything. A topic is split into N partitions; each is an append-only log living on a broker (with replicas on others). Producers pick the partition by hash(key) % N — so all events for one key (one order, one user) land in one partition, in order. That is the whole Kafka ordering story: order per key, no order across keys. Partitions are also the unit of parallelism (one consumer per partition within a group), of replication, and of hot-spotting.

Consumer groups & rebalancing. A group's consumers divide the partitions; a group coordinator (a broker) tracks membership via heartbeats. Join/leave/crash triggers a rebalance — classically stop-the-world (every consumer drops all partitions, re-assigns, resumes), which at scale means seconds of paused consumption; modern clients use cooperative/incremental rebalancing (only moved partitions pause) and static membership (group.instance.id) so a rolling restart doesn't thrash assignments. Consumers persist progress by committing offsets to an internal topic; commit after processing ⇒ at-least-once (crash re-reads a batch), commit before ⇒ at-most-once.

Durability knobs. Each partition has a leader and followers; followers in sync form the ISR (in-sync replica set). acks=1: leader ack only — fast, but a leader crash before replication loses the write. acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2 (with RF=3): ack when all ISR members have it — survives a broker loss, costs one extra intra-cluster RTT and becomes unavailable for writes if ISR shrinks below 2 (durability chosen over availability). Throughput levers: producers batch (batch.size, linger.ms=5–100 ms trades latency for batching) and compress per batch (lz4/zstd, often 3–5× on JSON); brokers do sequential appends and zero-copy sends, which is why a modest partition sustains tens of MB/s.

Sizing & sharp edges. Partition count: max(target_throughput / per-partition_throughput, target_consumers) with 2–3× headroom — you can add partitions later but that reshuffles key→partition mapping (breaks "same key, same partition" history), so over-provision upfront; thousands of partitions per broker also cost memory/leader-election time. Hot partitions: one celebrity key floods one partition — fixes: composite keys (key+bucket), salting with consumer-side merge, or keyless round-robin where ordering doesn't matter. Compacted topics keep the latest record per key forever (changelog/table semantics — great for caches and Kafka Streams state). Tiered storage (one line): brokers offload old segments to object storage, making months-long retention affordable without giant broker disks.

LeverSetting / ruleTrade-off
Durabilityacks=all + min.insync.replicas=2, RF=3+1 intra-cluster RTT; writes fail if ISR < 2 (chooses consistency)
Producer speedlinger.ms 5–100, big batch.size, zstd/lz4Adds up to linger-worth of latency; big CPU/net win (3–5× on JSON)
Partition countmax(throughput need, consumer count) × 2–3 headroomAdding later remaps keys; too many → broker memory + slow elections
Rebalance painCooperative assignor + group.instance.idSlightly slower to evict a truly dead consumer
History semanticsCompacted topic (latest per key) vs time retentionCompaction loses intermediate events; time retention loses old keys
Long retentionTiered storage → old segments in object storeReads of cold data slower; near-infinite replay window cheaply
Interview angle: the phrase that lands: "Kafka gives me an ordered, replayable log per key, and I size partitions for the consumers I'll need, not the bytes — the bytes are rarely the constraint." Then quote one number: a single partition comfortably does 5–10+ MB/s, so 100 MB/s of 1 KB events needs ~10–20 partitions for throughput — but 50 partitions if I need 50 parallel consumers.

Pitfalls

  • Claiming "Kafka guarantees ordering" unqualified — only per partition; a repartition (adding partitions, or a keyless producer) silently breaks it.
  • Auto-commit with default settings while processing asynchronously — offsets can be committed for messages you haven't finished, turning crashes into data loss (at-most-once by accident).
  • acks=all without setting min.insync.replicas — with ISR shrunk to just the leader, acks=all degrades to acks=1 semantics.
  • Scaling consumers past partition count and wondering why the extras idle; or fixing a hot partition by "adding partitions", which doesn't split an existing hot key.
  • One slow message stalls its whole partition (head-of-line blocking) — long tasks belong in a work queue or behind a per-partition worker pool with care for ordering.
Interview questions
  • Your topic has a hot partition from one huge tenant — options? — Composite key (tenant+bucket) to spread while keeping per-bucket order; salt the key and merge consumer-side; isolate the tenant to its own topic; or drop keyed ordering for that flow. Adding partitions alone does nothing — the hot key still hashes to one.
  • What exactly does acks=all wait for? — All current ISR members to have the record, not all replicas: a lagging follower drops out of ISR and stops being waited on — which is why min.insync.replicas is needed to keep the guarantee meaningful.
  • What happens during a consumer group rebalance, and why do you care? — Partitions are revoked and reassigned; with the eager protocol all consumption pauses (seconds), and uncommitted messages get reprocessed by the new owner. Care: latency spike + duplicates on every deploy unless you use cooperative rebalancing and static membership.
  • How do you pick partition count for a new topic? — Two constraints: throughput (need ÷ per-partition MB/s) and parallelism (max consumers you'll ever want in one group); take the max, multiply 2–3× because repartitioning breaks key ordering. Say the arithmetic out loud.
  • Compacted topic vs normal retention — when each? — Compaction when the topic is a changelog and only latest-state-per-key matters (user profiles, config, Streams state stores — new consumers bootstrap current state). Time retention when every event matters (orders, audit, analytics).
  • Producer throughput is low but brokers are idle — first two knobs? — linger.ms > 0 and larger batch.size to stop sending one-record batches, then compression (zstd). Most "Kafka is slow" cases are an unbatched producer, not the cluster.
  • Why not one partition per user for perfect ordering? — Millions of partitions melt the controller and broker memory; partitions are a broker-level resource. Keyed hashing gives per-user order with a bounded partition count.

Delivery & processing guarantees in real pipelines

Why interviewers ask: "how do you guarantee exactly-once?" is a trap laid in almost every event-driven design interview. The expected shape: exactly-once delivery is impossible; the production recipe is at-least-once transport + idempotent processing, with Kafka transactions as a special case whose scope you must state precisely.

Recap from §5 delivery semantics: an ack can be lost after the work happened, so a sender must choose — never retry (at-most-once, loses data) or retry (at-least-once, duplicates data). Pipelines compound this at every hop: producer→broker (producer retries duplicate the record unless the idempotent producer's sequence numbers dedupe them), broker→consumer (redelivery after crash before offset commit), and consumer→downstream (your HTTP call to the payment provider times out…). The default recipe: make every hop at-least-once, then make the final effect idempotent (mechanics in §5 idempotency) — natural idempotency (SET status='shipped'), unique keys (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on event_id), or a dedupe store: transactionally record processed event_ids alongside the state change, skip if seen. The dedupe key must live in the same transaction/store as the effect — a Redis "seen" set beside a Postgres write reintroduces the dual-write problem.

Kafka "exactly-once" (EOS), scoped honestly: the idempotent producer (default on) dedupes broker-side retries via producer-id + sequence numbers; transactions (transactional.id, consumer isolation.level=read_committed) make "consume from topic A, process, produce to topic B, commit offsets" atomic. That is exactly-once within a Kafka→Kafka pipeline (the Kafka Streams model). The moment processing touches an external system — a DB, an email API — the transaction cannot cover it, and you are back to idempotency/outbox at that boundary. Saying that sentence is the difference between senior and mid.

Ordering across partitions is the other silent killer: at-least-once plus retries plus multiple partitions means "OrderCancelled" can be processed before "OrderCreated" if they took different paths. Defenses: key everything about one entity to one partition (the main fix); version/sequence numbers in events so consumers detect and park out-of-order arrivals; or design state machines that tolerate reordering (a cancel for an unknown order id waits or is retried). Never assume cross-partition or cross-topic order.

GuaranteeHowHonest scope
At-most-onceAck/commit before processing; never retryLoses messages on any crash — OK for metrics ticks, not money
At-least-onceProcess, then ack/commit offset; retry on doubtThe default; duplicates guaranteed eventually
Effectively-onceAt-least-once + idempotent/deduped consumerWhat "exactly-once" means in practice, works across any boundary
Kafka EOSIdempotent producer + transactions + read_committedKafka-in → Kafka-out only; external side effects not covered
Interview angle: when asked "the email service must send exactly one email", walk the chain: at-least-once everywhere; consumer checks a dedupe store keyed by event_id before calling the mail API; the mail API call itself can still double-send if its ack is lost — so pass an idempotency key to the provider too (SES/SendGrid support this). Guarantees are per-hop; the chain is as strong as its weakest hop.

Pitfalls

  • Dedupe state in a different store than the effect (Redis set + Postgres write) — a crash between them re-creates the duplicate or, worse, marks unprocessed work as done.
  • Believing Kafka transactions protect a DB write or HTTP call inside the processing step — EOS ends at Kafka's edge.
  • TTL-ing the dedupe store shorter than the maximum redelivery horizon (retries + DLQ reprocessing weeks later ⇒ duplicate sails through).
  • Relying on order between "Created" and "Cancelled" events that traverse different partitions or topics.
Interview questions
  • Interviewer: "just use Kafka exactly-once" — your response? — Agree for Kafka→Kafka stages (transactions make consume-process-produce atomic), then point out our sink is Postgres/an email API, which the transaction can't span — so the boundary still needs idempotent writes or outbox-style dedupe.
  • Where do you store dedupe keys and for how long? — In the same transactional store as the effect (a processed_events table with the business tables); retain longer than the max possible redelivery window — retries + DLQ replay horizon, typically days to weeks — then archive/prune.
  • How does the idempotent producer dedupe retries? — Broker tracks (producer id, partition, sequence number); a retried batch with an already-seen sequence is acked but not re-appended. It covers producer→broker retries only, in-session.
  • Events for one order arrive out of order — how? — They crossed partitions or topics (or a repartition remapped keys mid-history). Fix by keying on order_id into one partition, or carry a sequence/version so consumers can buffer or reject stale transitions.
  • What does isolation.level=read_committed change? — Consumers skip records from aborted transactions and won't read past the first open transaction (last stable offset), giving atomic visibility of transactional writes at some latency cost.
  • Ack before or after processing — who decides? — The data's tolerance: ack-first = at-most-once (droppable telemetry), process-first = at-least-once (anything that matters). Per-queue policy, stated explicitly in the design.

The dual-write problem & the transactional outbox / CDC

Why interviewers ask: every event-driven design contains the line "the service saves to its DB and publishes an event" — and that sentence, taken literally, is a bug. Spotting the dual-write problem unprompted and reaching for outbox/CDC is one of the highest-signal moves in the whole interview.

The bug: a database and a message broker are two independent systems with no shared transaction. Whatever order you write them in, a crash between the two writes leaves them disagreeing: DB-then-publish ⇒ crash loses the event (order exists, fulfillment never hears about it — silently, forever); publish-then-DB ⇒ crash announces an order that doesn't exist. Retries don't fix it (the crash is between operations) and 2PC between a DB and a broker is essentially unsupported and unwanted (see §3 distributed transactions).

Transactional outbox: use the one transaction you actually have. In the same local DB transaction as the business change, insert the event into an outbox table — atomicity for free, since it's one database. A separate relay then moves outbox rows to the broker: either a poller (SELECT unpublished ORDER BY id → publish → mark published; simple, adds up to the polling interval of latency) or CDC — change data capture: a connector like Debezium tails the DB's replication log (MySQL binlog / Postgres WAL) and publishes committed changes to Kafka with no polling and near-zero DB load. CDC can also skip the outbox table entirely and stream the business tables themselves — that's how you get a log-as-source-of-truth pipeline feeding caches, search indexes, and warehouses from the same change stream.

The fine print: the relay is itself a sender with lossy acks, so it publishes at-least-once — a crash after publish but before marking the row re-publishes it. Combined with the previous card: outbox gives you no lost events; consumer idempotency gives you no duplicated effects; together they are the standard correctness recipe. Ordering: publish outbox rows keyed by aggregate id so per-entity order survives into the broker's partitions.

Analogy: instead of promising to mail a letter every time you update your ledger (and sometimes forgetting), you write the letter into the ledger itself — and a clerk who never sleeps mails everything the ledger contains, twice if unsure.

Interview angle: drop the pattern name early: "I'll write the event through a transactional outbox — I don't want the save-then-publish dual write." If asked to go deeper: outbox table (id, aggregate_id, type, payload, created_at, published_at), relay = Debezium on the WAL publishing to Kafka keyed by aggregate_id, consumers dedupe on event id. Mention the operational upside of CDC-of-business-tables: one change stream feeds search, cache invalidation, and the warehouse without touching application code.

Pitfalls

  • "Fixing" dual write by reordering the two writes — both orders fail, just with different wreckage (lost event vs phantom event).
  • Publishing inside the DB transaction (before commit) — the commit can still fail after the event is out; and broker latency now sits inside your DB transaction holding locks.
  • Forgetting the relay is at-least-once and skipping consumer dedupe — outbox alone does not give effectively-once.
  • Letting the outbox table grow forever — prune published rows, or use CDC + a short retention since the log, not the table, is the transport.
  • Raw CDC of business tables leaks your schema as a public contract — wrap it (outbox with an explicit event payload, or a transform layer) so internal migrations don't break consumers.
Interview questions
  • Why not just publish the event first, then save? — Symmetric failure: crash after publish ⇒ downstream reacts to an order that was never created (email for a nonexistent order, reserved inventory). Neither ordering fixes atomicity across two systems.
  • Poller vs CDC for the relay? — Poller: trivial to build, adds poll-interval latency and query load, fine at modest scale. CDC (Debezium): ms latency, no polling load, ordering from the log — but new infrastructure (connector cluster) and binlog/WAL access to operate. Start with a poller, move to CDC at scale.
  • How does the event's partition key survive from outbox to Kafka? — The relay publishes with key = aggregate_id from the outbox row, so all events of one order land in one partition in commit order.
  • Could two relay instances double-publish? — Yes — run the relay leader-elected (or use Debezium's single-connector-task model), and accept that failover still re-publishes a window; consumers dedupe. Never require exactly-once from the relay.
  • What is "log as source of truth"? — Invert the arrow: the change log (CDC stream) becomes the canonical record of what happened, and DBs, caches, search indexes are all just materialized views subscribing to it — replayable, rebuildable, consistent-eventually.
  • When is dual write actually acceptable? — When the event is advisory and loss is tolerable (cache-warm hints, best-effort analytics) — say so explicitly and log the failure; never for money, orders, or anything another team's correctness depends on.

Sagas: distributed transactions without 2PC

Why interviewers ask: "the order spans order, payment, and inventory services — how do you keep them consistent?" is the canonical microservices question. The expected answer is a saga — a sequence of local transactions with compensations — plus the follow-ups that separate readers from practitioners: who coordinates, what happens on timeout, and what other requests see mid-saga.

A saga replaces one distributed ACID transaction (unavailable/unwanted across services — §3) with a chain of local transactions: T1 create order → T2 charge payment → T3 reserve inventory. If step k fails, you cannot roll back committed steps — you run compensating transactions C(k−1)…C1 in reverse: refund the charge, cancel the order. Compensations are new forward actions ("refund"), not undo — they must be idempotent and should be designed to (almost) never fail; if one does, it retries until it succeeds or a human intervenes.

Two coordination styles. Choreography: no coordinator — each service reacts to events (OrderCreated → payment listens, PaymentFailed → order listens…). Zero extra infrastructure, but the workflow exists nowhere: it's implicit in N services' subscriptions, hard to see, hard to change, prone to cycles. Orchestration: a saga orchestrator (a state machine — Temporal, Camunda, Step Functions, or a hand-rolled table) sends commands and records each transition durably. One place to read the flow, explicit timeout handling, and — critically — a queryable answer to "where is saga #4412 stuck?". Rule of thumb: choreography for 2–3 steps, orchestration beyond that or when money is involved. The orchestrator's own state changes must use the outbox pattern too — it is also a service doing dual writes.

Failure & isolation, the deep-dive layer. Timeouts: a step that never replies (service down, message in a dead-letter queue) must trigger a timeout transition → compensate or park the saga for operator review; stuck-saga detection (scan for sagas in a non-terminal state older than X) is a required batch job. Isolation anomalies: sagas have no I in ACID — between T1 and T3 other requests can see a half-done order (a dirty read at business level), or a parallel saga can modify the same inventory (lost update). Mitigations: semantic locks / pending states (order status=PENDING, inventory "reserved" not decremented — other flows treat pending as untouchable), commutative operations, and re-validation at each step ("is the order still PENDING?" before charging).

Analogy: booking a trip — you book the flight, then the hotel, then the car. If the car falls through you don't "roll back time"; you cancel the hotel and the flight, pay any cancellation fees (compensation is a new transaction, and imperfect), and until it's all confirmed your itinerary says "pending", so your spouse doesn't book a second trip.

Choreography (events)Orchestration (coordinator)
CouplingLoose — services only know eventsServices know the orchestrator's commands
Visibility of flowImplicit, scattered across subscriptionsExplicit state machine; "where is saga X?" is a query
Adding a stepTouch multiple services' subscriptionsChange one definition
Timeout / stuck handlingEach service DIYCentral timers, retries, escalation
Fits2–3 steps, simple flowsMoney, ≥3 steps, audits, SLAs (Temporal/Step Functions)
Interview angle: narrate the failure path, not the happy path — that's where the signal is: "payment fails ⇒ compensate in reverse; payment times out ⇒ I can't know if it charged (§5's lost-ack ambiguity), so the compensation is 'refund-if-charged', idempotent, keyed by order id; saga stuck > 15 min ⇒ sweeper escalates to an ops queue." Then mention what a checkout page shows during PENDING.

Pitfalls

  • Treating compensation as rollback — the charge happened; a refund is a second money movement with its own failure modes (and sometimes fees). Some actions (sent email) are uncompensatable — order steps so those come last.
  • No timeout transitions: a lost reply leaves the saga (and the customer's money) in limbo forever. Every waiting state needs a timer.
  • Ignoring isolation: showing half-created orders to users, or letting two concurrent sagas reserve the same last item — use pending states and re-validation.
  • An orchestrator that updates its state and publishes commands as a dual write — the coordinator needs the outbox pattern as much as anyone.
  • Compensating on business failure vs retrying on technical failure confused: card declined ⇒ compensate; payment service 503 ⇒ retry with backoff, don't refund anything.
Interview questions
  • Payment step times out — refund or retry? — Neither blindly: a timeout is ambiguous (charged or not?). Retry the charge idempotently (same idempotency key ⇒ no double charge) a bounded number of times; if still unknown, run a query/reconciliation step, then compensate with an idempotent refund-if-charged.
  • Choreography or orchestration for a 5-step order flow with refunds? — Orchestration: the flow is long, involves money, and needs auditability and central timeout policy. Choreography's looser coupling isn't worth an invisible workflow here.
  • What stops another request reading a half-completed order? — Semantic locks: the order is PENDING until the saga completes, and every read path treats PENDING as "not yet real" (or shows it as processing). Sagas don't give isolation — you build it into the data model.
  • A compensation itself fails — then what? — Retry forever with backoff (compensations are designed idempotent and eventually-succeeding); if a business rule makes it truly impossible, park in a manual-intervention queue with full saga context. Never silently drop it.
  • How do you find sagas stuck for hours? — Because every saga has a durable state row, a sweeper queries non-terminal sagas older than a threshold, emits metrics (count by state), retries or escalates. With Temporal/Step Functions this is built in.
  • Saga vs 2PC in one sentence each? — 2PC: atomic and isolated but blocking and coordinator-fragile — fine inside one database ecosystem, wrong across services. Saga: available and non-blocking, but eventually consistent with business-level compensation — the microservices default.

Event sourcing & CQRS: events as the state

Why interviewers ask: both terms are résumé bait, and interviewers use them to test judgment: can you explain the mechanics (events → projections → replay), the operational costs (eventual read models, versioned events forever), and — the senior part — when not to use them?

Event sourcing flips persistence: instead of storing current state and overwriting it (UPDATE balance=80), you store the immutable sequence of events that happened (AccountOpened, Deposited(100), Withdrawn(20)) and derive state by replaying them. Current state is a fold over the event stream; new writes append an event after validating the command against replayed state. You get a perfect audit log by construction, time travel (state as of any moment), and the ability to answer questions retroactively ("how many carts contained item X before checkout?" — replay with a new fold). Replaying millions of events per entity is too slow, so you take periodic snapshots (state at event #N; load snapshot + replay the tail).

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is the companion: separate the write model (commands validated against the event stream, optimized for correctness) from read models — projections that consume the event stream and maintain query-shaped views (an orders-by-customer table in Postgres, a search index in Elasticsearch, a leaderboard in Redis). Each projection is rebuildable by replay: deploy a bug fix, drop the view, replay from event 0 (or a snapshot), and the read model heals. The costs: the read side is eventually consistent (a user who just placed an order may not see it in the list for ~100 ms–seconds — the UI must fake it or read-your-write from the write side), and events are forever: every historical event version must remain parseable, making schema evolution a permanent tax.

When it's overkill — the judgment answer: most services need none of this. CRUD + outbox (previous card) already yields a reliable event feed for other teams while keeping simple state management. Reach for event sourcing when the event history is the business value: ledgers/payments (auditors demand it), inventory movements, anything requiring retroactive queries or legal audit; reach for CQRS-without-ES when read and write shapes/scales genuinely diverge. Adopting both for a settings service is architecture cosplay — say so (politely) in the interview.

Analogy: your bank account is event-sourced — the balance is not a stored number you overwrite, it is the sum of the transaction history; the "balance" on your app is a projection, and a mid-month statement is a snapshot.

CRUD + outboxEvent sourcing (+CQRS)
Source of truthCurrent-state rowsImmutable event log
HistoryOnly what you explicitly log/auditComplete, by construction
Retroactive queries / rebuildsNo (state overwritten)Replay into new projections
Read-your-writeNaturalNeeds care (read from write side, or UI optimism)
Complexity taxLowHigh: versioned events forever, projections, snapshots
Use whenDefault for most servicesLedgers, inventory, audit-heavy, retroactive analytics
Interview angle: the strongest move is scoping: "I'd event-source the ledger — money demands an audit trail and replay — and keep the profile service as CRUD with an outbox. CQRS only where read shapes diverge: order history in Postgres, seller analytics in a warehouse projection." Whole-system event sourcing is a red flag you can call out.

Pitfalls

  • Deleting or mutating events to "fix" data — corrections are new compensating events (like accounting: you post a correcting entry, never erase).
  • Underestimating schema evolution: five-year-old events must still deserialize — upcasters/versioned types are a forever commitment.
  • GDPR vs immutability: personal data in events can't be erased by design — use crypto-shredding (per-user keys, delete the key) or keep PII out of events.
  • Reading your own projection right after a command and "losing" the write — the read side lags; design the UX for it.
  • Projections consuming at-least-once must be idempotent too (track last-applied event position per view).
Interview questions
  • User places an order and their order list doesn't show it — what happened and what do you do? — The list is a lagging projection. Options: read-your-write from the write model for that user's recent commands, return the created entity in the command response and render optimistically, or block until the projection reaches the command's position (per-request consistency token).
  • How do snapshots interact with correctness? — Pure optimization: state must equal fold(events); a snapshot is a memoized prefix. If snapshot logic changes, you can always discard snapshots and re-fold from zero.
  • How do you change an event's schema? — Additive fields with defaults where possible; otherwise version the event type and add an upcaster that converts old versions on read. Never rewrite the log.
  • Event sourcing vs the outbox's event stream — aren't they the same? — No: outbox events are derived notifications; state lives in tables and events could be lossy/incomplete without breaking the service. In ES the events ARE the state — completeness is existential.
  • Rebuilding a projection takes 6 hours — how do you deploy a fix without downtime? — Build the new projection in parallel (new consumer group from offset 0 / snapshot), let it catch up, then atomically switch reads to it and retire the old one — a blue/green for read models.
  • Where does Kafka fit? — As the transport/backbone (and compacted topics for changelogs). But a per-entity event store needs efficient "read all events for aggregate X", which Kafka partitions don't give per key — dedicated stores (EventStoreDB, DynamoDB streams-style tables) or a DB table per aggregate are the usual write-side store, with Kafka fanning out.

Backpressure, consumer lag & poison messages

Why interviewers ask: "the queue keeps growing — what do you do?" is the operational follow-up to any async design. It tests whether you know the one metric that matters (consumer lag / oldest-message age), the difference between buffering and drowning, and what happens to the message that crashes every consumer.

A pipeline is stable only while drain rate ≥ arrival rate on average. Queues hide short imbalances; a sustained imbalance grows the backlog without bound — memory/disk pressure on the broker, and worse, staleness: if lag is 2 hours, you are processing the world as it was 2 hours ago. That's why consumer lag is THE health metric of async systems — measured in messages (Kafka: log-end-offset − committed offset) and, more usefully, in time (age of oldest unprocessed message, or lag ÷ drain rate = time-to-catch-up). CPU on the consumers can look idle while lag explodes (e.g. consumers blocked on a slow downstream) — alert on lag, not on utilization.

Flow control toolkit, in escalation order: bounded queues everywhere (an unbounded in-memory queue converts overload into an OOM — bound it and make producers block or fail fast); autoscale consumers on lag (works until you hit the partition ceiling — beyond partition count, extra consumers idle, so scale partitions ahead of need or fan out to a second stage); speed up the consumer (batch downstream calls, parallelize per partition where ordering allows, cache); and when arrival still exceeds any achievable drain: shed load — drop or sample low-value messages (telemetry), reject new work upstream (429 at the API), or route overflow to cold storage for later. The buffering-vs-shedding decision is a product question: an email 30 minutes late is fine; a fraud check 30 minutes late is useless — shed or prioritize instead.

Poison messages: one malformed or bug-triggering message makes the consumer crash → redelivery → crash, blocking its partition/queue forever (an infinite-retry hot loop). The fix is standard: retry with backoff N times (delivery-count on SQS/Rabbit; retry topics on Kafka), then move the message to a dead-letter queue with error context. A DLQ is only half a design without reprocess tooling: alerting on DLQ depth > 0, a viewer to inspect payloads, and a replayer that sends fixed/retried messages back to the source — otherwise the DLQ is where data goes to die quietly.

Interview angle: when an interviewer says "traffic doubles", answer in rates: "consumers currently drain 5k/s against 4k/s arrival; at 8k/s I need 60% more consumer throughput — I have 40 partitions and 25 consumers, so I can scale to 40 before repartitioning; my lag alert is oldest-message age > 60 s with page at 5 min." Rates and ceilings, not adjectives.

Pitfalls

  • Alerting on queue depth alone — depth 100k might be 10 seconds of work or 10 hours; age/time-to-drain is the actionable number.
  • Unbounded in-memory buffers inside the consumer (prefetching thousands of messages) — a crash loses them all back to redelivery, and memory becomes the failure mode.
  • Autoscaling consumers past the partition count and reporting "we scaled" while the extras sit idle.
  • Retrying poison messages forever "to avoid data loss" — you lose everything behind them instead; bounded retries + DLQ preserves both.
  • A DLQ without alerting and replay tooling — discovered full three weeks later, past the dedupe TTL and the retention window.
Interview questions
  • Lag is climbing after a deploy — first three checks? — (1) per-message processing time vs before (the deploy made it slower?), (2) error/retry rate (crash loops or a poison message pinning a partition?), (3) downstream dependency latency (consumer healthy but blocked). Then: partition skew and whether arrival rate itself spiked.
  • Buffer or shed — how do you decide? — By the value-decay of the work: durable value (emails, invoices) ⇒ buffer, it's still worth doing late; fast-decaying value (fraud scores, live recommendations, presence) ⇒ shed or prioritize, late results are worthless or harmful.
  • How would you implement priorities on Kafka? — Kafka has no per-message priority: use separate topics per priority class with dedicated (or weighted) consumer capacity, so a P0 backlog never waits behind P2 bulk.
