  • What makes a message "poison" and how do you keep one from stopping the world? — It deterministically fails processing (bad schema, bug-triggering data). Bounded retries with backoff, then DLQ with the error attached; the partition proceeds. Alert on first DLQ arrival, replay after fixing.
  • Producers are faster than any possible consumer scale-out — now what? — Push backpressure upstream: bounded intake with 429/blocking at the API edge, admission control by customer/priority, and per-tenant quotas — better to slow the source than to build an infinite buffer.
  • Time-to-recover formula after an incident? — backlog ÷ (drain − arrival). If it's negative or measured in hours beyond SLO, that's your case for emergency shedding or borrowing capacity.

Scheduling & delayed work at scale

Why interviewers ask: "send a reminder 24h later", "retry in 5 minutes", "run this nightly across the fleet" — deferred work appears in almost every design, and the follow-ups probe classic traps: who fires the timer when there are 20 instances, and what happens to timers when that node dies?

Delayed delivery: the simplest tool is broker-native delay — SQS DelaySeconds (≤15 min) or per-message visibility timeout, RabbitMQ delayed-message exchange or TTL+DLX (message expires from a wait queue into the real one). Kafka has no delay primitive: teams build retry-tier topics (retry-5m, retry-1h — a consumer pauses until each message's due time) or store due-times in a DB scanned by a dispatcher. For huge numbers of in-process timers (connection timeouts, per-request deadlines), the classic data structure is the timer wheel — a ring of buckets indexed by (due_time mod wheel_size), O(1) insert/expire vs O(log n) for a heap; it's what Kafka and Netty use internally, worth one name-drop.

Cron at scale: a cron on one box is a SPOF; naive cron on N boxes runs the job N times. The pattern: a leader-elected scheduler — instances compete for a lock/lease (see §5 distributed locks) and only the leader enqueues the work; the work itself goes onto a queue so workers (not the scheduler) execute and scale. Alternatives: DB-backed claims (ShedLock-style UPDATE jobs SET owner=? WHERE due<now() AND owner IS NULL — the row lock is the election), or managed schedulers (EventBridge Scheduler, Cloud Scheduler, Temporal timers) which move the HA problem to the vendor. Two rules regardless: schedulers enqueue, never execute (a slow job must not block the tick), and every fired job carries an idempotency key (fire-time + job-id) because failover can double-fire a tick.

Pacing outbound work: a drained backlog of 1M emails must not hit a partner API at full speed. Put a token bucket in front of outbound calls — refill at the partner's allowed rate (say 500/s), spend one token per call, and let consumers block on tokens; burst capacity = bucket size. This turns your rate limit compliance into backpressure that flows naturally back into the queue instead of into 429-retry storms.

Analogy: a restaurant kitchen — the expeditor (leader-elected scheduler) decides when each ticket fires, the line cooks (workers) actually cook, and the pass (token bucket) releases plates at the rate the servers can carry.

NeedToolWatch out
Delay one message minutes–hoursSQS delay/visibility, Rabbit TTL+DLX / delayed exchangeSQS DelaySeconds caps at 15 min; TTL queues deliver in order of expiry only if FIFO-per-TTL-tier
Delay on KafkaRetry-tier topics, or DB of due-times + dispatcherA paused consumer must not trigger rebalance (use pause(), not sleep past max.poll.interval.ms)
Millions of soft timers in-processTimer wheel (hashed/hierarchical)Coarse tick granularity; timers die with the process — persist what must survive
Fleet-wide cronLeader-elected scheduler → queue; DB claim (ShedLock); managed (EventBridge/Temporal)Failover double-fires: idempotency key per (job, tick); missed ticks need catch-up policy
Pacing outbound callsToken bucket at the client (shared via Redis if multi-instance)Distributed buckets need atomic take (Lua script); leave headroom below the partner's hard limit
Interview angle: for "send a reminder 24h after signup", the senior answer is boring and correct: write a row (user_id, due_at, status) — the DB is the timer store; a leader-elected dispatcher scans due_at < now() AND status='pending' every 30 s and enqueues; workers send idempotently and mark done. It survives restarts, is inspectable with SQL, and scales to millions of timers. Fancy in-memory timers are for sub-second precision, not for tomorrow.

Pitfalls

  • Scheduling by sleeping in a worker (sleep 24h) — dies with the process, blocks a thread, invisible to ops.
  • Cron on every instance without a lock — N instances, N duplicate runs (the classic "why did every customer get 8 emails" incident).
  • Scheduler executes jobs inline — one slow job delays every subsequent tick; always enqueue.
  • Ignoring the missed-tick policy: after 2h of scheduler downtime, do the 2h of nightly jobs run once, all, or not at all? Decide per job (catch-up vs skip).
  • Draining a backlog at full speed into a rate-limited partner — you trade your outage for their ban; pace with a token bucket.
Interview questions
  • How do you run a nightly job exactly once across 20 instances? — Leader election via a lock/lease (§5) or a DB claim with an atomic UPDATE; loser instances skip. Since failover can double-fire, the job is also idempotent keyed by (job, date). "Exactly once" = at-least-once fire + idempotent run.
  • Design "remind me in 30 days" for 100M users. — Not 100M in-memory timers: a due-time table/index (or time-bucketed partitions), a leader-elected sweeper enqueueing due batches each minute, idempotent send. Storage math: 100M rows × ~50B ≈ 5 GB — trivial for a DB.
  • Why a timer wheel over a priority heap? — O(1) insert/cancel/expire at millions of timers vs O(log n), at the cost of tick-granularity precision — the right trade for network timeouts, which are approximate anyway.
  • Your retry queue delays messages 5 min — how on Kafka specifically? — A retry topic whose consumer reads a message, computes due = ts+5m, calls pause() until due (staying under max.poll.interval or using an external store), then republishes to the main topic. Or sidestep: use SQS for the retry path even in a Kafka shop.
  • How do you pace 1M queued emails through a 500/s provider limit? — Shared token bucket (Redis + Lua for atomic take) refilled at 450/s (10% headroom); consumers block on tokens so the queue absorbs the wait. ETA: 1M ÷ 450/s ≈ 37 min — say the number.

Designing events: contracts, fat vs thin, schema evolution

Why interviewers ask: events are APIs — published once, consumed by teams you've never met, forever. Interviewers probe whether you treat the payload as a designed contract (semantics, size, evolution, PII) or as "whatever the ORM serializes".

Event vs command: an event is a fact in past tense, owned by the producer, with zero expectation — OrderPlaced: "this happened; react if you care". A command is an instruction addressed to one handler — ChargePayment: "you, do this". The grammar drives the topology: events fan out to N subscribers on streams; commands go point-to-point on queues, usually with a reply. Mixing them ("SendEmail" published as an 'event' to exactly one consumer) creates hidden coupling — the producer secretly depends on a specific reaction it pretends not to know about.

Fat vs thin events: a thin event carries identity only ({orderId: 42, status: PLACED}) — small, never stale, but every consumer calls back to the producer's API, re-coupling availability and creating a thundering herd on hot events. A fat event (Event-Carried State Transfer) embeds the needed state (items, totals, address) — consumers are autonomous and can rebuild local views, but payloads bloat, may be stale by delivery time, and every added field becomes contract surface. Pragmatic default: carry the state consumers commonly need plus ids for the rest; version the answer per event type, not globally.

Schema evolution: with many consumers you can never coordinate a simultaneous upgrade, so schemas evolve under compatibility rules enforced by a schema registry (Confluent SR, AWS Glue) at produce time: backward compatible (new schema reads old data — consumers upgrade first), forward (old readers read new data — producers upgrade first; means: only add optional/defaulted fields, never remove/rename/retype required ones), or full. Binary formats (Avro/Protobuf) make this checkable; JSON needs discipline plus explicit eventType/version fields. Breaking changes ship as a new versioned topic (orders.v2) with a migration window, not as a mutation. PII: events are copied into brokers, DLQs, replicas, lake archives — either keep PII out (ids only, fetch on demand), tokenize it, or encrypt fields with per-user keys so deletion = key destruction (crypto-shredding) — otherwise GDPR erasure meets an immutable log and loses.

Analogy: an event is a newspaper headline — published to whoever reads, immutable, archived forever (so don't print someone's SSN in it); a command is a work order handed to a specific contractor.

DecisionOption AOption B
SemanticsEvent (fact, fan-out, no reply)Command (instruction, one handler, often replies)
PayloadThin: ids only — fresh but re-couples via callbacksFat: embedded state — autonomy, bigger/stale-able contract
CompatibilityBackward (consumers first)Forward (producers first; add-only fields)
Breaking changeNew versioned topic + migration window— (never mutate in place)
PIIExclude / tokenizeField-encrypt + crypto-shred keys
Interview angle: sketch a real envelope: {eventId (uuid, dedupe key), eventType: "order.placed", version: 2, occurredAt, aggregateId (partition key), traceId, payload {…}}. Mentioning that eventId feeds consumer dedupe and aggregateId feeds partitioning shows the envelope is engineered, not decorative.

Pitfalls

  • CDC-ing internal tables straight to other teams — your DB schema silently becomes a public API; migrations now break strangers.
  • Renaming or retyping a field "because it's just JSON" — breaks consumers you can't see; compatibility must be checked mechanically at produce time.
  • Thin events + a hot topic = self-DDoS: 50k OrderPlaced/s × 4 consumers calling GET /orders = 200k RPS on your own API.
  • Email addresses in events replicated into a 2-year data-lake archive — erasure requests become archaeology; design PII handling before the first event ships.
Interview questions
  • OrderPlaced: what goes in the payload? — The commonly-needed projection (order id, customer id, line items with sku/qty/price, totals, timestamps) plus ids for rarely-needed detail; no card numbers, no raw address if avoidable (fulfillment can fetch by id). Justify each field as "≥2 consumers need it".
  • How do you evolve an event schema with 12 consumer teams? — Registry-enforced compatibility (typically backward or full): add optional fields freely; for breaking shape changes, publish orders.v2 alongside v1, dual-write during migration, deprecate v1 with a date.
  • Event vs command — why does the difference matter architecturally? — Ownership and coupling direction: events couple consumers to the producer's fact schema (producer evolves freely); commands couple the sender to the handler's API (sender must know the handler). Getting it backwards creates producers that break when a consumer changes.
  • Where does a schema registry sit in the write path? — Producer serializes against a schema id; the registry validates compatibility at registration and the id travels in the message header — consumers fetch the schema by id and cache it. Incompatible schema ⇒ producer fails at deploy/publish, not consumers at 3am.
  • User invokes GDPR erasure but events are immutable — options? — Best: PII never entered events. Else: tokenization (delete the token mapping) or per-user field encryption with key destruction. Retention-based expiry alone rarely satisfies "without undue delay".

Async request-reply: correlation ids, webhooks, polling

Why interviewers ask: the moment you make an operation async, someone still needs the answer — the user staring at "processing…", or the partner system awaiting a result. The probe: how does the reply find its way back, and how do you make callbacks reliable when the receiver is down?

Correlation ids are the backbone: the requester attaches a unique correlationId (and, in messaging, a replyTo address); every message, log line, and eventual reply carries it, letting the requester match responses to requests and letting on-call trace a request across five services. In-process this is a map of pending futures keyed by correlation id; across services it rides message headers (and doubles as the trace id).

Three reply-delivery patterns. (1) Polling: the request returns 202 Accepted + Location: /operations/{id}; the client polls a status endpoint (pending → succeeded/failed + result link), ideally with backoff and a Retry-After hint. Simple, firewall-proof, but latency = poll interval and hot polling is load. (2) Callback / webhook: the requester registers a URL; you POST the result when done. This makes you a producer with all of this section's problems: the receiver can be down, so you need retries with exponential backoff over hours (and a DLQ + dashboard for undeliverable hooks), the receiver gets duplicates so the payload carries an event id and the receiver must be an idempotent receiver, and the payload must be authenticated — HMAC signature over the body with a shared secret plus a timestamp against replay (the Stripe webhook model: Stripe-Signature: t=…,v1=…). Deliver the thin version and let the receiver fetch details to dodge payload-tampering and ordering issues. (3) Server push: WebSocket/SSE to the waiting client — best UX for humans, needs connection state (see §2). Real systems combine: webhook for machines, polling as the fallback, push for the browser tab.

Analogy: dry cleaning — the ticket number is the correlation id; you can call the shop every hour (polling), leave your number for a text (webhook — and they text twice if unsure you got it), or wait in the shop for your name to be called (push).

PatternLatencyReliability burdenFits
Polling a status endpoint≈ poll intervalOn the client (keep polling); server just stores statePublic APIs, simple clients, firewalled receivers
Webhook callbackms after completionOn the sender: retries+backoff, signatures, DLQ, receiver idempotencyB2B/machine integration (payments, CI, shipping)
WebSocket / SSE pushmsConnection state, reconnect + resume, fan-out infraHuman UIs awaiting results
Interview angle: for "video upload with async transcoding": respond 202 + operation id immediately; browser subscribes via SSE (falls back to polling every 5 s with backoff); if the uploader is an API partner, fire a signed webhook with event id, retry 1m/5m/30m/2h/6h, surface failures in a deliveries dashboard with manual redrive. One sentence each for signature, idempotent receiver, and retry schedule covers 90% of follow-ups.

Pitfalls

  • Webhooks without signatures + timestamp — anyone who finds the URL can forge "payment succeeded"; HMAC the body and reject stale timestamps.
  • Fire-once webhooks: receiver down for a 2-minute deploy silently loses the notification; retries over hours + DLQ are mandatory.
  • Assuming webhook order — retries reorder events; receivers must key on ids/versions, or fetch current state instead of trusting the payload.
  • Unbounded polling (every 500 ms forever from every client) — enforce backoff and Retry-After, or your status endpoint becomes your top traffic source.
  • Status stored only in memory — a restart strands every in-flight operation in "pending"; operation state belongs in a store.
Interview questions
  • Design reliable webhook delivery as the sender. — Outbox the completion event; a delivery worker POSTs with HMAC signature + timestamp + event id, retries on non-2xx with exponential backoff and jitter across hours, parks in a DLQ with a redrive UI, and exposes per-endpoint health (disable endpoints failing for days). Consumers told: idempotent by event id, verify signature, respond 2xx fast (enqueue internally).
  • Why does the receiver need idempotency if you retry only on failure? — The lost-ack ambiguity again: a timeout after the receiver processed but before the 200 arrived forces a retry ⇒ duplicate. Same rule as every hop: at-least-once + idempotent receiver.
  • Polling interval trade-off for a status endpoint? — Latency vs load: n clients ÷ interval = RPS (10k waiting clients at 2 s = 5k RPS). Use exponential backoff per client, Retry-After hints, and cheap responses (ETag/304 or cached status) — or upgrade hot waiters to SSE.
  • What goes in the webhook payload? — Prefer thin: event type, event id, resource id, timestamp, signature — the receiver fetches the authoritative object. It shrinks the trust surface, avoids stale embedded state, and keeps the contract small.
  • How does a correlation id differ from a trace id? — Same mechanism, different scope: the trace id follows the request through infrastructure for observability; the correlation id is the application-level key that matches a business reply to its request — commonly one value doing both jobs.

A checkout service saves the order to Postgres, then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. The process crashes between the two operations. What is the state of the system?

This is the dual-write problem: the DB commit already happened and cannot be undone by a later crash, and no component knows an event was ever intended — nothing retries it. (a) is wrong because the DB and broker share no transaction; (b) is wrong because the idempotent producer only dedupes retries of sends that were attempted — this send never happened. The fix is the transactional outbox: event written in the same DB transaction, relayed asynchronously.

A Kafka topic has 12 partitions. Your consumer group scales from 12 to 20 instances during a lag incident. What happens?

Partition count is the parallelism ceiling per consumer group: 12 partitions ⇒ at most 12 active consumers; the rest get no assignment. (a) describes queue-model competing consumers (SQS/Rabbit), which is exactly the contract Kafka does not offer. Partitions are never auto-split (c) — adding them is a manual, key-remapping operation. This is why you provision partitions ahead of the consumer count you'll ever need.

An email consumer reads a "send confirmation" event, sends the email, then crashes before committing its offset. After restart, what does the standard recipe rely on to avoid a second email?

Transport is at-least-once, so the message WILL be redelivered — correctness comes from idempotent processing: check a processed-events record and pass an idempotency key to the provider. (a) is the classic overreach: Kafka transactions scope to Kafka-in/Kafka-out and cannot cover an SMTP/API call. (b) avoids the duplicate by switching to at-most-once — crash after commit but before sending loses the email entirely. (d) is fiction: brokers know nothing about your side effects.

In an order saga, the payment service times out (no reply). What is the correct next move?

A timeout is ambiguous: the charge may or may not have happened. Retrying with the same idempotency key is safe (a duplicate attempt is absorbed) and resolves the ambiguity; only after bounded retries do you compensate — with a refund designed to be a no-op if no charge exists. (a) can refund money that was never taken (or double-refund on redelivery); (c) is impossible — the step is committed locally or not, you can't reach in; (d) is at-most-once wishful thinking.

Which situation is the strongest case for choosing a stream/log (Kafka) over a queue (SQS)?

Multiple independent readers of the same data, future subscribers, and replayable history are exactly the log contract: non-destructive reads, consumer groups, offset rewind. (a) and (c) are the queue contract (competing consumers, delete-on-ack; slow jobs also cause head-of-line blocking on Kafka partitions), and (b) names queue-native features (delay, priority) that Kafka lacks and must hand-build.

Consumer lag on a payments topic has grown steadily since 14:00 with CPU on consumer hosts at 15%. What is the most likely cause to check first?

Lag growing while CPU is idle is the signature of consumers waiting on I/O — a downstream dependency got slower (deploy, DB, external API), so each message takes longer and drain rate fell below arrival rate. This is why lag (or oldest-message age), not utilization, is the health metric: (d) inverts the logic — idle CPU is fully consistent with a drowning pipeline. (a) would show broker errors, not consumer lag; (c) is not a thing.

A malformed message crashes the consumer every time it is delivered, and the partition behind it is stalling. What is the production-grade handling?

Bounded retries + DLQ preserves both the poison message (inspectable, replayable after the fix) and everything queued behind it. (a) trades one message for the whole partition — infinite crash-loop; (b) loses data invisibly, which for payments is worse than an outage; (d) destroys all the healthy data with it. The half everyone forgets: a DLQ needs alerting and a redrive path, or it's just a slower way to lose data.

Twenty app instances each run an internal cron that fires a nightly settlement job. Customers received the settlement email up to 20 times. What is the standard fix?

The pattern is single-fire via leader election plus idempotency as the safety net — "exactly once" is engineered as at-least-once firing + idempotent execution. (b) still fires 20 times, just spread out; (c) fixes duplication by installing a SPOF; (d) misuses FIFO dedupe — its 5-minute dedupe window and content-based scope aren't a distributed-cron mechanism and the 20 sends would need identical dedupe ids within the window to be suppressed.

Which change to an Avro event schema is safe under backward compatibility (new schema must read old data) with consumers upgrading first?

Adding a field with a default is the canonical safe evolution: the new reader schema fills the default when reading old records that lack the field. A rename (a) is a remove+add of required data — old records have no custId; a type change (b) breaks decoding; removing a required field (c) is backward-OK in Avro only if the old data is still readable without it, but as a contract change it strands any consumer still reading it — registries under stricter modes reject it. The operational rule stands: add-with-default is free; everything else is a versioned migration.

You deliver payment webhooks to partner systems. A partner's endpoint returns 500s for 40 minutes during their deploy. What must your delivery system have done for them to end up correct?

Webhook sending is producing over an unreliable channel: durable retries with backoff (spanning outages), authentication (HMAC over body + timestamp against forgery/replay), and a stable event id so the inevitable duplicate attempt — e.g. their 200 lost in transit — is absorbed by an idempotent receiver. (a) is the exactly-once delivery myth wearing a webhook costume; (c) makes a 2-minute deploy lose money events; (d) is nonsense. Undeliverable-after-hours goes to a DLQ with a redrive dashboard.

Practice

Design the order saga: order / payment / inventory

An e-commerce checkout spans three services: order (creates the order), payment (charges the card), inventory (reserves stock, must come after payment per business rules). Design the saga: coordination style, the happy path, every failure path with compensations, timeout handling, and how you find and fix stuck sagas. State what a concurrent "cancel order" request sees mid-saga.

Covers: orchestration vs choreography · compensating transactions · timeouts · semantic locks · stuck-saga recovery

Hint 1

Three steps involving money ⇒ pick orchestration and justify it. Write the state machine first: states, and for each waiting state, a timeout transition. Then ask for each step: business failure vs technical failure — which compensates, which retries?

Hint 2

Inventory fails after payment succeeded — what runs, in what order? And what stops a second saga selling the same last unit while this one is mid-flight?

Solution

Coordination: orchestration — 3 steps, money, need auditability and central timeouts. The orchestrator persists saga state (saga_id, order_id, state, step_attempts, updated_at) and communicates via messages; its own state-change + command-publish uses the outbox pattern. All commands/replies are at-least-once; every handler is idempotent keyed by (saga_id, step).

Happy path: CREATED: T1 order service creates order status=PENDING (semantic lock) → AWAITING_PAYMENT: command charge(order_id as idempotency key) → on PaymentCharged → AWAITING_INVENTORY: command reserve(order_id) → on StockReserved → T-final: order status=CONFIRMED → saga COMPLETED.

Failure paths (reverse-order compensations):

• Payment declined (business failure): no compensations needed for money; run C1 cancel order (PENDING→CANCELLED). Saga FAILED.
• Payment timeout (technical): retry charge with same idempotency key ×N with backoff; still unknown ⇒ query payment provider (reconciliation step); if charged proceed, else C1. Never blind-refund.
• Inventory out of stock after successful charge: C2 refund(charge_id) — idempotent, retried until success — then C1 cancel order. Saga FAILED with reason=OOS; customer notified.
• Refund itself fails repeatedly: park saga in NEEDS_ATTENTION, page ops with full context. Compensations must be designed to almost-always succeed; a declining refund is a human problem.

Timeouts & stuck sagas: every AWAITING_* state has a timer (e.g. payment 30 s soft, 10 min hard). A sweeper job scans sagas in non-terminal states with updated_at < now−15 min: re-drives the pending command (idempotent, so safe), escalates after M re-drives. Replies that can't be processed go to a DLQ; DLQ depth > 0 alerts. Metrics: sagas by state (gauge), time-in-state histogram, compensation rate.

Isolation: the order is PENDING until COMPLETED — the storefront treats PENDING as "processing" (not cancellable through the normal path, not visible as confirmed); a user cancel during the saga is itself a command to the orchestrator, which either aborts cleanly at the next transition or queues the cancel to run post-completion as a normal refund flow. Inventory uses reservations (reserved_qty), not decrements, so a failed saga releases stock via compensation and concurrent sagas contend on an atomic reserve operation — the last unit goes to exactly one.

Exactly one confirmation email, end to end

"When an order is placed, the customer must receive exactly one confirmation email." Design the pipeline from the order service to the customer's inbox. Enumerate every place a duplicate or a loss can occur and the mechanism that closes it.

Covers: outbox · at-least-once hops · consumer dedupe · provider idempotency keys · DLQ

Hint 1

Walk the hops: order DB → event out → broker → email consumer → mail provider API → inbox. At each arrow ask: what if the ack is lost right here?

Solution

Pipeline: (1) Order service commits order + OrderPlaced row into an outbox in one transaction — closes the dual-write loss (crash after commit still publishes later). (2) Relay (poller or Debezium CDC) publishes to the broker keyed by order_id — relay is at-least-once ⇒ possible duplicate events, never loss. (3) Broker → email consumer at-least-once (commit offset only after processing). (4) Consumer, in one DB transaction: INSERT INTO sent_emails(event_id) — ON CONFLICT abort — then call the mail provider with an idempotency key = event_id; on success commit, then ack/commit offset.

Duplicate/loss audit: outbox crash-replays ⇒ duplicate event ⇒ consumer dedupe (sent_emails) absorbs. Consumer crash after provider call, before offset commit ⇒ redelivery ⇒ dedupe row already committed? Careful: if the crash was between provider call and local commit, the dedupe row is absent — this is why the provider-side idempotency key is required too (SES/SendGrid dedupe on it); the retried call becomes a no-op. Provider accepts but our timeout fires ⇒ retry with same key ⇒ provider dedupes. Mail provider → inbox is the provider's at-least-once problem (rare duplicate deliveries can still occur at SMTP level — acknowledge this honestly; "exactly once" beyond your boundary is best-effort).

Failure containment: malformed events → bounded retries → DLQ + alert + redrive tool. Dedupe rows retained ≥ max redelivery horizon (retries + DLQ replay window, e.g. 30 days). Monitoring: consumer lag age, DLQ depth, provider error rate, and an end-to-end canary (place a test order, expect exactly one email).

The one-line summary for the interviewer: loss is eliminated by outbox + at-least-once everywhere; duplication is eliminated at the two effect boundaries (our DB via dedupe table, provider via idempotency key). Every hop in between is allowed to duplicate freely.

Consumer lag climbing after a deploy — hypotheses in order

Thirty minutes after a routine deploy of the enrichment consumer, oldest-message age on its topic has gone from ~2 s to 9 minutes and is climbing. Give five hypotheses in the order you would check them, and for each: how to confirm in under two minutes.

Covers: lag triage · rebalance storms · poison messages · downstream latency · partition skew

Hint 1

The deploy is the prime suspect — but "the deploy made code slower" is only one of several ways a deploy hurts a consumer group. What does a rolling restart do to partition assignments?

Solution

1. Rebalance storm from the rolling deploy. Each instance restart triggers rebalances; with eager assignment the whole group pauses repeatedly. Confirm: broker/consumer logs for repeated "rebalance"/generation bumps, lag climbing in stair-steps during the deploy window then flattening. Fix: cooperative assignor + static membership; verify lag now drains.

2. New code is slower per message. A new blocking call (feature flag, extra lookup) cut drain rate below arrival. Confirm: compare per-message processing time / max.poll duration metrics before vs after deploy (p50 and p99); consumer CPU low + downstream call time up is the signature. Fix: rollback or optimize; lag ETA = backlog ÷ (drain−arrival).

3. Crash loop / poison message. New deserialization or validation rejects a message and the consumer dies repeatedly, pinning its partitions. Confirm: restart counts / crash-loop status, error logs showing the same offset re-attempted, lag concentrated in specific partitions. Fix: hotfix the handler or route the message to DLQ manually, then redrive.

4. Downstream dependency slowed (correlated, not caused — or caused by config change in the deploy). The enrichment API/DB the consumer calls got slower or is rate-limiting the new version (e.g. connection pool shrunk in new config). Confirm: downstream latency/error dashboards, connection pool saturation metrics. Fix: restore pool/timeout config, add batching, or temporarily shed enrichment.

5. Offset reset / auto.offset.reset surprise. The deploy changed group id or reset offsets, so the "lag" is actually the group reprocessing history (earliest) — alarming but self-healing — or metrics changed meaning. Confirm: committed offset positions vs log-end; did the group id change in config? Fix: if intentional replay, silence the alert with an ETA; if accidental, reset offsets to a timestamp.

Wrap: state the recovery arithmetic once the cause is fixed (backlog ÷ net drain), and the permanent fixes: canary consumer with lag SLO as a deploy gate, cooperative rebalancing, DLQ on deserialization failure.

Estimation drill: partitions & consumers for 1M events/min

A pipeline must process 1M events/min. Each event takes ~30 ms of consumer processing (mostly a downstream call), average size 1 KB. Size it: consumers needed, partition count, and broker throughput sanity check — with headroom for a 3× peak and a rebuild/replay scenario. Show the arithmetic.

Covers: throughput math · partition sizing · headroom · replay capacity

Hint 1

Convert to per-second first. A single-threaded consumer at 30 ms/event does how many events/s? Parallelism must come from somewhere — partitions.

Solution

Base rate: 1,000,000 / 60 ≈ 16,700 events/s. Bytes: 16.7k × 1 KB ≈ 17 MB/s — trivial for a Kafka cluster (a single partition does ~5–10+ MB/s); throughput of bytes is NOT the constraint. The constraint is processing latency.

Consumer math: one single-threaded consumer at 30 ms/event ⇒ ~33 events/s. Needed: 16,700 ÷ 33 ≈ ~505 consumer-threads just for average load. With 3× peak headroom: ~1,515. That number says: don't buy it with raw partition-per-thread scale-out alone — first shrink the 30 ms.

Lever 1 — batch the downstream call: if the consumer batches 50 events per downstream request at ~60 ms/batch, per-event cost ≈ 1.2 ms ⇒ one thread does ~830/s ⇒ 16.7k needs ~20 threads, 3× peak ⇒ ~60. Lever 2 — pipeline/async I/O within a partition (careful with ordering: only if per-key order is preserved via per-key serialization).

Partition count: must cover max concurrent consumers ever wanted. With batching: peak ~60 consumers ⇒ 2× headroom ⇒ ~128 partitions (round to a power-of-two-ish operable number). Without batching you'd be staring at 1,500+ partitions — quote that as the reason batching wins. Also check per-partition rate: 16.7k/s ÷ 128 ≈ 130 events/s ≈ 130 KB/s per partition — far under limits; fine.

Replay scenario: rebuilding a projection over 7 days of retention = 1M × 60 × 24 × 7 ≈ 10B events (~10 TB). At the batched rate with 128 consumers × 830/s ≈ 106k/s ⇒ ~94,000 s ≈ 26 hours to replay — acceptable for a planned rebuild; if the SLO is tighter, replay with a temporarily larger group (needs partitions — another reason for the 128 headroom) or from a snapshot.

Answer shape for the interview: "17k/s and 17 MB/s — bytes are trivial, latency is the problem; batch the downstream call to turn 505 required threads into ~20, provision 128 partitions for peak+replay headroom, and monitor lag age with a 60 s alert."

Rapid-fire: async & event-driven one-liners

Why: last-hour revision — the one-line answers that keep an interview moving. Say them crisply, then expand only if asked.

  • Queue vs stream in one line? — Queue: message deleted on ack, work distribution; stream: append-only log with offsets, replayable fan-out.
  • What does async buy you? — Temporal decoupling, load leveling of spikes, and failure isolation — paid for with latency and eventual completeness.
  • Kafka's ordering guarantee? — Per partition only; per key if you key the producer. Never across a topic.
  • Max useful consumers in a group? — One per partition; extras idle.
  • What triggers a rebalance? — Membership change (join/leave/crash/timeout) or subscription/partition change; cooperative assignor keeps unaffected partitions flowing.
  • acks=all really means? — All current in-sync replicas — pair it with min.insync.replicas=2 or it can degrade to leader-only.
  • Commit offset before or after processing? — After ⇒ at-least-once (default); before ⇒ at-most-once.
  • Exactly-once delivery? — Impossible over a lossy network; ship at-least-once + idempotent consumer = effectively once.
  • Kafka EOS scope? — Consume→process→produce within Kafka (transactions + read_committed); ends the moment you touch an external system.
  • Dual-write problem? — DB write and broker publish can't be atomic; a crash between them loses or fabricates events.
  • Outbox pattern? — Event row committed in the same local transaction as the state change; a relay publishes it at-least-once.
  • CDC? — Tail the DB's binlog/WAL (Debezium) and publish committed changes as a stream — outbox relay without polling.
  • Saga? — A distributed transaction as a chain of local transactions, each with an idempotent compensation run in reverse on failure.
  • Orchestration vs choreography? — Central state machine commanding steps vs services reacting to each other's events; pick orchestration for long/money flows.
  • Compensation ≠ rollback because…? — The step committed; compensation is a new forward action (refund), possibly imperfect, sometimes impossible (sent email).
  • Saga isolation problem? — No I in saga: other requests see intermediate state — hide it with pending states / semantic locks.
  • Hot partition fix? — Better key (composite/salted), isolate the tenant, or drop ordering — adding partitions alone doesn't split a hot key.
  • THE async health metric? — Consumer lag as time (oldest-message age / time-to-drain), not queue depth or CPU.
  • Poison message handling? — Bounded retries with backoff → DLQ with error context → alert → redrive tool.
  • Backpressure options in order? — Bound queues, scale consumers (≤ partitions), cheapen processing, then shed or push back on producers.
  • Event vs command? — Past-tense fact fanned out vs imperative addressed to one handler.
  • Fat vs thin event? — Embedded state (autonomy, staleness risk) vs ids-only (fresh, but callbacks re-couple and can herd).
  • Safe schema change? — Add optional fields with defaults via a registry compatibility check; breaking shapes go to a new versioned topic.
  • Event sourcing in one line? — Store the events, derive the state; projections are rebuildable views; snapshots make replay cheap.
  • When is event sourcing overkill? — When history isn't the product — default to CRUD + outbox.
  • Webhook reliability trio? — Retries with backoff over hours, HMAC signature + timestamp, stable event id for an idempotent receiver.
  • Cron on a fleet? — Leader-elect the tick, enqueue the work, make jobs idempotent per (job, tick) — failover may double-fire.
  • Correlation id? — The key that lets an async reply find its request — carried on every message and log line.

7️⃣ Reliability, Scale & Operations

Designing the boxes is half the interview; keeping them up is the other half — and the half where senior candidates separate from mid-level ones. This section builds the operational spine of any design: what "99.99%" actually costs, why averages lie about latency, how to refuse work gracefully (rate limits, shedding, breakers) instead of collapsing, how to ship changes and survive region loss, and how you would observe, scale, and run the thing on-call. Learn the math cards first — availability composition and tail latency drive almost every other decision here.

Availability math: nines, and the serial-multiplication trap

Why interviewers ask: "we need four nines" is a requirement candidates accept without doing the two multiplications that show whether it is even possible. The interviewer wants to see you convert nines to minutes, compose availabilities across a call chain, and notice that redundancy math assumes independence.

Availability = uptime ÷ total time, quoted in nines. The numbers to know cold: 99% ≈ 3.65 days down/year, 99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year (43 min/month), 99.95% ≈ 4.4 h/year, 99.99% ≈ 52.6 min/year (4.3 min/month), 99.999% ≈ 5.3 min/year. Each nine is roughly 10× the engineering and operational cost of the previous one — at five nines a human cannot be in the recovery loop at all (paging + login already spends the year's budget), so everything must auto-heal.

Serial composition: if a request must pass through services A → B → C and each is independent, the path availability is the product: five services at 99.9% give 0.9995 ≈ 99.5% ≈ 44 h down/year — you quietly lost a whole nine by drawing five boxes in a row. Add the database, DNS, the load balancer and the cloud provider itself and "99.99% overall" becomes arithmetic fiction unless the parts are better than the target or the chain gets shorter. Analogy: a convoy over five bridges — the trip fails if any one bridge is out, so trip reliability is worse than the worst bridge.

Parallel composition: redundancy multiplies unavailabilities: two independent 99.9% replicas where either can serve give 1 − (0.001)2 = 99.9999%. That is why the standard recipe is "shorten the serial chain, widen everything into redundant pools". The trap word is independent: two replicas behind the same bad deploy, the same overloaded database, the same AZ power feed, or the same expired TLS certificate fail together, and the real-world availability collapses back toward single-instance numbers. Correlated failure is why multi-AZ and multi-region exist, and why config/deploy pipelines (which touch all replicas at once) cause a large share of big outages.

AvailabilityDown/yearDown/30-day monthWhat it implies operationally
99% ("two nines")3.65 days7.2 hManual recovery fine; nightly maintenance windows OK
99.9%8.8 h43 minOn-call humans can still fix things; single region survivable
99.99%52.6 min4.3 minAutomated failover mandatory; multi-AZ; no downtime deploys
99.999%5.3 min26 sHumans out of the loop entirely; multi-region active-active; very expensive
Interview angle: when given an availability target, do the two computations out loud: "99.95% is ~4.4 h/year. Our path has 6 serial dependencies, so each needs ~99.99%, or we shorten the chain — cache pricing so it's off the critical path, make recommendations optional with a timeout, and pool every stateless tier." Turning nines into a design constraint is exactly the senior signal.

Pitfalls

  • Promising an SLA higher than the product of your critical dependencies (your DB's SLA, your cloud LB's SLA) — you cannot out-promise your own serial chain.
  • Counting redundancy as independent when replicas share a deploy pipeline, a config source, a cert, or a database — correlated failure is the norm, not the exception.
  • Quoting availability without a definition: measured how (probe success? request success rate?), over what window, and does degraded-but-serving count as up?
  • Chasing five nines on a product whose clients (mobile networks, browsers) fail more often than that — the extra nines are invisible to users and very expensive.
Interview questions
  • Your request path has 5 services at 99.9% each — what availability can you promise? — 0.999⁵ ≈ 99.5% (~44 h/year), assuming independence. To do better: shorten the chain (caches, async, optional dependencies), make each part better than the target, and add redundancy within each tier.
  • How much downtime is 99.99% per month? — About 4.3 minutes per 30-day month, 52.6 minutes per year. One botched 10-minute deploy blows two months of budget.
  • Two replicas at 99.9% — is the pair really 99.9999%? — Only if failures are independent. Same bad release, same AZ, same overloaded downstream all correlate; realistic gain is far smaller, which is why you separate failure domains (AZs, regions, staggered deploys).
  • How do you raise availability without touching the services themselves? — Remove serial dependencies from the critical path: serve stale from cache when a dependency is down, make non-essential calls best-effort with tight timeouts, precompute, and degrade features instead of failing requests (see graceful degradation).
  • Why does each extra nine cost ~10×? — The failure modes you must now survive get rarer and more correlated (AZ loss, region loss, operator error), and the remaining downtime budget gets too small for human response, forcing automation, redundancy, and drills.

SLI, SLO, SLA & error budgets: reliability as a number you spend

Why interviewers ask: "how reliable should it be?" has a professional vocabulary, and using it correctly signals you have run services, not just designed them. The error budget is the piece most candidates miss — it is what turns reliability from a religion into an engineering trade-off.

Three terms, three different things. An SLI (service level indicator) is a measurement: "fraction of HTTP requests answered successfully in < 300 ms, measured at the load balancer". An SLO (objective) is the internal target on that SLI: "99.9% over a rolling 28 days". An SLA (agreement) is the external contract with money attached: "< 99.5% monthly → 10% service credit". The SLA is always looser than the SLO — the SLO is your tripwire, the SLA is the lawyer's line. Good SLIs measure what users experience (success ratio, latency percentile at the edge), not what machines feel (CPU, node up/down).

The error budget is the SLO inverted: 99.9% over 28 days means 0.1% of requests — roughly 40 minutes of full outage, or proportionally more of partial failure — are allowed to fail. That budget is spent by incidents, risky deploys, and planned migrations alike. The classic budget policy: while budget remains, ship fast; when the budget is exhausted, feature launches pause and the team works on reliability until the window recovers. This resolves the eternal dev-vs-ops fight with arithmetic instead of arguments. Analogy: a monthly spending allowance — you can spend it on deploy risk or on outages, but when it's gone, austerity until payday.

Budgets also give you the right alerting signal: burn rate = how fast you are consuming budget relative to plan (burn rate 1 = exactly on budget). Page when the burn is fast (e.g. 14× — budget gone in 2 days) rather than on every blip; details in the observability card.

SLISLOSLA
WhatA measurement (ratio of good events / all events)Internal target for the SLI over a windowExternal contract with penalties
Example% of requests OK and < 300 ms at the LB99.9% over rolling 28 days99.5%/month or 10% credit
AudienceEngineers, dashboardsTeam + product (drives paging & budget)Customers, lawyers, sales
Breach means—Stop feature work, fix reliabilityPay out; reputational damage
Interview angle: when asked "how would you set the reliability target for this design", answer as a product question: "checkout gets a tight SLO (99.95%, p99 < 500 ms) because failures cost revenue; the recommendations panel gets 99% and is allowed to vanish. Then each SLO buys its own architecture — checkout gets multi-AZ and shed-everything-else priority; recommendations get a timeout and a fallback." Differentiated SLOs per endpoint is a strong senior move.

Pitfalls

  • SLOs on causes ("CPU < 80%") instead of user-visible symptoms (success rate, latency) — users don't experience your CPU.
  • 100% as a target. It forbids all deploys and all maintenance; every real system needs a nonzero failure allowance to change safely.
  • Measuring the SLI inside the service — you miss LB, DNS and network failures the user saw. Measure as close to the user as practical.
  • Having an error budget but no policy — a budget nobody acts on is a dashboard decoration, not a control loop.
Interview questions
  • Difference between SLO and SLA? — SLO is the internal engineering target that drives alerting and the error-budget policy; SLA is the looser external contract with financial penalties. You want to breach the SLO occasionally (it means it's honest), the SLA never.
  • What is an error budget and what is it for? — 1 − SLO over the window: the amount of failure you are allowed. It prices risk: deploys, migrations and experiments spend it; when it's gone, velocity yields to reliability work. It ends the "ops says freeze, dev says ship" argument with a number.
  • Pick SLIs for a checkout API. — Availability: % of requests with 2xx/expected-4xx at the edge; latency: % under 500 ms (a threshold SLI, not "p99 < 500", so the SLI stays a ratio); optionally durability/correctness for orders persisted. Windowed 28 days, measured at the LB.
  • Your team exhausted the month's error budget in week one. What happens? — Per policy: freeze risky launches, ship only reliability fixes, do a postmortem on the spend, and page thresholds tighten for the rest of the window. If this recurs, the SLO is wrong or the system needs investment.
  • Should internal microservices have SLAs? — SLOs yes (dependency planning needs them: your availability is capped by your serial dependencies — see nines math); contractual SLAs internally are theater, but published SLOs + error budgets per internal service work well.

p50/p95/p99 & tail-latency amplification in fan-outs

Why interviewers ask: latency questions are where "we'll add more servers" answers die. Averages hide the users who suffer; and the moment your design fans one request out to N backends, rare slowness stops being rare — the interviewer wants the 0.99100 insight and the mitigations by name.

Percentiles, not averages. p50 (median) is the typical experience; p95/p99 are the worst 5%/1%. Latency distributions are heavily right-skewed — GC pauses, cache misses, page faults, queueing, a hot row — so the mean is dragged by outliers yet tells you nothing actionable: a service with mean 20 ms can have p99 = 2 s. Worse, your best customers hit the tail most: heavy users make more requests, so the probability that a session contains a p99 event approaches 1. That's why SLOs bind percentiles ("99% of requests < 300 ms"), never means. Also know that percentiles don't average across hosts or windows — you must aggregate histograms, not average each node's p99.

Amplification. A request that fans out to N backends and must wait for all of them runs at the speed of the slowest. If each backend is slow (worse than its own p99) 1% of the time, the probability that a fan-out of 100 avoids all slowness is 0.99100 ≈ 37% — so 63% of user requests experience at least one backend's p99. The backend's 1% tail becomes the front end's median. This is Dean & Barroso's "The Tail at Scale" result, and it is the hidden cost of every scatter-gather search, feed aggregation, and 100-shard query in your design. Even a fan-out of 10 pays: 0.9910 ≈ 90%, so p99-level slowness now hits ~10% of requests — your p99 became your p90.

Mitigations, in the order to say them: shrink the fan-out (better partitioning, denormalized/precomputed views); cut the per-node tail (bound queues, avoid GC spikes, separate hot paths); hedged requests — after ~p95 waiting, duplicate the straggler to another replica and take the first answer, cancelling the loser (a few % extra load for a huge p99 cut; idempotent reads only — mechanics in §2 timeouts & retries); and partial results — answer with 98 of 100 shards inside the deadline and mark the response incomplete (search engines do exactly this). Analogy: a group photo where each person blinks 1% of the time — with 100 people, most photos have someone blinking; you fix it by taking two shots (hedging) or cropping the blinkers out (partial results).

Interview angle: drop the arithmetic proactively whenever your design fans out: "feed read hits ~40 shards; 0.99⁴⁰ ≈ 67%, so a third of reads would see a shard's p99 — I'll hedge at p95 and cap fan-out latency with a 150 ms partial-results deadline." One sentence, and you've pre-empted the entire latency probe. Also say how you'd see it: latency histograms per shard, not averages.

Pitfalls

  • Reporting or alerting on average latency — it hides bimodal distributions entirely (fast cache hits + slow misses average to a number nobody experiences).
  • Averaging p99s across hosts or time windows — percentiles don't compose; merge histograms/HDR sketches instead.
  • Hedging writes, or hedging without cancellation — you duplicate load precisely when replicas are struggling (see retry storms).
  • Fixing tail latency by raising timeouts — you've converted "fast failure" into "slow success at best, thread exhaustion at worst".
Interview questions
  • Why do we track p99 instead of average latency? — Distributions are right-skewed, so the mean describes nobody: it's dragged up by outliers but hides them. p99 bounds what your unluckiest 1% — and your heaviest users, who make the most requests — actually experience.
  • Your service fans out to 30 backends, each with p99 = 400 ms. What's the user's experience? — 0.99³⁰ ≈ 74%: about a quarter of requests wait ~400 ms+. Mitigate: hedge stragglers at ~p95, use partial results with a deadline, reduce fan-out, and attack each backend's tail causes.
  • What are hedged requests, and when are they safe? — Send a duplicate to another replica after waiting ~p95, keep the first answer, cancel the other. Safe for idempotent reads with capacity headroom; unsafe for writes or an already-overloaded fleet.
  • Why might p99 be terrible while p50 is great? — Tail causes are episodic: GC/compaction pauses, cold caches, lock contention, queue buildup, hot keys, connection re-establishment. Bimodality is the signature — look at the histogram, not summary stats.
  • How do you aggregate p99 across 200 pods? — You can't average per-pod p99s. Export histograms (Prometheus buckets, HDRHistogram, t-digest) and compute the percentile over the merged distribution.
  • Interviewer: "just cache it" — does caching fix tail latency? — It lowers p50 and can worsen relative tails: misses now include a failed lookup plus the origin call, and stampedes on hot-key expiry create tail spikes. Caching helps only with coalescing and stampede protection designed in.

Rate limiting algorithms: token bucket, leaky bucket & the window bug

Why interviewers ask: "design a rate limiter" is a complete interview question at many companies, and inside any design "how do you protect this API?" is guaranteed. The discriminating detail is the fixed-window boundary burst and knowing which algorithm tolerates bursts on purpose.

Token bucket (the industry default — Guava RateLimiter, Envoy, AWS API Gateway, NICs): a bucket holds up to B tokens, refilled at r tokens/sec; each request takes one token, no token → reject (or briefly wait). Two knobs, two meanings: r is the sustained rate, B the burst allowance — a client that was idle can spend saved-up tokens in one burst of B, then is held to r. State per key is tiny: token count + last-refill timestamp (refill computed lazily on access). Leaky bucket is the mirror image: requests enter a queue that drains at a fixed rate — output is perfectly smooth, bursts wait in the queue (adding latency) or overflow. Use token bucket to admit bursty-but-bounded traffic; leaky bucket to shape a perfectly even outflow toward a fragile downstream.

Fixed window: a counter per key per interval — "100 per minute" as INCR user:42:12:05 with a 60 s expiry. Cheap and obvious, but it has the boundary-burst bug: 100 requests at 12:05:59 and 100 more at 12:06:01 are both legal — 200 requests in two seconds, 2× the intended limit, exactly the kind of burst limits exist to stop. Sliding window log fixes it exactly by storing every request timestamp and counting the last 60 s — correct but O(rate) memory per key. The practical compromise is the sliding window counter: keep this window's and the previous window's counters and weight them — count = curr + prev × (overlap fraction) — approximately correct, two integers of state, no boundary hole. Analogy: token bucket is a prepaid card that tops up steadily and lets you splurge your balance; fixed window is a bouncer who forgets everyone at the top of each hour.

Rejecting well is part of the algorithm: respond 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header (seconds until tokens exist) and quota headers (X-RateLimit-Limit / -Remaining / -Reset, or the standardized RateLimit-* drafts) so well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering; a limiter without Retry-After converts polite clients into a retry storm. Rejection must be cheap — the whole point of admission control is refusing work in microseconds at the edge instead of failing it after burning a thread, a DB connection and 500 ms.

AlgorithmState per keyBurstsBoundary bug?Use when
Token bucket2 numbers (tokens, last refill)Allowed up to B, then sustained rNoDefault for APIs; burst-friendly admission
Leaky bucket (queue)Queue + drain rateSmoothed — queued or droppedNoShaping outflow to a fragile downstream
Fixed window1 counterUp to 2× limit across a boundaryYesCheap rough limits; long windows (quotas)
Sliding window logAll timestamps in windowExactNoLow-rate, high-value limits (logins)
Sliding window counter2 counters~Exact (weighted approx.)NoHigh-rate limits needing fairness cheaply
Interview angle: the model answer shape: "token bucket per API key, B = 20, r = 10/s, enforced at the gateway; 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-Remaining headers; login endpoint gets a sliding-window log per user+IP because exactness matters more than memory there." Naming B and r separately — burst vs sustained — is the detail that reads as senior.

Pitfalls

  • Fixed windows for short intervals — the 2×-at-the-boundary leak defeats the protective purpose; keep fixed windows for long-period quotas only.
  • Rejecting without Retry-After — clients guess, guess wrong, and synchronize into a retry wave (see §2).
  • B = r (no burst headroom) breaks legitimate clients that batch; B ≫ r makes the "limit" meaningless for a whole burst window. Size B as ~1–2 s of r for interactive APIs.
  • Limiting after expensive work (auth, deserialization, DB touch) — admission control must be the first, cheapest gate in the request path.
Interview questions
  • Token bucket vs leaky bucket in one line each? — Token bucket admits bursts up to B while capping the sustained rate at r; leaky bucket emits at a perfectly constant rate, queueing or dropping bursts. Admission vs traffic shaping.
  • Explain the fixed-window problem with "100 req/min". — 100 requests at 0:59.9 and 100 at 1:00.1 both pass — 200 in ~0.2 s, 2× the limit, because the counter forgets history at the boundary. Sliding window log/counter or token bucket fix it.
  • A client bursts 1000 requests after being idle an hour — should they pass? — Product decision encoded in B: with token bucket, at most B pass instantly and the rest are paced at r. If replays after downtime are legitimate (IoT flushes), size B for them or offer a bulk endpoint instead.
  • What should a 429 response contain? — Retry-After (seconds or date), remaining-quota headers, and a machine-readable error body naming the limit hit. Well-behaved SDKs then back off with jitter instead of hammering.
  • Quota vs rate limit? — Rate limits protect systems over seconds (10 req/s, token bucket, in-memory/Redis); quotas meter business usage over long windows (1M calls/month, durable counter, billing-grade accuracy, warn-then-block UX). Different windows, different storage, different failure stakes.
  • Where would you NOT rate limit? — Internal hop-by-hop between your own services as a first resort — prefer backpressure, load shedding and circuit breakers (next cards); layered hard limits inside a call chain amplify partial failure and are hard to reason about.

Distributed rate limiting: local vs global, keys, and where in the stack

Why interviewers ask: "10k req/s per customer, enforced across 40 edge nodes" is a mini distributed-systems problem hiding inside an ops feature: shared state, races, hot keys, and a failure-mode decision (fail open or closed?). It's a favorite because the naive answer — "just count in Redis" — invites every follow-up.

Local limiting (each node divides the limit by node count) is free and fast but wrong under skew: with 40 edges and a 10k/s customer limit, 250/s per node throttles a customer whose traffic happens to concentrate on a few nodes long before they reach 10k globally — and autoscaling changes the divisor under you. Global limiting keeps the counter in a shared store, almost always Redis: the naive GET-then-SET is a textbook race window (two nodes read 99, both admit, both write 100), so the check-and-decrement must be atomic — a Lua script (or Redis functions/CL.THROTTLE in redis-cell) that reads the bucket, computes lazy refill from the stored timestamp, decides, and writes back in one server-side step. Cost: one Redis round trip (~0.3–1 ms same-DC) per decision plus a hot key per big customer — shard buckets by key across a Redis cluster, and remember one customer's bucket still lands on one shard.

The production pattern is a hybrid: local token buckets that sync asynchronously with the global store — each edge serves decisions from its local bucket and periodically (e.g. every 100 ms) reconciles spent tokens with Redis, or a central service pushes per-node allowances based on observed distribution (Envoy's global rate limit service, Kong/Cloudflare-style "eventually consistent" counters). You trade a small, bounded overshoot (a burst can exceed the global limit by roughly one sync interval's worth) for zero added latency and survival of the limiter's own outages. Which leads to the question you must answer in an interview: fail open or fail closed? If Redis is down, protective rate limits should fail open (serve traffic, log loudly) — the limiter must never be the outage; billing quotas and abuse/login limits fail closed.

Choosing the key is a design decision, not a detail: per-user/API-key for fairness and billing; per-IP only as an anti-abuse backstop (NATs and CGNAT make IPs shared, botnets make them plentiful); per-tenant to stop one noisy tenant starving a multi-tenant cell; and compound keys for precision (tenant:endpoint so a bulk-export endpoint can't consume the tenant's interactive budget). Placement is layered: CDN/edge kills volumetric abuse cheaply; the API gateway holds the authoritative per-customer business limits (it knows identity after auth); services keep small self-protective concurrency limits; and per-dependency limits shield fragile downstreams. Analogy: stadium security — a perimeter fence (edge), ticket gates (gateway), and per-section stewards (service), not one giant queue at a single gate.

ApproachAccuracyAdded latencySurvives limiter outage?Use for
Local only (limit ÷ N nodes)Poor under skew; breaks on autoscaleNoneYesPer-node self-protection
Global sync (Redis + Lua per request)Exact (atomic)~0.5–1 ms/requestMust choose fail-open/closedStrict business limits, login throttles
Local buckets + async global syncBounded overshoot (~1 sync interval)None on hot pathYes (degrades to local)High-volume edges/gateways — the default
Interview angle: the crisp answer to "40 edge nodes, 10k/s per customer": "local token buckets per customer on each edge, async-reconciled to Redis every 100 ms; worst-case overshoot ≈ one interval of the aggregate burst (~1k requests), which I'll accept; login and payment endpoints use synchronous atomic Redis checks; Redis down → protective limits fail open with an alert, billing quota decisions queue for reconciliation." You've named the consistency trade-off, the race fix, and the failure policy in three sentences.

Pitfalls

  • Non-atomic read-modify-write on the shared counter — the race window admits bursts precisely at the limit boundary; use Lua/CAS server-side.
  • One global Redis in another region — you added 60 ms to every request to save a counter; keep the limiter store region-local (limits are per-region anyway, or reconciled).
  • Rate limiting by IP as the primary key — corporate NATs get throttled as one "user" while attackers rotate through thousands of IPs.
  • Failing closed on limiter-store outage for ordinary traffic — the rate limiter becomes your lowest-availability serial dependency (see nines math).
Interview questions
  • Why not just divide the global limit across nodes? — Traffic skew: consistent hashing, geography, and sticky connections concentrate a customer on few nodes, throttling them far below the promised aggregate; and the divisor changes whenever the fleet autoscales.
  • How do you make a Redis rate-limit check race-free? — Do the whole read-refill-decide-write as one atomic server-side operation: a Lua script (or redis-cell's CL.THROTTLE) keyed on the bucket; never GET then SET from the client.
  • What happens to rate limiting when Redis dies? — Decide per limit class ahead of time: protective limits fail open (never be the outage), abuse/billing limits fail closed or degrade to conservative local limits; alert either way. Saying "it depends, and here's the split" is the senior answer.
  • A single customer is 30% of your traffic — what breaks in the limiter? — Their bucket is a hot key on one Redis shard. Fixes: local+async-sync for that key, split the bucket into per-node sub-allowances, or move the tenant to a dedicated cell (blast radius card).
  • Rate limit before or after authentication? — Both: a cheap per-IP/connection ceiling before auth (or you can be DoS'd by unauthenticated traffic), the real per-identity limits right after auth at the gateway.
  • How does a customer-facing quota differ in implementation from a rate limit? — Quota needs durable, exactly-reconciled counting (billing disputes), long windows, warning thresholds at 80/90%, and grace behavior; a protective rate limit tolerates approximation and forgets state in seconds.

Overload protection: shedding, breakers, bulkheads & graceful degradation

Why interviewers ask: every system is eventually offered more load than it has capacity — the question is whether it degrades or collapses. "Black Friday hits, you're at 120% capacity — what happens?" checks whether you'd rather serve 80% of users well than 100% of users a timeout.

The core theorem of overload: past saturation, trying to serve everything means serving nothing — queues grow, latency exceeds client timeouts, clients retry, and goodput falls toward zero while the servers are 100% busy doing work nobody is waiting for. Load shedding is the fix: explicitly reject a slice of offered load, cheaply and early, to keep the rest inside capacity. Shed by priority first — tag requests at the edge (checkout > browse > recommendations > batch/crawler) and drop lowest tiers first; shed by percentage when priorities tie ("drop 30% of tier-3"); and trigger on saturation signals — queue depth, concurrency in flight, p99 vs SLO — not CPU alone. A shed request costs microseconds and gets an honest 503/429 + Retry-After; an accepted-then-timed-out request costs a thread, downstream work, and a retry.

Circuit breakers protect the caller from a sick dependency: track the recent error/slow-call rate per dependency; past a threshold, open — fail fast or serve fallback without calling at all — then after a cool-down go half-open, letting a few probes through; success closes the breaker. This removes pressure from the struggling service (letting it recover) and stops your own threads queueing on a black hole. In the Java world this is Resilience4j — sliding windows, state machine, thresholds and Spring annotations are covered in the Spring Boot guide's Resilience4j card. Bulkheads bound the blast radius inside your process: give each downstream its own connection/thread/semaphore pool so a hung Payments API can exhaust its 20 permits, not the shared 200 — the ship-compartment principle: flood one compartment, not the hull.

Graceful degradation is the product-visible tier of the same idea — decided before the incident, executed by switches during it: read-only mode (browsing works, writes disabled during a DB failover); stale-while-degraded — serve cached/last-known-good data past its TTL with a banner rather than erroring (prices from 10 minutes ago beat no prices); feature kill switches — flags that instantly turn off recommendations, search facets, or image richness to shed their cost; and simplified fallbacks (default shipping estimate instead of the ML model). Analogy: a hospital in a disaster switches to triage — it does not treat patients in arrival order until the ER collapses.

MechanismProtectsTriggerUnit of sacrifice
Load sheddingThe service itselfSaturation: queue depth, in-flight concurrency, SLO burnLow-priority requests
Circuit breakerThe caller (and the sick callee)Error/slow rate to one dependencyCalls to that dependency (fallback instead)
BulkheadOther paths in the same processPer-dependency pool exhaustedConcurrency for that dependency only
Graceful degradationThe user experienceOperator switch or automated brownoutFeatures, freshness, write ability
Interview angle: for an e-commerce design, enumerate the degradation ladder unprompted: "at 100% capacity: shed crawlers and batch; at 110%: kill recommendations and reviews (flag), serve prices from cache with 10-min staleness; at 130%: read-only browse + queue orders for async confirmation; checkout is the last thing standing." Having a pre-decided ladder is the difference between an outage and a brownout — and interviewers score it as operational maturity.

Pitfalls

  • Shedding late and deep in the stack — by then the request has burned edge, gateway and service resources; reject at the first hop that can make the decision.
  • Uniform shedding — dropping 20% of everything drops 20% of checkouts; priority tags must ride the request from the edge.
  • Breakers without fallbacks — an open breaker that just throws converts "slow" into "instant error"; pair it with cache/stale/default responses where the product allows.
  • One shared thread/connection pool for all downstreams — the slowest dependency eventually owns every thread; that's the anti-bulkhead.
  • Kill switches that were never tested — a flag flipped for the first time during an incident is itself a deploy (see config as a deploy).
Interview questions
  • Load shedding vs rate limiting — aren't they the same? — Rate limiting enforces a per-client contract at admission regardless of health; shedding is a health-triggered global valve that drops load by priority when saturated. You want both: limits for fairness, shedding for survival.
  • How does a circuit breaker decide to open, and what does half-open mean? — It tracks failure/slow-call rate over a sliding window (e.g. ≥50% of the last 100 calls); open = fail fast, no calls; after a wait, half-open admits a few probe calls — success closes it, failure re-opens. (Implementation details: Resilience4j.)
  • What saturation signal would you shed on, and why not CPU? — In-flight concurrency or queue depth/wait-time against a measured capacity limit; CPU misses I/O-bound saturation (threads all blocked on a slow DB at 15% CPU) and lags the queue growth that is already killing latency.
  • Design read-only mode for a shopping site. — A global flag checked at the write edges: carts become session-local, orders queue to a durable buffer with "confirmation by email", browse/search serve from replicas and cache. Practice the flag monthly; make banners honest.
  • Why serve stale cache data during an incident? — Availability beats freshness for most read paths: a 10-minute-old product page is worth ~a fresh one; an error page is worth zero. Bound the staleness, label it, and exclude correctness-critical reads (account balance, inventory at checkout).
  • When do bulkheads matter most? — Fan-out services calling many dependencies with shared pools: one hung dependency plus unbounded concurrency = total thread starvation. Per-dependency semaphores/pools cap the damage at that dependency's allotment.

Retry storms & metastable failures: why systems stay down after the cause is fixed

Why interviewers ask: the scariest production pattern is the outage that persists after the trigger is gone — the DB recovered an hour ago and the site is still down. Explaining why (retry amplification + cold caches sustain the overload) and how to exit (shed, don't scale) is deep operational signal that reads as "has lived through one".

A metastable failure has three parts: a system running in a fragile-but-fine state; a trigger (a slow query, a deploy, a brief network blip) that pushes it into overload; and — the defining part — a sustaining effect that keeps it overloaded after the trigger is removed. The commonest sustaining effect is the retry storm: latency exceeds client timeouts → every request becomes 3–4 attempts (multiplied per layer — see the 3N math in §2) → offered load triples exactly when capacity halved. Close behind: cold caches (a restarted cache turns 95% hits into 100% DB misses — the DB now needs 20× its steady-state capacity to warm the cache it normally hides behind) and connection re-establishment storms (TLS handshakes are 10–100× the CPU of a request on an idle pool).

The mechanism is a feedback loop through your own clients: work amplification grows with latency, so the overloaded state is self-reinforcing — the system has two stable equilibria (healthy: 1× load, low latency; congested: 3–4× offered load, timeouts, ~zero goodput) and cannot climb back to the good one on its own because every unit of work it completes has already been abandoned and retried. Servers show 100% utilization and 0% goodput. Analogy: a crowd-crush at an exit — the fire (trigger) is out, but everyone pushing (retries) keeps the door jammed; the only fix is fewer people pushing, not a wider door.

Exit and prevention. You exit by breaking the loop, which is counter-intuitive: shed load below true capacity (reject 50%+ cheaply at the edge), open circuit breakers to stop internal retries, disable client retries via a flag, and let queues drain — then ramp admission back up gradually. Scaling out mid-storm often fails: new instances arrive with cold caches and empty connection pools and are instantly drowned. Prevention is the whole toolbox wired together as end-to-end backpressure: bounded queues and concurrency limits at every hop (so overload surfaces as fast rejection, not queued latency), deadline propagation (stop working on abandoned requests), retry budgets not retry counts, jitter everywhere, breakers between layers, and shed-by-priority at the front door. Backpressure in async pipelines is the same principle on queues — see §6.

Interview angle: this is the model answer to "walk me through a production outage you'd expect at scale". Name the three phases (trigger → amplification → sustaining effect), give the numbers (3× retry load, 95%→0% cache hits = 20× DB load), and state the counter-intuitive fix: "recovery required rejecting most traffic for four minutes — the hardest part is convincing people that serving less is the way to serve more." Facebook/Meta's metastable-failures papers made this vocabulary standard.

Pitfalls

  • Unbounded queues anywhere in the chain — they convert overload into latency, which converts into timeouts, which convert into retries: the storm's fuel line.
  • Retry counts per layer instead of a retry budget — 3 retries at each of 4 layers is 81× amplification at the bottom during a brownout.
  • Responding to the storm by autoscaling — cold instances raise aggregate demand (cache fill, connection setup) before they add capacity.
  • No admission ramp after recovery — lifting the shed at once re-drowns the warm-but-fragile system; step back up 10–20% at a time watching goodput.
Interview questions
  • Define a metastable failure. — An overload state that persists after its trigger is removed because a feedback loop (retries, cold caches, reconnect storms) sustains demand above capacity; the system is stable in the bad state and won't recover without intervention that breaks the loop.
  • Why did goodput go to zero while CPU stayed at 100%? — All completed work belonged to requests whose callers had already timed out and retried; the system was busy producing answers nobody was waiting for, and each abandonment spawned more offered load.
  • Cache cluster restarted and the DB fell over — connect the dots. — At 95% hit ratio the DB sees 5% of reads; cold cache sends it 100% — a 20× read spike it was never sized for. Prevention: cache warm-up before taking traffic, request coalescing, replica pools sized for a bounded miss surge, gradual key-space cutover.
  • What single mechanism best prevents retry storms? — A retry budget (retries ≤ ~10% of requests, per client) with full jitter, plus circuit breakers so layered retries can't compound. Deadline propagation then stops work on abandoned requests.
  • How would you get out of one, step by step? — Declare the incident, shed to well below measured capacity at the outermost layer, disable retries via flag, open breakers, drain queues, re-warm caches, then raise admission gradually watching goodput and p99 — and afterwards fix the sustaining loop, not just the trigger.
  • How do you test that you're not vulnerable? — Load tests past saturation (does goodput plateau or collapse?), chaos drills that slow — not kill — a dependency (brownouts find these bugs; blackouts don't), and verifying every queue and pool has a bound and a shed path (game days).

Deployment safety: blue/green, canary, flags & expand/contract migrations

Why interviewers ask: change causes most outages — far more than hardware. "How do you ship without breaking your SLO?" tests whether you treat deploys as a controlled experiment (small blast radius, automatic verdict, instant undo) or as a leap of faith.

Three traffic-shifting strategies. Rolling: replace instances a few at a time (k8s' default; maxSurge/maxUnavailable) — cheap, no extra fleet, but both versions serve mixed traffic for a while and rollback means rolling again (slow). Blue/green: run the full new fleet (green) beside the old (blue), switch traffic atomically at the LB, keep blue warm for instant rollback — fastest undo, but 2× capacity during the deploy and the "atomic" switch sends 100% of users to a version that has served 0% of them. Canary: the senior default — send 1% → 5% → 25% → 100% to the new version, comparing the canary's metrics against the baseline at each step, with automated rollback when the canary's error rate or latency burns the SLO (Argo Rollouts, Spinnaker's automated canary analysis, Flagger). The judge must be a machine: humans watching dashboards at 2 am approve everything.

Feature flags decouple deploy (code reaches production, dark) from release (users see it): ship continuously, enable per-cohort (employees → 1% → region → all), and kill a bad feature in seconds without a rollback — the fastest MTTR of any mechanism. Costs: flag debt (dead flags must be deleted), combinatorial testing, and the discipline that a flag flip is a deploy — staged, observed, revertible. Which generalizes: config is a deploy. Config and flag pushes cause a large share of famous outages precisely because they skip the deploy pipeline — so canary config changes too, version them, validate schemas before push, and never push config globally in one shot.

Schema migrations are where "just roll back" dies: during any rollout, old and new code run simultaneously against one database, so every schema change must be compatible with both. The expand/contract pattern: (1) expand — add the new nullable column/table/index (backwards-compatible, no code depends on it yet); (2) migrate — deploy code that writes both old and new, backfill history in batches; (3) switch reads to the new shape behind a flag, verify; (4) contract — after the old path has been cold for a full rollback horizon, drop old columns. Never rename in place, never add NOT NULL without a default, never drop anything the previous release still reads. Analogy: renovating a bridge while traffic drives on it — build the new lane alongside, shift traffic, then demolish the old lane; you never close the bridge.

StrategyExtra capacityRollback speedBlast radiusCatch
Rolling~0 (surge 1–2 pods)Slow (roll again)Grows with each batchMixed versions serve together; slow undo
Blue/green2× during deployInstant (switch back)100% at the moment of switchNo gradual validation; DB shared by both
Canary + auto-analysis~1 pod + toolingInstant (weight to 0)1–10% per stageNeeds enough traffic for significance; metrics discipline
Feature flag release0Seconds (flip off)Chosen cohortFlag debt; flips are themselves risky changes
