Interview angle: tie it back to the error budget: "99.99% gives us 4.3 min/month; a bad full rollout with a 10-minute MTTR spends 2 months of budget, a 10% canary auto-rolled-back in 4 minutes spends ~1%. So the SLO effectively mandates canaries + automated rollback." Deriving process from arithmetic is exactly what staff-level interviewers reward.

Pitfalls

  • Canary judged by a human dashboard — at 2 am everything "looks fine"; codify pass/fail thresholds and let the controller act.
  • Schema change and code change in one release — the previous version instantly becomes un-deployable, so rollback (your main safety net) is gone at the worst moment.
  • Canary too small to detect anything: 1% of 1000 RPS = 10 RPS; at 0.5% error rate you need minutes for significance — size stages and dwell times to traffic.
  • Config/flag pushes bypassing the pipeline — global, instant, unversioned config is how you take down all regions at once; stage it like code.
  • State-mutating jobs (migrations, backfills) treated as deploys without their own rollback plan — a backfill needs rate limits, checkpoints, and an abort switch.
Interview questions
  • Blue/green vs canary — when each? — Blue/green for instant-switch needs, small fleets, or stateful cutovers where mixed versions are unacceptable (and you can afford 2×); canary when you want statistical validation with minimal blast radius — the default for high-traffic stateless services.
  • Walk me through a zero-downtime column rename. — Expand/contract: add new column (nullable) → deploy dual-write → backfill in batches → switch reads via flag → verify parity → stop old writes → after a full rollback horizon, drop the old column. Five deploys, each individually revertible.
  • What triggers your automated rollback? — Canary-vs-baseline deltas (error rate, p99) and SLO burn rate over short windows, evaluated per stage; plus hard gates like crash-loop/readiness failures. Thresholds pre-agreed, action automatic, humans notified after.
  • Feature flags vs deploys — how do they interact? — Deploy = code to prod (dark); release = flag on per cohort. You ship small diffs continuously and control exposure independently; kill switch MTTR is seconds. Discipline: flags expire, flips are staged and observed like deploys.
  • Why do config changes cause so many major outages? — They're global, instant, often unvalidated and outside the canary pipeline — the exact opposite of safe code deploys — while being just as able to change behavior. Treat config as code: schema-validate, version, canary, auto-rollback.
  • Both old and new versions are serving during a rollout — what must be compatible? — The DB schema (expand/contract), API/event contracts with peers (additive changes only), cache entry formats (version keys), and session/state blobs — anything both versions read or write concurrently.

Multi-region architecture: active-passive vs active-active & the failover

Why interviewers ask: "what if the region goes down?" is the final boss of availability probes. The answer forces every trade-off you know — consistency vs latency (you cannot sync-replicate OLTP writes across 70 ms), cost vs RTO, and the ugly truth that failover itself is the riskiest operation you own.

Start with the physics: cross-region RTT is ~50–150 ms (us-east↔us-west ~60–70 ms, US↔EU ~80–100 ms) vs ~0.5 ms within a DC. Synchronous cross-region replication for OLTP writes is therefore off the table for interactive traffic: every commit would pay ≥1 cross-region round trip — 70 ms+ added to each write, and row locks held ~100× longer collapse throughput on contended rows. So per tier you choose: stateless services — run everywhere, trivially active-active; caches — region-local, warm independently (never replicate a cache across regions); OLTP data — asynchronous replication with seconds of lag (accepting RPO > 0), or consensus-per-shard systems (Spanner, CockroachDB) that pay quorum latency on writes for RPO = 0; async/event traffic — replicate topics (MirrorMaker-style), tolerate reordering at the seams.

Topologies. Active-passive: one region serves everything, a standby replicates asynchronously; simple mental model, 100% of paid standby capacity idle, and the failover path is rare and scary (see §5 HA topologies for warm/hot variants and who decides). Active-active: all regions take traffic — capacity fully used, region loss is "shift the weights" — but writes need an answer to "which region owns this row?" The workable middle is region-local reads, home-region writes: every user (or tenant) is pinned to a home region that owns their writes (routing layer maps user → home); reads serve region-locally from async replicas with bounded staleness; cross-user interactions become async messages between regions. This gives active-active capacity for the read-heavy 95% while keeping single-writer semantics per key — and it doubles as a data-residency answer (EU users homed in EU). Truly global mutable state (a worldwide username set, global inventory counts) is minimized, then handled with consensus or CRDTs (§3 multi-leader).

The failover itself is a rehearsed runbook, not an if-statement: detect (external multi-vantage probes, not the sick region's own monitors) → decide (a human or quorum declares — automatic full-region failover is rare because false positives are catastrophic) → fence the old region's writers (revoke leases, block writes — split brain across regions is unrecoverable divergence) → promote replicas → shift traffic (DNS with 60 s TTLs honored loosely — budget minutes; anycast/global LBs converge in seconds and are why big platforms front with them) → reconcile: the async lag at failure time (say 2 s) is orphaned committed writes — recover them from the old region's WAL when it returns, replay idempotently, or compensate (apology email beats silent loss). Cost: multi-region ≈ ≥2× infra + egress fees + the engineering tax of testing failover quarterly — which is why the honest senior answer is often "this product needs multi-AZ, not multi-region". Analogy: a second airport for a city — you don't build it to be half-empty "just in case"; you either route real traffic through both every day, or accept that the emergency-only one won't work when you finally need it.

TierMulti-region strategyWhy
Stateless servicesActive-active everywhereNo state → free to replicate; capacity where users are
CachesRegion-local, independent warm-upReplicating caches ships staleness at RTT cost for no benefit
OLTP writesHome-region per user/tenant, async replicas elsewhere (or consensus DB paying write latency)Sync cross-region = +70 ms/commit and lock-throughput collapse
ReadsRegion-local from async replicas, bounded staleness95% of traffic gets local latency; staleness is priced in
Events/queuesPer-region clusters + cross-region mirroringOrdering guaranteed within region; seams are async anyway
Object storageCross-region replication (async, provider-managed)Immutable blobs tolerate lag; cheap relative to DB replication
Interview angle: the latency math is your opening move: "US↔EU is ~90 ms RTT, so synchronous writes are out — I'll pin each user to a home region for writes, serve reads region-locally with ~2 s staleness, and accept RPO ≈ replication lag for region loss, RTO ≈ 5 min via runbook + global LB. Truly global state — the username namespace — goes in a small consensus store because it's low-write." Then volunteer the cost caveat: "if the SLA only needs 99.9%, multi-AZ single-region is the right answer and saves 2×."

Pitfalls

  • "We'll sync-replicate to be safe" — across regions this adds RTT to every commit and destroys contended-row throughput; nobody runs interactive OLTP this way.
  • A passive region that never takes real traffic — config drift, stale capacity, expired quotas: the failover fails at the worst moment. Route some real traffic through it or drill quarterly.
  • Failing over the app tier but not its dependencies (feature-flag service, auth, rate limiter store) — the app comes up in B and dies calling A.
  • Auto-failback the moment A looks healthy — you re-split the brain during A's flapping recovery; fail back deliberately, off-peak, as its own runbook.
  • Forgetting the humans: if the failover tooling itself runs only in region A, you cannot fail over out of A.
Interview questions
  • Why can't you synchronously replicate OLTP writes across regions? — Each commit waits ≥1 cross-region RTT (~70–150 ms), and locks held that long serialize contended rows to ~10 writes/s. Either accept async (RPO > 0) or pay quorum write latency in a consensus DB for the data that truly needs RPO = 0.
  • Active-active writes to the same row from two regions — what happens? — Multi-leader conflict: last-writer-wins silently loses data, CRDTs need commutative semantics, app-level merge is per-field pain (§3). The standard dodge: don't — pin each key's writes to one home region.
  • Define RTO and RPO for your design and what sets each. — RPO = data-loss window = replication lag at failure (async: seconds; sync/quorum: 0). RTO = detection + decision + fencing/promotion + traffic switch + warm-up; dominated by decision (humans) and DNS unless you have global LBs and drilled runbooks. (Also §5.)
  • DNS failover vs anycast — trade-off? — DNS is universal and cheap but converges in minutes (TTL disobedience, resolver caches, apps caching lookups); anycast/global LB withdraws the sick region in seconds but requires owning that layer. Serious RTOs use anycast/GSLB with DNS as fallback.
  • How do you handle the writes lost to replication lag? — Fence A, then when it returns diff its WAL past B's applied position: replay idempotently where safe (idempotency keys — §5), compensate where not (notify user, refund), and report the realized RPO in the postmortem.
  • Interviewer pushes: "make it five regions, active-active, strongly consistent, fast writes." — Name the impossibility politely: consistency + cross-region quorum = write latency ≥ RTT to a majority; you can pick per-dataset. Propose: home-region writes + local reads for user data, a consensus store for the tiny global-invariant set, CRDTs for counters/presence.
  • What does multi-region actually cost? — ≥2× infrastructure (capacity to absorb a region's load), cross-region egress on every replicated byte, plus the ongoing tax: quarterly failover drills, dual-region deploy pipelines, per-region quotas — which is why the first question is whether the SLO requires it at all.

Disaster recovery: backups that restore, and practicing failure on purpose

Why interviewers ask: replication is not backup — replicas faithfully replicate your DROP TABLE, your ransomware encryption, and your buggy migration to every copy in milliseconds. "How do you recover from an operator deleting the users table?" tests the layer below HA that most designs forget.

Backup tiers. Snapshots — periodic full/incremental images (nightly + hourly incrementals): cheap, simple, but RPO = the interval (up to 24 h of loss) and restores are all-or-nothing. PITR (point-in-time recovery) — a base snapshot plus a continuous WAL/binlog archive: replay the log to any second, so RPO ≈ seconds and, crucially, you can stop replay at 13:59, one second before the bad migration ran. That "restore to just before the mistake" ability is the whole reason PITR exists — a replica can never give it to you, because the replica already applied the mistake. Layer them: PITR for the OLTP tier, snapshots for everything else, with retention laddered (hourly for days, daily for a month, monthly for years/compliance).

"Backups you haven't restored don't exist." Untested backups fail in boring ways: silent job failures for months, missing WAL segments, backups that depend on a KMS key that was deleted, restore times of 20 hours discovered during the outage, schema/version mismatches. So: automated restore testing — periodically restore into a scratch environment, run checksums/row counts, and record the measured restore time; that number, not hope, is your DR RTO (restoring 10 TB at ~200 MB/s is ~14 hours — if your RTO is 1 h you need warm standbys or parallel/partitioned restore, not just "we have backups"). Guard the data's write path too: deletion protection — soft delete with delayed purge, MFA/two-person deletes on backup storage, provider deletion-protection flags on databases.

Ransomware & the malicious case change the threat model: an attacker (or compromised admin credential) who can encrypt your data can also delete your backups — unless they physically can't. Immutable backups: object-lock/WORM storage (S3 Object Lock compliance mode), a separate account/tenant with independent credentials that production cannot write-delete, ideally air-gapped or cross-cloud — the modern reading of the 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site/off-account). Finally, chaos engineering & game days are DR for your organization: deliberately kill instances/AZ links in production-like conditions (chaos, continuous, automated) and run scheduled incident simulations with the humans — "region A is gone, go" — to find that the runbook is stale, the standby's quota is too small, and the one person who knows the failover left last quarter. Analogy: fire drills — the building's sprinklers (HA) are automatic, but you still practice evacuating, because the plan that exists only on paper fails when the alarm is real.

MechanismProtects againstRPORestore timeDoes NOT protect against
Replication / HAHardware, node, AZ loss~0Seconds (failover)Bad writes, deletes, bugs, ransomware — all replicated
SnapshotsData corruption/loss since last snapshotSnapshot interval (hours)Minutes–hours (size-dependent)Anything in the last interval; slow for huge datasets
PITR (snapshot + WAL)Bad migrations, fat-finger deletes — restore to the second beforeSecondsBase restore + log replayBackup-store compromise if not isolated
Immutable/off-account copyRansomware, malicious/compromised adminCopy intervalSlowest tierNothing it can't — that's the point; costs extra
Interview angle: the layered answer: "replication for machines dying, PITR for humans erring, immutable off-account copies for attackers, and quarterly restore drills so the RTO is a measurement, not a guess." If asked for numbers: "PITR gives RPO ≈ 30 s; measured restore of our 2 TB primary is 70 min, so DR RTO is ~90 min with runbook overhead — if the business needs 15 min we add a delayed-apply replica (applies WAL 1 h late: fat-finger protection at failover speed)." The delayed replica is a nice senior flourish.

Pitfalls

  • Calling replicas a backup strategy — replication ships the disaster to every copy at wire speed.
  • Backups encrypted with a key stored… in the system being backed up (or deletable by the same credentials). Key escrow must be independent.
  • Never measuring restore time — a 20-hour restore discovered mid-incident converts a bad day into a company-threatening one.
  • Game days that always pass — if drills never find problems, they're scripted theater; rotate scenarios and include the humans, not just the software.
Interview questions
  • Snapshots vs PITR — when do you need the latter? — Whenever RPO must be seconds or you need "restore to just before the mistake": PITR = base snapshot + continuous WAL archive replayed to an exact moment. Snapshots alone leave up to an interval of loss and can't stop before the bad statement.
  • Someone ran a migration that corrupted 3 tables at 14:02. Walk me through recovery. — Freeze writes to the affected scope; PITR-restore to 14:01:59 in a parallel instance; diff and re-apply legitimate post-14:02 writes (from WAL/outbox) that didn't touch corrupted rows; swap in; postmortem the migration gate. Never restore in place over your only copy.
  • How do backups survive ransomware? — Immutability + isolation: object-lock/WORM retention that no credential can shorten, in a separate account with independent auth, monitored for backup-job silence. Assume production creds are the attacker's creds.
  • What do you actually verify in a restore test? — That it completes (measured duration = real RTO), integrity (checksums/row counts vs source), usability (app boots against it, schema version matches), and freshness (latest recovery point within RPO). Automated, scheduled, alerting on failure.
  • Chaos engineering vs game days? — Chaos = automated fault injection against the system (kill instances, add latency, drop an AZ) run continuously with steady-state hypotheses; game day = scheduled exercise for the people (simulate a region loss, follow runbooks, find stale docs and missing access). Mature orgs do both; start with game days.

Observability at scale: metrics, logs, traces — and alerting that doesn't cry wolf

Why interviewers ask: "how would you know this design is broken?" ends many interviews, and weak answers ("we'd have monitoring") are conspicuous. Strong answers name the three signals, which questions each answers, the two acronym methods, and why you page on symptoms and SLO burn — not on CPU.

The three signals, by the question they answer. Metrics — cheap pre-aggregated numbers over time (counters, gauges, histograms; Prometheus-style) — answer "is something wrong, how much, since when?": they're the alerting and dashboard substrate because they cost O(series), not O(requests). Logs — structured per-event records — answer "what exactly happened to this request/entity?": full detail, searchable, expensive at volume. Traces — a request's tree of timed spans across services (OpenTelemetry) — answer "where in the chain did the time or error go?": the only signal that explains cross-service latency. The glue is correlation: trace-id on every log line, exemplars linking histogram buckets to sample traces — so you pivot alert → dashboard → trace → logs in four clicks.

What to measure: for every service, RED — Rate (RPS), Errors, Duration (latency histogram); for every resource (CPU, disk, pool, queue), USE — Utilization, Saturation (queue/wait — the leading indicator), Errors. What to page on: symptoms, not causes — page when users hurt (SLO-relevant error rate or latency at the edge), not when a cause-metric twitches (CPU 85%, one pod restarting): cause-alerts fire without user impact (alert fatigue → real pages ignored) and miss novel causes entirely; causes belong on dashboards for diagnosis, not in the pager. The refined version is SLO burn-rate alerting: page when the error budget is burning at, say, 14× plan over both a 1 h and a 5 min window (fast-burn: budget gone in ~2 days — wake someone), ticket at 3× over 6 h+30 min (slow leak — fix in business hours). Multi-window = fires fast, un-fires fast, and a 0.2% blip that self-heals never pages anyone.

The costs at scale are real interview material: cardinality — a metric's cost is its label-combination count, so one user_id label on a request counter turns 100 series into 10 million and kills the TSDB (rule: labels only for dimensions you'd group by — endpoint, region, status class; never unbounded IDs — those belong in logs/traces); and trace sampling — tracing 100% of 100k RPS is prohibitive, so head sampling (decide at ingress, e.g. 1%, cheap but blind — the decision predates knowing if the request was interesting) vs tail sampling (buffer, then keep errors + slow requests + a baseline sample: keeps everything you care about at collector cost). Analogy: metrics are the hospital's vital-sign monitors, traces are the CT scan for one patient, logs are the doctor's notes — you don't CT-scan everyone, but the monitor decides who gets scanned. For the interview wrap-up, the dashboard answer is: edge RED per endpoint against SLO lines, then per-service RED, then USE for the stateful tiers (DB connections, queue lag, cache hit ratio), plus deploy markers overlaid — "and I page on exactly two things: edge availability burn and edge latency burn."

SignalAnswersCost modelRetentionTrap
MetricsIs it broken? How much? Trend?O(series × resolution) — cheap until cardinalityMonths (downsampled)Unbounded labels (user_id) explode series count
LogsWhat happened to this one request?O(events × size) — expensive at volumeDays–weeks hot, archive coldUnstructured text nobody can query under pressure
TracesWhere in the call tree did time/errors go?O(sampled requests × spans)DaysHead-sampling away the exact requests you needed
Interview angle: when closing a design, give the two-pager answer: "I page on SLO burn for edge availability and latency — multi-window, 14× fast / 3× slow. Dashboards: RED per endpoint with deploy markers; USE for DB, cache, queues — saturation first, it leads. Traces tail-sampled: 100% of errors and >1 s, 1% baseline. Logs structured JSON with trace-ids." Thirty seconds, and it signals you've held a pager.

Pitfalls

  • Paging on causes (CPU, pod restarts, disk 80%) — fatigue trains on-call to ignore the pager; the one real page drowns among 40 false ones.
  • Averaging latency in dashboards — plot histogram percentiles (p50/p95/p99); the mean is a number no user experiences (see tail card).
  • High-cardinality labels on metrics "because it might be useful" — that query belongs in logs; the TSDB bill and query slowness arrive within weeks.
  • No deploy/config-change markers on graphs — the first diagnostic question is always "what changed?"; make the answer visible.
Interview questions
  • Metrics vs logs vs traces — one line each? — Metrics: cheap aggregates that tell you something is wrong; traces: the cross-service map of where; logs: the per-event detail of why. Correlate with trace-ids so you can pivot between them.
  • What would you page on for this design, concretely? — Edge SLO burn only: availability burn (error ratio vs budget) and latency burn (% over threshold vs budget), multi-window multi-burn-rate. Everything else — queue lag, saturation, DLQ depth — is tickets or dashboards.
  • Explain burn-rate alerting like I'm the on-call. — Burn rate 1 = spending budget exactly on plan. Page at 14×+ sustained minutes (monthly budget gone in ~2 days); ticket at ~3× over hours. Two windows (long + short) so the alert clears as soon as the bleeding stops.
  • Why is per-user request count a bad Prometheus metric? — Cardinality: each user id is a new time series; 10M users × endpoints × status = TSDB death. Track per-user detail in logs or a purpose-built analytics store; metrics get bounded labels only.
  • Head vs tail trace sampling? — Head decides at request start (cheap, uniform, misses interesting requests); tail decides after completion (keep all errors and slow traces + baseline) at the cost of buffering in collectors. High-scale default: tail for value, head as a pre-filter.
  • RED vs USE? — RED (rate, errors, duration) for request-serving things; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources. Saturation — queue depth, wait time — is the leading indicator: it rises before latency and errors do.

Capacity & autoscaling: the right signal, warm pools, and honest headroom

Why interviewers ask: "it autoscales" is the modern "it's in the cloud" — a phrase that ends thinking. The follow-ups (scale on what signal? how fast? from what floor?) expose whether you know autoscaling is a slow feedback loop that must be aimed at the right metric and backstopped by provisioned headroom.

The signal matters more than the mechanism. CPU-based scaling (the k8s HPA default) works only for CPU-bound services. An I/O-bound service melts at 20% CPU — every thread blocked on a downstream — while the HPA sees nothing; and once you shed load (overload card) CPU drops, so the autoscaler may scale in during your outage. Better signals, in order of directness: queue depth / queue wait time for worker fleets (scale on lag — see §6); in-flight concurrency per instance for request servers (Knative-style: target N concurrent per pod); request rate against a measured per-instance capacity; and always latency as a guardrail, not a trigger (it's the lagging symptom). Horizontal vs vertical: horizontal (more instances) is the default — it composes with redundancy and has no ceiling — but needs statelessness or rebalancing; vertical (bigger boxes) is underrated for the stateful tier (a 2× DB instance is a config change; re-sharding is a quarter) until you hit the biggest machine.

Autoscaling is slow. The loop is: metric ages (15–60 s) → decision dwell → instance boot: container pull + JVM start + warm-up (JIT, connection pools, caches) can be 1–5 min; VM-based, worse; serverless cold starts push p99 per request instead. A traffic spike that doubles in 60 s beats every reactive autoscaler — which is why real systems pair autoscaling with: warm pools (pre-booted, pre-JIT-ed instances waiting to attach), scheduled scaling (pre-scale for the 9 am ramp, the marketing email, Black Friday), a min-capacity floor sized for the largest instant spike you must absorb (never scale to near-zero on a spiky service), and headroom policy — run at ≤60–70% of measured capacity so you can absorb a spike, an AZ loss (N+1: lose one AZ of three and the survivors take +50%), and a deploy surge simultaneously. Capacity planning proper is arithmetic you should show: measured per-instance capacity (from load tests, e.g. 600 RPS/pod at SLO latency) × peak forecast × headroom.

Pitfalls have names. Flapping: scale-out raises capacity → metric dips → scale-in → metric spikes → repeat; fix with asymmetric policies (fast out, slow in), cooldowns/stabilization windows, and scaling on a smoothed metric. Wrong-metric scaling: the classic is CPU for a blocked-thread service (see above), or scaling web tier on requests while the real constraint is DB connections — every new pod adds a pool and worsens the DB. Scaling into a bottleneck: autoscaling the stateless tier cannot add DB or downstream capacity; pair every autoscale policy with the question "what does this push the load onto?" Analogy: a thermostat with a 5-minute-lag radiator — point it at the room's actual temperature (not the hallway's), don't let it toggle every 30 seconds, and keep the pilot light on.

Scaling signalBest forFails when
CPU utilizationCPU-bound compute (encoding, scoring)I/O-bound services (blocked threads, idle CPU); post-shedding CPU dips
Queue depth / lag ageAsync workers, batch fleetsScaling past partition/ordering parallelism ceiling
In-flight concurrencyRequest-serving tiers (most APIs)Per-request cost varies wildly (mixed cheap/expensive endpoints)
RPS vs measured capacityPredictable per-request costCapacity number goes stale after code/dependency changes
Latency (p99)Guardrail/alarm onlyAs a trigger: it lags — by the time it fires you're already burning SLO
Interview angle: show the arithmetic once: "load test says 600 RPS/pod at SLO p99; forecast peak 60k RPS ⇒ 100 pods at 100%; at 65% headroom target ⇒ ~154 pods; min floor 50 (largest observed 2-min spike), HPA on concurrency target 40/pod, scale-out fast/scale-in over 10 min, warm pool of 20 for the flash-sale calendar, and the DB is provisioned for 160 pods' worth of connections via a pooler." Numbers → policy in one breath.

Pitfalls

  • Autoscaling as the spike plan — reactive loops take minutes; instant spikes are absorbed by headroom and floors, or shed. Pre-scale for known events.
  • Scale-to-zero (or near) on latency-sensitive services — the first user of the morning pays every cold start in the chain.
  • Scaling the stateless tier into a fixed-size database — more pods, more connections, more contention; the bottleneck just moves and worsens.
  • Symmetric scale-in — tearing capacity down as eagerly as you added it is how flapping starts; scale in at ~¼ the speed you scale out.
Interview questions
  • Your service is at 20% CPU and timing out — why won't the autoscaler help? — It's I/O-bound: threads are blocked on a slow downstream, so CPU never rises and the HPA never triggers — and more replicas would just multiply pressure on the sick downstream. Scale on concurrency/queue wait, and fix the downstream (breaker + shed).
  • Horizontal vs vertical scaling — how do you choose? — Horizontal for stateless tiers (composability, no ceiling, redundancy included); vertical first for stateful tiers where resharding is expensive — until the biggest box, then you must partition (§3).
  • How much headroom is right? — Target ~60–70% utilization at forecast peak: enough to absorb an AZ loss (N+1), a deploy surge, and a 1.5× spike while the autoscaler reacts. Five-nines-critical paths run fatter; batch fleets run near 90%.
  • What causes autoscaler flapping and how do you stop it? — The scaling action moves the metric it's watching, oscillating around the threshold. Fix: stabilization windows/cooldowns, fast-out/slow-in asymmetry, smoothed metrics, and target-tracking rather than step thresholds.
  • Black Friday is Friday. What do you do this week? — Forecast peak from last year × growth; load test to re-measure per-instance capacity; pre-scale floors (don't trust reactive scaling), pre-provision the un-autoscalable (DB, caches, quotas, rate-limit configs); agree the degradation ladder and freeze deploys (details in the practice problem).

Security & abuse at scale: edge auth, secrets, bots & blast-radius isolation

Why interviewers ask: a design interview rarely goes deep on crypto, but "where does auth happen?", "what if a node is compromised?", and "one tenant is attacking you — who else suffers?" are fair game in any senior loop. The goal is a credible security posture, not a security lecture.

AuthN/AuthZ at the edge. Terminate TLS and authenticate at the gateway: validate the token (JWT signature/expiry against cached JWKS keys, or opaque-token introspection with caching) once, then forward an internal identity context; services re-verify cheaply (signature check, no user-DB hit) and apply authorization locally — authn is "who are you" (edge concern), authz is "may you do this" (owned by each service near its data, or a central policy engine like OPA for consistency). Internally, don't trust the network: mTLS between services (usually via mesh) plus per-service identities means a compromised pod can't impersonate the payments service — the zero-trust posture in one sentence. Never let raw internal headers (X-User-Id) cross the edge unauthenticated — classic header-injection hole; the gateway must strip and re-set them.

Secrets: no secrets in code, images, or env-var dumps — a central manager (Vault, cloud secret managers) issuing short-lived, auto-rotated credentials (dynamic DB creds valid hours, IAM roles instead of static keys). Rotation must be a non-event: services fetch/refresh at runtime and hold two valid versions during overlap — if rotating a secret requires a deploy freeze and a prayer, you'll never rotate, and leaked-credential incidents last months. Bot & abuse basics: layered like rate limiting — WAF + managed bot rules at the CDN/edge for the crude 90% (signatures, IP reputation), per-identity rate limits and anomaly detection behind auth (impossible travel, scraping patterns, credential-stuffing velocity — login gets sliding-window-log limits per user and per IP), CAPTCHAs/proof-of-work as friction of last resort on the endpoints attackers love (login, signup, coupon, gift-card balance).

Blast-radius isolation is the architectural security idea interviewers reward most: assume any component or tenant will be compromised or go berserk, and bound what it can take down. Per-tenant quotas on everything (rate, storage, concurrency, queue depth) so one tenant's incident isn't your outage; cell-based architecture — partition the whole stack into independent cells (each cell: its own services, DB, cache; a thin routing layer maps tenant → cell) so a poison workload, bad deploy wave, or data-plane bug takes out one cell (say 5% of tenants), not everyone — cells are the availability and security containment unit, and they make blast radius a number you choose. Refinement: shuffle sharding — give each tenant a random small subset of nodes; two tenants rarely share their full set, so a targeted attack degrades the attacker's shard, not yours. Analogy: a ship's watertight compartments again — but for tenants and credentials, not threads: any one breach floods a compartment you already decided you could afford to lose.

Interview angle: when the interviewer says "let's talk security" in a design loop, give posture in four beats: "authn once at the gateway with cached JWKS, authz per service near the data; mTLS + workload identity inside; secrets short-lived from a manager, rotation as a non-event; and blast radius: per-tenant quotas, cell-based partitioning so any incident is capped at one cell." Then invite depth: "happy to go deeper on token design or tenant isolation." You've shown the map without derailing the interview.

Pitfalls

  • Trusting the internal network ("it's behind the VPC") — one SSRF or compromised pod then has free lateral movement; identity + mTLS inside is the fix.
  • Long-lived static credentials (API keys in env vars, year-old DB passwords) — the leak you'll never detect; short TTLs turn leaks into 1-hour problems.
  • Rate limiting login per-IP only — credential stuffing rotates IPs; limit per-account too, and alert on aggregate failure-rate anomalies.
  • Multi-tenant SaaS with no tenant-level quotas — the first tenant with a runaway script becomes everyone's outage, and the first compromised tenant becomes everyone's breach headline.
Interview questions
  • Where do you authenticate — gateway or each service? — Both, cheaply: gateway does full validation (and strips spoofable headers), services verify the forwarded signed context locally without a network hop. Authorization stays with each service (or a shared policy engine) because it needs domain context.
  • JWT vs opaque session tokens at scale? — JWT: stateless verification (cached public keys), no session store on the hot path, but revocation is hard — keep TTLs short (minutes) with refresh tokens, and a small denylist for emergencies. Opaque: instant revocation, but every check hits/introspects the session store — cache it.
  • How does secrets rotation work without downtime? — Overlapping validity: issue v2 while v1 still works, services refresh from the manager on a timer, retire v1 after the overlap. Dynamic per-service DB credentials with hours-long TTLs make rotation continuous and automatic.
  • One customer's API key leaked and is being hammered — contain it. — Their quota/rate limits cap total damage (that's why limits exist per key, not just per IP); revoke and reissue the key, check anomaly logs for data accessed, and if tenants map to cells, the noisy traffic saturated one cell at worst.
  • What is cell-based architecture and why do interviewers love it? — The stack partitioned into N independent full-stack cells with tenant→cell routing; any failure — bad deploy, poison tenant, data bug — is capped at one cell. It converts "blast radius" from a hope into a dial (cell size), and it composes with staged deploys (one cell first).

Operational excellence: runbooks, on-call, incidents & blameless postmortems

Why interviewers ask: senior loops often end with "and how would you run this?" — because architecture that no one can operate at 3 am is a diagram, not a system. A crisp answer here also feeds the behavioral interview ("tell me about an incident you handled").

Runbooks: every alert links to a runbook — what the alert means, how to confirm impact, the 3 most likely causes with checks, the mitigation commands (copy-pasteable, tested), and escalation contacts. The standard for a mitigation that matters (region failover, read-only mode, cache flush) is that it's rehearsed — an unexecuted runbook is a hypothesis (see game days). On-call that works: a rotation with a primary and secondary, pager load bounded (if a shift regularly gets >2–3 pages, that's an engineering problem to fix, not a staffing one), symptom-based pages only (observability card), and the authority to mitigate first, diagnose later — MTTR falls when on-call reaches for "roll back / flip the flag / shed" instead of debugging live.

Incident management borrows fire-department structure: an Incident Commander who coordinates and decides but doesn't type, an ops/subject lead doing the hands-on work, and a communications lead updating stakeholders on a cadence — so engineers aren't context-switching into status meetings mid-mitigation. Severity levels (SEV1 = users down, all hands; SEV3 = degraded, business hours) set the response, and mitigation always precedes root cause. Afterwards, the blameless postmortem: timeline, impact quantified against the error budget, contributing causes (plural — big incidents are never one mistake), and action items with owners and dates. Blameless isn't kindness, it's epistemics: name-and-shame teaches people to hide information, and the postmortem's product is information — the assumption is that the person acted reasonably given what the system showed them, so you fix the system (guardrails, validation, better alerts), not the person. "You build it, you run it" closes the loop: the team that owns the code carries its pager, so operational pain (noisy alerts, toil, flaky deploys) lands on the people empowered to eliminate it — with an ops-review cadence (pager stats, SLO status, toil budget) so it actually happens. Analogy: aviation safety culture — pilots self-report near-misses precisely because reports are blameless, and that reporting is why flying got safe.

Interview angle: the one-paragraph close for any design: "Operationally: symptom-based paging on SLO burn, every alert linked to a rehearsed runbook, incidents run with an IC and comms lead, mitigation before diagnosis — rollback and kill switches are the first moves — then a blameless postmortem with actions that spend or defend the error budget. The team that builds it carries the pager." It signals lived experience in five lines.

Pitfalls

  • Runbooks written once and never executed — commands rot, permissions expire; drill them or delete them.
  • Root-causing during the fire — mitigate first (roll back, shed, flip flags); the logs will still be there at 10 am.
  • Postmortems that end in "engineer will be more careful" — that's a blame document with extra steps; actions must change the system.
  • On-call for a service owned by another team ("ops runs it") — the feedback loop from operational pain to code fixes is severed, and both sides rot.
Interview questions
  • What makes a postmortem blameless, and why bother? — It assumes actors behaved reasonably given the information the system gave them, and targets systemic fixes (guardrails, validation, alerts) instead of individuals. The payoff is honesty: people surface what actually happened, which is the raw material of prevention.
  • What roles exist in a serious incident? — Incident Commander (coordinates, decides, doesn't debug), ops/tech lead (hands on keyboard), comms lead (stakeholder updates on cadence), scribe (timeline for the postmortem). Roles, not ranks — the IC may be the most junior person trained for it.
  • Mitigation vs root cause — order and why? — Mitigate first: users are hurting and the top mitigations (rollback, feature kill, shed, failover) don't require understanding the bug. Root cause comes after, in the postmortem, with the luxury of time.
  • What's in a good runbook entry for an alert? — Meaning of the alert, how to confirm real user impact, top likely causes with one check each, exact mitigation commands (tested, least-privilege), rollback of the mitigation, and when/whom to escalate.
  • "You build it, you run it" — always? — It's the default for product services (aligns pain with power to fix). Shared platforms (DB fleets, k8s, observability) get their own owning teams with SLOs; the anti-pattern is a generic ops team paged for code it can't change.

A request path crosses 5 services, each independently 99.9% available. Roughly what availability can the path promise?

Serial composition multiplies: 0.999⁵ ≈ 0.995 → ~44 h of downtime a year. Option (a) is the trap — the chain is worse than every part, because any one failure fails the path. A load balancer (d) adds redundancy within a tier, not across the serial chain.

A backend has p99 = 800 ms, and you fan each user request out to 100 such shards, waiting for all. What fraction of user requests experience ≥ 800 ms from at least one shard?

P(all 100 shards fast) = 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.37, so ~63% of requests wait on at least one shard's tail — the backend's p99 becomes the front end's typical case. (a) is the intuition tail-at-scale breaks: percentiles don't survive fan-out. (d) overshoots: 37% of requests do dodge every tail.

Why is average latency a poor dashboard/alerting metric?

Skewed distributions (GC pauses, misses, queueing) drag the mean into a no-man's land: higher than the median most users see, far lower than the tail your unluckiest (and heaviest) users see. Percentiles from histograms are the fix. (d) has it backwards — fast requests pull the mean down, masking the tail.

An API promises "100 requests per minute" using a fixed-window counter. What's the worst burst a client can legally push in a few seconds?

The boundary-burst bug: the counter forgets everything at the window edge, so 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 at 1:01 both pass — 2× the promised rate in ~2 s. Sliding-window counters (weighting the previous window by overlap) or a token bucket close the hole. (a) is what the config claims; the boundary is where it lies.

You enforce 10k req/s per customer across 40 edge nodes with a naive per-node GET counter; if < limit then SET counter+1 against shared Redis. What's the bug?

Redis serializes each command, not your GET-then-SET sequence — two nodes read 9,999 concurrently and both admit. The check-refill-decrement must be one atomic server-side unit (Lua script / redis-cell). (c) is the tempting half-truth: single-threaded execution doesn't make multi-command sequences atomic.

A 30-second database brownout ended an hour ago, but the service is still down: servers at 100% CPU, goodput near zero. What best explains it?

Trigger gone, outage persisting = the signature of metastability: retry amplification plus cold caches hold demand above capacity, so the bad state is self-sustaining. The exit is counter-intuitive — shed hard below true capacity and stop retries, then ramp admission back. (c) is the trap that worsens it: new instances join cold and drown.

During a rolling deploy, why must a schema change follow expand/contract instead of renaming a column in place?

Mid-rollout, both versions read and write the one schema; a rename instantly breaks whichever version doesn't know it — and makes rolling back the code impossible. Expand (add new, dual-write, backfill) → switch reads → contract (drop old after the rollback horizon). (a) can also be true on some engines, but it's not the architectural reason.

Why is synchronous replication of OLTP writes between us-east and eu-west not a real option for an interactive product?

It's latency physics, not networking quality or law: a sync commit waits a full cross-region round trip, and a lock held ~100× longer serializes hot rows to a crawl. Hence async replication (RPO > 0), home-region write pinning, or consensus stores that knowingly pay quorum latency for the few datasets that need RPO = 0.

Which paging policy best follows "alert on symptoms, not causes"?

(d) pages only when users are measurably hurt at a rate that threatens the SLO — and the dual window makes it fire fast and clear fast. (a)–(c) are causes: they fire without user impact (fatigue) and stay silent for novel failure modes; they belong on diagnosis dashboards, with (c) at most a ticket.

Your worker service is timing out at 15% CPU while its queue backlog grows. The HPA scales on CPU. What's the production-correct change?

Blocked-on-I/O threads saturate the service while CPU idles — the scaling signal must be the thing that's actually queueing (lag, wait time, concurrency). (a) is a kludge that still tracks the wrong quantity and invites flapping; (c) adds CPU the workload doesn't use. Also check what the workers are blocked on — more workers may just pound a sick downstream.

Practice

Checkout spans 6 services — hit 99.95%

Your checkout request path is: edge gateway → auth → cart → pricing → inventory → payments, in series. Each service independently achieves 99.9%. (1) Compute the composite availability and downtime per 30-day month. (2) The business demands 99.95% for checkout. Redesign the path to get there — with arithmetic showing your redesign plausibly meets the target.

Covers: serial/parallel availability math · dependency pruning · graceful degradation

Hint 1

Serial availability is the product. For the redesign: which of the six calls must be synchronous and fresh at checkout time? A dependency you can cache, default, or defer stops multiplying.

Hint 2

Two levers: remove links from the serial chain (cache/async/optional), and improve the links that remain (redundancy inside each tier multiplies unavailabilities).

Solution

1. Composite: 0.999⁶ = 0.99402 ≈ 99.4%. A 30-day month is 43,200 min; 0.598% ≈ 258 min ≈ 4.3 h/month. Target 99.95% allows 21.6 min/month — we're 12× over budget.

2. Redesign — shorten the chain:

• Pricing: serve from a region-local cache with bounded staleness (prices change rarely); on miss/outage use last-known-good. Off the critical path.
• Inventory: soft-check from cache at checkout ("likely in stock"), enforce the hard reservation asynchronously with a compensating "sorry" flow for the rare oversell — a business trade-off worth saying out loud.
• Auth: validate JWTs locally at the gateway with cached JWKS keys — no synchronous call to the auth service (it's only needed for issuing, not verifying).

Remaining serial chain: gateway → cart → payments (3 links). At 99.9% each: 0.999³ ≈ 99.7% — still short. Now improve the links: run each tier redundantly across 2+ AZs with health-checked failover so each tier reaches ~99.99% (two nodes at 99.9%, if reasonably independent: 1 − 0.001² = 99.9999% theoretical; call it 99.99% honestly, allowing for correlated failures like deploys — mitigated by staggering deploys across AZs). Payments includes an external processor: wrap it with a second provider as failover, or accept it as the dominant term.

Result: 0.9999³ ≈ 99.97% ≈ 13 min/month — meets 99.95% with margin for the external processor's bad months. Answer shape: "compute (99.4%), prune the chain (6 → 3 sync deps: cache pricing, async inventory, local JWT), then widen what remains (multi-AZ per tier ⇒ ~99.99% each) → 99.97%, and I'd protect the margin with staggered deploys and a degradation ladder so partial failures don't count as downtime."

Design global rate limiting: 10k req/s per customer, 40 edge nodes

Your public API serves ~2M req/s through 40 edge nodes worldwide. Contract: each customer gets 10,000 req/s (with reasonable burst); large customers' traffic is geographically skewed. Design the rate limiter: algorithm, state placement, consistency model, hot-key handling, failure behavior, and the client-facing contract. State your accuracy guarantee.

Covers: token bucket · local vs global state · race windows · fail-open policy · 429 semantics

Hint 1

Synchronous global consistency costs a Redis RTT on 2M req/s. What accuracy does the contract actually require — and over what timescale?

Hint 2

Per-node static division (10k/40 = 250/s per node) breaks under skew. What if the division were dynamic, based on each node's recently observed share of that customer's traffic?

Solution

Algorithm: token bucket per customer — r = 10k/s, B ≈ 20k (2 s of burst) — because the contract is a sustained rate with honest bursts, and bucket state is two numbers per key.

Placement — hybrid local + async global: every edge node keeps a local bucket per active customer and answers from it in-process (~µs, nothing added to the hot path). Every 100 ms, nodes report tokens spent per customer to a region-local aggregator (Redis cluster or a small limiter service, buckets sharded by customer id); the aggregator returns each node's allowance for the next interval proportional to its observed share of that customer's traffic — so a customer concentrated on 3 nodes gets ~all 10k/s across those 3, solving skew without static division. All aggregator updates are atomic server-side (Lua) — never read-then-write from the nodes (that race admits over-limit bursts precisely at the boundary).

Accuracy guarantee: overshoot ≤ roughly one sync interval of aggregate burst: 100 ms × 10k/s ≈ 1,000 extra requests worst-case (~10% for one interval), decaying immediately. State that number; "eventually consistent within 100 ms, bounded overshoot 10%" is a contract engineers and lawyers can both read. Endpoints needing exactness (login throttles, purchase abuse) bypass the hybrid and do synchronous atomic checks — they're low-rate, so the RTT is affordable.

Hot keys: a 300k req/s customer's bucket is one Redis shard's problem only in the aggregator (10 updates/s per node × 40 = 400 writes/s per customer — trivial, because the hot path never touches Redis). If aggregator load grows, shard customers across aggregator instances; each customer still maps to exactly one owner (single-writer per key).

Failure behavior: aggregator unreachable → nodes fail open degrading to conservative local buckets (last-known allowance, floor 10k/40 per node), log and alert — the limiter must never become the outage. Billing quotas reconcile later from access logs, which are the durable source of truth for metering anyway.

Client contract: 429 + Retry-After + RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers; documented burst B; SDKs with jittered backoff. Interview close: "µs-latency local decisions, 100 ms-consistent global fairness, 10%-bounded overshoot, fail-open with alerts, exact only where exactness pays."

Black Friday 10× playbook: pre-provision, auto-scale, degrade

Your e-commerce platform normally peaks at 20k req/s; Black Friday will bring ~200k req/s, with a doors-open spike from 0 → 120k req/s in under two minutes at midnight. Write the playbook: what you pre-provision (and why autoscaling can't cover it), what auto-scales, what degrades and in what order, and what you do in the two weeks before.

Covers: headroom vs reactive scaling · un-autoscalable tiers · degradation ladder · ops preparation

Hint 1

List which tiers can add capacity in minutes (stateless pods) vs hours/days (databases, caches, quotas, external contracts). The second list is your pre-provisioning list.

Solution

Pre-provision (autoscaling cannot save you here): the midnight spike (0→120k in <2 min) beats any reactive loop (metric lag + boot + JVM warm-up ≈ 3–5 min), so the floor at 23:45 must already hold ~120k req/s: at a measured 600 req/s/pod that's ~200 pods minimum before midnight (vs ~35 normally). Also pre-provisioned because they scale in hours/days, not minutes: database capacity (read replicas, IOPS, connection budgets via poolers), cache clusters pre-warmed with the sale catalog (a cold cache at midnight = self-inflicted metastable failure — 95%→0% hit ratio is a 20× DB spike), cloud quotas (instance limits, LB capacity — request raises weeks ahead), external contracts (payment-processor TPS ceilings — the classic forgotten bottleneck), and rate-limit/WAF configs tuned for legitimate bursts plus the bot wave that accompanies every sale.

Auto-scales: stateless tiers (web, search-read, recommendations) on concurrency/RPS with fast-out/slow-in and floors raised for the event; async workers (order confirmation, email) on queue lag — these are allowed to fall behind, that's what the queue is for.

Degradation ladder (pre-agreed, flag-driven, in order): 1. shed crawlers/bots and batch/analytics traffic; 2. kill recommendations, reviews, recently-viewed (flags); 3. serve product pages and prices from cache with extended TTL (minutes of staleness, labeled); 4. queue orders for async confirmation ("order received — confirmation by email") instead of synchronous end-to-end checkout; 5. waiting room / admission queue at the edge as the last resort — an honest queue beats a timeout storm. Checkout is last to degrade, first to get capacity.

Two weeks before: load test to 250k req/s (past target — find the collapse point and verify goodput plateaus rather than collapses, i.e. shedding works); re-measure per-pod capacity (it drifts with every release); game-day the ladder including actually flipping every kill switch; deploy freeze from T-3 days (change causes most outages — don't spend the budget that week); staffed war room with the runbook, dashboards (edge RED vs SLO, DB/queue saturation, payment success rate), and pre-authorized decision owners for each ladder rung.

Region failover drill: RTO 5 min, RPO 30 s

Two regions, active-passive. The business signs off on RTO ≤ 5 min and RPO ≤ 30 s for a total region loss. Design (1) the data plan per tier, (2) the traffic-switch plan, and (3) the failover runbook with a time budget per step — then show the design actually fits inside 5 minutes and 30 seconds.

Covers: RPO/RTO decomposition · replication lag budgeting · fencing · DNS vs global LB · runbook design

Hint 1

RPO ≤ 30 s is a constraint on replication lag, continuously — not something you do during the failover. What do you monitor and alert on to keep it true?

Hint 2

Budget the RTO backwards: detection + decision + fencing + promotion + traffic switch + validation ≤ 300 s. Which step is the least controllable, and what technology choice fixes it?

Solution

1. Data plan (RPO ≤ 30 s = "replication lag never exceeds 30 s"): OLTP: async streaming replication to the standby region with lag as a paged SLI — alert at 10 s, page at 20 s, and throttle/queue bulk writers when lag climbs (protecting RPO costs write throughput; say so). Object storage: provider cross-region replication (verify its lag SLA fits 30 s for critical buckets; pre-write critical blobs synchronously dual-region if not). Queues: mirrored topics; consumers must be idempotent since mirror offsets differ (§5). Caches: not replicated — accept a cold-cache surge in region B and pre-warm the hottest keys continuously from the replication stream so failover doesn't trigger a metastable collapse (card above). Also replicated continuously: secrets, feature-flag state, rate-limiter configs, deploy artifacts — the app must be able to run in B, and the failover tooling itself lives outside region A.

2. Traffic switch: DNS alone can't make 5 min reliably (TTL disobedience → minutes, uncontrolled). Front with a global load balancer / anycast layer that health-checks per region and shifts weights in seconds; DNS (TTL 60 s) remains as the fallback path. Clients get retry-with-jitter so the switch itself doesn't thundering-herd region B — whose floors are pre-scaled to absorb 100% of traffic (capacity you pay for all year; that's the price of the RTO).

3. Runbook with time budget (total ≤ 300 s):
• T+0–60 s — Detect: external multi-vantage probes (3+ locations) fail hard; page fires; auto-diagnosis bundle (per-region SLIs) attached. [60 s]
• T+60–120 s — Decide: on-call IC applies a pre-agreed decision rule ("both probe sets red AND region-B probes green for 60 s ⇒ fail over — no consensus meeting"). Practiced monthly, so the human step is 60 s, not 20 min. [60 s]
• T+120–150 s — Fence A: one command: revoke A's write lease at the routing layer + block writes at A's proxies, so a zombie A can't split-brain. [30 s]
• T+150–210 s — Promote B: scripted: promote replica (orchestrated, e.g. Patroni-style), verify read-write, point region-B services at it (already configured, just a health-gate flip). [60 s]
• T+210–240 s — Switch traffic: set global-LB weights A→0/B→100; watch B's edge RED dashboards. [30 s]
• T+240–300 s — Validate & announce: synthetic checkout passes in B; comms lead posts status; begin monitoring B's saturation. [60 s]
Fit check: 300 s total with each step scripted and rehearsed; RPO: lag-SLI enforcement keeps loss ≤ 30 s (realized RPO = lag at T+0; measured in the drill). Afterwards: A returns as a replica — no auto-failback; extract A's WAL beyond B's applied position, replay idempotently or compensate, and record realized RPO/RTO in the postmortem. Quarterly drills execute this runbook against production (game day) — an unrehearsed 5-minute RTO is fiction.

Rapid-fire: reliability & operations one-liners

Why: last-hour revision — the one-line answers that keep an interview moving. Say them crisply, then expand only if asked.

  • 99.9% vs 99.99% in downtime? — ~8.8 h/year vs ~53 min/year (43 min vs 4.3 min per month).
  • 5 services at 99.9% in series? — 0.999⁵ ≈ 99.5%: serial availabilities multiply, chains are worse than their parts.
  • Two redundant 99.9% replicas? — 1 − 0.001² = 99.9999% — but only if failures are independent (deploys and shared deps aren't).
  • SLI vs SLO vs SLA? — Measurement, internal target on it, external contract with penalties — each looser than the last.
  • Error budget? — 1 − SLO: the failure you're allowed; spend it on deploys or outages, freeze features when it's gone.
  • Why p99 over average? — Skewed distributions: the mean describes nobody and hides the tail your heaviest users hit most.
  • Fan-out of 100, each 1% slow? — 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63% of requests see a tail: p99 becomes the norm.
  • Two tail-latency fixes? — Hedge stragglers at ~p95 (idempotent reads, cancel the loser); partial results at the deadline.
  • Token bucket knobs? — r = sustained rate, B = burst allowance; state is two numbers per key.
  • Fixed-window bug? — Counter resets at the boundary: 2× the limit in seconds. Sliding-window counter fixes it with two counters.
  • Global rate limiting without an RTT per request? — Local buckets + async sync (~100 ms): bounded overshoot, zero hot-path latency, degrades to local.
  • Rate limiter store down — allow or deny? — Protective limits fail open (never be the outage); abuse/billing limits fail closed.
  • Proper 429? — Retry-After + RateLimit-Remaining/Reset headers + machine-readable body, decided cheaply at the edge.
  • Quota vs rate limit? — Billing-grade counting over months vs protective throttling over seconds.
  • Load shedding vs rate limiting? — Health-triggered priority drop when saturated vs per-client contract at admission.
  • Circuit breaker states? — Closed → open on error-rate threshold (fail fast/fallback) → half-open probes → closed on success.
  • Bulkhead? — Per-dependency pools/semaphores so one hung downstream exhausts its allotment, not every thread.
  • Graceful degradation examples? — Read-only mode, stale-from-cache with a label, feature kill switches, simplified fallbacks.
  • Metastable failure? — Overload that outlives its trigger because retries + cold caches sustain it; exit by shedding below capacity, never by scaling cold instances in.
  • Retry storm math? — 3 retries at each of N layers ⇒ 3^N amplification; fix with retry budgets (~10%), jitter, breakers, deadlines.
  • Canary in one line? — 1→5→25→100% with automated metric comparison vs baseline and auto-rollback on SLO burn.
  • Expand/contract? — Add-compatible schema → dual-write + backfill → switch reads → drop old after the rollback horizon; never rename in place.
  • Feature flag vs deploy? — Deploy puts code in prod dark; the flag releases it per cohort — and a flag flip is itself a deploy.
  • Why no sync replication cross-region? — +70–150 ms per commit and locks held ~100× longer collapse contended-row throughput.
  • RTO vs RPO? — Time to be back up vs data-loss window; async replication makes RPO = lag at failure.
  • DNS vs anycast failover? — Minutes (TTLs loosely honored) vs seconds (withdraw the route); serious RTOs need the latter.
  • Why isn't replication backup? — It replicates the DROP TABLE too; PITR restores to the second before the mistake.
  • Ransomware-proof backups? — Immutable (object-lock/WORM), separate account/credentials, restore-tested — assume prod creds are the attacker's.
  • Metrics vs logs vs traces? — Is it broken / what happened to this event / where in the call tree it went wrong.
  • RED vs USE? — Rate-Errors-Duration for services; Utilization-Saturation-Errors for resources; saturation leads.
  • Page on what? — Symptoms: SLO burn rate, multi-window (14× fast, ~3× slow). Causes go on dashboards.
  • Metric cardinality rule? — Labels only for bounded dimensions you group by; user-ids belong in logs/traces.
  • Wrong autoscaling signal? — CPU for I/O-bound services: threads block, CPU idles, HPA sleeps. Scale on concurrency or queue lag.
  • Why floors/warm pools? — Reactive scaling takes minutes; instant spikes are survived by pre-paid headroom or not at all.
  • Cell-based architecture? — Full-stack partitions with tenant→cell routing: blast radius becomes a dial you set.
  • Blameless postmortem in one line? — Assume people acted reasonably on what the system showed them; fix the system, and the truth keeps flowing.

8️⃣ Classic Designs, End to End

Everything before this was building blocks; this section is the exam. Twelve classic interview designs, each walked through the 4-step framework: requirements with real numbers, a compact API and data model, the architecture, and the 2–3 deep dives interviewers actually probe. Notice how little is new — every design is "pick the right cards from sections 1–7 and defend the trade-offs with the numbers you estimated". Study the pattern of reuse as much as the designs themselves.

Design a URL shortener (TinyURL / bit.ly)

Why interviewers ask: the classic warm-up — small enough to finish, rich enough to expose whether you can do estimation, choose a key-generation scheme with a reason, and notice that the read path is 100× the write path.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Shorten a URL (optionally custom alias, optional expiry), redirect fast, click analytics. Assume 100M new URLs/month ≈ 40 writes/s; read:write 100:1 → 4k redirects/s (peak ~3×: 12k/s). Row ≈ 500 B → 100M × 12 × 5 y × 500 B ≈ 3 TB over 5 years — one sharded KV table, not "big data". Redirect latency target p99 < 100 ms.

Step 2 — API & data model. Two endpoints and one table; per API design, the code goes in the path, creation is a POST returning 201.

POST /api/urls   {"longUrl":"https://…", "customAlias?":"promo24", "expireAt?":…}
  → 201 {"code":"aZ3kQ9x"}                     (409 if alias taken)
GET  /{code}     → 302 Location: longUrl       (404 / 410 if expired)

urls: code PK (7 chars base62) | long_url | user_id | created_at | expires_at
      62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12 codes — enough for ~2900 years at 100M/month

Deep dive — key generation. Three defensible schemes. Counter + base62: unique by construction, but a single counter is a SPOF and codes are sequential (enumerable — competitors can scrape your URLs; mitigate by XOR-ing with a fixed secret or skipping randomly). Scale the counter by handing each app server a range lease (server takes 1M ids from ZooKeeper/DB, hands them out from memory — one coordination call per million codes). Hash (MD5/SHA-256 of URL, take 7 base62 chars): no coordination, same URL → same code (free dedupe), but 627 birthday-collides around ~2M random codes, so you MUST check-and-retry with a salt on collision — and the check is a read-before-write race unless the insert is conditional (INSERT IF NOT EXISTS). Pre-generated key service (KGS): offline job fills a pool of random unused codes; app servers grab batches. Random (not enumerable), no per-request coordination — the pool table becomes the thing you monitor.

Deep dive — 301 vs 302. A 301 (permanent) lets browsers and intermediaries cache the redirect: subsequent clicks never reach your servers — great for load, fatal for analytics, and you can never remap or expire the code for that user. A 302/307 (temporary) keeps every click on your servers: you count clicks, honor expiry, and can kill malicious links. Interviews want the trade-off stated and a pick justified by the requirement — analytics was a requirement, so 302 (with Cache-Control tuned so CDNs don't over-cache).

Pitfalls

  • Jumping to "hash the URL" without handling collisions — at billions of rows, 7-char collisions are routine, and unchecked ones silently point users at the wrong site.
  • Answering 301 "because it's a redirect" — you just deleted your own analytics requirement. State the trade-off.
  • Auto-increment DB key exposed directly as the code: enumerable AND ties you to one writer; at least base62 + offset/obfuscate it, or use ranges.
  • Designing a 20-service architecture for 40 writes/s — this problem is a test of restraint (over-engineering); one KV table + cache + counter is the honest answer.
Interview questions
  • How many characters does the code need? — 626 ≈ 57B, 627 ≈ 3.5T. At 100M/month = 1.2B/year, 6 chars lasts ~47 years but gets crowded (more collision retries if hashing); 7 is the safe default.
  • Your redirect p99 is 800 ms — where do you look? — Cache hit ratio first (miss → DB on the hot path), then DB hot shard (a viral code hammering one partition — but that's exactly what the cache should absorb), then connection setup (TLS, cross-region client→server RTT; put the redirect behind a CDN/edge PoP, CDN).
  • How do you shard the table? — Hash of code (hash sharding): perfectly uniform, and the only query is by exact code so losing range scans costs nothing.
  • How do custom aliases coexist with generated codes? — Same table, same uniqueness constraint; conditional insert returns 409 on conflict. Reserve a namespace (e.g. length or prefix) so generated codes never collide with future aliases.
  • Expired links: delete or keep? — Keep and return 410 Gone; lazy-expire on read plus a background sweep. Never resell an expired code soon after — cached 301s elsewhere may still point at it.
  • What breaks first at 100× read load? — Nothing interesting: add cache replicas and app servers; the DB still sees only misses. That answer — "this design scales reads trivially, here's why" — is the senior signal.

Design a rate limiter as a service

Why interviewers ask: you already know the algorithms from rate-limiting algorithms — this question tests whether you can productize one: shared state across N gateways, atomicity under concurrency, a 1–2 ms latency budget, and the fail-open/fail-closed judgment call.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Limit requests per API key/user/IP across a fleet of ~50 gateway nodes handling 50k RPS total; rules like "100 req/min per user, burst 20". The check sits on EVERY request, so its budget is ~1–2 ms and its availability must exceed the services it protects. State per key is tiny (two numbers for a token bucket) but there are ~10M active keys → ~100s of MB — one Redis cluster, sharded by key.

Step 2 — API & placement. A library/sidecar in each gateway calling a shared store beats a separate "rate-limit microservice" (which would add a network hop AND still need the shared store). Config is rules-as-data, hot-reloadable.

check(key="user:42:POST/orders", cost=1) → {allowed: true, remaining: 17, resetSec: 31}
response on deny: 429 + Retry-After: 31 + RateLimit-Remaining: 0

rule: {match: "POST /orders", scope: user, rate: 100/min, burst: 20}
state per key in Redis: {tokens: float, lastRefillMs: long}   (~50 B, TTL = 2× window)

Deep dive — why Lua, not GET+SET. Two gateways read tokens=1 concurrently, both decide "allowed", both SET tokens=0 → the limit leaks under exactly the load it exists for. Fixes in order of preference: one atomic Lua script (refill+check+decrement server-side); or INCR-based fixed/sliding-window counters (atomic by nature, coarser semantics); or local buckets with async sync (bounded overshoot, zero hot-path RTT) when even 0.5 ms is too much. Mention Redis Cluster hash tags ({user:42}) so a key's state and script execute on one shard.

Deep dive — hot keys and multi-tenancy. One abusive API key = one Redis shard's key getting hammered — fine, that's ~100k ops/s per shard headroom; the danger is a scan attack across millions of distinct keys inflating memory. TTL every key (2× window) and cap the keyspace. Per-tenant rule lookup must be O(1): compile rules to a trie/exact-match map in gateway memory, hot-reload on config push, version the config so a bad rule rolls back like a deploy.

Pitfalls

  • Designing a standalone "rate limit service" that every request must call — you added a hop and a SPOF; the service is a library + shared store.
  • GET-then-SET token math in the client — racy; atomicity must live where the state lives.
  • One global fail-open/fail-closed answer — the correct answer is "depends on what the limit protects", stated per rule class.
  • Forgetting the response contract: a 429 without Retry-After turns polite clients into a retry storm (retries).
Interview questions
  • Token bucket vs sliding window log — when does each win? — Bucket: O(1) memory, allows bursts, the default for API limits. Log (a ZSET of timestamps): exact, no boundary artifacts, but O(rate) memory per key — use for low-rate, high-value limits (login attempts, OTP sends).
  • The limiter itself is at 50k RPS — does Redis cope? — Yes: ~50 B/key, in-memory ops at 100k+/s per shard; 50k RPS spread over a few shards is comfortable. Scale by adding shards — keys hash-distribute evenly.
  • How would you rate-limit by IP behind a proxy/CDN? — Trust only your own edge's client-IP header (X-Forwarded-For is client-forgeable); at the CDN layer, do it in the edge itself.
  • User bursts exactly at a minute boundary and gets 2× the limit — which algorithm has this bug? — Fixed window; sliding-window counter (weighted two windows) fixes it with the same O(1) memory.
  • How do you roll out a stricter limit without breaking good clients? — Shadow mode first: evaluate + log would-be denials for a week, alert affected tenants, then enforce — a limiter change is a breaking API change.
  • Where does the limiter sit relative to auth? — Coarse IP/anonymous limits before auth (cheap protection from junk traffic), per-user/per-key limits after auth (identity needed). Two layers, both cheap.

Design a distributed unique ID generator (Snowflake)

Why interviewers ask: it is a 15-minute sub-question inside almost every other design (message ids, order ids, tweet ids) and it quietly tests bit arithmetic, clock skew (time in distributed systems), and "why not just the database?".

Requirements & numbers. Globally unique 64-bit ids (fits a bigint, sorts as a number), roughly time-ordered (so B-tree inserts append instead of random-writing — index locality), 10k+/s per node with no coordination on the hot path, no single point of failure. UUIDv4 fails the ordered requirement (128 random bits shred index locality); a single DB AUTO_INCREMENT fails the SPOF/throughput one.

Snowflake layout (Twitter's, the canonical answer): 1 sign bit (0, keeps it positive) + 41 bits timestamp in ms since a custom epoch (241 ms ≈ 69 years) + 10 bits machine id (1024 workers) + 12 bits per-ms sequence (4096 ids/ms/worker = 4M ids/s per worker theoretical). Ids from different workers in the same ms interleave arbitrarily — ordering is k-sorted (ordered to ~ms precision), not total, and that is fine for feeds and pagination.

Snowflake (64-bit)UUIDv7 (128-bit)DB sequences
CoordinationWorker-id assignment onlyNone at allEvery id (or every batch)
Ordered?k-sorted by msk-sorted by ms (48-bit ts + random)Strictly, per sequence
Size / index cost8 B, append-friendly16 B, append-friendly (v4 is NOT)8 B, append-friendly
Throughput ceiling4M/s/worker × 1024Effectively unboundedOne writer; batch ranges help (Flickr ticket servers: two DBs, odd/even ids)
Pick whenNeed compact bigint ids at scaleNeed zero infrastructure; 16 B acceptableSingle-DB app; simplicity wins (don't over-build)

Pitfalls

  • Proposing UUIDv4 for a primary key at scale — random keys turn every B-tree insert into a random page write and bloat every secondary index (16 B repeated per index entry).
  • Ignoring worker-id assignment — two pods with the same worker id silently duplicate ids; the lease/registration step IS part of the design.
  • Claiming Snowflake ids are totally ordered — they are k-sorted; two ids in the same ms from different workers have no defined order.
  • Timestamp leaks: Snowflake ids reveal creation time (and volume, if sequences are guessable) — fine internally, think twice for public-facing ids.
Interview questions
  • Why not just Redis INCR? — Works (atomic, fast) but adds a network RTT per id, a SPOF unless clustered, and ids reveal exact global count; batch-fetching ranges fixes the RTT and is a legitimate lightweight answer.
  • How does Instagram's variant differ? — Same idea inside Postgres: 41 bits time + 13 bits logical shard + 10 bits per-shard sequence, generated in a PL/pgSQL default — no extra service.
  • What if you need strict global ordering? — No decentralized generator gives it; you need a single sequencer or consensus (Raft) and you pay its throughput/latency. Interview answer: challenge the requirement — per-key ordering usually suffices.
  • 241 ms from a 2020 epoch runs out when? — ~2089. State the epoch choice; reusing Twitter's 2010 epoch wastes a decade.
  • Why is time-ordering worth the clock headaches? — Ids double as cursors for pagination (WHERE id < ?), rough created-at, and index-append locality; random ids give up all three.

Design a chat system (WhatsApp / Messenger scale)

Why interviewers ask: chat forces every hard topic at once — stateful connections, per-conversation ordering, delivery guarantees to flaky mobile clients, fan-out, and an enormous write volume — and there is a crisp, well-known good answer to compare you against.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. 1:1 and group chat (≤1024 members), delivery states (sent/delivered/read), presence, media, offline delivery, optional E2EE. 500M DAU × 100 msgs/day = 50B msgs/day ≈ 580k msg/s average, ~1.5M/s peak; ~300 B/message → ~15 TB/day of message writes. Each online user holds one persistent connection: hundreds of millions of concurrent sockets. Latency target: sender→recipient p95 < 500 ms. Ordering: per conversation only — nobody needs global order (causal beats linearizable here).

Step 2 — API & data model. Clients keep a WebSocket to a gateway; everything else is stateless services behind it. Messages land in a write-optimized store using exactly the wide-column chat schema: partition (chat_id, bucket), clustering sent_at DESC — "last N messages of a chat" is one partition read.

WS frames:  send {chatId, clientMsgId, body} → ack {msgId, ts}     (clientMsgId = idempotency key)
            recv {msgId, chatId, from, body} → client acks → server marks delivered
HTTP:       GET /chats/{id}/messages?before=cursor      (history, paging)

messages:   PK ((chat_id, bucket)), sent_at DESC | msg_id (snowflake) | sender | body | state
inbox/sync: per-user queue of undelivered msg ids (drained on connect)
registry:   user_id → {gateway_id, device_ids}   (Redis, TTL by heartbeat)

Deep dive — the gateway fleet. A tuned server holds ~500k–1M mostly-idle sockets (memory-bound: ~10 KB/conn); 300M concurrent users ⇒ ~300–600 gateways. Gateways do almost nothing — auth the socket, heartbeat, forward frames — precisely so they rarely deploy (every deploy = mass reconnect storm; drain slowly and stagger, rolling deploys). Presence: client heartbeats every ~30 s refresh a TTL'd registry entry; "online" = entry exists, "last seen" = last heartbeat. Presence fan-out to watchers is the hidden load — batch it and only notify chats currently on screen.

Deep dive — groups. Sender writes ONE copy of the message to the conversation partition; fan-out happens at delivery: look up each member's gateway and push, inbox-append for offline members. For a 1024-member group that's ≤1024 registry lookups + pushes per message — bounded and parallel. Contrast with feeds (next card) where fan-out-on-write to millions is the problem. Per-conversation ordering: all appends go to one partition, ordered by (sent_at, msg_id); concurrent sends in the same ms get an arbitrary but consistent order that all members see identically.

Deep dive — E2EE in one paragraph. With the Signal protocol, clients exchange keys (X3DH) and ratchet per message (Double Ratchet); the server relays ciphertext it cannot read. Design consequences: the server can't index or search message bodies, receipts/typing indicators stay plaintext metadata (who-talks-to-whom is still visible), multi-device means encrypting per device key, and spam/abuse detection must move client-side or onto metadata. Everything else in the architecture is unchanged — E2EE is a payload property, not a topology change.

Pitfalls

  • Acking "sent" before persisting — a chat system's one unforgivable sin is losing an acked message; durability precedes the ack, always.
  • Using push notifications as the delivery path — they're best-effort hints; the inbox + reconnect-sync is the real offline path.
  • Polling ("client checks every 5 s") — 500M users × 0.2 QPS = 100M QPS of mostly-empty polls; persistent connections exist for exactly this (realtime transports).
  • Global message ordering via one sequencer — unnecessary (per-chat is the requirement) and a 1.5M/s bottleneck. Requirements first.
  • Storing group messages once per recipient — 1024× write amplification at 15 TB/day; store once, track per-member delivery cursors.
Interview questions
  • A gateway with 800k connections dies — walk me through recovery. — Clients detect via missed heartbeats and reconnect (with jitter, or they thundering-herd the LB — least-connections helps); registry entries TTL out; messages sent meanwhile follow the offline path, so nothing is lost — reconnect sync drains them. Recovery time ≈ heartbeat interval + reconnect backoff.
  • How do you order messages when two people send at the same instant? — Server order wins: the partition append order (sent_at, msg_id) is the truth all clients converge to; client timestamps are display-only (clocks lie).
  • Why Cassandra-style storage for messages? — 1.5M/s append-only writes with reads of recent slices per chat is the LSM sweet spot; (chat_id, bucket) partitioning caps partition size and makes history paging one-partition reads.
  • Where does media go? — Client uploads to object storage via a presigned URL, sends only the reference through chat; recipients fetch via CDN. Never through the message pipeline.
  • Read receipts for a 500-member group? — Don't fan out every member's read event to every other member (O(n²)); store per-member cursors and aggregate ("read by 47") lazily on demand.
  • What's your typing indicator design? — Ephemeral: throttled events over the socket to online chat-open members only, never persisted, drop on any failure — correctness class "who cares", say so explicitly.
  • 50k messages/day chat app for one enterprise — same design? — No: one Postgres, one WebSocket tier, no Cassandra, no registry sharding. Saying which parts of the big design you'd delete is a senior signal (right-sizing).

Design a news feed (Twitter / Instagram)

Why interviewers ask: the fan-out decision is the purest scale trade-off in the canon — write amplification vs read latency — and the celebrity problem forces you to admit no single strategy works, which is exactly the "hybrid thinking" senior interviews screen for.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers.
