Post (text/media), follow, and read a home feed of recent posts from followees; feed p99 < 200 ms; eventual consistency fine (a post appearing after 10 s is acceptable — say this out loud, it licenses the whole design). 200M DAU: writes ~5k posts/s; feed reads ~10 loads/user/day ≈ 25k reads/s avg, 100k/s peak — read:write ~20:1, and each read wants the merged, ranked top-of-feed from ~400 followees in one round trip.

Step 2 — API & data model. POST /posts, GET /feed?cursor=…, POST /follows. Tables: posts (by author), follows (two indexes: my followees for read-path merge, my followers for write-path fan-out — two access paths, two indexes), and a per-user feed cache: a Redis list/zset of ~800 post ids per user (ids only — hydrate post bodies from a separate post cache; never duplicate bodies 400×).

Deep dive — the trade-off table you must say. Fan-out on write: reads are O(1), writes are O(followers) — dies on celebrities; also wasteful for inactive users (precomputing feeds nobody loads — skip fan-out to users inactive >30 days, rebuild on their return). Fan-out on read: writes O(1), reads merge O(followees) timelines — 400 fetches per feed load at 100k loads/s is 40M lookups/s; dies on read latency. Hybrid: push for the many-small, pull for the few-huge. The threshold is tunable — it's the knob trading write amplification against read fan-in.

Deep dive — pagination & ranking. Cursor = opaque (rank_score/timestamp, post_id) of the last item, NOT offset — offsets shift as new posts arrive, giving duplicates/skips (cursor pagination). Ranking: fetch ~800 candidate ids, hydrate features, score with a model, return top 50 — done at read time so scores are fresh; the feed list stays chronological and ranking is a layer on top. Keep a "ranking pointer" per user (last-served position) so refresh shows new-since-last-visit first.

Pitfalls

  • Pure fan-out-on-write with "we'll handle celebrities later" — the interviewer WILL ask; the hybrid split is the expected answer, volunteer it.
  • Storing full post bodies in every follower's feed list — 800 posts × 1 KB × 200M users ≈ 160 TB of duplicated cache; store ids, hydrate from one post cache.
  • OFFSET pagination on a moving feed — duplicates on every refresh; cursors are non-negotiable.
  • Treating the feed cache as durable — it's rebuildable from posts+follows; losing a Redis shard means rebuild-on-read for those users, not data loss. Design the rebuild path.
  • Ignoring unfollow/delete: a deleted post must be filtered at read (tombstone/lookup) — you can't reach into 80M cached lists to remove it.
Interview questions
  • Walk me through the p99 of a feed load. — Registry-cached session → 1 Redis read (list of ids, ~1 ms) → multiget post bodies (cache, ~1–2 ms) → celebrity pull (cached, parallel) → rank (~10–20 ms model) → respond; budget dominated by ranking, not I/O. Misses (inactive user, evicted list) fall back to on-demand merge: slower but correct.
  • New user follows 200 accounts — feed is empty. Fix? — Backfill on follow: pull recent posts of new followees into the list asynchronously; the read-path merge covers the gap meanwhile.
  • Why Redis lists and not a DB table per user feed? — The feed is an ephemeral, capped, hot view — exactly cache-shaped; a 200M-row-churning table buys durability nobody needs (Redis structures).
  • How does Instagram's problem differ from Twitter's? — Same skeleton; media-heavy (CDN dominates, edge delivery), stronger ranking (engagement model), and fewer mega-broadcast accounts historically → they ran fan-out-on-write further.
  • What breaks first at 10×? — Fan-out write volume (15M pushes/s): shard fan-out workers by follower-list segment, batch pushes per Redis shard, and lower the celebrity threshold — the knob exists precisely for this.
  • Likes/comment counts on feed items? — Don't fan those out; they're read-time hydration from a counter cache, eventually consistent, rounded ("1.2K") — precision is wasted there.

Design a notification system

Why interviewers ask: it looks easy ("send an email") and is actually a masterclass in async design: multi-provider failover, exactly-one-send, user preferences as a filter pipeline, and delivery tracking through third parties you don't control.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. One internal API for all teams to send push/email/SMS; per-user preferences and quiet hours; templates; no duplicates (a double "payment failed" SMS is a support ticket, a double marketing push is churn); delivery tracking. Scale: 50M notifications/day ≈ 600/s average but extremely bursty — a marketing campaign wants 5M pushes in 10 minutes ≈ 8k/s sustained. Latency: transactional (OTP) < 5 s; campaigns can smear over minutes. That split — transactional vs bulk — is the first design decision: separate queues, separate priorities, so a campaign never delays an OTP.

Step 2 — API & model. Callers send an intent, not a channel: the system resolves channels from event type + user preferences.

POST /notify {idempotencyKey, userId, event:"order_shipped", data:{...}, class:"txn|bulk"}
prefs:     user_id | event_class → channels {push:on, email:on, sms:critical-only},
           quiet_hours 22:00–08:00 local (critical overrides)
devices:   user_id → [apns/fcm tokens], email, phone   (verified, with bounce state)
sent_log:  idempotency_key PK | status | provider_msg_id | timestamps   (dedupe + tracking)

Deep dive — "exactly one send". Three layers, none sufficient alone: (1) caller-supplied idempotency key deduped at the API (stops caller retries); (2) outbox + at-least-once queue delivery means workers may see a message twice → worker re-checks sent_log state and passes the key to the provider (most support idempotent send APIs); (3) crash after provider call but before recording → the provider-side key is the last line. Net: duplicates are possible in a vanishing window and harmless because the provider dedupes — this honest layering is the answer, not "we use exactly-once" (delivery guarantees).

Deep dive — preferences as a pipeline. Evaluate in order: device/address validity → user channel opt-ins per event class → quiet hours (defer, don't drop: schedule for 08:00 local via a delayed queue) → per-user frequency caps ("max 2 marketing pushes/day", a token bucket per user per class) → global campaign throttle. Every drop/defer is logged with a reason — "why didn't the user get it?" is the #1 ops question.

Pitfalls

  • One queue for everything — a 5M-message campaign delays every OTP by minutes; class-separated queues with priority is table stakes.
  • Synchronous provider calls in the API request — provider p99s are seconds; the API accepts, persists, returns 202. Always.
  • Quiet hours in server timezone — 22:00 UTC is midday for half your users; store user timezone, defer in local time.
  • No bounce handling — mailing dead addresses tanks sender reputation and then NOBODY gets email; webhooks aren't optional telemetry, they're a control loop.
Interview questions
  • How do you avoid double-sending when a worker crashes mid-batch? — At-least-once redelivery + sent_log state check + provider idempotency key; state transitions (claimed → sent → delivered) make redelivered work a no-op.
  • Provider gives you 100 msg/s; the campaign needs 5M. How long, and how do you enforce it? — ~14 hours at 100/s — surface that math to the campaign owner; enforce with a worker-side rate limiter per provider, and buy more throughput or a second provider if the business needs faster.
  • Push token is invalid — what happens? — APNs/FCM return an unregistered error → delete the token; it means the app was uninstalled. Retrying invalid tokens gets your sender throttled.
  • How do teams onboard a new notification type safely? — Templates + event-class registration as config with review, default opt-in rules per class, and a mandatory dry-run mode that renders and counts recipients without sending.
  • Where would you add batching? — Digest low-priority events per user ("5 new comments" instead of 5 pushes) with a short aggregation window keyed by (user, event class) — huge UX and cost win, cheap to build on the delayed-queue machinery.
  • What do you monitor? — Per-channel: queue lag (freshness), send rate vs provider limit, provider error rate (failover trigger), end-to-end delivery rate by provider, bounce/complaint rates (RED per channel).

Design a web crawler

Why interviewers ask: a crawler is a distributed systems problem where the internet itself is the adversary: you must go fast globally while being slow per host, dedupe an unbounded URL space, and survive malicious/broken sites. The frontier data structure is the heart, and few candidates know it.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Crawl 1B pages/month for a search index; be polite (respect robots.txt, ≤1 req/host/second — this is a hard correctness requirement, not a nicety); dedupe URLs and near-duplicate content; recrawl by freshness. 1B/month ≈ ~400 pages/s sustained; avg page ~100 KB → ~40 MB/s download bandwidth; storage ~100 TB/month raw (compressed ~20 TB) into object storage. The tension to name immediately: 400/s globally is easy, but politeness caps you at ~1/s per host — so you need thousands of hosts in flight concurrently, which is exactly what the frontier must arrange.

Step 2 — Components. Frontier (the smart queue) → fetchers (async I/O, thousands of concurrent connections) → parser/extractor → dedupe (URL-seen set + content fingerprints) → storage pipeline → scheduler (recrawl). Everything scales horizontally by partitioning URLs by host — one host is owned by one crawler node, which makes politeness enforceable locally without coordination (shard by the constraint).

Deep dive — dedupe at two levels. URL-seen: billions of URLs → a Bloom filter in front of a persistent KV: filter says "definitely new" for the common case at ~10 bits/URL (1% FP means ~1% of genuinely-new URLs wrongly skipped — acceptable; or confirm positives against the KV). Content-seen: exact dupes via checksum; near-dupes via simhash — 64-bit fingerprint where similar documents differ in ≤3 bits; find neighbors by splitting the 64 bits into 4 bands of 16 and indexing each band (Hamming distance ≤3 guarantees at least one identical band — that's the trick worth saying).

Deep dive — traps & freshness. Spider traps: infinite calendars, session-id URL spinners, link farms. Defenses are budgets, not detection: max depth (~15), max URLs per host per crawl cycle, max URL length, adaptive host penalty when content repeats. Freshness: recrawl interval adapts per page — halve it when a fetch shows change, double it (capped) when unchanged; news hits hourly, static pages settle at monthly. Conditional GETs (ETag/If-Modified-Since) make a "no change" check nearly free (HTTP validators).

Pitfalls

  • One global FIFO queue — 10,000 consecutive URLs from one big site either hammer it (rude, you get IP-banned) or stall the whole crawler waiting for politeness delays. The per-host back-queue structure IS the design.
  • Checking robots.txt per-URL against the live site — fetch it once per host per day; it's a cache with TTL, and its crawl-delay feeds the heap delay.
  • Dedupe on raw URL strings — example.com/a?utm=x vs /a explodes the frontier; normalization comes first, always.
  • Ignoring fetch failures taxonomy — DNS failure, 4xx, 5xx, timeout each need different retry/give-up policies; a naive uniform retry re-crawls the dead web forever.
Interview questions
  • How do you split work across 50 crawler nodes? — Consistent-hash hosts to nodes: each node owns its hosts' back queues, politeness needs no cross-node coordination, and robots/DNS caches get natural locality. Rebalance moves hosts, not URLs.
  • Your crawler does 40 pages/s instead of 400 — diagnose. — Almost always frontier starvation: too few distinct ready hosts (heap mostly in the future). Check hosts-in-flight metric; fixes: widen discovery, raise per-host parallelism where robots allows, lower priority-queue bias toward few big sites.
  • How big is the URL-seen structure for 10B URLs? — Bloom at 10 bits/URL ≈ 12.5 GB — fits in RAM per shard; the authoritative KV behind it is disk-based. That arithmetic is the expected answer.
  • Handle JavaScript-rendered pages? — A separate headless-browser fetch pool, 10–100× the cost per page — only for domains flagged as JS-dependent; never in the main fetch path.
  • How do you avoid crawling the same content behind different domains (mirrors)? — Content fingerprints catch it after one fetch per mirror; simhash clusters plus host-level "duplication ratio" metrics demote mirror hosts entirely.
  • What's in your storage pipeline? — Fetcher appends raw responses to WARC segments in object storage (immutable, cheap), a queue of "page stored" events feeds parsers/indexers downstream — log-structured handoff so re-indexing is a replay, not a re-crawl.

Design Top-K / trending (hashtags, hot products, most-played)

Why interviewers ask: "count views per video and show the top 10" sounds like a GROUP BY — at 10M events/s it cannot be. The expected move is trading exactness for bounded memory (sketches), and the follow-ups probe whether you understand what error you accepted.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Top 100 trending items over the last 5 minutes / 1 hour / 24 hours, refreshed every ~10 s, item space unbounded (hashtags, URLs), 10M events/s at peak. Approximate is explicitly fine — nobody audits position 87 of a trending list; say this, it licenses the sketch. Exact counting needs a counter per distinct key: 100M+ keys × per-window = memory blowup, and a hot key (celebrity skew) melts whichever shard owns it — exact global counting is the trap this question sets.

Step 2 — Shape. Events → Kafka partitioned by item id → stream aggregators, each holding a count-min sketch + min-heap of K candidates per window → periodic merge into a serving store; a batch layer (exact counts from the event log) corrects the realtime numbers for the long windows.

Deep dive — where the errors actually are. CMS error is one-sided (overcount) and proportional to total volume N — heavy hitters are barely affected relatively, tail items can be badly inflated: fine for top-K (we only rank heads), disastrous if you bill on it (then you need exact counts, which is a different, more expensive system — say so). Heap-miss error: an item that becomes hot late can be temporarily under-ranked until its estimate beats the heap min; mitigated by generous K (track top-1000, serve top-100). "Trending" vs "top": trending ranks by acceleration — score = countnow/expected (from same hour last week) — otherwise the list is permanently "login" and "weather".

Deep dive — celebrity skew. One item at 1M events/s overwhelms its partition's aggregator. Fix with two-stage aggregation: producers (or a first stream stage) pre-aggregate per-item counts locally over ~1 s and emit deltas — the hot item becomes N deltas/s instead of 1M raw events (hot-key splitting, same medicine).

Pitfalls

  • Proposing SELECT id, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 100 at 10M/s — the interviewer set this trap; walk into it and the rest is uphill.
  • Redis ZINCRBY per raw event — a single hot zset shard caps out around 100k ops/s; fine at small scale (say when!), not at 10M/s.
  • Sliding windows by storing per-key timestamps — unbounded memory; the ring-of-sketches is the answer.
  • Forgetting that CMS can't list keys — without the heap (or a second pass) you have counts for everything and a list of nothing.
Interview questions
  • Why count-min over just sampling 1% of events? — Sampling works for heads too and is even cheaper, but errors on mid-tail items are large and it can't answer point queries ("how hot is X?") with bounds; CMS gives every key an estimate with a provable one-sided bound. Combining both is legitimate.
  • Top-K per country and per topic too? — Key the sketch/heap per (dimension) — memory multiplies by cardinality of dimensions, which is fine because each sketch is small; don't try one sketch over composite keys you'll need to slice.
  • Exactly how stale is your trending list? — Event→Kafka (~ms) + aggregation tick (1 s) + merge tick (5 s) + serving refresh (10 s) ≈ ~15 s worst case; every stage is a knob trading cost for freshness.
  • An aggregator crashes — what's lost? — Its in-memory window state; recover by replaying its partitions from Kafka offsets since the window start (minutes of data) — sketches rebuild deterministically. Checkpoint sketches every ~30 s to cut replay time (offsets + replay).
  • Product asks for exact view counts on video pages alongside trending. — Different system: per-item counters, batched increments (aggregate 1 s of views into one +N), sharded counter rows for the hottest items, eventual display ("1.2M views") — never serve page counts from the sketch.

Design ride-hailing dispatch (Uber / Lyft)

Why interviewers ask: it introduces a whole dimension the other classics lack — geospatial indexing under a brutal write rate — plus a matching problem with real-world race conditions (two riders, one driver) and a money-bearing state machine.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Riders request; nearby drivers get offers; one accepts; trip runs to completion; surge pricing per zone. 1M drivers online, location ping every 4 s → 250k location writes/s — the defining number: this stream is too hot for a disk-based DB and too ephemeral to deserve one (only the latest position matters). Matching: ~10k requests/s peak, match latency target < 3 s. Trip state must be durable and consistent — that's where the real database lives.

Step 2 — Split hot from durable. Location service: in-memory geo index, sharded by cell, fed by the ping stream; TTL ~15 s (a driver who stops pinging vanishes from matching — heartbeat-style liveness). Trip service: Postgres-class store with the trip state machine. Surge service: consumes the same ping/request streams, computes demand/supply per cell per minute.

POST /rides {riderId, pickup:{lat,lng}, dest}  → 202 {rideId}   (match result pushed)
driver app  ── ping {driverId, lat, lng, heading} every 4s ──→ location ingest
trip states: REQUESTED → MATCHING → OFFERED → ACCEPTED → ARRIVING
             → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED | CANCELLED  (each transition audited, idempotent)

Deep dive — geohash vs S2 vs H3 (know one sentence each). Geohash: base32 prefix encoding of interleaved lat/lng bits — prefix = containment, works as plain string keys in Redis (GEOADD uses it) — but cells are rectangles that distort near poles and neighbor-finding at boundaries needs the 8-neighbor fix-up (two points meters apart can share no prefix across a cell edge — the classic gotcha). S2 (Google): projects the sphere onto a cube → quadtree of near-equal-area cells, great covering algorithms ("give me cells covering this circle"). H3 (Uber, built FOR this problem): hexagons — all 6 neighbors are equidistant (no diagonal bias in ring search), smooth multi-resolution — the natural fit for expanding-ring driver search and surge zones.

Deep dive — the state machine is the product. Every transition is a conditional update (WHERE state = 'OFFERED') so duplicate/late messages can't double-advance (idempotent transitions); illegal transitions are rejected and logged. Cancellations race accepts constantly — CAS decides, the loser gets a clean "already accepted/cancelled" answer. Payment holds/capture hang off COMPLETED via a saga. ETA in one line: precomputed road-graph routing (contraction hierarchies) corrected by live traffic from the ping firehose — the pings you already have are the traffic sensor.

Pitfalls

  • Writing every ping to Postgres/Cassandra — 250k writes/s of data that's stale in 4 s; latest-position belongs in memory (archive a sampled trail async to object storage for analytics/disputes).
  • Radius search via WHERE lat BETWEEN … AND lng BETWEEN … on a B-tree — a 2-D query on 1-D indexes scans huge stripes; that's precisely what cell indexes exist to avoid.
  • Offering one ride to 5 drivers with no lock and "first accept wins" — double-accept race → two drivers en route, one furious; the offer lock or atomic claim is required.
  • Forgetting driver-side state: a driver mid-trip must not be matchable; index membership is driven by the state machine, not just pings.
Interview questions
  • A location-index shard dies — what's the blast radius? — Drivers in those cells unmatchable for seconds; rebuild is trivial: the next ping wave (≤4 s) repopulates from scratch. Ephemeral data = cheap recovery; that's WHY it's separated from trip state.
  • How would you shard the location index? — By cell-prefix ranges so a query's ring of cells touches few shards; city-dense regions get more shards (range sharding, heat-aware splits).
  • Rider and driver both see "searching…" forever — debug. — Check: offer locks leaking (TTL not expiring), state machine stuck in MATCHING (worker died mid-saga — need a reaper for stale states), or index TTLs purging drivers whose pings are dropped upstream.
  • Why not match with a global optimizer instead of greedy-nearest? — Batch matching (collect requests for ~2 s, solve assignment across them) genuinely beats greedy on city-wide efficiency — mention it as the v2; greedy per-request is the interview-scale answer.
  • Where do WebSockets appear here? — Driver and rider apps hold persistent connections for offers, accept, live trip position — same gateway + registry pattern as chat; reuse that design wholesale.
  • Surge zones flicker between 1.0× and 1.8× — fix? — Hysteresis and smoothing: minimum dwell time per price level, average over trailing windows and neighbor cells; pricing stability is a product requirement, encode it in the aggregation.

Design distributed file storage & sync (Dropbox / S3-lite)

Why interviewers ask: it tests the metadata/data split — the pattern behind S3, HDFS, and every photo app — plus content-addressed dedupe and a sync protocol that must survive offline edits and conflicts.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Upload/download files (up to GBs), sync across devices within seconds, share folders with permissions, version history, never lose a byte (11-nines durability class). 100M users × 5 GB avg = 500 PB logical — but typical dedupe + compression cuts stored bytes 30–50% (same PDFs, installers, photos everywhere). Sync traffic is dominated by small edits to big files — the requirement that forces chunking.

Step 2 — The split. A small, strongly-consistent metadata service (namespace tree, file → ordered chunk list, versions, ACLs — Postgres-class, sharded by namespace) and a huge, dumb, immutable block store (chunks keyed by content hash, on object storage, erasure-coded). Clients talk to metadata for truth and move bulk bytes directly to/from the block store via presigned URLs — the control/data-plane split that keeps the metadata tier tiny.

file = ordered list of chunks (~4 MB), chunk id = SHA-256(content)
metadata: files(id, path, version, chunk_ids[], size, owner)
          namespaces + ACLs (folder → members → role)
          devices(cursor)              ← per-device sync position
block store: PUT/GET /blocks/{sha256}  (immutable, write-once, refcounted)

Deep dive — conflicts. Two devices edit offline and both commit "v7→v8". The metadata commit is conditional on the base version (optimistic concurrency): the first wins, the second gets a conflict and — for files — does NOT merge: it creates "report (Bob's conflicted copy)". That's a deliberate product decision: silent merges of binary files destroy data; surfacing the conflict is honest. (Google-Docs-style merging needs CRDTs/OT and is a different product — one sentence, offered.)

Deep dive — sharing & garbage. Sharing = adding members to a namespace with roles; moving a folder into a shared namespace re-parents metadata, moves no bytes. Permission checks live at the metadata layer (which also mints the presigned block URLs — short-lived, per-chunk, so the dumb block store needs no ACL logic). Deletes: decrement chunk refcounts; actual reclamation is a lazy background sweep after the version-retention window — never synchronous, and refcounting bugs are why you also run a periodic mark-and-sweep audit.

Pitfalls

  • Streaming file bytes through your API servers — the classic; bulk data goes client↔block-store direct with presigned URLs, or your app tier becomes a very expensive proxy.
  • Storing files whole — a 1-byte edit re-uploads 400 MB, versioning costs full copies, dedupe disappears; chunking is load-bearing for all three.
  • Metadata in the blob store "for simplicity" — listing a folder or renaming becomes a scan; the namespace needs a real transactional DB.
  • Last-writer-wins on file conflicts — you just silently discarded someone's afternoon; conflicted-copy is the acceptable default.
Interview questions
  • Why ~4 MB chunks and not 64 KB or 64 MB? — Small chunks: better dedupe granularity, but chunk-list metadata and per-request overhead balloon (a 1 GB file = 16k entries at 64 KB). Big chunks: tiny metadata, terrible delta efficiency. 1–8 MB is the sweet spot; state the trade-off, not the number.
  • How does the block store achieve durability? — Replicate ×3 or erasure-code (e.g. 6+3: survives 3 losses at 1.5× overhead vs 3× for replication), spread across failure domains, plus continuous scrubbing against bit-rot (object-store internals).
  • Client uploads 999 of 1000 chunks then dies — state? — No commit happened: the file doesn't exist at v8; orphaned chunks await GC. Resume is free: the diff call returns the 1 missing hash. Upload is naturally idempotent — content-addressed PUTs are safe to repeat.
  • Sync storm: a 10k-member shared folder gets one edit. — One metadata change, 10k notifications (cheap, tiny), 10k downloads of one 4 MB chunk — served from CDN/cache because chunk content is immutable → perfectly cacheable (immutability is the best cache policy).
  • Where does S3-lite differ from Dropbox-lite? — S3 exposes the flat blob API (bucket/key → bytes) with no sync/namespace tree — it IS roughly the block store + a metadata index; Dropbox is an application (namespaces, sync, conflicts) built atop one. Saying which you're designing scopes the interview.

Design typeahead / autocomplete

Why interviewers ask: a read-latency problem in its purest form — every keystroke is a query with a <50 ms end-to-end budget — so it tests whether you reach for precomputation instead of clever query-time work.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Top 5–10 suggestions per keystroke from popular queries; p99 < 50 ms end-to-end (perceived-instant threshold ~100 ms, and the network eats half — so the server has ~10 ms). 10M DAU × 20 searches × ~8 keystrokes ≈ 1.6B lookups/day ≈ ~20k QPS avg, 60k peak. Fresh-ish: a breaking-news query should suggest within ~30 min; per-keystroke freshness is NOT required — that asymmetry is the whole design.

Step 2 — Core insight: precompute top-K per prefix. The query-time work must be O(1): a hash lookup prefix → [top 10 completions]. A trie with top-K cached at every node is the textbook structure (walk to the prefix node, read its cached list — no subtree walk at query time); the production-flavored equivalent is the flattened form: every prefix (cap length at ~20) is a key in Redis/a KV store with the precomputed list as the value. Space math: 100M distinct queries × avg 15 prefixes × ~100 B entry ≈ 150 GB — shard by prefix, replicate hot shards (short prefixes are astronomically hotter — 1-char prefixes are ~26 keys taking a huge fraction of traffic → cache them in the API node's memory, local L1 cache).

Update pipeline: query logs → stream + hourly batch job aggregates counts (with time decay so yesterday's spike fades) → rebuild changed prefix lists → bulk-load into the serving store as a versioned dataset (build offline, flip a pointer — never mutate the serving copy in place, blue/green for data). A parallel streaming path boosts suddenly-hot queries into lists within minutes without waiting for the batch. Personalization in one line: re-rank the top-10 client/API-side against the user's recent history — never per-user precomputation. Also: filter offensive suggestions at build time (a policy service in the pipeline — cheaper and safer than query-time).

Trie in service memoryPrefix-hash in Redis/KV
Query costO(len) pointer walk + cached top-K at nodeOne GET, O(1)
MemoryCompact (shared prefixes stored once)Redundant (every prefix a key) — ~2–5×
Ops storyCustom service: sharding, rebuild, failover are yoursStandard cache ops; sharding/replication built in
UpdatesRebuild + atomic swap per shardWrite per changed prefix; versioned namespace flip
Pick whenYou control latency to the µs / huge scale (search engines)Almost everyone else — say this

Pitfalls

  • Query-time SELECT … WHERE query LIKE 'pre%' ORDER BY count LIMIT 10 — a range scan + sort per keystroke; even indexed, it blows a 10 ms budget at 60k QPS. Precompute.
  • Counting keystrokes as searches in the pipeline — log submitted queries, or "j", "ja", "jav" pollute the popularity model.
  • Ignoring the client: debounce (~100–150 ms), cancel in-flight requests on the next keystroke, and cache prefix→results in the browser — the cheapest QPS reduction in the whole design.
  • Rebuilding all 1.5B prefix keys hourly — rebuild only prefixes whose top-K actually changed (delta detection in the batch job); full rebuilds are a weekly event.
Interview questions
  • Walk through the <50 ms budget. — Client debounce aside: network to edge ~10–20 ms (put suggest API behind CDN PoPs / regional replicas — edge proximity), LB + API ~1 ms, L1 hit ~0 or Redis GET ~1 ms, serialize ~1 ms. The budget is spent on the wire, which is why geography (regional serving copies) matters more than server code.
  • How do trending queries appear within minutes? — Streaming path: a top-K/CMS aggregator over the live query stream flags risers; a fast lane patches just their prefix lists. The batch remains the source of truth and reconciles hourly.
  • Multi-language / unicode? — Normalize (NFC, casefold) at both build and query time; CJK has no useful "prefix" per keystroke → suggest on pinyin/romaji or after IME composition events.
  • Typo tolerance? — Not in the hot path: precompute common misspellings into the same lists (edit-distance-1 variants of head queries at build time); true fuzzy search per keystroke busts the budget.
  • What breaks at 10×? — Nothing structural: it's read-only, versioned, cacheable data — add replicas and edge caches. The pipeline (build time) strains before serving does; shard the batch job by prefix range.

Design ticket booking / flash sale (BookMyShow, concert on-sale)

Why interviewers ask: it inverts every other design in this section — here correctness under contention beats latency and availability: 500k people want 40k seats in the same minute, and selling seat 12F twice is the one unforgivable outcome. It's the applied exam for locking, transactions, and admission control.

Step 1 — Requirements & numbers. Browse events, view a live seat map, hold seats while paying, confirm on payment; zero oversell; fairness under a stampede. Steady state is boring (~100 bookings/s nationally); the design point is the flash sale: 500k users arriving in 60 s for one event's 40k seats — 8k+ RPS on ONE event's inventory rows, the definitional hot partition that sharding cannot fix (the contention is semantic: everyone wants the same seats).

Step 2 — API & data model. The three-step protocol IS the design: hold → pay → confirm, with the hold expiring on TTL so abandoned checkouts return inventory automatically.

POST /events/{id}/holds   {seats:["12E","12F"]} → 201 {holdId, expiresAt: +5min} | 409
POST /bookings            {holdId, paymentToken} → 202 (payment saga starts)
seats: event_id | seat_id | state: AVAILABLE→HELD→SOLD | hold_id | hold_expires_at | version
holds are the only writers of HELD; a reaper (and lazy checks) expire them

Deep dive — surviving the stampede: the virtual waiting room. 500k arrivals in 60 s must not reach the inventory DB. Admission control at the edge: arrivals get a queue token and a live position (WebSocket/polling); a gate releases users into the store at a rate the booking path measurably sustains (say 2k/s), everyone else waits with an honest ETA. This converts an overload problem into a queueing problem — and it's fairer than letting retry-storms win. Randomize within arrival cohorts to blunt bots; bind tokens to sessions so they can't be resold. The seat-map service, meanwhile, serves a cached, slightly-stale map (1–2 s) to everyone — only holds touch truth.

Deep dive — where the inventory lives. For seated events, rows in a transactional DB (one event's 40k seats fit one shard — contention, not volume, is the issue). For unseated inventory (general admission, flash-sale stock of 10k iPhones), a counter: atomic DECR in Redis with periodic reconciliation to the DB, or DB row with UPDATE stock = stock-1 WHERE stock > 0. Never oversell-then-apologize by default — but note the airline counter-example (deliberate overbooking is a business policy, not a bug), which shows "zero oversell" is a requirement to confirm, not assume.

Pitfalls

  • Read-then-write holds ("SELECT state; if AVAILABLE then UPDATE") — the check-then-act race sells the seat twice; the condition must live inside the write.
  • Holding seats in Redis only — a Redis failover can drop holds while payments are in flight → double-sell against the DB's view. Holds are money-bearing state: put them where the transactions are, use Redis for the seat-map cache.
  • No TTL on holds — one crashed client strands seat inventory until ops intervenes; every hold needs an expiry AND a reaper.
  • Autoscaling as the flash-sale answer — the bottleneck is 40k contended rows, not CPU; more app servers just deliver the stampede faster. Admission control is the lever.
  • Payment webhook applied twice → two confirmations: every transition keyed by hold_id/booking_id and conditional — idempotency end to end.
Interview questions
  • Payment succeeds but your confirm crashes — user charged, no ticket. Recover. — The saga's pending booking record + payment-provider idempotency key let a recovery worker re-drive the confirm (or void the auth); reconciliation jobs compare provider records vs bookings nightly. Never rely on the user's retry.
  • How do you show the seat map to 500k browsers without melting the DB? — Cached snapshot (Redis/CDN, 1–2 s TTL) + delta push for seat state changes; accept staleness because the hold path re-checks truth — display and correctness are decoupled on purpose.
  • Optimistic or pessimistic locking here — defend your choice. — By conflict rate: browsing-era (low contention) optimistic versioning is fine; flash sale (~everyone conflicts) makes optimistic retry loops a DoS on yourself — single-statement conditional writes or brief FOR UPDATE (with NOWAIT/skip-locked to fail fast) win.
  • Bots take 90% of the queue — what do you do? — Layered: bot-detection before token issuance (POW/captcha/risk scoring), per-account+payment-method purchase caps enforced at confirm (the only uncheatable point), token-session binding, and post-hoc cancellation sweeps. Be honest that it's an arms race.
  • Can you shard your way out of the hot event? — Not semantically — but you can partition the seat space (per-section shards) so contention spreads across N rows-sets, and route holds by section. Works because users want "a seat in section X", not one global counter.
  • What's different for a movie theater vs a 60k-seat concert on-sale? — Same schema, different regime: movies = steady low contention, no waiting room, longer holds; the design's flash-sale machinery (admission, map caching) should be a mode you can turn ON, not permanent complexity (design for the load you have).

Your URL shortener must report per-link click counts. Which redirect status do you return, and why?

Analytics requires seeing the clicks: a 302 keeps the browser coming back every time. (a) is the tempting one — 301 IS lighter on your servers, but browsers cache it and never return, silently deleting your analytics (and your ability to expire or kill the link). (b) addresses method preservation, irrelevant for GET redirects; (d) adds latency and is hostile to users and crawlers alike.

In a chat system, when is it correct for the server to mark a message "sent ✓" to the sender?

"Sent" means "the server owns it now and will not lose it" — which is only true after durable persistence. (a) risks the one unforgivable chat failure: an acked message lost in a gateway crash. (c) and (d) describe stronger states — (d) is exactly what "delivered ✓✓" means; conflating sent with delivered breaks the offline path, where messages are sent but not deliverable for hours.

Your feed system fans out on write. A user with 40M followers posts 20 times a day. What is the standard fix?

The hybrid split: push for normal users, pull for celebrities — their posts are so hot they're always cached, making the read-time merge cheap. (b) is the tempting "scale it" answer: 800M pushes/day for one user is possible but pure waste, and the follower lists keep growing. (a) makes celebrity posts an hour late — a product non-starter; (d) solves engineering by deleting the product.

A Snowflake-style ID generator's node observes the wall clock jump 200 ms backwards. What must it do?

Timestamps it already used may be re-issued with the same sequence values → duplicate ids; the only safe move is to not go back in time: spin for small skews, alert and refuse for large ones. (a) is wrong because sequence numbers restart per millisecond — the same (ms, seq) pair can recur. (c) breaks the k-ordering contract and risks collisions; (d) permanently corrupts the time encoding.

Two gateway nodes check the same user's token bucket in Redis with GET, both see 1 token, both allow, both SET 0. What's the fix?

The read-modify-write must be atomic where the state lives — one Lua script does refill, check, and decrement with no interleaving. (d) is the classic near-miss: MULTI/EXEC queues commands atomically but can't branch on the GET result inside the transaction (you'd need WATCH+retry — a worse Lua). (a) just narrows the race window; (b) breaks the stateless-gateway model and fails when the sticky node dies.

Your crawler's single global URL queue happens to contain 50,000 consecutive wikipedia.org URLs. What does the two-level frontier (front + back queues) fix?

Politeness (~1 req/host/s) means those 50k URLs represent 14 hours of legal fetching from one host — a FIFO would either violate politeness or stall the fleet. Back queues serialize per host while the heap of next-allowed-times keeps fetchers busy across many hosts. (c) confuses priority policy (front queues) with the politeness mechanism; (d) — robots.txt is still fetched and cached per host regardless.

Why does a count-min sketch read the MINIMUM across its d hashed counters as the estimate?

Every increment of a colliding key adds to a cell; nothing ever subtracts. Each cell is therefore truth + pollution, and min picks the least-polluted view — a one-sided (over-)estimate with a provable bound. (a) inverts the error direction: CMS never undercounts. (d) is false — it's always approximate; d controls the probability of a bad estimate, not exactness.

Ride-hailing: 1M online drivers ping locations every 4 seconds. Where does this data belong?

250k writes/s of data whose value dies in 4 seconds — only the latest position matters for matching, and losing it costs one ping interval to rebuild. That's the profile of ephemeral in-memory state, not durable storage. (a) works mechanically but pays LSM/compaction costs for data nobody will ever read back; (b) couples the hottest write stream to your most correctness-critical DB; (d) makes reads O(stream) — a queue is transport, not an index.

Ticket booking: which statement makes the seat-hold race-free when A and B click seat 12F simultaneously?

The condition inside the write makes check-and-claim one atomic statement: exactly one of the two UPDATEs matches a row; the other gets rowcount 0 → 409. (a) is the check-then-act race itself. (c) adds a second source of truth that can disagree with the DB across failovers — and the DB could have done it alone. (d) is a SPOF that dies precisely during the flash sale.

In Dropbox-style storage, a 400 MB file shared by 300 users gets a 4 MB edit. Roughly what gets stored and transferred, and why?

Content-addressed chunking makes both dedupe and delta sync fall out of one mechanism: the new version is a chunk list differing in one entry; the block store already has every other hash. Devices diff chunk lists and fetch only c3′. (a) describes whole-file storage — exactly what chunking exists to avoid; (d) misses that content addressing dedupes across users by construction: same hash, same stored chunk, refcounted.

Practice

Design Pastebin in 15 minutes — full dry run

Run the complete 4-step framework on Pastebin (share text snippets via short links, optional expiry, optional syntax view), compressed to a 15-minute screen. Produce: requirements + estimation (with arithmetic), API + data model, the architecture in words, and your ONE deep dive with a justified choice.

Skills: framework fluency · estimation · restraint (this is a small-numbers problem)
Hint 1

Pastebin ≈ URL shortener with bodies. What changes when the value is 10 KB of text instead of a 200-byte URL? Where do big pastes go?

Hint 2

Reads dominate again, but there's a new wrinkle: pastes can be MBs. Does everything belong in one table? What does the CDN see?

Solution

Requirements (2 min): create paste (≤10 MB, default 512 KB cap), read via short code, expiry (never/1h/1d/1mo), private (unlisted) pastes; no edits (immutable) — confirm that, it simplifies everything. Non-functional: read p99 < 200 ms, paste durability, read:write ~10:1 (lower than URL shortener — pastes are shared to fewer people).

Estimation (2 min): 10M pastes/month ≈ 4 writes/s; 40 reads/s — trivial QPS, so the interview is about storage: avg paste 10 KB → 10M × 10 KB = 100 GB/month ≈ 1.2 TB/year, plus metadata (~100 B/row, negligible). Numbers verdict: one Postgres + object storage + cache; anything more is over-engineering.

POST /pastes {body, lang?, expires?, visibility} → {code}    (code: 8-char base62, KGS or counter)
GET  /{code} → paste (404/410 after expiry)
pastes: code PK | owner? | lang | created | expires_at | size | storage_ref
bodies: < 64 KB inline in the row; larger → object storage, row keeps the key

Architecture (1 min): CDN → LB → stateless API → Redis (hot paste bodies+metadata, cache-aside) → Postgres (metadata + small bodies) + object store (large bodies). Async: expiry sweeper (lazy check on read + daily batch delete); view counters batched.

Deep dive pick — storage split (3 min): why not all-in-Postgres? MB-size TOASTed rows bloat the buffer pool and backups; why not all-in-S3? Per-object overhead and latency for the 90% of pastes under 64 KB, plus you'd still need the DB for codes/expiry. The split serves each size class from the medium that suits it — same metadata/blob split as Dropbox at 1/1000 scale. Second-choice dive: expiry (lazy + sweep, never synchronous deletes).

Wrap (1 min): failure = cache loss (rebuild from DB, brief latency blip); monitoring = read p99, cache hit ratio, storage growth; evolution at 100× = shard metadata by code hash, nothing else changes. Total: a deliberately boring design, delivered with numbers — that IS the senior answer here.

Parking-lot IoT + reservation system

A city operator runs 200 garages, 500k total spots. Each spot has an occupancy sensor reporting on change (plus a 5-min heartbeat). Drivers see live availability per garage, can reserve a spot for 30 minutes, and pay on exit by plate recognition. Design it: ingest, availability, reservations, payments. Where does this reuse the designs above?

Skills: IoT ingest sizing · counter vs per-spot state · reservation = seat hold · recognizing reused patterns
Hint 1

Compute the sensor message rate before designing ingest. 500k sensors on-change + heartbeat — is this actually a big number?

Hint 2

"Reserve a spot for 30 minutes" — which card in this section did you just re-read? What plays the role of the payment saga?

Solution

Estimation first: heartbeats: 500k / 300 s ≈ 1.7k msg/s; occupancy changes: 500k spots × ~10 events/day ≈ 60/s. Total ~2k msg/s — small! MQTT/HTTP ingest → Kafka → one consumer group updates state. No exotic ingest tier needed; say so.

Availability = two-tier state: per-spot truth table (spot_id, state: FREE/OCCUPIED/RESERVED/OUT_OF_SERVICE, last_seen) in Postgres, and a per-garage counter cache in Redis (free = total − occupied − reserved) maintained by the consumer — drivers' map queries read counters (eventually consistent, seconds stale, fine), never scan spots. A sensor silent past ~2 heartbeats → spot flagged UNKNOWN and excluded from "free" counts (liveness by heartbeat, same as chat presence).

Reservations = the seat-hold pattern verbatim (ticket booking): conditional write FREE→RESERVED WHERE state='FREE', TTL 30 min, reaper returns expired reservations. Contention is trivial (two drivers rarely race for one spot — but the race exists, so the mechanism must too). Assign a specific spot or garage-level reservation with spot assigned at gate — offer the simpler garage-level variant; it dodges "reserved spot is physically blocked" disputes.

Payments: plate-read at exit → session lookup (entry camera/reservation) → charge via provider with idempotency key = session_id (idempotency, saga for auth/capture/receipt: exactly the notification + booking machinery). Failed plate reads → gate ticket fallback; reconciliation job matches unclosed sessions nightly.

Reused designs: heartbeat liveness (chat presence), counter cache over truth table (feed counter hydration), hold-with-TTL + reaper (booking), idempotent payment saga (booking), multi-channel receipts (notifications). A strong answer names the reuse explicitly — it demonstrates the framework, not memorized designs.

Metrics ingestion at 10M points/sec

Design the storage side of a metrics platform (think Prometheus-at-scale / M3): 10M data points/sec across 50M active series, dashboard queries over arbitrary ranges, 13-month retention. Cover: ingest path, compression, downsampling, retention tiers, and why a row-store is the wrong shape. Include the storage arithmetic.

Skills: write-path batching · columnar/time-series layout · downsampling math · storage tiering
Hint 1

A point is (series_id, timestamp, float64). Raw: ~16 B. What's 10M/s for 13 months raw? Now what do delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR float compression (Gorilla) do to that?

Hint 2

Nobody renders 1-second resolution for a 30-day chart — a screen has ~2000 pixels. What resolution does each query range actually need?

Solution

The arithmetic that shapes everything: raw = 10M/s × 16 B = 160 MB/s ≈ 14 TB/day ≈ 5.5 PB for 13 months — untenable. Gorilla-style compression (delta-of-delta timestamps since scrape intervals are regular ≈ 1–2 bits; XOR floats since values change slowly) averages ~1.4 B/point ≈ 1.2 TB/day — a 12× cut before any downsampling. This is why every serious TSDB is a custom columnar format, not rows: a B-tree row per point would spend 10× the bytes on structure than on data and die on random inserts (write patterns).

Ingest path: agents → LB → ingesters, sharded by hash(series_id) so one series always lands on one ingester (in-order, compressible). Ingesters buffer the head block in memory (last ~2 h per series), WAL for crash recovery, then flush immutable compressed blocks to object storage — LSM-shaped by design. Queries fan out to ingesters (recent) + block store (historical) and merge — the split is invisible to the user.

Downsampling: a 2000-px chart of 30 days needs ~20-min resolution — raw 15 s data is 80× overkill. Background compactors produce rollups: raw (15 s) kept 15 days; 5-min aggregates (min/max/avg/count — keep all four, or you can never answer "max" later) kept 90 days; 1-h aggregates kept 13 months. Storage: raw 15 d ≈ 18 TB; 5-min ≈ 1/20 rate for 90 d ≈ 5.4 TB; 1-h ≈ 1/240 for 395 d ≈ 2 TB — ~26 TB total vs 5.5 PB naive: ~200×. Query planner picks resolution by range automatically.

Retention tiers: hot (NVMe on ingesters/recent blocks) → warm (standard object storage) → expiry. Cost roughly: 26 TB mostly in object storage ≈ $600/mo — worth saying out loud; capacity math is a reliability skill.

The trap to name: series cardinality, not point rate, kills these systems — 50M series × per-series index entries is the real memory bound, and one bad label (user_id!) can 100× it overnight (cardinality discipline). Guard with per-tenant series limits and label allowlists. Second trap: exact global percentiles across shards are impossible to pre-aggregate — store histograms (fixed buckets), merge buckets, then read percentiles off the merged histogram (same "approximate beats exact" move).

Rapid-fire: the whole guide in one-liners

Why: the night-before sheet for the entire guide — design picks, first bottlenecks, latency anchors, and sync-vs-async calls. One line each; expand only when probed.

  • Latency anchors? — RAM ~100 ns · SSD ~100 µs · same-DC RTT ~0.5 ms · cross-region ~50–150 ms · disk seek ~10 ms. Every design argument starts here.
  • DAU → QPS in one move? — DAU × actions/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ avg; ×2–3 for peak. 100M × 10 ÷ 86k ≈ 12k QPS avg.
  • DB for a URL shortener? — KV by code (or sharded SQL); the only query is exact-key GET.
  • DB for chat messages? — Wide-column LSM (Cassandra/Scylla), partition (chat_id, bucket), clustering by time DESC.
  • DB for orders/payments? — Relational with transactions; shard when numbers force it, not before.
  • DB for a social graph's follows? — Two indexes/tables: by follower AND by followee — you always need both directions.
  • Store for driver locations? — In-memory cell index with TTL; it's ephemeral — the next ping rebuilds it.
  • First bottleneck in a feed system? — Celebrity fan-out; answer is the hybrid push/pull split.
  • First bottleneck in chat? — Gateway connection count and reconnect storms, not message storage.
  • First bottleneck in a crawler? — Frontier host-diversity (politeness starvation), not bandwidth.
  • First bottleneck in a flash sale? — Contended inventory rows; admission control, not autoscaling.
  • 301 or 302 for a shortener? — 302 if you want analytics/expiry; 301 offloads you but browsers never come back.
  • Snowflake in one line? — 41-bit ms timestamp + 10-bit worker + 12-bit sequence = k-sorted 64-bit ids, no hot-path coordination.
  • Clock goes backwards on an id node? — Refuse/wait; never re-issue a used (ms, seq).
  • Rate limiter atomicity? — Lua script in Redis: refill+check+decrement as one op.
  • Limiter's Redis is down? — Fail open for protective limits, closed for abuse/billing; degrade to local buckets.
  • Exactly-once notification? — Idempotency key at API + outbox enqueue + provider-side key; duplicates possible, harmless.
  • Quiet hours bug everyone ships? — Server-timezone evaluation; store the user's timezone, defer in local time.
  • Sent vs delivered vs read? — Durable on server / acked by device / seen on screen — three different acks.
  • Offline chat delivery? — Inbox queue + push hint + reconnect cursor sync; push is never the delivery path.
  • Group-chat writes: per member? — No — store once per conversation, fan out at delivery with per-member cursors.
  • Feed pagination? — Cursor (ts, id) — offsets duplicate/skip as new items land.
  • Why ids-only in feed caches? — Bodies once in a post cache; 800 copies of a 1 KB post × 200M users is 160 TB of waste.
  • Count-min sketch error direction? — Overcounts only; read the min across rows; heap remembers which keys matter.
  • Sliding window at scale? — Ring of per-minute sketches; merge slots, drop the oldest — never per-key timestamps.
  • Exact "views: 1,234,567" at 1M/s? — Pre-aggregated deltas into sharded counters; never a sketch, never raw INCR per event.
  • Geohash vs H3 in one line? — Geohash = string prefixes, easy in Redis, edge-effect warts; H3 = hexagons, equidistant neighbors, built for ring searches.
  • Two riders, one driver? — Offer lock with TTL on the driver; CAS on trip state decides ties.
  • Two buyers, one seat? — Conditional UPDATE … WHERE state='AVAILABLE'; rowcount tells the loser.
  • Hold-with-TTL exists because…? — Abandoned checkouts must return inventory without humans; reaper + lazy expiry.
  • Waiting room in one line? — Token queue + metered release at measured capacity; converts overload into queueing with an honest ETA.
  • Dropbox dedupe mechanism? — Content-addressed chunks: SHA-256 keys make dedupe, delta sync, and versioning the same feature.
  • Why presigned URLs? — Bulk bytes go client↔blob store directly; metadata tier stays tiny and in charge.
  • Typeahead in one line? — Precompute top-K per prefix offline; serve as one GET; freshness via a fast lane for risers.
  • Sync or async: payment capture? — The authorize is sync (user waits for yes/no); capture/receipt/ledger are async saga steps.
  • Sync or async: analytics/click tracking? — Always async fire-and-forget; never add a failure mode to the user path.
  • Sync or async: cross-region replication? — Async (accept RPO = lag); sync cross-region murders commit latency ~100×.
  • The universal first question? — "What are the numbers?" — QPS, data size, read:write, latency target choose the architecture for you.
  • The universal last question? — "What breaks first at 10×, and what would I page on?" — have one crisp answer per design.
